title: Establishment of a Committee of Inquiry To Investigate Allegations of False Statements by Lisa DeNell Cook
full_text:
Memorandum of October 7, 2026
Establishment of a Committee of Inquiry To Investigate Allegations of False Statements by Lisa DeNell Cook
Memorandum for the Attorney General[,] the Counsel to the President[,] the Assistant to the President for Economic Policy[,] the Director of the Office of Government Ethics[, and] the Chairman of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, I hereby establish a committee of inquiry (Committee) to investigate allegations that Federal Reserve Governor Lisa D. Cook made false statements in connection with one or more mortgage instruments. The Assistant to the President for Economic Policy, the Chairman of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and the Director of the Office of Government Ethics shall serve as members of the Committee.
As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law. U.S. Const. Art. II, sec. 3. To assist me in carrying out that responsibility, the Committee shall investigate the allegations against Governor Cook and report to me whether there is “cause” for Governor Cook's removal within the meaning of
12 U.S.C. 242
, as construed in
Trump
v.
Cook,
146 S. Ct. 2234 (2026). The Committee may consult with appropriate personnel from executive departments and agencies, including the Department of Justice, to aid in its inquiry. The Committee shall, on November 5, 2026, conduct an in-person hearing to consider the evidence and allegations against Governor Cook. The hearing shall occur at the White House and shall last no longer than 4 hours.
Governor Cook may submit a written position statement to the Committee regarding the allegations, provided the statement is received at least 3 days before the hearing. Governor Cook shall appear at the hearing and be examined by the Committee, its representatives, and her legal counsel, if any. Governor Cook may present argument, written evidence, and written witness statements regarding the evidence and allegations. The Committee may also question Governor Cook about any representations she or her counsel make during the hearing, or it may authorize its representatives, including Department of Justice personnel, to conduct that questioning. The Committee may request documents or other evidentiary submissions from Governor Cook, as appropriate, and Governor Cook shall comply with any such requests.
Prior to the hearing, the Committee shall provide Governor Cook with the evidence it is considering in its inquiry. At the hearing, the Committee or its representatives may question Governor Cook or her counsel about the evidence and allegations against her. The hearing shall be closed to the public but shall be transcribed.
Governor Cook may submit a post-hearing written statement to the Committee by November 10, 2026. As soon as practicable after receipt of that statement, the Committee shall submit written findings of fact and conclusions of law to me and shall recommend whether there is cause to remove Governor Cook from her position on the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve. The Committee may establish additional procedures or make reasonable changes to the above procedures as necessary or appropriate and shall give Governor Cook adequate notice of any such changes.
(
printed page 65436)
The Counsel to the President shall transmit a copy of this memorandum to Governor Cook, to the members of the Committee, and to the Attorney General.
The Attorney General is authorized and directed to publish this memorandum in the
Federal Register
.
THE WHITE HOUSE,
Washington, October 7, 2026

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is proposing to amend its regulations to renew the AP1000 design certification and incorporate Revision 20 of the AP1000 design control document. The purpose of this rulemaking action is to update the AP1000 design to be consistent with changes made to the design during the
(
printed page 65134)
licensing, construction, and operation of Vogtle Electric Generating Plant, Units 3 and 4. This rulemaking incorporates AP1000 design control document Revision 20, which includes updates made to the AP1000 design to represent a current, construction-validated design. The NRC also proposes to issue an environmental assessment supporting this rule.

I. Obtaining Information and Submitting Comments
A. Obtaining Information
Please refer to Docket ID NRC-2026-2377 when contacting the NRC about the availability of information for this action. You may obtain publicly available information related to this action by any of the following methods:

or call 1-800-397-4209 or 301-415-4737, between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. eastern time, Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
B. Submitting Comments
The NRC encourages electronic comment submission through the Federal Rulemaking Website (
https://www.regulations.gov
). Please include Docket ID NRC-2026-2377 in your comment submission.
The NRC cautions you not to include identifying or contact information that you do not want to be publicly disclosed in your comment submission. The NRC will post all comment submissions at
https://www.regulations.gov
as well as enter the comment submissions into ADAMS. The NRC does not routinely edit comment submissions to remove identifying or contact information.
If you are requesting or aggregating comments from other persons for submission to the NRC, then you should inform those persons not to include identifying or contact information that they do not want to be publicly disclosed in their comment submission. Your request should state that the NRC does not routinely edit comment submissions to remove such information before making the comment submissions available to the public or entering the comment into ADAMS.
II. Rulemaking Procedure
Because the NRC considers this action to be non-controversial, the NRC is publishing this proposed rule concurrently with a direct final rule in the Rules and Regulations section of this issue of the
Federal Register
. The direct final rule will become effective on December 28, 2026. However, if the NRC receives significant adverse comments by November 13, 2026, then the NRC will publish a document that withdraws the direct final rule. If the direct final rule is withdrawn, the NRC will address the comments in a subsequent final rule. Absent significant modifications to the proposed revisions requiring republication, the NRC will not initiate a second comment period on this action in the event the direct final rule is withdrawn.
A significant adverse comment is a comment where the commenter explains why the rule would be inappropriate, including challenges to the rule's underlying premise or approach, or would be ineffective or unacceptable without a change. A comment is adverse and significant if:
(1) The comment opposes the rule and provides a reason sufficient to require a substantive response in a notice-and-comment process. For example, a substantive response is required when:
(a) The comment causes the NRC to reevaluate (or reconsider) its position or conduct additional analysis;
(b) The comment raises an issue serious enough to warrant a substantive response to clarify or complete the record; or
(c) The comment raises a relevant issue that was not previously addressed or considered by the NRC.
(2) The comment proposes a change or an addition to the rule, and it is apparent that the rule would be ineffective or unacceptable without incorporation of the change or addition.
(3) The comment causes the NRC to make a change (other than editorial) to the rule.
For procedural information and the regulatory analysis, see the direct final rule published in the Rules and Regulations section of this issue of the
Federal Register
.
III. Background
The NRC originally approved the AP1000 design certification in a final rule published on January 27, 2006 (
71 FR 4464
). On December 30, 2011 (
76 FR 82079
), the NRC published a final rule amending appendix D, “Design Certification Rule for the AP1000 Design,” to part 52, “Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for
(
printed page 65135)
Nuclear Power Plants,” of
title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(10 CFR) to incorporate AP1000 Design Control Document (DCD), Revision 19, APP-GW-GL-702, dated June 13, 2011. On September 22, 2021 (
86 FR 52593
), the NRC published a direct final rule extending the duration of the AP1000 design certification by five years, with an effective date of December 6, 2021.
On July 2, 2025 (
90 FR 28869
), the NRC amended its regulations to replace the 15-year duration of design certifications with a 40-year duration, both for existing design certifications currently in effect and generically for future design certifications, including renewals. The NRC did not change the date of issuance or renewal for existing design certifications but changed their expiration dates based on the most recent date of issuance or renewal. The current AP1000 design certification expires on February 27, 2046.
On February 10, 2012, the NRC issued combined licenses (COLs) to Southern Nuclear Operating Company (SNC) for the Vogtle Electric Generating Plant (VEGP) Units 3 and 4 (COLs NPF-91 and NPF-92). During the licensing, construction, and operation of VEGP Units 3 and 4, SNC submitted over 180 license amendment requests (LARs) to the NRC addressing design changes, construction-discovered issues, and operational refinements. The NRC reviewed and approved these LARs through safety evaluations for each approved amendment. In addition, SNC implemented numerous Tier 2 departures under the section VIII.B.5 of appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 change process that did not require prior NRC approval. The VEGP licensing process also resolved the COL action items identified in DCD Revision 19 with site-specific design details, operational program descriptions, and as-built information. The VEGP Unit 3 entered commercial operation on July 31, 2023, and Unit 4 did so on April 29, 2024.
In SECY-26-0034, “NRC Regulatory Pathways and Licensing Readiness for Near Term Large Light-Water Reactor Deployment,” dated March 9, 2026, the NRC staff informed the Commission, among other things, that it anticipated submission of the Westinghouse Electric Company LLC (Westinghouse) application to update and renew the AP1000 design certification. The NRC staff also informed the Commission of its plan to incorporate the as-built changes incorporated into VEGP Units 3 and 4, previously approved safety findings, and lessons learned into a revised AP1000 design certification. The NRC's verification review determined that no new changes were incorporated into AP1000 DCD Revision 20 that require additional technical review, and that all changes incorporated into the AP1000 DCD Revision 20 were either previously reviewed and approved by the NRC or were incorporated using a process that does not require NRC approval. Therefore, the NRC is using the direct final rule process to update appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 to include AP1000 DCD Revision 20. This renewal would improve regulatory clarity, avoid unnecessary re-review, and streamline future AP1000 licensing activities by providing applicants with an updated, standardized design basis. The NRC is amending appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 to include AP1000 DCD Revision 20. The NRC is also retaining the incorporation by reference of AP1000 DCD Revision 19 in appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 because several combined license holders were licensed to AP1000 Revision 19 and the incorporation of the AP1000 DCD Revision 19 in appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 remains part of the licensing basis for those combined license holders. Applicants could reference either revision in future applications.
While
10 CFR 52.63(a)
imposes restrictive limits on the types of changes that may be made while a design certification rule is in effect,
10 CFR 52.59(c)
allows a design certification renewal applicant greater flexibility in seeking changes to the design certification. Thus, a design certification renewal application that includes amendments to a certified design is not required to address the criteria in
10 CFR 52.63
, “Finality of standard design certifications.” However, if the amendment request entails such an extensive change to the design certification that an essentially new standard design is being proposed,
10 CFR 52.59(c)
provides that an application for a design certification must be filed. The AP1000 amendment request does not propose an essentially new standard design.
The NRC is amending the design certification for the AP1000 standard plant design to renew the AP1000 design certification for 40 years from the effective date of the direct final rule. The NRC determined the submitted application for incorporation by reference of DCD Revision 20 into appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 is acceptable. Further, the Commission granted an exemption from
10 CFR 52.57(a)
to allow renewal more than 36 months before expiration of the current design certification rule (
91 FR 40596
; July 2, 2026). The requirements of
10 CFR 52.55
, “Duration of certification,” govern the duration of a design certification and the effect of timely renewal. The AP1000 design certification rule does not expire until 2046.
The NRC is amending section VIII.B.6 of appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 to incorporate the alternative change process that was previously reviewed and approved for Vogtle Units 3 and 4 into appendix D to 10 CFR part 52. The license amendments and exemptions included in AP1000 DCD Revision 20 include a previously reviewed and approved change process for Tier 2* information. On December 21, 2017, SNC submitted LAR-17-037, and an associated exemption request, seeking changes to the Vogtle Units 3 and 4 COLs to add a license condition that would apply the change process for Tier 2 information for a proposed departure from Tier 2* information provided that specific criteria are not met. If one of the criteria were met for the proposed departure, then the proposed departure would continue to require prior NRC approval. On September 20, 2018, the NRC granted the amendments and exemptions to Vogtle Units 3 and 4 that effectively replaced the Tier 2* change process with an alternative process (reflected in a license condition) that applied the Tier 2 change process along with nine additional criteria to determine whether a license amendment was required. Inclusion of this change process in section VIII.B.6 of appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 promotes regulatory efficiency by eliminating the need for unnecessary licensing actions for applicants referencing either AP1000 DCD Revision 19 or AP1000 DCD Revision 20.
IV. Plain Writing
The Plain Writing Act of 2010 (
Pub. L. 111-274
) requires Federal agencies to write documents in a clear, concise, and well-organized manner. The NRC has written this document to be consistent with the Plain Writing Act as well as the Presidential Memorandum, “Plain Language in Government Writing,” published June 10, 1998 (
63 FR 31885
). The NRC requests comment on this proposed rule with respect to clarity and effectiveness of the language used.
V. National Environmental Policy Act: Environmental Assessment and Proposed Finding of No Significant Impact
The NRC has determined under the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969, as amended (NEPA), and the NRC's regulations in subpart A, “National Environmental Policy Act—Regulations Implementing Section 102(2),” of
10 CFR part 51
,
(
printed page 65136)
“Environmental Protection Regulations for Domestic Licensing and Related Regulatory Functions,” that this proposed rule, if issued, would not be a major Federal action significantly affecting the quality of the human environment and, therefore, an environmental impact statement is not required. The NRC's generic determination in this regard, reflected in
10 CFR 51.32(b)(1)
, is based upon the following considerations: (1) A design certification rule does not authorize the siting, construction, or operation of a facility referencing any particular design, but only codifies a standard design certification in a rule (extending the AP1000 design certification and incorporating changes to the design in this case); (2) the NRC will evaluate the environmental impacts and issue an environmental finding in a Record of Decision as appropriate under NEPA as part of the application for the construction and operation of a facility referencing any particular design certification rule; and (3) comments on the environmental assessment will be limited to the consideration of severe accident mitigation design alternatives as required by 10 CFR 51.30(d). The environmental assessment is available in the companion direct final rule published in the Rules and Regulations section of this issue of the
Federal Register
. In keeping with Commission policy, that environmental assessment also updates the agency's consideration of severe accident mitigation design alternatives.
VI. Paperwork Reduction Act
This proposed rule does not contain any new or amended collections of information subject to the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
). Existing collections of information were approved by the Office of Management and Budget, control number 3150-0151.
Public Protection Notification
The NRC may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information unless the document requesting or requiring the collection displays a currently valid Office of Management and Budget control number.
VII. Executive Orders
The following are Executive orders that are related to this proposed rule:
A.
Executive Order 12866
: Regulatory Planning and Review (as amended by
E.O. 14215
, Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies)
The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) has determined that this direct final rule is not a significant regulatory action.
B.
Executive Order 14154
: Unleashing American Energy
The NRC has examined this proposed rule and has determined that it is consistent with the policies and directives outlined in
E.O. 14154
.
C.
Executive Order 14192
: Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation
This action is determined to be a deregulatory action as defined by
E.O. 14192
. The AP1000 renewal and amendments will facilitate future reactor licensing by resolving design issues generically, which will lead to shorter and more efficient reviews yielding savings to the agency and future applicants.
D.
Executive Order 14267
: Reducing Anti-Competitive Regulatory Barriers
E.O. 14267
requires the NRC to identify anti-competitive regulations for recission or modification. The purpose of a design certification rule is to facilitate the licensing process for future applicants that reference the certified design. Therefore, there are no anti-competitive regulatory barriers associated with this rule.
E.
Executive Order 14270
: Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting To Unleash American Energy
E.O. 14270
, “Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting to Unleash American Energy,” requires the NRC to insert a conditional sunset date into all new or amended NRC regulations provided the regulations are (1) promulgated under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended (AEA), the Energy Reorganization Act of 1974, as amended (ERA), or the Nuclear Waste Policy Act of 1982, as amended (NWPA); (2) not statutorily required; and (3) not part of the NRC's permitting regime. The NRC determined that the regulatory changes proposed in this rule are part of the NRC permitting regime as future licensing applicants may reference the AP1000 certified design to obtain operating licenses. Therefore, the NRC views this rulemaking to be outside the scope of
E.O. 14270
and did not insert conditional sunset dates for the regulatory changes in this direct final rule.

II. Rulemaking Procedure
Because the NRC considers this action to be non-controversial, the NRC is using the “direct final rule procedure” for this rule. This amendment is effective on December 28, 2026. However, if the NRC receives significant adverse comments on this direct final rule by November 13, 2026, then the NRC will publish a document that withdraws this action and will address the comments received in a subsequent final rule as a response to the companion proposed rule published in the Proposed Rules section of this issue of the
Federal Register
. Absent significant modifications to the proposed revisions requiring republication, the NRC will not initiate a second comment period on this action.
A significant adverse comment is a comment where the commenter explains why the rule would be inappropriate, including challenges to the rule's underlying premise or approach, or would be ineffective or unacceptable without a change. A comment is adverse and significant if:
(1) The comment opposes the rule and provides a reason sufficient to require a substantive response in a notice-and-comment process. For example, a substantive response is required when:
(a) The comment causes the NRC to reevaluate (or reconsider) its position or conduct additional analysis;
(b) The comment raises an issue serious enough to warrant a substantive response to clarify or complete the record; or
(c) The comment raises a relevant issue that was not previously addressed or considered by the NRC.
(2) The comment proposes a change or an addition to the rule, and it is apparent that the rule would be ineffective or unacceptable without incorporation of the change or addition.
(3) The comment causes the NRC to make a change (other than editorial) to the rule.

III. Background
The NRC originally approved the AP1000 design certification in a final rule published on January 27, 2006 (
71 FR 4464
). On December 30, 2011 (
76 FR 82079
), the NRC published a final rule amending appendix D, “Design Certification Rule for the AP1000 Design,” to part 52, “Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants,” of title 10 of the
Code of Federal Regulations
(10 CFR) to incorporate AP1000 Design Control Document (DCD), Revision 19, APP-GW-GL-702, dated June 13, 2011. On September 22, 2021 (
86 FR 52593
), the NRC published a direct final rule extending the duration of the AP1000 design certification by five years, with an effective date of December 6, 2021.
On July 2, 2025 (
90 FR 28869
), the NRC amended its regulations to replace the 15-year duration of design certifications with a 40-year duration, both for existing design certifications currently in effect and generically for
(
printed page 65093)
future design certifications, including renewals. The NRC did not change the date of issuance or renewal for existing design certifications but changed their expiration dates based on the most recent date of issuance or renewal. The current AP1000 design certification expires on February 27, 2046.
On February 10, 2012, the NRC issued combined licenses (COLs) to Southern Nuclear Operating Company (SNC) for the Vogtle Electric Generating Plant (VEGP) Units 3 and 4 (COLs NPF-91 and NPF-92). During the licensing, construction, and operation of VEGP Units 3 and 4, SNC submitted over 180 license amendment requests (LARs) to the NRC addressing design changes, construction-discovered issues, and operational refinements. The NRC reviewed and approved these LARs through safety evaluations for each approved amendment. In addition, SNC implemented numerous Tier 2 departures under the section VIII.B.5 of appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 change process that did not require prior NRC approval. The VEGP licensing process also resolved the COL action items identified in DCD Revision 19 with site-specific design details, operational program descriptions, and as-built information. The VEGP Unit 3 entered commercial operation on July 31, 2023, and Unit 4 did so on April 29, 2024.
In SECY-26-0034, “NRC Regulatory Pathways and Licensing Readiness for Near Term Large Light-Water Reactor Deployment,” dated March 9, 2026, the NRC staff informed the Commission, among other things, that it anticipated submission of the Westinghouse Electric Company LLC (Westinghouse) application to update and renew the AP1000 design certification. The NRC staff also informed the Commission of its plan to incorporate the as-built changes incorporated into VEGP Units 3 and 4, previously approved safety findings, and lessons learned into a revised AP1000 design certification. The NRC's verification review determined that no new changes were incorporated into AP1000 DCD Revision 20 that require additional technical review, and that all changes incorporated into the AP1000 DCD Revision 20 were either previously reviewed and approved by the NRC or were incorporated using a process that does not require NRC approval. Therefore, the NRC is using the direct final rule process to update appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 to include AP1000 DCD Revision 20. This renewal would improve regulatory clarity, avoid unnecessary re-review, and streamline future AP1000 licensing activities by providing applicants with an updated, standardized design basis. The NRC is amending appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 to include AP1000 DCD Revision 20. The NRC is also retaining the incorporation by reference of AP1000 DCD Revision 19 in appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 because several combined license holders were licensed to AP1000 Revision 19 and the incorporation of the AP1000 DCD Revision 19 in appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 remains part of the licensing basis for those combined license holders. Applicants could reference either revision in future applications.
While
10 CFR 52.63(a)
imposes restrictive limits on the types of changes that may be made while a design certification rule is in effect,
10 CFR 52.59(c)
allows a design certification renewal applicant greater flexibility in seeking changes to the design certification. Thus, a design certification renewal application that includes amendments to a certified design is not required to address the criteria in
10 CFR 52.63
, “Finality of standard design certifications.” However, if the amendment request entails such an extensive change to the design certification that an essentially new standard design is being proposed,
10 CFR 52.59(c)
provides that an application for a design certification must be filed. The AP1000 amendment request does not propose an essentially new standard design.
The NRC is amending the design certification for the AP1000 standard plant design to renew the AP1000 design certification for 40 years from the effective date of this direct final rule. The NRC determined the submitted application for incorporation by reference of DCD Revision 20 into appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 is acceptable. Further, the Commission granted an exemption from
10 CFR 52.57(a)
to allow renewal more than 36 months before expiration of the current design certification rule (
91 FR 40596
; July 2, 2026). The requirements of
10 CFR 52.55
, “Duration of certification,” govern the duration of a design certification and the effect of timely renewal. The AP1000 design certification rule does not expire until 2046.
The NRC is amending section VIII.B.6 of appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 to incorporate the alternative change process that was previously reviewed and approved for Vogtle Units 3 and 4 into appendix D to 10 CFR part 52. The license amendments and exemptions included in AP1000 DCD Revision 20 include a previously reviewed and approved change process for Tier 2* information. On December 21, 2017, SNC submitted LAR-17-037, and an associated exemption request, seeking changes to the Vogtle Units 3 and 4 COLs to add a license condition that would apply the change process for Tier 2 information for a proposed departure from Tier 2* information provided that specific criteria are not met. If one of the criteria were met for the proposed departure, then the proposed departure would continue to require prior NRC approval. On September 20, 2018, the NRC granted the amendments and exemptions to Vogtle Units 3 and 4 that effectively replaced the Tier 2* change process with an alternative process (reflected in a license condition) that applied the Tier 2 change process along with nine additional criteria to determine whether a license amendment was required. Inclusion of this change process in section VIII.B.6 of appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 promotes regulatory efficiency by eliminating the need for unnecessary licensing actions for applicants referencing either AP1000 DCD Revision 19 or AP1000 DCD Revision 20.

).
VII. Regulatory Analysis
The NRC has not prepared a regulatory analysis for this direct final rule. The NRC prepares regulatory analyses for rulemakings that establish generic regulatory requirements applicable to all licensees. Design certifications are not generic rulemakings in the sense that design certifications do not establish standards or requirements with which all licensees must comply. Rather, design certifications are NRC approvals of specific nuclear power plant designs by rulemaking, which then may be voluntarily referenced by applicants for combined licenses or construction permits. For these reasons, the NRC concludes that preparation of a regulatory analysis is neither required nor appropriate.

X. National Environmental Policy Act: Environmental Assessment and Final Finding of No Significant Impact
A. Introduction
The NRC is renewing the design certification for the AP1000 standard plant design for 40 years from the effective date of this direct final rule. The NRC also is updating the design certification to reflect changes provided by Westinghouse, by letter dated March 27, 2026. The NRC issues design certification rules as appendices to
10 CFR part 52
. The purpose of this amendment is to renew the period that the AP1000 design certification is valid for referencing by an applicant and includes incorporation of VEGP Units 3 and 4 license amendment approvals under their respective COLs. Specifically, Revision 20 of the AP1000 DCD incorporates the issuance of Amendments 142 and 141 for VEGP Units 3 and 4 granting changes to the Tier 2* departure evaluation process with a
10 CFR 51.22(c)(9)
categorical exclusion determination and is incorporated by reference into this NEPA evaluation. This rule amends Section VIII.B.6 of appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 to include changes to the Tier 2* departure evaluation process for the AP1000 design. With the renewal approval, the AP1000 design certification rule would remain valid for referencing until 40 years after the effective date of this direct final rule.
The NRC developed in section X, “National Environmental Policy Act: Environmental Assessment and Final Finding of No Significant Impact,” of this document containing this evaluation of the environmental impacts of the renewal request. The NRC has documented its finding of no significant impact in accordance with the requirements of
10 CFR 51.21
, “Criteria for and identification of licensing and regulatory actions requiring environmental assessments”;
10 CFR 51.31
, “Determinations based on environmental assessment”; and the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969, as amended (NEPA). This evaluation also addresses the severe accident mitigation design alternatives (SAMDAs) that the NRC has previously evaluated for the Westinghouse AP1000 design in the environmental assessment (EA) dated September 1, 2021. The evaluation does not address the site-specific environmental impacts of constructing and operating any facility that references the AP1000 design certification at a particular site. The
(
printed page 65095)
SAMDA analysis completed as part of this direct final rule can be incorporated by reference into the environmental determination related to an application for siting, construction, or operation of a nuclear plant that references the AP1000 standard design. The NRC would evaluate those impacts as part of any application(s) for the siting, construction, or operation of such a facility.
As discussed later in this section of this direct final rule, the NRC has determined that issuing the subject renewal does not constitute a major Federal action significantly affecting the quality of the human environment. This determination is based on the generic finding made in
10 CFR 51.32(b)(2)
that there is no significant environmental impact associated with this renewal of the AP1000 design certification. This renewal does not authorize the siting, construction, or operation of a facility referencing the AP1000 design; it only codifies an extension of the period an applicant can reference the AP1000 design in a COL application. Furthermore, because the certification and update of the design constitute a rule change rather than a physical action, it does not involve the commitment of any resources that have alternative uses. The
10 CFR 51.32(b)(2)
generic finding of no significant impact is, essentially, the legal equivalent of a categorical exclusion (
72 FR 49427
; August 28, 2007). Therefore, the NRC has not prepared an environmental impact statement (EIS) for this direct final rule.
Under
10 CFR 51.30(d)
, an EA for an amendment, of which a renewal is, to a design certification is limited to the consideration of whether the design change that is the subject of the proposed amendment renders a SAMDA previously rejected in the earlier EA to become cost beneficial, or results in the identification of new SAMDAs, in which case, the costs and benefits of new SAMDAs and the bases for not incorporating new SAMDAs in the design certification must be addressed.
This amendment renewal request brings the AP1000 design certification up to date. Revision 20 to the DCD includes construction and operating experience from current AP1000 nuclear power plants operating in the U.S. today (
i.e.,
Vogtle Units 3 and 4) and will allow for consistency and standardization in future AP1000 plant applications. Although DCD Revision 20 does not affect the overall risk profile for the AP1000 design (
i.e.,
Revision 20 to the AP1000 DCD does not change the risk insights and conclusions of the AP1000 design certification or COL probabilistic risk assessments), as discussed in this section of the direct final rule, the NRC updated its SAMDA evaluation and performed sensitivity analyses in section X.B.2 of this document to determine whether any SAMDAs previously rejected in the earlier AP1000 design certification EAs could become cost beneficial due to updated cost parameter information.
B. Severe Accident Mitigation Design Alternative Evaluation
Consistent with the objectives of standardization and early resolution of design issues, the Commission decided to evaluate SAMDAs as part of the original design certification for the AP1000 design. In its “Policy Statement on Severe Reactor Accidents Regarding Future Designs and Existing Plants” (
50 FR 32138
; August 8, 1985), the Commission defined the term “severe accident” as an event that is “beyond the substantial coverage of design-basis events (DBEs),” including events where there is substantial damage to the reactor core (whether or not there are serious offsite consequences). These DBEs are analyzed in accordance with NUREG-0800, “Standard Review Plan for the Review of Safety Analysis Reports for Nuclear Power Plants: LWR Edition,” and documented in several chapters of the AP1000 DCD, such as Chapters 2, 3, 15, and 19.
B.1 Westinghouse's DCD Revision 20 Assessments of SAMDAs
In the transmittal letter for the AP1000 renewal, Westinghouse states that Appendix 1B of the AP1000 DCD Revision 19 fulfills this requirement and addresses the costs and benefits of 15 SAMDAs that are not included in the AP1000 plant design. Revision 19 Appendix 1B has been retained in AP1000 DCD Revision 20. Westinghouse continues to find that the previously considered SAMDAs, which were deemed to be non-cost beneficial, remain non-cost beneficial and that no new design alternatives were identified. Their evaluation concludes that the SAMDA review performed in AP1000 DCD Revision 19 with regard to the viability of the proposed SAMDAs remains valid and applicable to the AP1000 plant design presented in AP1000 DCD Revision 20.
B.2 NRC Evaluation
The NRC conducted an audit of Appendix 1B as part of its DCD Revision 20 application review. During that review, the NRC found that Westinghouse did not evaluate the effect of applying current dollar values to the cost analysis in Appendix 1B of Revision 20 of the AP1000 DCD. An environmental evaluation considers the present conditions at the time of the application submission and this would include cost evaluations related to SAMDAs. Several recent new reactor construction permit applications have used appropriate current cost values in their initial SAMDA evaluations. For example, these applicants applied the updated dollar-per-person-rem value in accordance with NUREG-1530, “Reassessment of NRC's Dollar per Person-Rem Conversion Factor Policy,” Revision 1, issued February 2022. These new reactor applicants also applied current dollar inflation adjustments to undiscounted dollar parameter values in the cost formulas in Section 5.7 as directed in Section 5.8 of NUREG/BR-0184, “Regulatory Analysis Technical Evaluation Handbook,” published in January 1997.
The NRC uses the dollar-per-person-rem value to monetize the impact of a potential severe accident, which the agency then compares to the costs of a mitigation measure to determine if it is cost beneficial. Significantly, the agency published the revised dollar-per-person-rem values in 2022, after the agency reviewed Revision 19 of the AP1000 DCD, but before Westinghouse submitted Revision 20. Thus, consideration of this new information could change the agency's determination on whether any of the proposed SAMDAs are cost beneficial.
Similarly, Westinghouse did not provide a discussion on adjusting for inflation for undiscounted cost parameters as recommended in Section 5.8 of NUREG/BR-0184. Therefore, the NRC conducted a review of Appendix 1B to DCD Revision 20 to determine if the Westinghouse SAMDA conclusion is still valid when applying the noted updated monetary values.
The NRC reviewed the information in Appendix 1B to Tier 2, Chapter 1, of the AP1000 DCD, Revision 20, and in the EAs issued for the original AP1000 design certification rule in January 2006, for the amendment to the AP1000 design certification in January 2011, and for the amendment to extend the design certification in September 2021. Due to the intervening time between when Westinghouse originally developed Appendix 1B and the submission of Revision 20, the NRC examined, with respect to the guidance in Section 5.8 of NUREG/BR-0184 and Revision 1 of NUREG-1530, whether the revised dollar values have the potential to change the cost-benefit conclusions for any of the SAMDAs. The NRC evaluated new cost information on updates to a dollar-per-person-rem value of $7,300
(
printed page 65096)
consistent with guidance in NUREG-1530, Revision 1, and inflated to 2026 dollars the previously undiscounted cost parameters used in the maximum benefit valuation formulas of NUREG/BR-0184. Based on the updated maximum benefit valuation with sensitivity analyses, the NRC concluded that the new cost information would not change the conclusions reached in the EAs issued for the original, amended AP1000 design certification rules and the renewal AP1000.
For any future application referencing the AP1000 design certification, the inflation of cost parameters (
e.g.,
the dollar-per-person-rem value) and revised cost-benefit guidance should be considered in determining the subsequent AP1000 applicability of the SAMDA conclusions previously described. This clarification for future AP1000 applications is noted in paragraph VI.7 of appendix D of
10 CFR part 52
.
C. Summary of the Environmental Impacts of the Direct Final Rule
On the basis of
10 CFR 51.32(b)
and the evaluation in section X.B of this document, the NRC concludes that the direct final rule will not have a significant effect on the quality of the human environment. Accordingly, the NRC is not required to prepare an EIS for this direct final rule.
Since no physical changes would occur in the human environment, the agency action (rulemaking) would not affect any threatened or endangered species or historic properties. Accordingly, the NRC finds that the direct final rule would have no significant environmental impact.
D. Finding of No Significant Impact
The NRC has prepared this evaluation to determine the environmental effects of the agency action (rulemaking). This rule is primarily administrative or procedural in nature and therefore would not have any physical environmental effect. As explained in sections X.A through C of this document, the NRC has determined that the rulemaking would not change the conclusions in Appendix 1B of Revision 20 to the AP1000 DCD and would result in no new or different environmental effects. Therefore, the NRC concludes that the rule's action would not have a significant effect on the quality of the human environment. Based on this conclusion, the NRC has determined there is no need to prepare an environmental impact statement. Accordingly, the NRC finds the direct final rule would have no significant environmental impact. This environmental assessment and finding of no significant impact can be tracked with identification number NEPA ID EAXX-429-00-000-1784080234.

XV. Voluntary Consensus Standards
The National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act of 1995,
Public Law 104-113
, requires that Federal agencies use technical standards that are developed or adopted by voluntary consensus standards bodies unless the use of such a standard is inconsistent with applicable law or otherwise impractical. Design certifications are not generic rulemakings establishing a generally applicable standard with which all
10 CFR parts 50
and
52
nuclear power plant licensees must comply. Design certifications are Commission approvals of specific nuclear power plant designs by rulemaking. Furthermore, design certifications are initiated by an applicant for rulemaking, rather than by the NRC. This action does not constitute the establishment of a standard that contains generally applicable requirements.

XVII. Procedures for Access to Proprietary and Security-Related Information for Preparation of Comments on the Direct Final Rule
This section contains instructions regarding how the non-publicly available documents related to this rule, and specifically the information contained in Enclosure 2 of the March 27, 2026, letter from Westinghouse, “AP1000 Design Certification Renewal Request,” may be accessed by interested persons who wish to comment on the design certification renewal. These documents contain proprietary information and security-related information.
Interested persons who desire access to proprietary information or security-related information on the AP1000 design certification extension should first request access to that information from Westinghouse Electric Company LLC, the design certification applicant. A request for access should be submitted to the NRC if the applicant does not either grant or deny access by the 10-day deadline described in the following section.
Submitting a Request to the NRC for Access
Within 10 days after publication of this direct final rule, any individual or entity who believes access to proprietary information or security-related information is necessary in order to submit comments on this rule may request access to such information. Requests for access to proprietary information or security-related information submitted more than 10 days after publication of this document will not be considered absent a showing of good cause for the late filing explaining why the request could not have been filed earlier.
The requestor shall submit a letter requesting permission to access proprietary information or security-related information to the Office of the Secretary, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Attention: Rulemakings and Adjudications Staff, Washington, DC 20555-0001. The email address for the Office of the Secretary is
Rulemaking.Comments@nrc.gov
.
The requestor must send a copy of the request to the design certification applicant at the same time as the original transmission to the NRC using the same method of transmission. Requests to the applicant must be sent to Zachary S. Harper, Manager, Licensing Engineering, Westinghouse Electric Company LLC, 1000 Westinghouse Drive, Cranberry Township, Pennsylvania 16066.
The request must include the following information:
(1) The name of this design certification, AP1000 Design Certification; the rulemaking identification number, RIN 3150-AL70; the rulemaking docket number, NRC-2026-2377; and the
Federal Register
citation for this rule.
(2) The name, address, and email of the requestor.
(3) The identity of the individual(s) to whom access is to be provided, including the identity of any expert, consultant, or assistant who will aid the requestor in evaluating the information.
(4) The requestor's need for the proprietary information or security-related information in order to prepare meaningful comments on the design certification extension must be demonstrated. Each of the following areas must be addressed with specificity:
(a) The specific issue or subject matter on which the requestor wishes to comment.
(b) An explanation why information which is publicly available is insufficient to provide the basis for developing meaningful comment on the AP1000 design certification extension rule with respect to the issue or subject matter described in paragraph 4.a. of this section.
(c) The technical competence (demonstrable knowledge, skill, training or education) of the requestor to effectively utilize the requested information to provide the basis for meaningful comment. Technical competence may be shown by reliance on a qualified expert, consultant, or assistant who satisfies these criteria.
(d) A chronology and discussion of the requestor's attempts to obtain the information from the design certification applicant, and the final communication from the requestor to the applicant and the applicant's response, if any was provided, with respect to the request for access to proprietary information or security-related information must be submitted.
Based on an evaluation of the information submitted under paragraph (4) of this section, as applicable, the NRC will determine within 10 days of receipt of the request whether the requestor has established a legitimate need for access to proprietary information or security-related information.
Determination of Legitimate Need for Access
If the NRC determines that the requestor has established a legitimate need for access to proprietary information or security-related information, the NRC will notify the requestor in writing that access to proprietary information or security-related information has been granted. The written notification will contain instructions on how the requestor may obtain copies of the requested documents and any other conditions that may apply to access to those documents. These conditions may include, but are not limited to, the signing of a Non-Disclosure Agreement or Affidavit by each individual who will be granted access.
Filing of Comments on the AP1000 Design Certification Renewal Rule Based on Non-Public Information
Any comments on this final rule that are based upon the disclosed proprietary information or security-related information must be filed by the requestor no later than 25 days after receipt of (or access to) that information, or the close of the public comment period, whichever is later. The commenter must comply with all NRC requirements regarding the submission of proprietary information and security-related information to the NRC when submitting comments to the NRC (including marking and transmission requirements).
Review of Denials of Access
If the request for access to proprietary information or security-related information is denied by the NRC after a determination on requisite need, the NRC staff shall immediately notify the requestor in writing, briefly stating the reason or reasons for the denial.
The requestor may challenge the NRC staff's adverse determination by filing a challenge within five days of receipt of that determination with the NRC's Executive Director for Operations under
10 CFR 9.29(d)
.
XVIII. Incorporation by Reference—Reasonable Availability to Interested Parties
The NRC is incorporating by reference a document submitted by Westinghouse that updates the AP1000 design certification to Revision 20. As discussed in the “Discussion” section of this document, DCD Revision 20 includes updates made to the AP1000 design to represent a current,
(
printed page 65099)

The Office of the Federal Register's requirements for incorporation by reference are set forth in
1 CFR part 51
. These regulations require an agency to include in a direct final rule a discussion of the ways that the materials the agency incorporates by reference are reasonably available to interested parties or how it worked to make those materials reasonably available to interested parties. The discussion in this section complies with the requirement for direct final rules as set forth in
1 CFR 51.5(b)(2)
.
The NRC considers “interested parties” to include all potential NRC stakeholders, not only the individuals and entities regulated or otherwise subject to the NRC's regulatory oversight. These NRC stakeholders are not a homogeneous group but vary with respect to the considerations for determining reasonable availability. Therefore, the NRC distinguishes between different classes of interested parties for the purposes of determining whether the material is “reasonably available.” The NRC considers the following to be classes of interested parties in NRC rulemakings with regard to the material to be incorporated by reference:
Individuals and small entities regulated or otherwise subject to the NRC's regulatory oversight (this class also includes applicants and potential applicants for licenses and other NRC regulatory approvals) and who are subject to the material to be incorporated by reference by rulemaking. In this context, “small entities” has the same meaning as a “small entity” under
10 CFR 2.810
.
Large entities otherwise subject to the NRC's regulatory oversight (this class also includes applicants and potential applicants for licenses and other NRC regulatory approvals) and who are subject to the material to be incorporated by reference by rulemaking. In this context, “large entities” are those that do not qualify as a “small entity” under
10 CFR 2.810
.
Non-governmental organizations with institutional interests in the matters regulated by the NRC.
Other Federal agencies, States, local governmental bodies (within the meaning of
10 CFR 2.315(c)
).
Federally-recognized and State-recognized

6. a. An applicant who references the AP1000 design certification rule may depart from Tier 2 * information, which is designated with italicized text or brackets and an asterisk in the AP1000 design control document, without NRC approval, except for departures that:
(1) Involve a deviation from a code or standard credited in the plant-specific DCD for establishing the criteria for the design or construction of a structure, system, or component (SSC) important to safety;
(2) Result in a change to a design process described in the plant-specific DCD that is material to implementation of an industry standard or endorsed regulatory guidance;
(3) (i) Result in a change to the fuel criteria evaluation process, the fuel principal design requirements, or the nuclear design of the fuel or the reactivity control system that is material to a fuel or reactivity control system design function; or
(ii) Result in any change to the maximum fuel rod average burn-up limits or the small break LOCA analysis information in DCD Subsections 15.6.5.4B.2.2 or 15.6.5.4B.2.3;
(4) Adversely affect the containment debris limits or debris screen design criteria;
(5) Change the Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) type from a canned motor to a different type of RCP;
(6) Result in a change to the Passive Residual Heat Removal Heat Exchanger natural circulation test (first plant test), the Core Makeup Tank Heated Recirculation Tests (first three plants test), or the Automatic Depressurization System Blowdown Test (first three plants test) that is material to the test objectives or test performance criteria;
(7) Involve structural materials or analytical or design methods, including design codes and analytical assumptions, that deviate from those credited in the plant-specific DCD for critical sections;
(8) Result in a change to the design of the steel faceplates, internal trusses, tie bars, or headed studs of the steel-concrete (SC) module walls in the Nuclear Island or the Shield Building, including SC-to-reinforced concrete (RC) connections; or
(9) Result in an increase in the demand to capacity (D/C) ratio of a critical section of the structure. The licensee must determine the D/C ratio under this condition for each critical section structural member including, but not limited to, wall segments, wall sections, concrete panels, slabs, or basemat sections, affected by a departure by:
(i) Using the Tier 2 * information in the DCD Section 3.8 or Appendix 3H table that directly states the D/C ratio or states the area of steel provided and the area of steel required for the affected structural member; or
(ii) Providing the same total area of steel across the entire critical section using any combination of rebar sizes and spacing allowed by the design basis codes used in the DCD as the total area of steel specified in DCD Section 3.8 and Appendix 3H tables marked Tier 2 *.
b. For a departure from Tier 2 * information that does not require prior NRC approval, the licensee must comply with the requirements for Tier 2 departures in paragraph B.5 of this section. The departure or change to Tier 2 * information must remain Tier 2 * information in the plant-specific DCD.
c. Departures from Tier 2 * information that are made under paragraph B.6 of this section do not require an exemption from this appendix.

AGENCY:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (“ICE”), Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”); Executive Office for Immigration Review (“EOIR”), Department of Justice (“DOJ”).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
On June 27, 2025, the Departments issued an interim final rule (“IFR”) to streamline assessment of civil penalties under the Immigration and Nationality Act (“INA”) for aliens who fail to depart during a voluntary departure period, willfully fail or refuse to depart after a final removal order and certain other proscribed activities, or are apprehended while improperly entering or attempting to enter the United States. This final rule addresses comments and finalizes the IFR with one change: it permits acceptance of a late-filed appeal based on documented mail delivery delays that ICE finds were beyond the alien's control.
DATES:
The effective date of this final rule is October 14, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For DHS:

For DOJ:
Jamee E. Comans, Assistant Director, Office of Policy, Executive Office for Immigration Review, 5107 Leesburg Pike, Suite 2500, Falls Church, VA 22041; telephone (703) 305-0289.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
A. Basis and Purpose of the IFR
On January 20, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order (“E.O.”) 14159,
Protecting the American People Against Invasion.
E.O. 14159
,
90 FR 8443
(Jan. 29, 2025). In Section 2 of that E.O., President Trump directed that it is “the policy of the United States to faithfully execute the immigration laws against all inadmissible and removable aliens” and “to achieve the total and efficient enforcement of those laws, including through lawful incentives and detention capabilities.”
90 FR 8443
. Section 8 of
E.O. 14159
directs the Secretary of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Secretary of the Treasury, to “take all appropriate action to ensure the assessment and collection of all fines and penalties that the Secretary of Homeland Security is authorized by law to assess and collect from aliens unlawfully present in the United States, including aliens who unlawfully entered or unlawfully attempted to enter the United States.”
90 FR 8444-45
. Section 12 of
E.O. 14159
directs the Secretary of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Secretary of State and the Attorney General, “to take all appropriate action . . . to adopt policies and procedures to encourage aliens unlawfully in the United States to voluntarily depart as soon as possible, including through enhanced usage of the provisions of section 240B of the INA (
8 U.S.C. 1229c
), international agreements or assistance, or any other measures that encourage aliens unlawfully in the United States to depart as promptly as possible”.
90 FR 8445
. In Section 2 of

,

One such authority is civil monetary penalties. As explained in more detail in the IFR, Congress has authorized DHS to impose civil penalties on: (1) aliens who willfully fail or refuse to depart the United States after a final order of removal or take other action to thwart removal; (2) aliens who fail to comply with a voluntary departure order; and (3) aliens who are apprehended entering or attempting to enter the United States unlawfully (“unlawful entry penalties”).

8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1)

8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1)
;

;
8 CFR 280.53(b)(14)
. As the IFR explains, DHS believes that robust application of these civil penalties will deter future unlawful entries and encourage greater compliance with removal and voluntary departure orders, in line with Congress's intent and this Administration's focus on securing the border and restoring integrity to the immigration system.

Prior to the IFR, however, DHS was required to use the general civil penalty procedures at
8 CFR part 280
to impose these penalties. These procedures were promulgated by the former Immigration and Naturalization Service (“INS”) decades before Congress authorized the specific failure-to-depart and unlawful entry penalties covered by the IFR.
See
90 FR 27440-41
. Those regulations were designed primarily for penalties imposed on airlines and other carriers that violate INA provisions governing the transport of aliens into the United States, rather than for penalties against individual aliens for failure-to-depart or unlawful entry.
Id.
Under those regulations, DHS had to provide a written notice of intent to fine (“NIF”), served in person or by certified mail, and then wait at least 30 days for a response.
Id.
If the alien did not respond or did not contest the fine, a DHS officer could issue a final decision imposing the penalty.
Id.
If the alien contested the fine, the alien could request an in-person interview or submit a sworn written response; a supervisory immigration officer would then issue a written decision; the alien could seek reconsideration within DHS; after exhausting DHS procedures, the alien could appeal to the BIA.
Id.
As discussed in the IFR, these procedures are lengthy, resource intensive, and not tailored to the failure-to-depart and unlawful entry penalties that Congress later authorized.
See
90 FR 27444-46
.
The IFR streamlined and simplified the process DHS uses to impose civil penalties for failure-to-depart and unlawful entry and eliminated unnecessary procedures that are not required by statute.
See
90 FR 27449-52
. The IFR changed only the way DHS issues and adjudicates civil monetary penalties and the way an alien may contest such penalties for these specific fines.
90 FR 27454
. The IFR did not require the imposition of any new penalties or otherwise change the substantive criteria for issuing civil penalties.
Id.
Under the IFR, the new
8 CFR 281
allows a DHS immigration officer to initiate the penalty process by issuing a written decision and order imposing the civil monetary penalty.
8 CFR 281.1(b)
,
(c)
. The decision and order must identify the statutory basis for the penalty, state the type and amount of the penalty, and provide a brief
(
printed page 65393)
explanation of the reasons for the decision.
8 CFR 281.1(c)(1)
. The decision and order must also advise the alien of the right to appeal; the process for filing an appeal; the right to be represented by counsel at no expense to the government; and the opportunity to submit written arguments and supporting documentation challenging the penalty.
8 CFR 281.1(c)(2)
. The alien may file a written defense and supporting evidence or may simply submit a written notice of appeal.
8 CFR 281.1(c)(2)
,
(e)(1)
. DHS may serve the decision and order in person or by regular mail.
8 CFR 281.1(d)
.
The IFR also replaced the elaborate review process before DHS set forth in
8 CFR part 280
and appeal process before EOIR set forth at
8 CFR 1280.1

11

for these three specific civil penalties with an appeal process that takes place solely before DHS. Under the IFR, an alien must file a notice of appeal within 15 business days of service of the initial decision and order.
8 CFR 281.1(e)(1)
. If the alien does not file a timely appeal with DHS, the initial decision and order become final.
8 CFR 281.1(f)(3)
. If the alien files a timely appeal with DHS, a supervisory immigration officer who did not issue the initial decision and order will review the appeal.
8 CFR 281.1(e)(2)

Id.
At the alien's request, the supervisory officer will generally provide copies of pertinent documents and records relevant to the penalty.
8 CFR 281.1(e)(3)
. The supervisory officer will decide the appeal on the written record; the IFR does not provide for in-person interviews.
Id.
The record must include the initial decision and order, evidence in DHS's administrative files, and any timely written submissions, briefs, documentary evidence, or other relevant materials submitted by the alien.
Id.
The supervisory officer will review this record de novo, including the initial decision and order and any written arguments and evidence submitted by the alien, and will issue a final decision within 45 days.
8 CFR 281.1(e)(2)

(f)(1)-(3)

As explained in the IFR, the Departments reasoned that these updated procedures will allow DHS to impose these civil penalties more swiftly on more aliens who unlawfully enter the United States and on those who disregard removal and voluntary departure orders.
See
90 FR 27442
. In turn, this will help support DHS's efforts to maintain border security and enforce immigration laws by deterring unlawful entries and encouraging compliance with removal and departure orders.
See
90 FR 27445-46
. Compared to the general procedures in
8 CFR part 280
, the revised process reduces unnecessary administrative burdens and allows DHS to reach final decisions more quickly while at the same time reducing unnecessary burdens on the BIA's caseload.
See
90 FR 27444-45
. The IFR explained that these changes are needed to ensure that DHS can efficiently employ these statutory penalties while continuing to prioritize, without diverting resources away from, border security and the apprehension, detention, and removal of aliens who have violated the Nation's immigration laws, consistent with this Administration's policy objectives and the President's direction.
See
90 FR 27444-46
.
To further advance the IFR's goal of encouraging compliance with removal and departure orders, DHS has announced that it will rescind most failure to depart fines if an alien uses the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (“CBP”) Home app to arrange and complete self-departure from the United States.
[
12
]
This policy, coupled with DHS's expanded use of these civil penalties, is intended to provide an additional clear incentive for aliens to comply with removal and departure orders and avoid civil monetary penalties by doing what the law requires: departing the United States as ordered.
[
13
]
At the same time, the Departments determined that the revised procedures are consistent with due process. For the reasons discussed more fully in the IFR and in response to comments in Section III of this preamble, the Departments have concluded that a shortened appeal period, removal of in-person interviews, and the shift from BIA review to internal DHS review are appropriate and consistent with due process given that these civil penalties typically turn on routine and straightforward factual and legal determinations and aliens have limited grounds to contest them.
90 FR 27451-55
. In addition, ICE will now also permit acceptance of a late-filed appeal based on documented mail delivery delays that ICE finds were beyond the alien's control.
First, INA 275(b),
8 U.S.C. 1325(b)
, authorizes DHS to impose a civil penalty on any alien who is apprehended while entering or attempting to enter the United States at an improper place or time. Aliens apprehended while entering unlawfully have, by definition, violated INA 275(b),
8 U.S.C. 1325(b)
, and the documented encounter provides the only fact necessary to impose these penalties. Additionally, when USBP agents apprehend an alien entering unlawfully, the agents prepare a Form I-213,
Record of Deportable/Inadmissible Alien,
which documents the apprehension and is sufficient to demonstrate liability for these penalties.
See
90 FR 27442
. As a matter of practice, USBP issues these penalties at the time that it apprehends the alien. In these circumstances, the Departments do not believe that a lengthy, multi-step appeal process is necessary.
See id.
The IFR's appeal structure preserves an alien's meaningful ability to contest an unlawful entry penalty if the alien believes a penalty was issued erroneously.
Second, the nature of the failure to depart penalties also supports the IFR's changes. Congress has authorized DHS to impose civil monetary penalties on aliens for failure to depart, subject to the general federal statute of limitations, 28
(
printed page 65394)
U.S.C. 2462, if two elements have been satisfied: (1) the alien is subject to a final order of removal or was granted voluntary departure and (2) the alien willfully fails or refuses to depart under a removal order or voluntarily fails to comply with a voluntary departure order. INA 274D(a)(1),
8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1)
; INA 240B(d)(1)(A),
8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(1)(A)
. DHS maintains records of an alien's immigration history, including removal and voluntary departure orders, and has ready access to information about any pending appeals needed to verify that the alien is subject to a final removal or departure order.
90 FR 27442-43
. Before issuing a penalty, ICE guidance requires the immigration officer to verify that there are no DHS records of the alien's departure from the United States and reviews the alien's immigration records for information suggesting that the alien's failure to depart was not willful or voluntary. This includes information about: automatic stays resulting from motions to reopen; certain immigration benefits under the Violence Against Women Act (“VAWA”) that stay the alien's removal; for aliens on an order of supervision, efforts the alien has made to secure travel documents at DHS's request; whether DHS has affirmatively approved the alien for deferred action; whether the Immigration Courts, DHS, or a federal court has granted a stay of removal; and whether DHS or EOIR has granted the alien protection that excuses the alien's failure to depart while the alien maintains that protection, including temporary protected status (“TPS”), protection under the Convention Against Torture (“CAT”), and withholding of removal under INA 241(b)(3),
8 U.S.C. 1231(b)(3)
when no alternative country of removal is available.
Absent evidence in records accessible to DHS showing that the alien is permitted to remain in the United States, or that the alien has departed, DHS believes the statutory prerequisites to issue a penalty will have been met where an alien ordered removed or granted voluntary departure is physically present in the United States beyond the time frame specified by the Immigration Judge. As the IFR explains, civil penalties for failure to depart are generally issued after completion of section 240 removal proceedings that resulted in a final order requiring the alien's departure from the United States immediately or within a certain time frame specified by the Immigration Judge.
See
90 FR 27440
. These aliens have received due process through section 240 removal proceedings where they had an opportunity to contest the charges against them, to seek relief, and to be informed by an Immigration Judge of their obligation to depart and of the consequences of failing to do so.
Id.
Aliens granted voluntary departure prior to the conclusion of section 240 removal proceedings have already agreed to forgo challenging removal or seeking relief in exchange for being allowed to depart voluntarily.
Id.
In these circumstances, and when DHS records show the removal order is executable, the Departments reasoned that an alien's continued presence in the United States is generally sufficient to establish liability for these civil penalties, absent the alien providing evidence on appeal
[
14
]
to demonstrate otherwise.
See
90 FR 27442-43
.
In addition, Immigration Judges are required by law to inform aliens of their departure obligations and the consequences for failing to comply. Under INA 240(c)(5),
8 U.S.C. 1229(a)(5)
, when an Immigration Judge orders removal, the Immigration Judge must inform the alien of the consequences for failure to depart under the order of removal, including civil penalties described at sections INA 274D,
8 U.S.C. 1324(d)
.
See
8 CFR 1240.13(d)
. Likewise, for voluntary departure, the INA requires that an Immigration Judge “shall inform the alien of the penalties” that will apply if the alien voluntarily fails to depart within the time allowed, including civil monetary penalties and ineligibility for certain forms of relief. INA 240B(d)(3),
8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(3)
. These advisals are mandatory components of 240 removal proceedings, not discretionary steps.
These statutory and regulatory requirements are directly relevant to the willfulness and voluntariness elements in the civil penalty statutes. Before DHS considers imposing a failure to depart penalty, the alien will ordinarily have been advised, on the record, that the law requires the alien to depart the United States and that failure to do so may result in civil fines and other adverse consequences. When an alien remains in the United States after such clear, legally required notice, his or her continued presence strongly supports the conclusion that the alien has “willfully fail[ed] or refuse[d]” to depart under a removal order or “voluntarily” failed to comply with a voluntary departure order, as required by the failure to depart civil penalty statutes. In making this assessment, DHS also relies on the presumption of regularity that attaches to official acts of government officers, including Immigration Judges.
See United States Postal Serv.
v.
Gregory,
534 U.S. 1, 10 (2001). Under this presumption, DHS may reasonably assume that Immigration Judges complied with their legal obligations under the INA and implementing regulations and provided the required advisals concerning departure obligations and the consequences of noncompliance, absent specific evidence to the contrary in the record. In all cases, ICE considers the willfulness of an alien's violation in determining whether to impose a penalty.
Taken together—(1) the procedural protections provided in section 240 removal proceedings, (2) the mandatory Immigration Judge advisals of departure obligations and penalties, (3) the presumption of regularity applicable to those advisals, and (4) DHS's careful review of U.S. Government records to confirm that the alien is subject to a final, executable order and lacks lawful permission to remain—DHS concludes that an alien's continued presence in the United States is generally sufficient to establish the willful or voluntary failure to depart required to impose these civil penalties, absent evidence provided by the alien on appeal to demonstrate that the alien is not liable. Therefore, the Departments reasoned that streamlining the issuance and adjudication of these civil penalties, and the associated appeals process, aligns more closely with the nature and intent of these straightforward civil penalties. While in most cases, DHS records sufficiently establish the facts necessary to demonstrate that the alien is subject to these civil penalties, the alien retains the right to contest them on limited grounds.
See
90 FR 27442-46
.
To the extent an alien believes that DHS issued a penalty erroneously—for example, because the alien is not subject to a removal order, is legally permitted to remain in the United States, or did not willfully or voluntarily fail to depart—the Departments determined that the IFR provides sufficient notice and an opportunity to contest the decision before DHS, and that further review before EOIR is unnecessary.
See
90 FR 27451-55
. Under the IFR, a DHS immigration officer must issue a written decision that sets forth the statutory and factual basis for the penalty and informs the alien of the requirements and deadlines for filing an appeal.
See Mullane
v.
Cent. Hanover Bank & Tr. Co.,
339 U.S. 306, 314 (1950) (stating
(
printed page 65395)
that notice under due process must be of a sufficient nature as to reasonably convey the required information). The revised appeal process also preserves an alien's opportunity to contest a civil penalty. Under the IFR's procedures, the alien has 15 business days to appeal using the DHS-developed Form 281,
Notice and Violation of Order,
and a supervisory immigration officer who did not issue the initial decision will review the record de novo and may request additional evidence before making a final determination.
See
90 FR 27452-54
.
As explained in the IFR and in response to comments in Section III of this preamble, the Departments believe that additional procedures, beyond those contained in the IFR, would not enhance the accuracy, fairness, or reliability of the process given the straightforward nature of these penalties and the limited grounds that an alien may have to contest them.
See id.
Thus, for the reasons discussed in the IFR and in response to comments in Section III of this preamble, the Departments believe that the revised procedure preserves an alien's ability to contest the fine while better ensuring that the BIA does not unnecessarily expend resources in areas where DHS is better positioned to review such determinations, and that DHS can reach final decisions efficiently and apply these statutory penalties swiftly and at the scale necessary to address the large number of aliens who have entered or remain unlawfully in the United States. Accordingly, after carefully considering comments received on the IFR, the Departments are finalizing this rule with one change discussed in more detail below to account for U.S. postal delays.
B. The Departments' Experience With the IFR
The IFR is working as intended. As a result of the IFR, DHS has been able to issue a significantly greater number of civil penalties compared to the pre-IFR process under
8 CFR part 280
. From March 26, 2025, through June 26, 2025, ICE issued 12,135 civil penalties under the pre-IFR process.
[
15
]
From June 27, 2025, after the IFR took effect, through September 14, 2026, ICE issued approximately 110,000 failure to depart civil penalties, and CBP issued an additional 66,000 civil penalties for unlawful entry. Thus, DHS increased the number of civil penalties issued from approximately 930 per week under the pre-IFR process to nearly 2,800 per week under the IFR process.
[
16
]
Accordingly, the IFR has allowed DHS to impose more civil penalties more quickly on a greater scale, while retaining procedural safeguards designed to promote accurate penalty assessments without diverting resources away from border security, and the apprehension, detention, and removal of aliens who have violated our immigration laws.
Second, DHS's robust use of civil penalties appears to be shifting incentives for aliens with removal and departure orders who might otherwise remain unlawfully in the United States. DHS data indicates that over 82,000 aliens with removal orders and voluntary departures orders have self-departed from the United States since DHS began issuing civil penalties in March 2025 through September 14, 2026.
[
17
]
In that same period, over 7,700 aliens have self-departed after receiving a civil penalty.
[
18
]
Further, the number of aliens with removal orders or voluntary departure orders who have self-departed since the IFR took effect has increased significantly, as has the number of aliens who have departed after receiving a civil penalty. In the pre-IFR period from March 26, 2025, through June 26, 2025, approximately 8,600 aliens with removal or voluntary departure orders self-departed, and approximately 540 aliens self-departed the United States after receiving a civil penalty during this period.
[
19
]
In the post-IFR period from June 27, 2025, through September 14, 2026, over 74,000 aliens with removal orders or voluntary departure orders self-departed in total, and approximately 7,180 aliens self-departed after receiving a civil penalty during this period. This data indicates that DHS's robust use of civil penalties, as facilitated by the IFR's streamlined procedures, is encouraging illegally present aliens to depart the United States on their own, consistent with the IFR's objectives.
Finally, DHS's experience implementing the civil penalties covered by this rule since March 26, 2025, confirms that many pre-IFR procedures were unnecessary and that the IFR's procedures provide a meaningful opportunity to contest penalties believed to be erroneous without unnecessarily diverting BIA resources away from adjudicating its existing pending caseload to conduct review better addressed by DHS. As discussed above, the IFR shortens the appeal period, eliminates in-person interviews, and shifts appeals from the BIA to DHS. DHS data support these changes:
Under the pre-IFR process, aliens filed written answers pursuant to
8 CFR 280.12
contesting failure to depart penalties for only 222 of the 12,135 notices of intent to fine that ICE issued, a less than 2 percent appeal rate. Under the post-IFR process through September 10, 2026, aliens appealed failure to depart civil penalties in 3,072 cases of the approximately 110,000 penalties that ICE issued between June 27, 2025, through September 14, 2026, a nearly 3 percent appeal rate. The appeal rate has therefore increased under the post-IFR process.
[
20
]
Only 4 aliens requested an in-person interview out of the 222 penalty notices that aliens contested under the pre-IFR process, indicating that in-person interviews are generally unnecessary and that aliens can adequately contest these decisions through written submissions based on information in the alien's possession.
Under the pre-IFR process, only 44 aliens appealed DHS's penalty decision to the BIA under
8 CFR part 1003
, further supporting the Departments' assessment that the legal issues associated with these penalties are relatively straightforward and appeals can be handled by DHS. As of September 10, 2026, the BIA has issued only two decisions in these appeals, including a published decision which
(
