As discussed in the IFR, Congress has not required EOIR or the BIA to review these civil penalty decisions, and nothing in the INA precludes the Attorney General from exercising his authority to remove the BIA's regulatory appellate authority over these penalties.
90 FR 27448
.
Comment:
Several commenters argued that replacing BIA appellate review with DHS appellate review impermissibly consolidates enforcement and adjudication powers within one agency. They further argued that the IFR's appeal structure creates an inherent conflict of interest because DHS cannot be impartial when reviewing its own actions. One commenter argued that this consolidation of enforcement and adjudication functions violates due process. The commenter explained that the Supreme Court has long recognized that due process requires impartiality from adjudicators, and that any arrangement that gives rise to even a “possible temptation” to act in a biased way that benefits the decisionmaker violates due process.
See Ward
v.
Village of Monroeville,
409 U.S. 57, 60 (1972). The commenter asserted that DHS assessing these penalties and reviewing appeals raises at least a possibility of temptation to impermissibly affirm the determinations, noting that the IFR itself was issued to allow DHS to impose these penalties more swiftly and at scale. Another commenter noted that these civil penalties are deposited into a DHS account that directly funds immigration detention, removal operations, and border wall construction. They suggested that this creates a powerful institutional incentive for DHS to maximize fine revenue, and, therefore, BIA review is needed to mitigate this potential conflict of interest. To address these concerns, this commenter urged the Departments to restore BIA review or to create an independent review board, separate from ICE and CBP, to review civil penalty appeals. They also suggested that if the IFR's structure is preserved, the rule should, at minimum, sever the financial interest DHS has in imposing these fines by redirecting civil penalty revenue to the Department of the Treasury's general fund rather than retaining it in DHS's enforcement accounts.
Response:
DHS strongly rejects commenters' speculative suggestion that DHS immigration officers cannot be impartial and neutral when adjudicating civil penalty appeals. DHS has designed the appeal process to ensure that an alien's appeal is fairly and fully considered on the merits alone. Indeed, the IFR makes clear that any appeal of a penalty decision must be reviewed by a separate supervisory immigration officer who was not involved in the initial civil monetary penalty decision. Additionally, the IFR instructs the supervisory officer to review the appeal record de novo, which ensures that officers decide each appeal solely on the law and facts presented without providing any weight in favor of the initial decision. There is a presumption of regularity that attaches to the actions of government agencies,
see U.S. Postal Serv.,
534 U.S. at 10, and commenters have offered no support for their claim that immigration officers will deny otherwise meritorious challenges to civil penalties simply because they are employed by the same agency that issues and enforces these penalties.
Moreover, the Supreme Court has long held that it does not violate due process to combine enforcement and adjudication functions within a single agency.
See Withrow
v.
Larkin,
421 U.S. 35, 56-58 (1975) (holding that the fact that the initial charge in an administrative proceeding is brought by the same agency that later adjudicates the matter is not, in and of itself, violative of due process);
see also Marcello
v.
Bonds,
349 U.S. 302 (1955) (rejecting the argument that the former INS's comingled prosecutorial and adjudicative functions, under a prior version of the INA, deprived aliens of due process in deportation proceedings). Thus, the Departments disagree with commenters' suggestion that the consolidation of enforcement and adjudication functions within the same agency violates due process or inherently increases the risk of biased decision-making.
The caselaw cited by one commenter does not undermine the Departments' conclusion that the IFR's appeal procedures comport with due process. At most, the cited cases stand for the principle that an agency's adjudicatory procedures could violate due process if the adjudicator has a direct financial or pecuniary interest in the outcome of the case, has prejudged the case, or has some other concrete conflict of interest. These cases, however, do not support the commenter's broad argument that DHS immigration officers cannot be neutral and unbiased merely because they are part of DHS. Rather the caselaw is clear: there is a presumption of honesty and integrity in administrative officials exercising adjudicative functions, even where there is a combination of investigative and adjudicative functions, and some evidence of actual bias must be presented to overcome this presumption.
See Marcello,
349 U.S. at 311;
Withrow,
421 U.S. at 47;
see also Baran
v.
Port of Beaumont Navigation District,
57 F.3d 436, 446 (5th Cir. 1995). The commenter has not offered any actual and non-speculative reason to think that DHS officers cannot be neutral but will instead be “tempted” to impermissibly affirm penalty decisions issued by other DHS officers.
The other concerns cited by commenters do not support their
(
printed page 65419)
contention that civil penalty appeals must be adjudicated by the BIA or an agency outside of DHS. The Departments acknowledge that INA 280(b),
8 U.S.C. 1330(b)
, provides that any civil monetary penalties collected from aliens shall be deposited into a DHS account that funds immigration detention, removal operations, and border wall construction. DHS disagrees, however, with one commenter's view that DHS officers adjudicating civil penalty appeals will be encouraged to maximize fine revenue for this DHS fund. DHS officers adjudicating civil penalty appeals are bound by strict legal and procedural standards to ensure impartiality and fairness in their decision-making processes.
[
49
]
These officers are tasked with applying the law and evaluating the facts of each case independently, without regard to the financial implications of their decisions.
[
50
]
DHS has robust supervisory review mechanisms in place to ensure that adjudications are conducted in compliance with applicable laws, regulations, and ethical standards. The fine amounts are governed by statute and regulations and, once an immigration officer determines that a civil penalty should be issued, the officer's discretion in choosing the fine amount is bound by those statutory and regulatory limits, and this rule does not alter the penalty amounts themselves authorized by statute. Furthermore, the primary purpose of civil monetary penalties under the INA is to enforce compliance with immigration laws, not to generate revenue. DHS remains committed to upholding the integrity of the adjudication process and ensuring that decisions are made based solely on the merits of each case, rather than any external considerations related to funding.
Similarly, DHS disagrees that officers will have an incentive to affirm penalty decisions on appeal because the IFR's preamble emphasizes DHS's desire to maximize the use of these penalties. The Departments agree that the IFR was designed to maximize DHS's ability to impose civil penalties in proportion to the scale of illegal aliens in the United States—not the total amount of the penalties. The IFR achieves this purpose by streamlining the penalty process, but it does not dictate the outcome of any penalty appeal or otherwise pressure immigration officers to affirm initial penalty decisions. Rather, as discussed above, the IFR makes clear that a supervisory officer must review appeals de novo based solely on DHS records and any evidence or argument submitted by the alien. Moreover, the IFR provides officers with a 45-day period to adjudicate appeals, which will ensure that they have ample time to consider all of the evidence and arguments provided by the alien. Accordingly, DHS believes that statements in the IFR's preamble will not cause immigration officers to prejudge appeals or impermissibly affirm penalty decisions. DHS clarifies that it expects each supervisory immigration officer to decide individual appeals based solely on the law and the facts presented.
Finally, the Departments note that BIA review is not needed to ensure that immigration officers comply with these regulatory requirements and decide each appeal on the basis of its own facts and circumstances. If an alien believes that an immigration officer's decision was erroneous and not based on the applicable law and the facts of the case, then after exhausting administrative remedies, the alien may seek judicial review under the APA or may challenge the decision in connection with any enforcement action brought by DOJ to collect the penalty.
For all of these reasons, individually and collectively, the Departments decline to modify the IFR to restore BIA review. Similarly, DHS declines to create an independent body, separate from ICE and CBP, to adjudicate civil penalty appeals because DHS believes that ICE and CBP supervisory officers are fully capable of deciding each appeal on the basis of its individual facts and circumstances without bias or prejudgment. Additionally, creating an independent board or body would conflict with the purpose of the IFR to streamline the civil penalty process, including the appeal process, because it could take additional time to create and to put in place processes that would ensure that the board receives filings and records in a timely manner. Finally, with respect to one commenter's claim that, in order to remove any conflict of interest, DHS should redirect penalty revenue to a general Treasury fund rather than retaining it in DHS accounts, DHS notes that it cannot redirect funds in contravention of INA 280(b),
8 U.S.C. 1330(b)
.
Comment:
Several commenters characterized the IFR's appeal process as lacking transparency and accountability. They noted that the BIA makes its decisions publicly available and has a well-established process for publishing decisions on emerging legal issues. In contrast, commenters noted that the IFR does not require DHS to make its civil fine decisions public or treat them as precedential in cases raising similar issues. Commenters argued that this will contribute to arbitrary and inconsistent decisions and a lack of accountability.
Response:
As discussed in the IFR and above, the civil penalties covered by this rule typically turn on straightforward issues of fact, rather than complicated questions of law.
See
90 FR 27453
. Accordingly, the Departments disagree with commenters that there is a need for DHS to establish a process for publishing decisions on emerging legal issues involving these penalties. DHS also notes that ICE and CBP have issued guidance to immigration officers regarding these penalties, including guidance on the various legal issues that commenters have identified and that are discussed throughout this preamble. Finally, nothing in this rule prevents an alien from bringing a federal court challenge to a penalty decision or from raising any legal defense that may be available to the alien in connection with a DOJ enforcement action to collect the penalty. DHS will comply with any adverse court ruling and will apply any legal precedent applicable to these penalties that results from such a challenge.
To the extent that commenters are suggesting that DHS must publish civil penalty decisions to provide transparency, accountability, and consistency in the penalty amounts being assessed, ICE and CBP are applying a uniform practice of assessing the maximum statutorily authorized penalty amount in each case, consistent with the statute of limitations. DHS has an interest in issuing these penalties quickly and at the maximum authorized amount to encourage aliens to comply with removal and voluntary departure orders. To achieve these dual objectives, DHS has determined that ICE and CBP should assess the maximum penalties authorized by law.
7. Mitigation Factors; Motions To Reopen
Comment:
Commenters argued that the rule should allow aliens to seek mitigation, and it should clarify that DHS should consider mitigating factors when assessing penalties. One commenter recommended a tiered penalty system based on severity and good faith compliance efforts. Another commenter recommended that the agencies adopt a means-tested fine structure that considers the recipient's
(
printed page 65420)
financial capacity. Another commenter points out that the government considers mitigating factors for employers subject to penalties. They state that in assessing fines against employers of aliens under the Immigration Reform and Control Act, the government considers factors such as the size of their business, their good faith, the seriousness of the violations, whether the employee is an alien, and the employer's history of previous violations. Finally, one commenter argues that the rule undermines procedural fairness by eliminating any right for aliens to request reopening while preserving reopening authority for DHS.
Response:
The Departments disagree that the IFR should authorize aliens to seek mitigation of penalty amounts, create a tiered penalty structure, or adopt a means-tested framework for assessing penalties. The civil monetary penalties addressed in this rule arise under INA 240B(d), 274D, and 275(b),
8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)
,
1324d
, and
1325(b)
. These statutory provisions do not require DHS or DOJ to adjust penalty amounts based on mitigating circumstances, financial capacity, or subjective good-faith factors, nor do they provide a means for aliens to request discretionary mitigation. In contrast, several of the statutes cited by commenters, including those governing certain employer sanctions under the IRCA, explicitly establish mitigating factors that DHS or DOJ must consider when assessing penalties. Congress included no such language in the statutory provisions at issue here. Additionally, President Trump's Executive orders direct DHS to “ensure the assessment and collection of all fines and penalties [DHS] is authorized by law to assess and collect from aliens unlawfully present in the United States”
[
51
]
and to “take all appropriate action to secure the borders of our Nation . . . [including by] deterring and preventing the entry of illegal aliens into the United States.”
[
52
]
At the same time, the IFR does not foreclose DHS from rescinding or reopening decisions on its own initiative, where doing so is necessary to ensure administrative accuracy, correct an error, or address other considerations relevant to sound enforcement. This internal authority is procedural in nature and serves the agency's interest in consistency, fairness, and error correction. Allowing aliens to file motions to reopen before DHS for the purpose of seeking mitigation, particularly after the supervisory review process, would undermine the Department's legitimate interests in finality, administrative efficiency, and the timely initiation of the collection process, which are essential to administering a nationwide penalty scheme. The civil monetary penalties addressed in this rule arising under INA 240B(d), 274(D), and 275(b),
8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)
,
1324d
, and
1325(b)
, do not confer a statutory right on aliens to request reopening of a final civil monetary penalty determination. The Departments therefore decline to create a new regulatory mechanism that would effectively grant aliens a right to reopen final decisions or seek mitigation after supervisory review has concluded.
The Departments also disagree with commenters who argued that fairness requires adopting mitigation factors analogous to those applicable to employers sanctioned under the IRCA. That comparison is misplaced. IRCA explicitly directs the government to consider certain mitigating factors when assessing employer penalties. By contrast, the penalties at issue here are based on statutory conditions, such as failure to comply with voluntary departure or the presence of a prior removal order, that turn on objective, records-based facts. These provisions do not require a discretionary, multi-factor penalty assessment. The Departments are not required to import into these statutes mitigation frameworks that Congress has chosen to include elsewhere but omitted here.
For these reasons, the Departments conclude that the IFR appropriately reflects the statutory framework governing civil penalties under INA 240B(d), 274D, and 275(b),
8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)
,
1324d
, and
1325(b)
, and that adopting a mitigation regime, a tiered fine system, a means-tested structure, or respondent-initiated motions to reopen is not required by the governing statutes, and is administratively impractical and beyond the scope of this rulemaking.
8. Civil Penalty Amounts;
8 CFR 281.1(g)
Comment:
Some commenters argued that the fines imposed by the IFR implicate the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Fines Clause. They contend that, under U.S. Supreme Court precedent, even if a penalty is deemed “civil,” it constitutes punishment for purposes of the Excessive Fines Clause if it serves retributive or deterrent purposes, rather than remedial ones. They broadly claimed that the IFR authorizes DHS to issue fines that serve no remedial purpose, and the IFR's self-expressed intent—to deter future unlawful entries and encourage greater compliance with removal and voluntary departure orders—reflects a punitive purpose. Commenters broadly stated that these penalties are excessive under the Eighth Amendment because they can result in sums “disproportionate” to the underlying immigration violations.
One commenter noted that there is a wide range of circumstances surrounding an alien's decision to come to the United States or remain in the country after a removal order or voluntary departure order and suggested that the Departments' failure to consider these circumstances violates the Excessive Fines Clause. The commenter listed examples, including aliens fleeing persecution or seeking a better life for their children, aliens who were unable to depart due to illness, financial problems, aliens with pending challenges to a removal order, and aliens who were removed in absentia and were unaware of the order. One commenter suggested that DHS should cap fines at levels that reflect the nature of the violation and an alien's ability to pay.
Response:
As an initial matter, the Departments note that the IFR did not change the scope or amount of the civil monetary penalties that Congress has established. It only changed the procedures for issuing and adjudicating these civil monetary penalties and for allowing an alien to contest them.
See
90 FR 27454
. DHS has imposed the maximum statutory penalties under both the IFR's streamlined penalty process and the prior penalty process in
8 CFR part 280
. This indicates that commenters' Eighth Amendment concerns are directed primarily at the penalty amounts authorized by Congress, not at the IFR's procedures, and are therefore outside of the scope of this rule. Nevertheless, in so far as commenters are suggesting the IFR is unlawful because it does not require DHS immigration officers to assess proportionality or consider mitigating factors before imposing the maximum penalty amount, the Departments respond as follows: (1) these civil monetary penalties do not fall within the Eighth Amendments Excessive Fines Clause, and (2) even if treated as “fines,” they are not excessive under the factors in
United States
v.
Bajakajian,
524 U.S. 321 (1998).
The Supreme Court has never held that civil monetary penalties for immigration violations are “fines” for purposes of the Excessive Fines Clause.
(
printed page 65421)
The Court's cases in this area have either involved sanctions ordered as penalties for criminal conduct, or civil forfeiture actions imposed after a criminal conviction, where the property was used in the commission of the crime.
See Alexander
v.
United States,
509 U.S. 544, 558 (1993) (criminal forfeiture of property);
Bajakajian,
524 U.S. at 328 (criminal forfeiture of currency);
Austin
v.
United States,
509 U.S. 602, 619-22 (1993) (civil forfeiture of property used to commit drug crimes). By contrast, the penalties covered by this rule are not imposed in connection with criminal offenses. They are civil measures designed to promote compliance with the immigration laws and support DHS's enforcement efforts. The Supreme Court has long recognized that Congress may impose civil monetary penalties for violations of the Nation's immigration laws, and that such penalties are not criminal in nature.
See, e.g., Oceanic Steam Nav. Co.
v.
Stranahan,
214 U.S. 320, 337 (1909). Moreover, the fact that these penalties are intended to serve a deterrence purpose does not render them subject to the Excessive Fines Clause because “deterrence may serve civil as well as criminal goals.”
Hudson
v.
United States,
522 U.S. 93 105, (1997) (internal quotation marks omitted);
see also Garner
v.
U.S. Dep't of Labor,
221 F.3d 822, 827 (5th Cir. 2000) (“That a statute serves to deter future conduct does not automatically render it punitive.”). In addition, Congress clearly intended these penalties to serve a remedial purpose. As explained in Section II of this preamble, apprehending, detaining, and removing removable aliens, and conducting section 240 removal proceedings imposes significant costs on the Departments, and a large number of unlawful entries strain resources at the border. Congress recognized these harms and authorized civil penalties to both encourage compliance with the immigration laws and to help fund DHS's border security and removal efforts.
See
INA 280(b)(3),
8 U.S.C. 1330(b)(3)
(providing that the Immigration Enforcement Account is available for removal of criminal aliens and structures along certain portions of the United States border);
see also
H. Rep. No. 104-469 pt. 1 at 155 (1996).
Even if these penalties were considered fines under the Excessive Fines Clause, DHS's decision to impose the maximum amount authorized by Congress without considering each alien's individual reasons for unlawful entry or failure to depart after a removal or departure order is neither excessive nor unconstitutional. Courts of appeals generally apply the following factors from
Bajakajian,
524 U.S. at 337-40, to determine whether a fine is “grossly disproportional” to the gravity of an offense: (1) the amount of the penalty authorized by Congress and the nature of the harm that results from a violation; (2) the class of persons to whom the statute principally applies; and (3) a comparison with potential criminal penalties. Taken together, these factors support the conclusion that the IFR need not be amended to limit DHS's authority to impose the maximum statutory penalties or to require a proportionality analysis before issuing a civil penalty or otherwise consider mitigating factors.
With respect to the first factor, judgments about the appropriate penalty amount for a violation “belong in the first instance to the legislature.”
Bajakajian,
524 U.S. at 322. The civil monetary penalties covered by this rule reflect Congress's considered judgment that the conduct involved—an alien's unlawful entry or failure to depart after a removal or departure order—is particularly serious and warrants substantial fines to promote compliance with immigration laws.
See
90 FR 27454
. Consistent with Congress's judgment and current enforcement priorities, DHS has determined that imposing the maximum authorized penalties is an appropriate response to the large number of aliens who have unlawfully entered the United States or have violated removal and departure orders in recent years.
See
Section II of this preamble. Courts have held that an agency's civil penalty decision is not excessive under the Eighth Amendment when it does not exceed the statutory maximum.
See Newell Recycling Co.
v.
EPA,
231 F.3d 204, 210 (5th Cir. 2000) (“No matter how excessive (in lay terms) an administrative fine may appear, if the fine does not exceed the limits prescribed by the statute authorizing it, the fine does not violate the Eighth Amendment”);
see also Pharaon
v.
Bd. of Governors of the Fed. Res. Sys,
135 F.3d 148, 155-57 (D.C. Cir. 1998).
The specific statutorily authorized penalty amounts are also proportionate to the underlying immigration law violations. For the unlawful entry penalty, the maximum penalty (adjusted for inflation) is $500 for each entry.
See
8 CFR 280.53(b)(15)
. That amount is not disproportionate to unlawful entries, including repeated unlawful entries, in violation of the immigration laws in light of Congress's concerns when enacting this penalty.
See
H. Rep. No. 104-469 at 155 (1996) (noting that unlawful entry “with no consequences undermines the credibility of our efforts to secure the border”).
For voluntary departure civil penalties, Congress has authorized Immigration Judges to set penalties between $1,992 and $9,970 (as adjusted for inflation).
See
8 CFR 280.53(b)(3)
. Under longstanding regulations, Immigration Judges or the BIA must select an amount within that range that reflects the likelihood that the alien will comply with voluntary departure or may apply a presumptive amount of $3,000.
See
8 CFR 1240.26(l)
;
73 FR 76927
,
76936
(Dec. 18, 2008). DHS adheres to the amount set by EOIR. That amount is not excessive because it reflects both the adjudicator's assessment of the incentive needed to secure compliance and Congress's desire to ensure consequences for violating departure orders.
See
H. Rep. No. 104-469, at 122 (noting how aliens with voluntary departure and had “very little incentive” to actually depart the United States prior to IIRIRA).
For failure to depart after a removal order, Congress has authorized DHS to impose a penalty of $998 per day (as adjusted for inflation) for each day an alien willfully fails to depart. Commenters argue that these penalties are excessive because the cumulative total may, in some cases, exceed $1,000,000. The Departments disagree. Congress designed this provision so that each day of willful failure to depart constitutes a separate, repeating violation.
See
Section III.E. of this preamble. In this context, proportionality is assessed by looking at each per day penalty, not the cumulative amount.
See e.g. United States
v.
Schwarzbaum,
127 F.4th 259, 276 (11th Cir. 2025). A $998 per diem penalty is not excessive compared to other immigration-related civil penalties. It reflects Congress's judgment as to the seriousness of the harm that flows from each day an alien remains in the United States in willful violation of a removal order and how these willful violations undermine the credibility of the immigration laws and warrant a separate penalty.
Even when viewed cumulatively, the per diem failure to depart penalty is not excessive. Congress added this authority in IIRIRA to strengthen immigration enforcement and to increase the consequences for ignoring removal orders, in response to the problem of aliens remaining in the United States—sometimes for years—after final deportation orders.
See
H.R. Rep. No. 104-469, pt. 1, at 160 (1996) (explaining when enacting IIRIRA that “aliens who have final orders of deportation [often]
(
printed page 65422)
remain in the United States indefinitely” and noting that “[a]s a result, the resources expended to identify, apprehend, and provide a hearing to a deportable alien are all too often wasted”). Against this backdrop, Congress expressly authorized DHS to impose per-day penalties that may reach substantial sums when an alien willfully remains in the United States for extended periods in violation of a removal order. In these circumstances, imposing the maximum daily amount, even where it results in a large total, is not excessive because the total directly reflects a long-running, repeated violation.
See Schwarzbaum,
127 F.4th at 284 (“when a cumulative fine is made up of constitutionally proportionate penalties, the cumulative fine “is, literally, directly proportionate to the offense”) (citation and internal quotations omitted).
Taken together, the three penalties covered by this rule reflect Congress's calibrated assessment of the harm associated with each type of violation. Lower penalties for unlawful entry generally apply to aliens apprehended while entering and who are often subject to prompt return or expedited removal, thereby conserving resources associated with section 240 removal proceedings. Higher penalties for failure to depart reflect Congress's judgment that remaining in the United States after a departure or removal order both seriously undermines the integrity of the immigration system and results in wasted enforcement and adjudicative resources.
See
H. Rep. No. 104 469, pt. 1, at 160. Accordingly, the Departments believe that imposing the maximum statutorily authorized amount of these penalties is both consistent with Congress's purpose in enacting these penalties and not excessive given those amounts reflect the value of the harm Congress placed on such violations.
See United States
v.
Chaplin's, Inc.,
646 F.3d 846, 852 (11th Cir. 2011) (“Congress, as a representative body, can distill the monetary value society places on harmful conduct”).
The second
Bajakajian
factor—whether the penalties apply to the class of persons for whom the statute was principally designed—also supports the Departments' position. Aliens subject to these penalties fall squarely within the class Congress targeted. For unlawful entry penalties, an alien's apprehension while attempting to enter the United States unlawfully is sufficient to support the penalty. For failure to depart penalties, ICE guidance instructs officers to confirm that the alien is subject to a final removal or voluntary departure order, that there is no DHS record of the alien's departure, and that, based on available records, there are no legal impediments or other circumstances that would negate a willful or voluntary failure to depart. For per diem penalties, ICE guidance further requires officers to exclude periods when the alien was lawfully permitted to remain in the United States, such as during the pendency of a stay of removal. This is all Congress has required. Congress has clearly provided that any alien who engages in the proscribed conduct—unlawfully entering the United States or willfully or voluntarily failing to depart after a removal or departure order—is subject to a civil penalty up to the statutory maximum. By contrast to other immigration-related civil penalties
[
53
]
and contrary to commenters' suggestion, Congress has not required DHS to adjust the penalty based on proportionality or to consider specific mitigating circumstances. To the extent that commenters are suggesting that DHS must consider factors such as an alien's inability to obtain travel documents, hospitalization, or other circumstances beyond the alien's control, such factors could negate the “willfulness” or “voluntariness” of an alien's conduct and, if the alien demonstrates them on appeal, the alien may not be subject to the penalty at all. However, the alien is best positioned to raise these considerations on appeal because DHS would generally not have knowledge of such circumstances. The second
Bajakajian
factor therefore supports DHS's decision to assess these penalties up to the maximum statutorily authorized amount without first conducting a proportionality analysis or considering mitigating circumstances.
The third
Bajakajian
factor—comparison to potential criminal sanctions—likewise weighs against a finding of excessiveness. In IIRIRA, Congress not only created the civil failure to depart penalty but also amended INA 243,
8 U.S.C. 1253
, to make it a criminal offense for an alien to willfully fail or refuse to depart within 90 days of a final removal order. Congress authorized imprisonment of up to four years, a fine, or both, with enhanced penalties for certain criminal aliens.
See
INA 243(a)(1),
8 U.S.C. 1253(a)(1)
. Congress has also authorized criminal penalties for unlawful entry, including up to six months' imprisonment, a fine, or both, with increased penalties for repeat offenses.
See
INA 275(a),
8 U.S.C. 1325(a)
. These criminal penalties are significantly more severe than the civil penalties at issue, and Congress specifically provided that the maximum civil penalties may be imposed in addition to any criminal sanctions.
See
INA 274D(b), 275(b),
8 U.S.C. 1324d(b)
,
1325(b)
. In light of this statutory framework, all three
Bajakajian
factors weigh strongly against commenters' arguments that imposing the maximum statutory civil penalties violates the Excessive Fines Clause.
For these reasons, the Departments decline to amend the rule to limit the discretion of DHS immigration officers to impose the maximum statutory penalty amounts or require that they apply proportionality factors before doing so. Finally, regarding one commenter's concern about “ability to pay,” the Departments note that Congress has not required DHS to consider an alien's ability to pay in assessing these penalties, and the Supreme Court has not held this factor must be analyzed under the Excessive Fines Clause. Absent a legal requirement for DHS to consider an alien's ability to pay, DHS believes that adjusting a fine amount lower based on an alien's ability to pay would diminish the rule's deterrent effect.
Comment:
One commenter alleged that
8 CFR 281.1(g)
is inconsistent with
8 CFR 1240.26(l)
mandating that the Immigration Judge or BIA advise the alien of the civil penalty amount at the time of granting voluntary departure or a presumptive amount of $3,000 will be set. Another commenter noted that DHS has increased the penalty amounts in
8 CFR 280.53
for failure to depart violations incrementally over time from $500 per diem penalty in 2011, to a $998 per diem penalty in 2025, with DHS making incremental adjustments each year in between. The commenter claims that “the amount of fines that allegedly accrued on any given day should have been limited to the amount authorized by the regulation in effect on that day.” The commenter acknowledges that the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Improvements Act of 2015 allows DHS to adjust civil penalty amounts for inflation each year and to apply adjustments retroactively, but the commenter argues that “charging a lump sum without itemizing the exact amounts that DHS alleges to have accrued on any specific dates nor any explanation for why DHS believes fines accrued during this particular timeframe
(
printed page 65423)
deprives respondents of critical information necessary to contest such charges.” The commenter argues the IFR is defective because it does not require DHS to itemize penalties that “DHS alleges to have accrued on any specific dates nor [provides] any explanation for why DHS believes fines accrued during this particular timeframe.”
Response:
First, DHS notes that the IFR does not direct immigration officers to apply the penalty amounts listed in
8 CFR 280.53
. Rather,
8 CFR 281.1(g)
merely refers them to that provision so that they have access to information concerning the current inflation adjusted amount for each penalty. Immigration officers must determine how to apply those inflation adjusted rates in the context of each individual case, or whether to apply those rates at all, consistent with ICE and CBP guidance. Indeed, contrary to one commenter's claim, ICE guidance directs immigration officers to apply the penalty amount set by an Immigration Judge or the BIA or a $3,000 amount if no penalty amount is included in the voluntary departure order when assessing voluntary departure civil penalties. Accordingly, DHS is assessing voluntary departure penalties consistent with
8 CFR 1240.26(l)
.
Further, the Departments do not agree that DHS should itemize penalty amounts in penalty decisions imposing fines for willful failure to depart under INA 274D(a)(1),
8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1)
. The commenter's suggestion that “the amount of fines that allegedly accrued on any given day should [be] limited to the amount authorized by the regulation in effect on that day” is inconsistent with the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Improvements Act of 2015,
Public Law 114-74
(Nov. 2, 2015),
28 U.S.C. 2461 note
. The 2015 Amendments amended section 6 of the Inflation Adjustment Act to provide that “[a]ny increase under this Act in a civil monetary penalty shall apply only to civil monetary penalties, including those whose associated violation predated such increase, which are assessed after the date the increase takes effect.” Congress's specific reference to applying the adjustments to civil monetary penalties “whose associated violation predated” the effective date of the adjustment clearly contemplates that inflation adjustments after 2015 can be applied to violations occurring prior to the effective date of the increased civil penalty amounts—but only if the civil penalties are “assessed after the date the increase takes effect.” That is precisely how DHS applies the failure to depart penalties under INA 274D(a)(1),
8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1)
. Specifically, DHS applies the inflation adjusted amount that is in effect on the day that the penalty is “assessed”—
i.e.,
when DHS issues the penalty decision—regardless of the date of the removal order or the amount that was authorized on any one day in the period for which the penalty applies—
i.e.,
any day that the alien willfully failed to depart the United States after the final removal order.
To the extent that the commenter is concerned about DHS applying the current inflation adjusted rate to violations that occurred prior to the Inflation Adjustment Improvements Act of 2015, DHS notes that the commenter's concern is misplaced. As discussed above in this preamble, an alien is liable for a per diem penalty for each day he willfully remains in the United States after a final removal order regardless of when the removal order first became final. However, DHS is applying the failure to depart penalty for only five years back from the date of the penalty decision. Therefore, DHS would only assess the per diem penalty at the adjusted rate in place at the time of the penalty decision for a total of five years back from the date of the decision, even if the alien's removal order became final prior to 2015.
Regarding commenters' suggestion that DHS needs to itemize penalty decisions because the alien may not be liable for a per diem penalty for some portion of the period that the alien remained in the United States, ICE guidance directs immigration officers account for any periods after the removal order became administratively final during which the alien was authorized to remain in the United States (
e.g.,
a stay of removal, a later approved immigration benefit).
See
Section III.E.2 of this preamble. To the extent that an alien's individual circumstances excused an alien's willful or voluntary failure to depart for some period of time (
e.g.,
the alien was hospitalized or incarcerated or otherwise was unable to depart due to circumstances beyond the alien's control), the alien is best positioned to raise these issues on appeal. DHS cannot be expected to know about an alien's individual circumstances that prevented the alien from departing.
E. Other Matters Related to the IFR
1. Statute of Limitations
Comment:
Several commenters asserted that the rule does not explain how the federal statute of limitations applies to the civil penalties imposed under the IFR. One commenter suggested that the IFR's streamlined penalty procedures make it difficult for aliens to raise statute of limitations defenses, and the complexity of these defenses undermines the IFR's assumption about the readily verifiable and straightforward nature of these penalties. One commenter argued that the IFR does not require DHS to include information in the penalty decision about when the violation occurred which makes it difficult for aliens and their counsel to determine if DHS is correctly applying the statute of limitations. The commenter suggested that the 15-day appeal period, combined with the use of ordinary mail to serve decisions, could prevent aliens and their attorneys from investigating statute of limitations issues and raising the statute of limitations as a defense to these penalties. The commenter argued that eliminating BIA review is particularly problematic because DHS immigration officers do not have the legal expertise to resolve complex statute of limitations issues, and DHS does not have a mechanism to issue binding decisions on legal issues including those involving statutes of limitation.
Commenters offered their views regarding how the federal statute of limitations,
28 U.S.C. 2462
, applies to the penalties covered by this rule. For the failure to depart penalties, commenters claimed that the five-year statute of limitations begins to run the moment the voluntary departure period ends or when a removal order becomes final. They stated that DHS cannot impose fines for conduct that happened more than five years ago, such as remaining in the United States after a voluntary departure order period expired or after a removal order became final, particularly when there is no caselaw or statute recognizing a “continuing violation” theory for these penalties. For the unlawful entry penalties, commenters said that the limitations period begins to run once an alien is apprehended while in the process of entering or attempting to enter the United States.
Response:
The Departments disagree that the rule should be rescinded because it fails to include a statute of limitations provision. As an initial matter, the Departments emphasize the IFR's limited scope. The IFR changed only the procedures by which DHS issues and adjudicates certain civil monetary penalties and the manner in which aliens may contest them. The IFR did not change or alter the criteria for issuing these penalties, including how DHS interprets or applies the general federal statute of limitations for these penalties. Indeed, the Departments note that none of the Departments' other civil
(
printed page 65424)
monetary penalty regulations contain a statute of limitations provision, including
8 CFR 280
, which, prior to the IFR, governed the process for assessing the penalties covered by this rule. Accordingly, the Departments believe that it was reasonable and appropriate to limit the scope of the IFR consistent with the scope of the Departments' other civil penalty regulations, especially because of the IFR's narrow purpose of streamlining the process for the failure to depart and unlawful entry penalties. Therefore, the Departments decline to amend the rule to add a statute of limitations provision. For the same reasons, the Departments do not agree with commenters' suggestion that failure to include a statute of limitations provisions renders the rule arbitrary or capricious.
[
54
]
The Departments also disagree that the IFR's streamlined proceedings make it too difficult for aliens to assert a statute of limitations defense. Consistent with
8 CFR 281.1(c)(1)
, each penalty decision lists the date when the alien became subject to a final removal or a voluntary departure order, or when the alien was apprehended entering or attempting to enter the United States unlawfully.
See
DHS Form 281,
Notice of Violation and Order.
Therefore, to the extent that an alien believes that the violation occurred outside of the statute of limitations, the penalty decision itself contains the relevant information to dispute the penalty. Further, aliens should already possess any documents needed to dispute the information contained in the penalty decision. For example, an alien who disputes the date of a final removal or voluntary departure order can simply provide a copy of his removal or departure order or any documents showing that the alien's removal order or voluntary departure period was delayed because of an appeal or a stay of removal. The same is true for aliens subject to civil penalties for unlawful entry: the relevant charging document will list the date that DHS apprehended the alien entering or attempting to enter the United States. Commenters do not explain why aliens cannot retain these important documents, and the Departments will not assume otherwise. Accordingly, the Departments believe that the penalty decision contains sufficient information to allow an alien to raise a statute of limitations defense, and the IFR's 15-day appeal period provides ample time for aliens and their attorneys, if any, to gather evidence to compliment or prepare such a defense.
Similarly, the Departments do not agree with commenters' position that BIA review is needed because legal questions regarding the statute of limitations cannot adequately be resolved by DHS immigration officers on appeal.
ICE and CBP both apply the statute of limitations for these penalties in a straightforward way that refutes commenters' arguments that additional procedures, including BIA review, are needed due to the complexity of statute of limitations issues. First, ICE only assesses penalties under INA 240B(d),
8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)
, if an alien's voluntary departure period expired within five years of the order imposing the penalty.
[
55
]
CBP only assesses penalties under INA 275(b),
8 U.S.C. 1325(b)
, against aliens apprehended in the last five years while entering (or attempting to enter) the United States. The Departments note these approaches are consistent with commenters' interpretation of the general statute of limitations,
28 U.S.C. 2462
, applicable to these penalties. This application ensures consistency in the assessment of these penalties and provides clear direction to immigration officers on how far back to assess these penalties. Therefore, aliens do not need to prepare, and immigration officers do not need to decide, complicated statute of limitations defenses for these penalties in light of this approach. If an alien believes a penalty is contrary to this approach, the alien can appeal the civil penalty decision and provide a copy of the voluntary departure order indicating the date of the violation or, in the case of an unlawful entry penalty, the charging document listing the date and location of apprehension.
With respect to penalties under INA 274D(a)(1),
8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1)
, for willful failure to comply with a removal order, immigration officers can impose these penalties regardless of the date of the post-IIRIRA final removal order, but the per diem penalty amount should be assessed only for the five-year period preceding the date that the penalty is issued. Contrary to commenters' arguments, this is consistent with the plain language of the statute and caselaw interpreting similar penalty statutes for the purposes of determining the application of the general five-year statute of limitations under
28 U.S.C. 2462
. Section INA 274D(a)(1) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1)
, provides that “any alien subject to a final removal order who—willfully fails or refuses to depart from the United States . . . shall pay a civil penalty of not more than $500 to [DHS]
for each day the alien is in violation of this section.”
(emphasis added). When a civil penalty statute imposes a per diem penalty, the “continuing violation” doctrine applies, and the Government may assess the penalty even if the first violation occurred more than five years back.
See Interamericas Invs., Ltd.
v.
Bd. of Governors of the Fed. Rsrv. Sys.,
111 F.3d 376, 382 (5th Cir. 1997) (explaining that “[w]here the civil penalty provision at hand contemplates per diem penalties for violations, then continuing violations are cognizable under the general statute of limitations.”). Similarly, when a statute contemplates “repeated violations,” each new violation restarts the statute of limitations, but penalties can be assessed only for the violations occurring within that limitations period.
See Hamer
v.
City of Trinidad,
924 F.3d 1093, 1100 (10th Cir. 2019) (explaining the repeated violation doctrine). Under either doctrine, INA 274D(a)(1),
8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1)
, plainly indicates that Congress intended for an alien to be subject to a continuing or new penalty each day he remains in the United States in violation of a removal order regardless of when the final removal order was issued. And, as a matter of policy, ICE is applying the per diem penalty amount only for the five-year period preceding the date that the penalty is issued, consistent with the “repeated violations” doctrine.
Additionally, the Departments note that aliens can seek judicial review of final penalty decisions, after exhausting administrative remedies. See
5 U.S.C. 704
. Aliens can also raise any available defense, including statute of limitations defenses, in connection with any enforcement action that DOJ brings to collect these fines.
For these reasons, individually and collectively, the Departments disagree with commenters' view that the IFR should be rescinded or revised because it does not address how the statute of limitations applies to these penalties. For the same reasons, commenters' views about the complexity of statute of limitations issues do not undermine the Departments' determination that the process for these penalties can be
(
printed page 65425)
streamlined because of their straightforward nature.
2. Implementation Matters and Alternatives
Comment:
Implementation concerns and alternatives were also raised. One commenter expressed concern that the rule lacks adequate safeguards to prevent civil monetary penalties from being applied to aliens who currently hold, or are eligible for, lawful or protected status. The commenter stated that the rule provides no clear guidance on how DHS will avoid imposing fines on individuals who have been granted TPS, asylum, or relief under the VAWA or the T and U visa programs. These groups, the commenter explained, often have pending or approved immigration benefits that authorize their continued presence in the U.S. or excuse prior periods of unlawful presence. The commenter also noted that the IFR does not address how DHS will handle cases where aliens are beneficiaries of prosecutorial discretion, deferred action, or stays of removal. According to the commenter, the absence of explicit instructions combined with the IFR's streamlined process, risks imposing fines on aliens who are lawfully present under DHS policy or court order. The commenter stated it was critical to recognize that individuals with lawful or protected status are not obligated to depart.
Another commenter suggested that DHS should implement this rule as a limited pilot program before implementing it nationwide. The commenter said that a pilot-and-evaluate model would allow DHS to collect empirical evidence to assess the impact of civil fines on compliance, family stability, and financial impact of these penalties on aliens and their families. Using this empirical evidence to guide adjustments would ensure that civil fine enforcement evolves in response to real-world outcomes rather than theoretical assumptions.
Response:
As an initial matter, the Departments reiterate that the IFR did not change the categories of aliens subject to civil penalties or ICE's process for deciding whether an alien is subject to a civil penalty. Rather, the IFR was issued as a procedural rule and governs only the procedures that apply to these penalties. Therefore, DHS declines to modify the IFR in this final rule to clarify the category of aliens who are or are not subject to these penalties. Immigration officers confirm an alien's current status based on available records before assessing a civil fine by referencing multiple platforms and immigration databases. ICE's guidance to immigration officers provides that aliens with approved applications for lawful or protected status—such as TPS, Form I-730 Refugee/Asylee Relative benefits, VAWA protections, DACA, and T-visas and U-visas—should not be issued a civil fine. ICE also accounts for any deferrals of removal triggered by the
filing
of certain applications before USCIS, consistent with applicable statutes and regulations. When calculating a fine under INA 274D, immigration officers account for any periods after the removal order became administratively final during which the alien was authorized to remain in the United States due to,
e.g.,
a stay or deferral of removal. As part of the individual case review process, immigration officers review documents and supporting information across multiple immigration systems, including systems and platforms of entities such as USCIS, CBP, and DOJ/EOIR. DHS clarifies that lawful status cannot be conferred through an immigration officer's exercise of discretion and that the immigration officer cannot excuse an alien's obligation to depart pursuant to a final removal order. Rather, this measure reflects a determination not to pursue enforcement action at the time such discretion is exercised. As such, individuals who are beneficiaries of this measure remain subject to the underlying immigration laws and obligations, including potential civil penalties for violations.
Comment:
One commenter asserted that the rule misinterprets and overextends the scope of the civil monetary penalty authorized by INA 275(b),
8 U.S.C. 1325(b)
. The commenter stated that, by statute, these penalties apply only to aliens who are “apprehended while entering (or attempting to enter)” the United States, and not to those later encountered within the interior after an unlawful entry. The commenter objected to language in the IFR suggesting that DHS may rely on Form I-213 or other records of interior apprehension to establish liability under INA 275(b),
8 U.S.C. 1325(b)
. The commenter argued that such an interpretation is inconsistent with the plain language of the statute and could lead to the improper assessment of fines against aliens who were not apprehended at the time of entry. The commenter urged DHS to revise the rule to clarify that INA 275(b),
8 U.S.C. 1325(b)
penalties cannot be imposed on aliens apprehended after entry or encountered away from the border. The commenter also stated that the rule should require DHS to include specific evidentiary information in any order imposing this penalty such as the date of the attempted entry and the date and location of the arrest, to ensure that the penalty is applied only in circumstances consistent with statutory authority.
Response:
The Departments disagree with the commenter's characterization that the rule overextends the scope of penalties under INA 275(b)(1),
8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1)
. The rule does not expand the statutory application of 275(b),
8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1)
but rather provides procedural clarity for the assessment and collection of civil monetary penalties. The Departments interpret INA 275(b),
8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1)
to apply to aliens who are apprehended while entering or attempting to enter the United States. In practice, CBP will assess an INA 275(b),
8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1)
, penalty only when it apprehends an alien who has entered (or attempted to enter) the United States without inspection in the past seven days and who has not yet reached their destination, consistent with the statutory language and legislative intent of INA 275(b)(1),
8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1)
. As indicated above, the applicable statute of limitations runs five years from the date of apprehension.
Comment:
Commenters expressed concern that the rule does not address how civil monetary penalties would apply to aliens whose prior removal orders are later reopened, vacated, or otherwise resolved in a manner that permits adjustment of status or other immigration relief. They noted that DHS often agrees to join motions to reopen removal proceedings to allow individuals to pursue lawful status or relief. They stated that it was “critical to recognize that those with lawful status in the U.S. are under no obligation to depart,” and that “[t]heir continued presence in the U.S. is not a willful failure to depart, but a lawful consequence of the status conferred upon them. Another commenter urged DHS to clarify that civil penalties assessed must be rescinded when a removal order is reopened and will not be used as a basis to deny the alien's future attempts to regularize their immigration status. The commenter suggested, without much elaboration, that the IFR should clarify that DHS should not apply fines against aliens with
in absentia
removal orders.
Response:
ICE's guidance to immigration officers provides that aliens whose removal order is stayed should not be issued an INA 274D,
8 U.S.C. 1324d
, failure to depart penalty. ICE confers with DHS's Office of the Principal Legal Advisor before issuing a
(
printed page 65426)
failure to depart penalty in any case in which a Motion to Reopen (“MTR”) has been adjudicated for review of the reasons for reopening asserted by the alien and any circuit-specific case law that may affect the viability of the penalty. ICE confirms an alien's current case status before assessing or collecting any fine by referencing its internal systems. DHS disagrees that fines should not apply to any alien with an
in absentia
removal order but notes that, where an alien files an MTR and claims that the alien did not receive notice, their removal order is stayed. INA 240(b)(5)(C),
8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)(C)
. DHS emphasizes that the assessment of civil penalties is tied to the existence of a valid removal order and the alien's willful failure or refusal to depart as required by law. If a removal order is reopened, vacated, or dismissed, DHS will review the circumstances to determine whether the assessed civil penalties remain appropriate.
F. Statutory and Regulatory Requirements
1. Administrative Procedure Act
i. Procedural Rule Exception
Comment:
Several commenters generally asserted that Departments lacked authority to issue the IFR without first publishing a notice of proposed rulemaking and providing a pre-promulgation comment period in accordance with the APA,
5 U.S.C. 553
. First, commenters argued that the Departments cannot properly characterize the IFR as a procedural rule under
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)
. Commenters identified changes such as eliminating the NIF before issuing a final penalty, reducing the time to respond from 30 days to 15 days, allowing service by regular mail instead of certified or personal service, and moving appeals from the BIA to DHS. They asserted that these changes remove or weaken existing protections, implicate due process, change rights and obligations of affected individuals, and therefore render the rule substantive, which would require compliance with the APA's notice and comment requirements.
Response:
The Departments disagree. This rule was properly issued without prior notice and comment under
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)
, which exempts from those requirements “rules of agency organization, procedure, or practice.” Under the APA, notice and comment is required for substantive rules. By contrast, agency rules that prescribe agency organization, procedure, or practice are exempt from the notice-and-comment requirement.
See
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)
. The “critical feature of the procedural rule exception is that it covers agency actions that do not themselves alter the rights or interests of parties, although it may alter the manner in which the parties present themselves or their viewpoints to the agency.”
JEM Broadcasting Co., Inc.
v.
FCC,
22 F.3d 320, 328 (D.C. Cir. 1994) (cleaned up). In
JEM Broadcasting,
the D.C. Circuit upheld a rule that changed the timing and processing of applications, not the substantive criteria for deciding them, and treated the rule as procedural and exempt from notice and comment.
Id.
As explained in the IFR, this rule fits within that procedural rule exemption.
See
90 27454. This rule merely prescribes how the Departments conduct internal penalty proceedings and administrative reviews. The IFR does not alter the statutory obligations under INA 240B(d), 274D(a)(1), and 275(b);
8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)
,
1324d(a)
, and
1325(b)
, that authorize civil monetary penalties against aliens who fail to depart voluntarily, who willfully refuse to depart after a final order of removal, or who are apprehended while unlawfully entering or attempting to enter. It does not change the amount of these penalties or create new categories of violators or new statutory rights. The substantive legal liability remains as defined by statute.
Rather, the IFR merely revised the process by which the Departments impose these civil monetary penalties. For example, allowing DHS to serve penalty notices by regular mail (and no longer only by certified mail or personal service); shortening the period within which a respondent must contest the fine or exercise appeal rights from 30 to 15 days, moving the appeals process from the BIA to DHS, and other procedural streamlining merely alters the manner in which parties present themselves or their viewpoints to the Departments. Under the IFR, aliens continue to receive written notice of the penalty by regular mail and a meaningful opportunity to present a written response with supporting evidence before any final determination is made. Likewise, replacing BIA review with review by a DHS supervisory official who was not involved in the initial decision preserves neutral, independent oversight while streamlining the adjudication process. Accordingly, this rule is properly classified as a procedural rule and exempt from prior notice and comment procedures under the APA.
Moreover, though not required to do so, the Departments nonetheless solicited post-promulgation comments following publication of the IFR on June 27, 2025, and accepted comments through July 28, 2025. The Departments have carefully reviewed and considered all comment submissions received at the docket in developing this final rule.
ii. Foreign Affairs Exemption
Comment:
Commenters also asserted that the Departments' reliance on the foreign affairs exemption under
5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1)
is legally unsupported. They argued that the rule's subject matter—imposing fines on aliens—is purely domestic enforcement activity that neither regulates nor directly impacts foreign affairs. Additionally, these commenters challenged the Departments' assertion that the rule supports U.S. foreign policy negotiations as vague, too attenuated, and overbroad. One commenter said that under the Departments' reasoning, nearly any domestic policy that “comes up in negotiations with a foreign country” could be exempt from notice and comment. The other commenter claimed that the Departments invoked the exception in bad faith, arguing that traditional examples of rules meeting the foreign affairs exemption involve rules relating to international trade and visa issuance.
One commenter suggested that the Departments did not demonstrate an immediate foreign affairs need to bypass the APA's notice and comment and delayed-effective-date requirements, noting that the fines covered by the IFR have been codified in law for years but only rarely used by DHS. The commenter also took issue with the Departments' assertion that immediate action is needed to address the shared problem of irregular migration to the southern border. The commenter asserted that the IFR will not have an appreciable impact on border operations because the Administration has already “shutdown asylum process at the Southern border” and the IFR is primarily targeted at aliens who are already illegally present within the United States.
Response:
The IFR is excepted from the APA's notice-and-comment and delayed-effective-date requirements because it involves a “foreign affairs function of the United States.”
5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1)
. As an initial matter, contrary to one commenter's claim, the foreign affairs exception is not limited to rules relating to international trade and visa issuance. The Supreme Court has never determined what constitutes a “foreign affairs function of the United States.” Lower federal courts have held that this exception applies when the rule in question is “clearly and directly
(
printed page 65427)
involve[d]” in “a foreign affairs function.”
E.B.
v.
U.S. Dep't of State,
583 F. Supp. 3d 58, 63 (D.D.C. 2022) (cleaned up). In addition, although the text of the APA does not require an agency invoking this exception to show that such procedures may result in “definitely undesirable international consequences,” some courts have required such a showing.
See, e.g., Rajah
v.
Mukasey,
544 F.3d 427, 437 (2d Cir. 2008) (quotation marks omitted). The IFR satisfies both standards. Even though the Departments issued an IFR, an opportunity for public comment after issuing the IFR was provided and this final rule responds to those comments.
See Little Sisters of the Poor Saints Peter and Paul Home,
591 U.S. 657, 683-84 (2020).
The Departments disagree with commenters' assertions that the IFR involves only domestic immigration enforcement and thus does not directly impact foreign affairs. First, as discussed in the IFR, the rule is directly and clearly connected to a foreign affairs function of the United States because it supports this Administration's efforts to address the shared international challenge of border security and illegal migration. The Secretary of State has made clear that “securing America's borders and protecting its citizens from external threats is the first priority foreign affairs function of the United States,” In this regard, the United States continues to work closely with foreign partner countries to address migration in the Western Hemisphere region to secure America's borders and protect its citizens, and this rule is clearly and directly related to, and responsive to, the United States efforts in this regard. Specifically, the IFR and this rule are intended to allow DHS to streamline and maximize its use of civil penalties against aliens who are apprehended entering or enter unlawfully at the southern border. DHS believes that this additional tool will allow it to discourage, prepare for, and respond to unlawful migration by increasing the consequences on aliens who make the dangerous journey to the United States and enter unlawfully. Therefore, measures like the IFR advance the United States' foreign policy objectives by demonstrating to partner countries that the United States is serious about the shared problem of irregular migration and border security and that the Administration is doing its part to address these challenges by using all available tools even if they originate from U.S. law. Further, the Departments disagree with one commenter's suggestion that the Departments invoked the exemption in “bad faith.” To the contrary, the Departments have relied on the foreign affairs exception, under several Administrations, when issuing rules designed to help address the shared international challenge of migration to the United States southern border.

The Departments acknowledge that this rule also applies to aliens in the interior of the United States who have violated the immigration laws by failing to depart after a removal or voluntary departure. The Departments disagree, however, that the problem that the IFR seeks to address is purely a domestic one. Rather, as explained in the IFR, the United States' ability to address the challenge of aliens remaining in the country unlawfully after removal and departure orders depends in part on the willingness of other nations to accept the return and repatriation of their citizens from the United States. Contrary to commenters' claims, the Departments have provided concrete examples of the United States' foreign negotiations and efforts aimed at encouraging other countries to support the return of their citizens, including those with outstanding removal and voluntary departure orders.
See
90 FR 27455
. These efforts include encouraging other countries to promptly issue travels documents that allow their residents to return home, and more broadly to cooperate with DHS's efforts to successfully implement Presidential Proclamation 10935,
Establishing Project Homecoming,
90 FR 20357
(May 9, 2025), which provides aliens with a process to voluntarily depart the United States and return to their home countries.
See
90 FR 27455-56
. All of these efforts indicate that the removal and voluntary return of aliens with no legal right to remain in the United States is a critical foreign policy objective of the United States. For these foreign policy efforts to continue to succeed, DHS must continue to demonstrate its own commitment to this foreign policy objective, including by encouraging aliens to take advantage of these expanded opportunities that the United States Government has secured through international efforts. The IFR directly and clearly serves this purpose by incentivizing aliens to comply with departure obligations, including through these expanded departure options, and by imposing consequences on those who fail to depart.
In addition to the IFR's clear and direct involvement in foreign affairs, the Departments believed that issuing the rule after notice and comment, and with a delayed effective date, could have led to definitely undesirable international consequences. As discussed in the IFR, these consequences include negative impacts to border security, which is a shared regional problem, and DHS's inability to capitalize on the momentum that the United States Government had achieved in encouraging countries to support the return of their citizens, including those with outstanding removal and departure orders. In this regard, the Departments disagree with commenters that claimed that the Departments did not demonstrate an immediate need for the IFR because this Administration's asylum policies at the southern border had already reduced irregular border encounters. The IFR acknowledged that encounters between POEs at the southern border had decreased significantly from their historic highs under the prior Administration.

27455-56

Further, the Departments also disagree with the claim that the Departments did not demonstrate an immediate need to implement the rule under the foreign affairs exception because these civil monetary penalties have been authorized for many years but rarely used, and DHS has mainly applied them to aliens in the interior. As an initial matter, regardless of the past administrations' policies, this Administration has made clear that that the rapid return of illegal aliens to their home countries is a critical foreign policy objective of the United States and
(
printed page 65428)
it has conducted its recent foreign policy efforts consistent with this objective. In the months prior to issuing this IFR, the Administration had been engaged in discussions with several countries aimed at ensuring that those countries promptly issue travels documents to facilitate the return of their nationals. Moreover, in the weeks prior to issuing the IFR, the President directed the Secretary of State and the Secretary of Homeland to take all appropriate “actions to enable the rapid departure of illegal aliens from the United States”

In light of these efforts, the Departments explained that by issuing the IFR immediately DHS would be able to capitalize on these recent foreign policy efforts by encouraging aliens, through the use of civil penalties, to take advantage of these expanded opportunities achieved through international discussions and cooperation, to depart the United States. The Departments also explained that the IFR would allow the U.S. Government to build on this foreign policy momentum by demonstrating to other countries that it is committed to using all necessary tools to facilitate the rapid departure of illegal aliens and that other nations should support the Administration's continued efforts to achieve this objective. Quite simply, if the United States is unable to demonstrate, through measures like the IFR, that it is committed to taking quick and robust action to remove aliens and encourage them to depart the United States voluntarily, which depends in large part on international cooperation, countries may be less inclined to engage with the United States on these ongoing efforts in the future.
