iii. Good Cause
Commenters also argued that the Departments lacked good cause to make the IFR effective immediately upon publication, and one commenter asserted that the Departments improperly invoked the good cause exception under
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
to issue and immediately implement the IFR without prior notice and comment. Commenters argued that the IFR does not respond to sudden or unforeseeable emergency, and any need for the IFR was an emergency of DHS's own making—
i.e.,
DHS's own decision to restart issuing civil penalty program despite previously ending that program in 2021 after determining that civil penalties were ineffective and legally vulnerable. Commenters also argued that the public burden imposed by immediate implementation, particularly on immigrant communities and service providers far outweighs any government benefit from accelerating enforcement.
Response:
As an initial matter, the Departments note that the IFR did not invoke good cause under
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
to dispense with notice and comment. Rather, the Departments issued the IFR under the procedural rule exception under
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)
and the foreign affairs exception under
5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1)
and invoked good cause under
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
solely to make the rule effective upon publication. Section 553(d)(3) permits an agency to waive the standard 30-day delayed-effective-date requirement when it finds good cause for the rule to take immediate effect, balancing the agency's need for immediate implementation against affected persons' need for a reasonable amount of time to prepare for the effective date of its ruling. As explained in the IFR and reaffirmed here, the Departments determined that the ordinary reason for delay in a rule's effective date, to give members of the regulated community time to prepare and adjust their behavior, does not apply here because the IFR does not affect any person's substantive rights. Rather, it merely modifies the manner in which DHS issues and adjudicates civil monetary penalties and how an alien may contest such penalties. Moreover, the Departments found that the benefits of immediate implementation, ensuring uniformity, and administrative efficiency in the imposition and collection of civil monetary penalties, outweighed any need for affected parties to prepare for the effective date and adjust their behavior accordingly as this rule does not affect substantive right. Thus, the Departments conclude that invocation of the good cause under 553(d)(3) was lawful and appropriate.
iv. Comment Period Duration
Comment:
Commenters argued that the 30-day post-promulgation comment window was inadequate given the breadth and complexity of the rule, which alters established practices related to assessing and collecting civil penalties under the three INA provisions. Commenters also cited
Executive Order 12866
, Regulatory Planning and Review,
58 FR 51735
,
51740
, directing agencies to “afford the public a meaningful opportunity to comment on any proposed regulation, which in most cases should include a comment period of not less than 60 days” and argued that the abbreviated timeframe prevented comprehensive analysis of the rule's many substantive changes.
Response:
As an initial matter, commenters did not suggest or indicate what additional issues the comment period precluded them from addressing; to the contrary, the comments received reflect both a breadth and a level of detail which suggests that the period was more than sufficient.
Cf. City of Waukesha
v.
EPA,
320 F.3d 228, 246 (D.C. Cir. 2003) (“In [showing prejudice] in the context of a violation of notice-and-comment requirements, petitioners may be required to demonstrate that, had proper notice been provided, they would have submitted additional, different comments that could have invalidated the rationale for the revised rule.”).
The APA does not prescribe any specific minimum duration for public comment periods. While agencies often provide a 30-day period for proposed rules, and sometimes longer for complex or economically significant rulemakings, the statute simply requires that agencies generally afford interested parties an opportunity to participate through submission of written data, views, or arguments.
Although not required to do so, the Departments nonetheless provided a 30-day comment period following publication of the IFR on June 27, 2025, accepting comments through July 28, 2025. That period afforded the public a meaningful opportunity to review the IFR and provide input. Indeed, federal courts have presumed 30 days to be a reasonable comment period length.
See Nat'l Lifeline Ass'n
v.
Fed. Commc'ns Comm'n,
921 F.3d 1102, 1117 (D.C. Cir. 2019). Here, the detailed public comments the Departments received are evidence that the 30-day period was sufficient for the public to meaningfully review and provide informed comments.
See, e.g., Little Sisters of the Poor Saints Peter and Paul Home,
140 S. Ct. at 2385 (“The object [of notice and comment], in short, is one of fair notice.”) (citation omitted).
The Departments received and carefully considered all timely submissions. Providing a 30-day
(
printed page 65429)
window for comments on a rule of limited procedural scope is consistent with longstanding administrative practice and the guidance reflected in Executive Orders 12866 and 13563, which encourage agencies to provide meaningful participation. The Departments' post-promulgation comment process thus satisfied the APA's requirements and furthered its purposes of transparency and public involvement, even though prior notice and comment were not legally required under
5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1)
and
(b)(A)
.
2.
E.O. 12866
Analysis
Comment:
One commenter asserted that the IFR would impose substantial new economic burdens on affected aliens and their households, with potentially significant aggregate impacts. They contended that the IFR's increased and accelerated civil monetary penalties, particularly daily fines approaching $1,000 for failure to depart following a final order of removal, could result in liabilities large enough to cause long-term financial hardship, including wage garnishment, asset seizure, and bankruptcy. They further stated that these costs would likely fall disproportionately on low-income individuals and mixed-status families, potentially creating spillover effects for U.S. citizen spouses and children and exacerbating economic insecurity in immigrant communities. The commenter also argued that the IFR may generate billions of dollars in annual penalties, and that DHS's retention of penalty revenues could create institutional incentives to maximize fine issuance. They maintained that the IFR was implemented without sufficient economic analysis or public input and recommend alternatives such as means-based penalties, hardship waivers, or installment plans, independent review mechanisms, and pilot implementation to evaluate real world economic effects before nationwide implementation.
Response:
The Departments do not agree that this rule needs additional economic analysis or that it was adopted without considering financial impacts. As previously discussed, the rule does not create any new fines, change who can be fined, or increase the dollar amounts Congress has already set; it only changes the internal process DHS uses to issue and review those fines. Any financial hardship, including possible collection actions, comes from the underlying law and from an alien's choice to remain in the United States after being ordered to leave, not from these procedural updates. DHS's goal is to encourage people to follow removal and departure orders and to deter unlawful entry, not to generate revenue, and DHS will cancel most failure to depart fines when eligible aliens use the CBP Home app to leave the country. OMB has reviewed the rule as significant under
Executive Order 12866
. DHS has weighed the limited added economic effects of these process changes against their enforcement benefits, and the Departments provided a 30-day comment period and considered economic and other feedback before finalizing the rule.
IV. Severability
The changes made by the IFR, as amended by this final rule, impact provisions that are not necessarily interrelated and can function independent of one another. As such, the Departments believe that most of the provisions of this final rule can function sensibly and independently of other provisions. Therefore, in the event that any provisions in this rule are invalidated by a reviewing court, the Departments intend the remaining provisions to remain in effect to the fullest extent possible.

D. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (“RFA”),
5 U.S.C. 601-612
, as amended, requires federal agencies to consider the potential impact of regulations on small entities during rulemaking. A regulatory flexibility analysis is not required when a rule is exempt from notice-and-comment rulemaking. This final rule finalizes an IFR that was exempt from the notice-and-comment rulemaking. Therefore, a regulatory flexibility analysis is not required.
However, even assuming that this rule is not exempt from notice-and-comment procedures and therefore not exempt from the requirements of the RFA, the Departments have reviewed this rule in accordance with the RFA. The Secretary of Homeland Security and the Acting Director of EOIR certify that this rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
See
5 U.S.C. 605(b)
.
First, aliens are not “small entit[ies]” as defined by the RFA.

5 U.S.C. 601(3)-(5)
).
Second, to the extent that legal service organizations qualify as “small entities,” any economic effects of this rule on such organizations would not be significant under the RFA. The rule will not economically impact representatives of aliens in contesting these penalties. It does not limit the fees they may charge or the number of cases a representative may ethically accept under the rules of professional responsibility. For example, the IFR's changes to the procedures for contesting a civil penalty do not change the overall requirement that aliens must respond to a civil penalty notice to challenge the penalty; rather the IFR simply changed the procedures for how that appeal is filed, in what time frame, and which U.S. Government officials are responsible for adjudicating the appeal. The IFR's changes to shorten the appeal period required legal service providers to adjust to these new timelines. The Departments expect, however, that legal service organizations have quickly acclimated to this change without substantial disruption. Indeed, the IFR was in effect for over a year, and the appeal rate increased under the IFR compared to the pre-IFR process for these civil penalties under
8 CFR part 280
. Thus, any costs incurred in adapting to the IFR's timelines were not significant under the RFA. And the one change in this final rule to the IFR's provisions is not expected to increase such costs significantly (if at all) given that it discretely applies to demonstrated mail delays.

v.
FERC,

Cir. 1985) (concluding “an agency may properly certify that no regulatory flexibility analysis is necessary when it determines that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities that are subject to the requirements of the rule” and stating that legislative history of the RFA “gives rise to an inference that Congress did not intend to require that every agency consider every indirect effect that any regulation might have on small businesses in any stratum of the national economy”).

(

DHS and its components analyze final actions to determine whether the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (“NEPA”),
42 U.S.C. 4321
et seq.,
applies to them and, if so, what degree of analysis is required. DHS Directive 023-01 Rev. 01

NEPA allows Federal agencies to establish categories of actions (“categorical exclusions”) that experience has shown do not, individually or cumulatively, have a significant effect on the human environment and, therefore, do not require an environmental assessment (“EA”) or environmental impact statement (“EIS”). An agency is not required to prepare an EA or EIS for a proposed action “if the proposed agency action is excluded pursuant to one of the agency's categorical exclusions.”
42 U.S.C. 4336(a)(2)
. The Instruction Manual, Appendix A, lists the DHS Categorical Exclusions. For an action to be categorically excluded under DHS's Instruction Manual, the action must satisfy each of the following three conditions: (1) the entire action clearly fits within one or more of the categorical exclusions; (2) the action is not a piece of a larger action; and (3) no extraordinary circumstances exist that create the potential for a significant environmental effect.
This final rule is categorically excluded from DHS's NEPA implementing procedures, because it satisfies all three relevant conditions. First, the Departments have determined that the IFR fits clearly within categorical exclusions A3(a) of DHS's Instruction Manual, Appendix A, for the promulgation of rules of a “strictly administrative or procedural nature.” This final rule merely changes the procedures that DHS and DOJ apply when assessing civil monetary penalties authorized under certain sections of the INA. This change in procedures does not result in a change in their environmental effect. Second, this final rule is a standalone rule and is not part of any larger action. Third, the Departments are not aware of any extraordinary circumstances that would cause a significant environmental impact. Therefore, this final rule is categorically excluded, and no further NEPA analysis or documentation is required.

If ICE determines that the appeal was filed after the deadline due to mail delay beyond the alien's control, ICE will accept the appeal as timely filed and consider it on the merits. In making this determination, ICE will consider the mailing and actual receipt dates, the cause and length of the delay, and the alien's good faith efforts in pursuing the appeal after receipt. ICE's determination will be case by case considering all evidence presented with the appeal.

AGENCY:
Postal Regulatory Commission.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Commission is noticing a recent Postal Service filing for the Commission's consideration concerning a negotiated service agreement. This notice informs the public of the filing, invites public comment, and takes other administrative steps.
ADDRESSES:
Submit comments electronically via the Commission's Filing Online system at
https://www.prc.gov
.
Those who cannot submit comments electronically should contact the person identified in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section by telephone for advice on filing alternatives.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
David A. Trissell, General Counsel, at 202-789-6820.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Table of Contents
I. Introduction
II. Public Proceeding(s)
III. Summary Proceeding(s)
I. Introduction
Pursuant to
39 CFR 3041.405
, the Commission gives notice that the Postal Service filed request(s) for the Commission to consider matters related to Competitive negotiated service agreement(s). The request(s) may propose the addition of a negotiated service agreement from the Competitive product list or the modification of an existing product currently appearing on the Competitive product list.
The public portions of the Postal Service's request(s) can be accessed via the Commission's website (
http://www.prc.gov
). Non-public portions of the Postal Service's request(s), if any, can be accessed through compliance with the requirements of
39 CFR 3011.301
.
[
1
]
Section II identifies the docket number(s) associated with each Postal Service request, if any, that will be reviewed in a public proceeding as defined by
39 CFR 3010.101(p)
, the title of each such request, the request's acceptance date, and the authority cited by the Postal Service for each request. For each such request, the Commission appoints an officer of the Commission to represent the interests of the general public in the proceeding, pursuant to
39 U.S.C. 505
and
39 CFR 3000.114
(Public Representative). The Public Representative does not represent any individual person, entity or particular point of view, and, when Commission attorneys are appointed, no attorney-client relationship is established. Section II also establishes comment deadline(s) pertaining to each such request.
The Commission invites comments on whether the Postal Service's request(s) identified in Section II, if any, are consistent with the policies of title 39. Applicable statutory and regulatory requirements include
39 U.S.C. 3632
,
39 U.S.C. 3633
,
39 U.S.C. 3642
,
39 CFR part 3035
, and
39 CFR part 3041
. Comment deadline(s) for each such request, if any, appear in Section II.
Section III identifies the docket number(s) associated with each Postal Service request, if any, to add a standardized distinct product to the Competitive product list or to amend a standardized distinct product, the title of each such request, the request's acceptance date, and the authority cited by the Postal Service for each request. Standardized distinct products are negotiated service agreements that are variations of one or more Competitive products, and for which financial models, minimum rates, and classification criteria have undergone advance Commission review.
See
39 CFR 3041.110(n)
;
39 CFR 3041.205(a)
. Such requests are reviewed in summary proceedings pursuant to
39 CFR 3041.325(c)(2)
and
39 CFR 3041.505(f)(1)
. Pursuant to
39 CFR 3041.405(c)-(d)
, the Commission does not appoint a Public Representative or request public comment in proceedings to review such requests.
II. Public Proceeding(s)
None.
See
Section III for summary proceedings.

Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation
29 CFR Part 4044
AGENCY:
Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This final rule amends the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation's regulation on Allocation of Assets in Single-Employer Plans to prescribe the spreads component of the interest assumption under the asset allocation regulation for plans with valuation dates of October 31, 2026-January 30, 2027. These interest assumptions are used for valuing benefits under terminating single-employer plans and for other purposes.
DATES:
Effective October 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jose Singer-Freeman (
singer-freeman.jose@pbgc.gov
), Attorney, Legislative and Regulatory Division, Office of the General Counsel, Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, 445 12th Street SW, Washington, DC 20024-2101, 202-229-5432. If you are deaf or hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
PBGC's regulation on Allocation of Assets in Single-Employer Plans (
29 CFR part 4044
) prescribes actuarial assumptions—including an interest assumption—for valuing benefits under terminating single-employer plans covered by title IV of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA). The interest assumption is also posted on PBGC's website (
www.pbgc.gov
).
PBGC uses the interest assumption in § 4044.54 to determine the present value of annuities in an involuntary or distress termination of a single-employer plan under the asset allocation regulation. The assumptions in part 4044 of PBGC's regulations are also used in other situations where it is appropriate for liabilities to align with private sector group annuity prices. For example, PBGC's regulations on Notice, Collection, and Redetermination of Withdrawal Liability (
29 CFR part 4219
) and Duties of Plan Sponsor Following Mass Withdrawal (
29 CFR part 4281
) provide that these assumptions are used to value liabilities for purposes of determining withdrawn employers' reallocation liability in the event of a mass withdrawal from a multiemployer
(
printed page 65111)
plan. Multiemployer plans that receive special financial assistance under the regulation on Special Financial Assistance by PBGC (
29 CFR part 4262
) must, as a condition of receiving special financial assistance, use the interest assumption to determine withdrawal liability for a prescribed period. Additionally, plan sponsors are required to use some, or all of these assumptions for specified purposes (
e.g.,
reporting benefit liabilities in filings required under PBGC's regulation on Annual Financial and Actuarial Information Reporting (
29 CFR part 4010
) or determining certain amounts to transfer to PBGC's Missing Participants Program on behalf of a missing participant of a terminating defined benefit plan under PBGC's regulation on Missing Participants (
29 CFR part 4050
)) and may use them for other purposes (
e.g.,
to ensure that plan spinoffs comply with section 414(l) of the Internal Revenue Code).
Part 4044 of PBGC's regulations provides that the interest assumption for part 4044 purposes is a yield curve (
i.e.,
the “4044 yield curve”) that is based on a blend of two publicly available bond yield curves that is adjusted to the extent necessary so that the resulting liabilities align with group annuity prices. The adjustments are referred to as “spreads.” PBGC determines and publishes spreads quarterly based on survey data on pricing of private-sector group annuities. PBGC posts the 4044 yield curve on its website at
www.pbgc.gov
each month shortly after its underlying data becomes available. In addition, practitioners are able to determine the 4044 yield curve as of the end of any month using the publicly available bond yield curves and the spreads specified in the regulation.
This rule amends the regulation to specify the spreads used to determine the 4044 yield curve as of the last days of October, November, and December of 2026 (
i.e.,
the “fourth quarter 2026 spreads”). Due to space constraints, table 1 to paragraph (e) shows spreads only for the most recent four quarters. Historical spreads are available on
www.pbgc.gov
,
along with more recent spreads.
Need for Immediate Guidance
PBGC has determined that notice of, and public comment on, this rule are impracticable, unnecessary, and contrary to the public interest. PBGC routinely updates the spreads component of the interest assumption in the asset allocation regulation so that the 4044 yield curve may be determined as soon as the underlying bond yield curves become available. These amendments are merely technical; they ensure that use of PBGC's interest assumption continues to yield liabilities in line with group annuity prices. The New England Fishery Management Council (Council) is scheduling a public hybrid meeting of its Scallop Joint Committee and Advisory Panel to consider actions affecting New England fisheries in the exclusive economic zone (EEZ). SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Agenda
The Scallop Committee and Advisory Panel will meet to discuss 2027 & 2028 (Default) Specifications and provide input on the range of potential access area and days-at-sea allocations for the 2027 and 2028 fishing years. This action will set specifications including Acceptable Biological Catch/Annual Catch Limits, days-at-sea, access area allocations, total allowable landings for the Northern Gulf of Maine management area, targets for General Category incidental catch, General Category access area trips, and set-asides for the observer and research programs for fishing year 2027 and default specifications for fishing year 2028. They will also discuss the draft 2027 Priorities and provide feedback for Council consideration at the December 2026 Council meeting. Other business will be discussed, if necessary.
Although non-emergency issues not contained on the agenda may come before this Council for discussion, those issues may not be the subject of formal action during this meeting. Council action will be restricted to those issues specifically listed in this notice and any issues arising after publication of this notice that require emergency action under section 305(c) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, provided the public has been notified of the Council's intent to take final action to address the emergency. 16 U.S.C. 1852
, a copy of the recording is available upon request.

The Gulf, South Atlantic, and Caribbean Fishery
(

Management Councils, in conjunction with the NMFS and the Atlantic and Gulf States Marine Fisheries Commissions have implemented the SEDAR process. SEDAR is a participatory process for developing, evaluating and reviewing information used for fisheries management advice. This multi-step process for determining the status of fish stocks in the Southeast Region may include (1) a data stage, (2) an assessment stage, and (3) a review stage. Each stage produces a report summarizing decisions made during that stage. A final stock assessment report is produced at the end of a SEDAR process documenting data sets used, model configurations, and the opinions from the independent peer review. Participants for SEDAR projects are appointed by the Gulf, South Atlantic, and Caribbean Fishery Management Councils and National Marine Fisheries Service Southeast Regional Office, Highly Migratory Species Management Division, and Southeast Fisheries Science Center. Participants may include data collectors and database managers; stock assessment scientists, biologists, and researchers; constituency representatives including fishermen, environmentalists, and non-governmental organizations; International experts; and staff of Councils, Commissions, and State and Federal agencies.

The New England Fishery Management Council (Council) is holding a hybrid public meeting of its Scientific and Statistical Committee (SSC) to consider actions affecting New England fisheries in the exclusive economic zone (EEZ). SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The FAA issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to amend
14 CFR part 39
by adding an AD that would apply to certain Bombardier, Inc., Model BD-700-2A12 airplanes. The NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
on March 4, 2026 (
91 FR 10522
). The NPRM was prompted by Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49, dated October 1, 2025 (Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49) (also referred to as the MCAI), issued by Transport Canada, which is the aviation authority for Canada. The MCAI states there have been reports of low clearance in the right wing between the fuel line flexible coupling and the harness support bracket clip-nut located in bay 3, between the fuel line flexible coupling and hydraulic system 3 line located in bay 18, and between the hydraulic system 3 lines and fuel vent tube located in bay 20. These low clearance conditions, if not addressed, may result in an ignition source developing in the fuel tank in the event of a lightning strike.
In the NPRM, the FAA proposed to require rectifying the low clearance condition between the fuel line flexible coupling and the harness support bracket clip-nut, rectifying the low clearance condition between the fuel line flexible coupling and the hydraulic system, and doing an inspection for adequate clearance between the hydraulic system and the fuel vent tube and applicable on-conditions actions, as specified in Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-2289.
Discussion of Final Airworthiness Directive
Comments
The FAA received comments from five individuals who supported the NPRM without change.
The FAA received additional comments from two other individuals. The following presents the comments received on the NPRM and the FAA's response to each comment.
Request To Clarify Why an Emergency AD Was Not Issued
Commenter #1 requested that the FAA clarify its determination that the unsafe condition does not meet the criteria for an emergency AD, given the potential interaction between fuel transfer systems, vibration-induced wear, and adjacent hydraulic and electrical components within the affected wing structure. Additionally, the commenter asked (1) if the low clearance condition could contribute to fuel starvation scenarios under certain operational conditions; (2) if interim inspections, operational limitations, or manufacturer service bulletins should be implemented while the rulemaking process proceeds; (3) if a shortened compliance period or immediate corrective action would better mitigate the identified risk; (4) if additional technical analysis regarding system interaction between fuel, hydraulic, and electrical components should be included in the final rulemaking record.
The FAA issues an emergency AD when an unsafe condition exists that requires immediate adoption, and the risk to the flying public justifies forgoing notice and comment prior to adopting an emergency AD. In developing this rulemaking, the FAA evaluated the compliance times and all the available information provided by Transport Canada and the manufacturer. The FAA has no additional data that would support reducing the compliance time below that specified in Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49, or issuing an emergency AD to address the unsafe condition.
Further, the FAA provides the following additional information:
(1) The low clearance condition would not contribute to fuel starvation. There is no potential fouling condition of the fuel vent line and, therefore, no effect on the fuel system operation.
(2) The corrective actions and compliance times in Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49 are adequate for addressing the unsafe condition. Therefore, no interim actions, operational limitations, or additional service bulletins need to be mandated. However, operators are permitted to accomplish the requirements of this AD at an earlier time, or may voluntarily adopt service information, operational limitations, or additional inspections to address the unsafe condition.
(3) Neither a shorter compliance time nor immediate corrective action are necessary to address the unsafe condition. Based on the risk evaluation conducted by the manufacturer, the corrective actions and compliance times in Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49 are sufficient for mitigating the identified risk.
(4) There is no system failure associated with this unsafe condition; therefore, no technical analysis regarding system interaction between the fuel, hydraulic, and electrical components needs to be included in the rulemaking docket.
(
printed page 65102)
Request To Reopen the Comment Period or Revise the Proposed AD
Commenter #2 requested that the FAA either (1) re-open the comment period and add to the AD docket all materials incorporated by reference and the basis for the cost assumptions and warranty offset, or (2) revise the proposed AD to add the operative standard and un-offset cost estimate. The commenter stated that the FAA did not provide adequate information for the public to meaningfully evaluate and comment on the proposed requirements and costs of compliance. The commenter further stated if the FAA cannot provide these elements, the proposed AD cannot be evaluated for comment or supported as a matter of reasoned decision-making and should be withdrawn and reissued with a complete record.
The FAA disagrees with the requests. The FAA provides summaries and access details in the preamble and regulatory text, makes materials available for inspection at FAA and National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) offices, offers publisher contact information, and obtains formal incorporation by reference (IBR) approval from the Office of the Federal Register. These efforts are intended to ensure that all IBR materials meet the “reasonably available” standard required by
1 CFR part 51
. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Further, the FAA notes that this AD incorporates by reference Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49, not the manufacturer service information referenced in Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49 (
i.e.,
non-IBR material). The FAA posted Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49 to the AD docket when the NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
. The non-IBR material may only be posted before the final rule's publication if it is already publicly available or if there is written consent from the owner of that material. Additionally, affected operators that must comply with the AD may obtain the non-IBR material directly from the manufacturer during the comment period through their normal course of business.
Further, the FAA based the estimated Costs of Compliance with this AD on information provided by the manufacturer. The number of estimated work hours and warranty terms are included in the manufacturer service bulletin, which is posted to the rulemaking docket upon publication of the final rule. The estimated parts cost was provided by the manufacturer. The FAA notes that no comments were received regarding the IBR material or estimated costs from any of the affected operators.
Conclusion
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA reviewed the relevant data, considered any comments received, and determined that air safety requires adopting this AD as proposed. Accordingly, the FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. Except for minor editorial changes, this AD is adopted as proposed in the NPRM. None of the changes will increase the economic burden on any operator.

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The FAA issued an NPRM that proposed to amend
14 CFR part 39
by adding an AD that would apply to certain The Boeing Company Model 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10 airplanes. The NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
on February 26, 2025 (
90 FR 10703
). The NPRM was prompted by reports that VHF radio frequencies transfer between the active and standby windows of the TCP without flightcrew input. The uncommanded frequency changes could result in missed communications between the flightcrew and Air Traffic Control. The NPRM proposed to require updating the TCP OPS and performing a software configuration check.
The proposed actions were intended to address uncommanded frequency changes, which could result in missed communications such as amended clearances and critical instructions for changes to flight path and consequent loss of safe separation between aircraft, collision, or runway incursion.
Actions Since the NPRM Was Issued
Since issuance of the NPRM, the FAA determined that the update to the TCP OPS specified in the NPRM does not correct the unsafe condition. The manufacturer informed the FAA that, based on fleet reports, it has concluded that the OPS version specified in the NPRM does not correct the unsafe condition. Also, multiple commenters reported concerns with the reliability of the software update or experienced service difficulties after accomplishing the service information. As a result, Boeing is conducting further analysis to determine the root cause of the new reports, and the FAA may consider other rulemaking when an adequate solution is developed to address the unsafe condition.
Withdrawal of the NPRM constitutes only such action and does not preclude the FAA from further rulemaking on this issue, nor does it commit the FAA to any course of action in the future.
Comments
The FAA received comments from Boeing, The Foundation for Aviation Safety, Kenya Airways, ProTech Aero Services Limited (ProTech), and Qatar Airways (Qatar). The following presents the comments received on the NPRM and the FAA's response.
Request To Delay Issuance of the AD
Boeing requested that the FAA delay issuance of the proposed AD until the next OPS version is incorporated into the airplane production line. Boeing stated that based on additional fleet reports, the OPS version specified in the proposed AD, as referenced in Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB230051-00 RB, Issue 001, dated May 20, 2024 (Issue 001 of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB230051-00 RB), does not completely address the TCP VHF uncommanded frequency change. Boeing also stated it is continuing to evaluate fleet reports to address the causes of the additional findings in the next OPS version.
The FAA agrees that the OPS version specified in the proposed AD does not correct the unsafe condition. For that reason, the FAA is withdrawing the NPRM and may consider other rulemaking when an adequate solution is developed to address the unsafe condition.
Request To Evaluate New Reports Before Issuing the AD
Qatar requested that the FAA evaluate new in-service reports before mandating the proposed AD. Qatar stated it has modified all of its affected Boeing Model 787 airplanes using Issue 001 of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB230051-00 RB, as proposed, but its flightcrews are reporting similar issues on the modified airplanes. Qatar believes the unsafe condition still exists on modified airplanes and has reported the events to Boeing and the parts manufacturer for further investigation and determination of the root cause.
The FAA is aware that multiple operators have reported concerns about the reliability of the software update or service difficulties after accomplishing Issue 001 of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB230051-00 RB. As stated previously, the FAA is withdrawing the NPRM and may consider other rulemaking when an adequate solution is developed to address the unsafe condition.
Request to Later Service Information
Kenya Airways and ProTech requested that the FAA revise paragraph (g) of proposed AD to require accomplishment of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB230051-00 RB, Issue 002, dated February 24, 2025 (Issue 002 of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB230051-00 RB) instead of Issue 001 of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB230051-00 RB.
The FAA disagrees. The FAA reviewed Issue 002 of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB230051-00 RB and noted it provides instructions for installing the same software part number identified in Issue 001 of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB230051-00 RB. Therefore, the FAA has determined Issue 002 of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB230051-00 RB is also not adequate for addressing the unsafe condition.
Request To Clarify the Root Cause
The Foundation for Aviation Safety noted that the FAA previously issued an NPRM on March 25, 2021 (
86 FR 17993
, April 7, 2021) to address the unsafe condition, and then withdrew that NPRM on August 31, 2021 (
86 FR 50484
, September 9, 2021), because the software update in that proposed AD was not effective. Since operators are reporting that the latest software update is still not effective, the commenter asked whether the problem is specific to
(
printed page 65144)
the software or if there also could be an electrical manufacturing defect.
The FAA is aware that multiple operators have reported concerns with the reliability of the software update or experienced service difficulties after accomplishing Issue 001 of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB230051-00 RB. Boeing is conducting further analysis to determine the root cause of the new reports. The FAA may consider other rulemaking when an adequate solution is developed to address the unsafe condition.
FAA's Conclusions
Upon further consideration, the FAA has determined that the NPRM does not adequately address the identified unsafe condition. Accordingly, the NPRM is withdrawn.
Regulatory Findings
Since this action only withdraws an NPRM, it is neither a proposed nor a final rule. This action therefore is not covered under
Executive Order 12866
, the Regulatory Flexibility Act, or DOT Regulatory Policies and Procedures (
44 FR 11034
, February 26, 1979).

Background

The costs for any repair that would be required by the proposed AD (including repairs for corrosion found outside the limits of the structural repair manual) would vary from airplane to airplane. Therefore, the FAA has no way of determining the cost estimate for such repairs
Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.
Regulatory Findings
The FAA determined that this proposed AD would not have federalism implications under
Executive Order 13132
. This proposed AD would not have a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
For the reasons discussed above, I certify this proposed regulation:

Executive Order 12866
,
(2) Would not affect intrastate aviation in Alaska, and
(3) Would not have a significant economic impact, positive or negative, on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

Description of Information Collection Requests
Title:
Disaster Assistance—General.
OMB Control Number:
0560-0170.
Expiration Date:
January 31, 2027.
Type of Request:
Revision of a currently approved information collection.
Abstract:
The Disaster Assistance-General information collection is needed to establish county eligibility for Secretarial disaster designations, which make emergency loans available to eligible farmers and ranchers and may also be used to qualify counties for other disaster assistance programs if required by statute or a program's regulations. The regulations in
7 CFR part 759
define the responsibilities of the Secretary of Agriculture in making disaster designations, the types of incidents that can result in a disaster designation, and the factors used in making disaster designations. Secretarial disaster designations must be requested in writing from a State governor (or authorized representative), Indian Tribal Council, or the FSA State Executive Director (SED) unless a county qualifies through the Fast Track process for drought using data from the U.S. Drought Monitor. For each county included in a request, the FSA county office and the County Emergency Board (CEB) will complete a Loss Assessment Report (LAR) that includes information about crop losses due to the disaster. If the LAR does not indicate a 30 percent or greater loss of at least one crop in the
(
printed page 65161)
county, FSA employees will conduct a survey of farmers in the county to assess whether other criteria justify a Secretarial disaster designation for the county.
FSA is requesting a revision of the approved information collection. The revisions are intended to accurately reflect the expected number of requests and need to conduct farmer surveys and will remove responses and burden hours for the collection of information from FSA employees rather than the public. For the following estimated total annual burden on respondents, the formula used to calculate the total burden hours is the estimated average time per response hours multiplied by the estimated total annual responses.
Estimate of Average Time To Respond:
Public reporting burden for the information collection is estimated to average 0.3724 hours per response.

Farms, Tribal Governments, and State Governments.

98.

1.

98.

37 hours.
Title:
Critical Customer Data.
OMB Control Number:
0560-0265.
Expiration Date:
January 31, 2027.
Type of Request:
Revision of a currently approved information collection.
Abstract:
FSA collects critical customer data (such as customer name, contact information, and taxpayer identification number) from new customers and updates records of existing customers with AD-2047, Customer Data Worksheet. This data is used by FSA and other USDA agencies to administer USDA programs and perform functions such as administering conservation compliance for federal crop insurance participants. The title of this information collection was formerly “Customer Data Worksheet Request for Business Partner Record Change”.
Critical customer data is typically provided directly to a service center employee while a customer is physically visiting the USDA Service Center. This approach minimizes the burden on customers by allowing them to provide this data as part of a routine office visit. AD-2047 is also available from the USDA e-Forms website for customers to download, complete, and submit to their local Service Center. Customers may submit the information by mail, fax, email, phone, or through Box or OneSpan (see
https://www.farmers.gov/​working-with-us/​signing-and-sharing-documents
).
FSA is currently reviewing how customers interact with USDA as part of the “One Farmer, One File” modernization initiative (see
https://www.fsa.usda.gov/​news-events/​news/​03-02-2026/​usda-launches-one-farmer-one-file-initiative-better-support-farmers
). Through “One Farmer, One File,” USDA's mission is to create a single, streamlined record that follows the farmer throughout the USDA system while reducing the administrative burden for farmers and making program delivery more efficient. As part of that initiative, FSA is establishing an electronic method for customer submission of critical customer data. The responses and burden hours associated with use of this electronic method are included in this information collection request.
The estimated number of respondents and responses increased by 170,981, and the burden hours increased by 8,549 due to the change in estimated responses since the last OMB approval. These changes reflect adjustments based on recent use of AD-2047. This increase is primarily due to an increase in the number of new customers who are participating in new programs. For the following estimated total annual burden on respondents, the formula used to calculate the total burden hours is the estimated average time per response multiplied by the estimated total annual responses.
Estimated Respondent Burden:
Public reporting burden for this collection of information is estimated to average 0.05 hours per response.
Type of Respondents:
Farms and Businesses.
Estimated Number of Respondents:
332,231.
Estimated Number of Responses per Respondent:
1.
Estimated Total Annual Number of Responses:
332,231.
Estimated Total Annual Burden on Respondents:
16,612 hours.
Request for Comments
FSA is requesting comments on all aspects of this information collection to help us to:
(1) Evaluate whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of FSA, including whether the information will have practical utility;
(2) Evaluate the accuracy of FSA's estimate of burden of the collection of information including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used;
(3) Evaluate the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected;
(4) Minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including using appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology.
All comments received in response to this notice, including names and addresses when provided, will be a matter of public record. Comments will be summarized and included in the submission for Office of Management and Budget approval.

Administrator, Farm Service Agency.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Statutory Authority
This proposed regulation is being issued under the authority granted to the Secretary of Health and Human Services by the Native American Programs Act of 1974, as amended (
42 U.S.C. 2991
et seq.
), hereafter referred to as the “Act.”
II. Background
The Native American Programs Act of 1974 (NAPA), as amended (
42 U.S.C. 2991
et seq.
), authorizes the Administration for Native Americans (ANA) to promote social development and economic self-sufficiency in Native communities through competitive grant funding. Under Section 803 of NAPA (
42 U.S.C. 2991b
), ANA provides financial assistance on a single-year or multi-year basis to public and nonprofit private agencies, including governing bodies of Indian Tribes on federal and state reservations, Alaska Native villages and regional corporations established under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (
43 U.S.C. 1601
et seq.
), and public and nonprofit agencies serving Native Hawaiians and Indian and Alaska Native organizations in urban or rural areas that are not reservations or Alaska Native villages. ANA implements its mission through competitive discretionary grants that support Native-led, community-based projects aimed at strengthening families and communities and reducing long-term dependency through social and economic development, Native language preservation, and environmental regulatory enhancement. ANA typically provides short-term “seed” funding ranging from 12 to 60 months to help communities launch or expand sustainable efforts. In Federal Fiscal Year (FFY) 2025, ANA awarded a total of $50,738,495, which included new awards and continued funding for previously awarded projects. The regulations that implement the NAPA,
45 CFR part 1336
, were last amended in 2026 by
91 FR 36756
.
III. Executive Summary
This would follow a final rule that was published in June 2026 (
see
91 FR 36756
) that repealed all of Part 1336 except for five sections. Those five sections now are fragmented and could be streamlined to ease readability and understanding. The five sections that currently remain in regulation are titled: Definitions, Notice of ineligibility, Appeal of ineligibility, Financial and administrative requirements, and Appeals. Many of these sections have language that is duplicative of statute, yet components of the section are not duplicative. Therefore, this rulemaking proposes to remove the language that is duplicative and streamline the remaining text.
Severability
The provisions of this NPRM, if finalized, are intended to be severable, such that, in the event a court were to invalidate any particular provision or deem it to be unenforceable, the remaining provisions would continue to be valid. The changes address a variety of issues relevant to the Administration for Native Americans. None of the provisions contained herein are central to an overall intent of the proposed rule, nor are any provisions dependent on the validity of other, separate provisions.
IV. Discussion of Proposed Changes
Subpart A—Definitions
§ 1336.10 Definitions
Section 1336.10 identifies the definitions that are applicable to part 1336, unless context otherwise requires. This proposal removes the definition for “Economic and social self-sufficiency” as the term is not used in the proposed new part. Further, this NPRM seeks to update the definition of “ANA” as the Administration for Native Americans is no longer under the Office of Human Development Services. Therefore, this proposal would remove that reference while maintaining the remainder of the definition. This rule proposes to also redesignate this section from § 1336.10 to § 1336.1 in accordance with the proposed streamlining of the part. There are no other proposed changes to definitions in this section.
Subpart C—Native American Projects
§ 1336.34 Notice of Ineligibility
Section 1336.34 states the process of notice for an organization if the Commissioner determines them to be ineligible for funding, or the activities proposed by the organization are ineligible. This NPRM proposes to streamline this section by maintaining the requirement that if an organization or activities proposed by an organization are determined to be ineligible for funding, the Commissioner must inform the applicant of this decision and must state the legal and factual grounds for which this decision was made. This NPRM seeks to remove the detailed requirements that state that a copy of part 1336 must be included in that letter, as well as requiring the letter to include the template paragraph that currently exists in regulation. The reason for this proposal is in part to simplify the regulatory text, which does not benefit from including template paragraphs, but also to recognize the fact that the address listed in the current section is no longer the appropriate office of ANA. This rule proposes to also redesignate this section from § 1336.34 to § 1336.2 and retitle it “Notices of ineligibility and appeals” in accordance with the proposed streamlining of the part.
§ 1336.35 Appeal of Ineligibility
Section 1336.35 currently identifies the process that must be followed to appeal a finding of ineligibility for funding. This section is proposed to be removed as the language detailing this appeals process conflicts with the Departmental Appeals Board (DAB) procedures which are identified in
45 CFR part 16
. To simplify the appeals process and ensure consistency among other ACF programs, we propose to add a new paragraph to proposed section 1336.2 entitled “appeals” (proposed 1336.2(b)) describing that an applicant who has had their application rejected because it has been found ineligible for funding or because the activities it is proposing are ineligible for funding by the Commissioner may appeal the Commissioner's ruling to the DAB following the process identified in
45 CFR part 16
.
Subpart E—Financial Assistance Provisions
§ 1336.50 Financial and Administrative Requirements
Section 1336.50 currently describes financial and administrative requirements applicable to grantees. This section is proposed to be streamlined and renumbered as section 1336.3 under the same name. This NPRM seeks to remove current § 1336.50(a) as the regulations identified in this subpart apply regardless of being cited here. HHS accepts that this list may be helpful for grantees to identify which requirements are applicable to them, and if this proposed rule is finalized, intends to provide training
(
printed page 65156)
and technical assistance to ensure grantees are still aware of applicable regulatory requirements.
Current section 1336.50(b)(1) details that recipients of financial assistance under sections 803, 804, and 805 of the Act must provide a matching share of 20 percent of the approved cost of the assisted project, unless a waiver is attained. This proposed rule removes this section because it is duplicative of
42 U.S.C. 2991b(c)
. We propose to streamline current section 1336.50(b)(2) by removing unnecessary language while preserving the all core aspects of the regulation and renumbering as § 1336.3(a)(1).
We propose to renumber current section 1336.50(b)(3) as 1336.3(a)(2) and retain in part. The language proposed for deletion is in paragraph (i) which was an overly wordy explanation for why an applicant could request a waiver for the non-Federal matching requirement and is proposed to be replaced with the proper statutory reference. Paragraph (ii) is proposed to be retained, but this NPRM seeks to remove the last two sentences of the paragraph which provide examples of allowable documentation, as opposed to requirements imposed on grantees. Current section 1336.50(b)(4) is proposed to be renumbered to 1336.3(a)(3) with no changes.
We propose to remove current section 1336.50(c)(1) as it does not contain any requirements but rather restates language from section 803(c) of the Act and other parts of the regulation. Paragraph (2) is then proposed to be renumbered as paragraph (1) with a minor edit to add a statutory reference. There are no other proposed changes to the rest of current section 1336.50, other than to renumber as appropriate.
§ 1336.52 Appeals
Section 1336.52 currently identifies the right to appeal decisions to suspend, terminate, or deny funding pursuant to the remedies for noncompliance under
2 CFR 200.339-200.343
and the process for which to do so. We propose to remove this section as the language detailing this appeals and hearing process is duplicative of the DAB procedures which are identified in
45 CFR part 16
. To ensure that grantees are still aware of the appeals process, without having to rewrite part 16 in this section, we propose to add a new paragraph to proposed section 1336.2 entitled “appeals” (proposed 1336.2(b)) which describes that a recipient who has had their financial assistance suspended or terminated, or whose non-competing continuation applications for refunding have denied under
2 CFR 200.339
and
200.340
may appeal the ruling to the DAB following the process identified in
45 CFR part 16
.
V. Regulatory Process Matters
Paperwork Reduction Act
Under the Paperwork Reduction Act (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.,
as amended) (PRA), all Departments are required to submit to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval any new or modified reporting or recordkeeping requirements inherent in a proposed or final rule. This NPRM does not contain any information collections requiring OMB approval under the PRA and, therefore, will not create any new paperwork burdens or modify existing burdens subject to OMB review.
Executive Order 13132
Executive Order 13132
requires federal agencies to consult with State and local government officials if they develop regulatory policies with federalism implications. Federalism is rooted in the belief that issues that are not national in scope or significance are most appropriately addressed by the level of government close to the people. This proposed rule would not have substantial direct impact on the States, on the relationship between the federal government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. This NPRM would not pre-empt State law. The changes proposed in the NPRM are removing unnecessary and obsolete regulations from the Native American Program rules. Therefore, in accordance with Section 6 of
Executive Order 13132
, it is determined that this action does not have sufficient federalism implications to warrant the preparation of a federalism summary impact statement.
Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families
Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families Section 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act of 1999 (
Pub. L. 105-277
) requires federal agencies to determine whether a policy or regulation may negatively affect family well-being. If the agency determines a policy or regulation negatively affects family well-being, then the agency must prepare an impact assessment addressing seven criteria specified in the law. HHS believes it is not necessary to prepare a family policymaking assessment because the actions proposed in this NPRM will not have any impact on the autonomy or integrity of the family as an institution.
VI. Regulatory Impact Analysis
We have examined the impacts of the proposed rule under
Executive Order 12866
,
Executive Order 13563
,
Executive Order 14192
, the Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 601-612
), and the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
Pub. L. 104-4
).
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct us to assess all benefits and costs of available regulatory alternatives and, when regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits.
Executive Order 14192
requires that any new incremental costs associated with significant new regulations “shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least ten prior regulations.” The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) has determined that this proposed rule is a significant action under
Executive Order 12866
Section 3(f).
The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) requires agencies to consider the impact of their regulatory proposals on small entities. Because this action would simply repeal obsolete and unnecessary language, we propose to certify that the proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA) generally requires that each agency conduct a cost-benefit analysis; identify and consider a reasonable number of regulatory alternatives; and select the least costly, most cost effective, or least burdensome alternative that achieves the objectives of the rule before promulgating any proposed or final rule that includes a Federal mandate that may result in expenditures of more than $100 million (adjusted for inflation) in at least one year by State, local, and tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector. Each agency issuing a rule with relevant effects over that threshold must also seek input from State, local, and tribal governments. The current threshold after adjustment for inflation is $193 million, using the most current (2025) Implicit Price Deflator for the Gross Domestic Product. This proposed rule would not result in an expenditure in any year that meets or exceeds this amount.
VII. Tribal Consultation Statement
Executive Order 13175
, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments,
requires agencies to consult with Indian Tribes when
(
printed page 65157)
regulations have “substantial direct effects on one or more Indian Tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes.” Similarly, ACF's Tribal Consultation Policy says that consultation is triggered for any legislative proposal, new rule adoption, or other policy change that significantly affects Tribes, meaning there exists a reasonable presumption that it has or may have substantial direct effects on one or more Indian Tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian tribes, on the amount or duration of ACF program funding, on the delivery of ACF programs or services to one or more Indian Tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes.
ACF conducted a Tribal consultation in August 2026, in which a panel on “Reducing Administrative Burden” was hosted. Commenters expressed general support for de-regulation and simplifying of regulatory text. This proposed rule begins another comment period by which we are requesting further input from Tribes on the proposed changes.

§ 1336.3
Financial and administrative requirements.
(a)
Cost sharing or matching.
(1)
Application.
If an applicant or recipient wishes to request a waiver of the requirement for a 20 percent non-Federal matching share for financial assistance under sections 803, 804, and 805 of the Act, the following conditions must be met:
(i) If an applicant for an initial award or an applicant for a non-competing continuation award anticipates that it will be unable to meet the cost-sharing or matching requirement, the applicant may request a waiver of the 20 percent non-Federal matching share. It must include with its application for funding, the submission of a revised SF424A, a written justification that clearly explains why the applicant cannot provide the matching share including the amount of non-Federal share to be waived, and how it meets the criteria indicated in paragraph (a)(2) of this section. For an applicant for an initial award, or an applicant seeking a non-competing continuation award, a request for a waiver must be submitted at the time of the initial application or non-competing continuation (NCC) application.
(ii) If a recipient is unable to contribute part or all of the required non-Federal matching share during a budget period due to an emergency situation the recipient may request a waiver of all or part of the requirement for a 20 percent non-Federal matching share. Any requests for an emergency waiver may be submitted at any time during a budget period as soon as the adverse effect is known to the recipient and must be submitted in accordance with the requirements specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section.
(2)
Criteria.

(i) Applicant or recipient documents an inability to meet requirements of
42 U.S.C. 2991b(c)
through an institutional audit if available, or a full disclosure of applicant's or recipient's total assets and liabilities.
(

(ii) Applicants or recipients can document that reasonable efforts to obtain cash or in-kind contributions for the purposes of the project from third parties have been unsuccessful, including evidence and the results of such attempts.

Maintenance of effort.

42 U.S.C. 2991b(d)(1)

On October 7, 2026, the Department of Justice lodged a proposed Fourth Amendment to the Consent Decree with the United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio in the lawsuit entitled
United States
v.
City of Akron, Ohio, et al.,
Civil Action No. 09-cv-00272.
In this action the United States, and the State of Ohio in a cross-claim, sought civil penalties and injunctive relief for violations of the Clean Water Act,
33 U.S.C. 1251
et seq.,
in connection with the City of Akron's (“Akron”) operation of its municipal wastewater treatment facility and sewer system. Under the Consent Decree, which was approved by the Court in January 2014, Akron was required to implement a comprehensive plan (the “Long Term Control Plan Update” or “LTCP Update”) to address overflows from its combined sewer system and bypasses around secondary treatment at the wastewater treatment facility.
The proposed amendment modifies certain provisions of the 2014 Consent Decree set forth in the LTCP Update. The proposed amendment (1) replaces a construction requirement for a new treatment facility with Performance Criteria limiting Akron to three untreated CSO discharges per Typical Year and volumetric discharge limits; (2) adds monitoring, modeling, and reporting requirements for evaluating achievement of the Performance Criteria; and (3) extends the requirement that Akron disinfect and dechlorinate certain discharges from six to eight months during a calendar year.

ACTION:

SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, the Corporation for National and Community Service (operating as AmeriCorps) is proposing a new information collection for AmeriCorps VISTA sponsors and certain categories of candidates for VISTA service.
DATES:
Written comments must be submitted to the individual and office listed in the
ADDRESSES
section by November 13, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection should be sent within 30 days of publication of this notice to
www.reginfo.gov/​public/​do/​PRAMain
. Find this particular information collection by selecting “Currently under 30-day Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the search function.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Elizabeth Southall, Acting Director VISTA Member Service Unit, AmeriCorps, 202-606-3835,
esouthall@americorps.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The OMB is particularly interested in comments which:
Evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of CNCS, including whether the information will have practical utility;
Evaluate the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions;
Propose ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and
Propose ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology.
A 60-day Notice requesting public comment was published in the
Federal Register
on July 15, 2026, at
91 FR 43364
. The comment period ended September 14, 2026. Three comments were received in response to that notice. One comment asked whether candidates are provided an opportunity to dispute inaccurate court records, clarify probation terms, or appeal a supervisor's negative Part C recommendation before being formally disqualified from AmeriCorps VISTA service. No change to the information collection is needed to address this comment because when the candidate receives their background check results directly from “Checkr”, they can dispute a finding through that system if they believe information on their background check is inaccurate, incomplete, or belongs to someone else. Additionally, the CHAF form provides a mechanism for candidates to address any discrepancies and provide clarification, encouraging dialogue between the candidate and Partner organization to engage in a transparent interactive process in which any discrepancies can be discussed, documented and elevated to VISTA if necessary. Another comment expressed concern that the form requires local non-profit or municipal site supervisors who are not trained in criminal record evaluations to justify acceptance or rejection based on a candidate's criminal history. In fact, the form does not require local site supervisors to make legal determinations regarding a candidate's criminal history. The criminal history information has already been processed through the criminal system. Site supervisors provide site-specific information and a recommendation concerning whether a candidate is suitable for service at that particular site; they do not make the final determination regarding the candidate's eligibility or suitability for VISTA service. AmeriCorps VISTA retains final decision-making authority consistent with the applicable statutory and program requirements as outlined in the Domestic Volunteer Service Act (DVSA), the National and Community Service Act of 1990, as amended. The third comment expressed concern regarding exposure of sensitive information to local host sites. AmeriCorps VISTA partners are required to comply with AmeriCorps and applicable federal regulations governing the handling of sensitive information.

Abstract:
The AmeriCorps VISTA Criminal History Acknowledgment Form (CHAF) is part of a new process that increases sponsor autonomy in AmeriCorps VISTA volunteer (member) selection and standardizes data collection for more efficient workflow and prompt adjudication of criminal history issues. The CHAF must be completed by VISTA sponsors when a candidate for VISTA service either fails to report their criminal history on their application or is noted to have a criminal history involving certain violent or serious offenses. In the latter case, a VISTA candidate reports the offense, its date, the final court judgment, and the legal status of each offense in Part A of the CHAF. In Part B, they accept the AmeriCorps VISTA conditions for serving with a criminal history special consideration.
On Part C of the form, the VISTA sponsor or site supervisor provides a recommendation to accept or reject the candidate based on the disclosed criminal history. They must include an explanation of why they consider the candidate to be (or not be) a good fit for their program in light of the disclosed criminal history and, if they recommend acceptance, what measures they will have in place to support a successful service term for the candidate and appropriate supervision.
Part D is a personal narrative that applicants who have noted a criminal history involving violence must complete.

Notice is hereby given that I have delegated to the Administrator, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), the authorities vested in the Secretary of Health and Human Services under section 1128(b) of the Social Security Act. This delegation revises the limitations from the March 14, 2011, delegation of authority (
76 FR 13618
), which superseded the September 6, 1984, DOA as to Section F.50.—Limitations of Authority, subsection (1)(c).
CMS requested that the permissive exclusion authority under Section 1128(b) of the SSA be formally delegated to the CMS Administrator. As the agency directly responsible for administering Medicare and Medicaid, CMS is uniquely positioned to investigate, identify, and develop the evidentiary basis underpinning permissive exclusion determinations. Formalizing this delegation aligns investigative and enforcement responsibilities within a single operating division, reducing redundancy and improving program integrity outcomes.
This delegation will be exercised in accordance with the Department's applicable policies, procedures, guidelines, and regulations. These authorities may be redelegated. Excluded from this delegation is the authority to conduct hearings and to issue regulations. This delegation does not affect or diminish the Secretary's previous delegation of these authorities to the Inspector General of the Department of Health and Human Services under
53 FR 12993
(Apr. 20, 1988), nor does it affect any actions taken pursuant to that earlier delegation.
All redelegations and edits to this authority are required to be reviewed by the Division of Performance and Organizational Programs, Office of Human Capital, CMS, or its successor. Exercise of this authority is in accordance with established policies, procedures, guidelines, and regulations as prescribed by the Secretary. The Secretary retains the authority to submit reports to Congress and promulgate regulations.
This delegation is effective immediately. I affirm and ratify any actions taken by the Administrator or subordinates that involve the exercise of the authorities delegated therein prior to the effective date of the delegation.
