SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Title:
Contact Lens Rule (Rule),
16 CFR part 315
.
OMB Control Number:
3084-0127.
Type of Review:
Extension of a currently approved collection.
Likely Respondents:
Contact lens prescribers and contact lens sellers.
Estimated Annual Labor Hours Burden:
3,216,888 hours (derived from 2,070,288 contact lens prescriber hours + 1,146,600 contact lens seller hours).
Contact Lens Prescribers:
750,000 hours (45 million contact lens wearers × 1 minute per prescription release/60 minutes) + 187,500 hours (33,750,000 contact lens wearers × 20 seconds per confirmation of prescription release/3600 seconds) + 62,500 hours (11,250,000 contact lens wearers × 20 seconds per affirmative consent to electronic prescription delivery/3600 seconds) + 320,288 hours (3,843,450 verification requests × 5 minutes per response/60 minutes) + 750,000 hours recordkeeping = 2,070,288 hours.
Contact Lens Sellers:
1,146,600 (derived from 1,067,625 hours (12,811,500 orders × 5 minutes per verification/60 minutes) + 78,975 burden hours (4,738,500 orders × 1 minute recordkeeping/60 minutes) = 1,146,600) hours.
Estimated Total Labor Cost Burden:
Approximately $133,334,992 (derived from $61,908,147 ($68.05 × 909,745 optometrist hours) + $23,514,733 ($146.47 × 160,543 ophthalmologist hours) + $47,912,112 ($22.32 × 2,146,600 prescriber and seller office clerk hours)).
Estimated Total Non-Labor Cost Burden:
$640,575 (derived from 12,811,500 orders × $.05 per automated message recording).
Estimated Total Annual Cost Burden:
$133,975,567 (derived from $133,334,992 labor cost + $640,575 non-labor cost).
The Contact Lens Rule was promulgated by the FTC pursuant to the Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act (“FCLCA”),
Public Law 108-164
(Dec. 6, 2003), which was enacted to enable consumers to purchase contact lenses from the seller of their choice. The Rule became effective on August 2, 2004, and was most recently amended in 2020.
[
1
]
As mandated by the FCLCA, the Rule requires the release and verification of contact lens prescriptions which are generally valid for one year and contains recordkeeping requirements applying to both prescribers and sellers of contact lenses.
Specifically, the Rule requires that prescribers provide a copy of the prescription to the consumer upon the completion of a contact lens fitting, even if the patient does not request it, and verify or provide prescriptions to authorized third parties. The Rule also mandates that a contact lens seller may sell contact lenses only in accordance with a prescription that the seller either: (a) has received from the patient or prescriber; or (b) has verified through direct communication with the prescriber. Additional provisions in the Rule that constitute collections of information as defined by
5 CFR 1320.3(c)
require that sellers who use calls containing automated verification messages record the entire call and preserve such recordings for at least three years. In addition, the Rule requires that prescribers: (a) obtain from patients, and maintain for a period of not less than three years, a signed confirmation of prescription release on a separate stand-alone document; or (b) obtain from patients, and maintain for a period of not less than three years, a patient's signature on a confirmation of prescription release included on a copy of a patient's prescription; or (c) obtain from patients, and maintain for a period of not less than three years, a patient's signature on a confirmation of prescription release included on a copy of a patient's contact lens fitting sales receipt; or (d) provide each patient with a copy of the prescription via online portal, electronic mail, or text message, and for three years retain evidence that such prescription was sent, received, or, if provided via an online-patient portal, made accessible, downloadable, and printable by the patient. For prescribers who choose to offer an electronic method of prescription delivery, the Rule requires that such prescribers maintain records or evidence of affirmative consent by patients to such digital delivery for three years. The Rule also requires prescribers to document, in their records, the medical reasons for setting a contact lens prescription expiration date of less than one year. Additionally, contact lens sellers are required to maintain records for three years of all direct communications involved in obtaining verification of a contact lens prescription, as well as prescriptions, or copies thereof, which they receive directly from customers or prescribers.
The information retained under the Rule's recordkeeping requirements is used by the Commission to substantiate compliance with the Rule and may also provide a basis for the Commission to bring an enforcement action. Without the required records, it would be difficult either to ensure that entities are complying with the Rule's requirements or to bring enforcement actions based on violations of the Rule.
As required by section 3506(c)(2)(A) of the PRA,
44 U.S.C. 3506(c)(2)(A)
, the FTC is providing this opportunity for public comment before requesting that OMB extend the existing clearance for the information collection requirements contained in the Rule.
Burden Statement
Estimated annual hours burden:
3,216,888 hours.
This figure is derived by adding 2,070,288 disclosure, verification, and recordkeeping-hours for contact lens prescribers to 1,146,600 verification and recordkeeping hours for contact lens sellers. This estimate is an increase from the 3,104,050 hours annual burden hours submitted to OMB in 2023.
1. Prescribers and Their Office Staff
The Rule requires prescribers to collect information and make disclosures in three ways. Upon completing a contact lens fitting, the Rule requires that prescribers (1) provide a copy of the contact lens prescription to the patient,
[
2
]
(2) collect a patient's signature on either a Confirmation of Prescription Release or a consent-to-electronic-prescription-release and preserve such record, and (3) as directed by any person designated to act on behalf of the patient, provide or verify the contact lens prescription. Prescribers can verify a prescription either by responding affirmatively to a request for verification, or by not responding at all, in which case the prescription will be “passively verified” after eight business hours. Prescribers are also required to correct an incorrect prescription submitted by a seller and notify a seller if the prescription submitted for verification is expired or otherwise invalid. Staff believe that the burden of complying with these requirements is relatively low.
The number of contact lens wearers in the United States is estimated by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to be approximately 45
(
printed page 65211)
million.
[
3
]
Therefore, assuming an annual contact lens exam for each contact lens wearer, approximately 45 million people would receive a copy of their prescription each year under the Rule and be required to either sign a Confirmation of Prescription Release or consent to electronic delivery of their prescription.
[
4
]
At an estimated one minute per prescription, the annual time spent by prescribers complying with the requirement to release prescriptions to patients would be approximately 750,000 hours. [(45 million × 1 minute)/60 minutes = 750,000 hours]. Since the Rule requires that prescriptions be released automatically at completion of a fitting, the Commission—for purposes of calculating the PRA burden—continues to assume that prescription releases to patients are handled by the prescriber rather than the prescriber's office staff.
[
5
]
In all likelihood, this estimate overstates the actual burden because it includes the time spent by prescribers who already release prescriptions to patients in the ordinary course of business. Furthermore, this estimate allocates the same time for both paper and electronic delivery of prescriptions, even though the latter likely takes less time for the prescriber.
The time required to collect a signature from a patient confirming release of a prescription is estimated at twenty seconds.
[
6
]
It is estimated that 25% of patients would opt for electronic delivery of their prescriptions and thus would not need to sign a Confirmation of Prescription Release.
[
7
]
Based on our knowledge of the industry and how the medical field operates, the Commission believes most signed patient confirmations are obtained by prescribers' office staff rather than by the prescribers themselves. The time spent by prescribers' staff complying with the requirement to obtain signed confirmations from the other 75% of patients is approximately 187,500 hours annually [(75% × 45 million prescriptions yearly × 20 seconds) / 3600 seconds = 187,500 hours].
As noted above, it is estimated that approximately 25% of patients would opt for electronic delivery of their prescriptions. In order to opt for electronic delivery, patients are required to sign an affirmative consent to receive their prescription via email, text, or patient portal. The time required to collect an affirmative consent signature is estimated at twenty seconds,
[
8
]
and the annual time spent complying with the requirement to obtain such signatures is approximately 62,500 hours [(25% × 45 million prescriptions yearly × 20 seconds) / 3600 seconds = 62,500 hours]. Based on our knowledge of the industry and how the medical field operates, the Commission believes most signed patient consents are obtained by prescribers' office staff rather than by the prescribers themselves.
As stated above, prescribers may also be required to provide or verify contact lens prescriptions to sellers. According to survey data, approximately 39% of contact lens purchases are from a source other than the prescriber.
[
9
]
Assuming that each of the 45 million contact lens wearers in the U.S. makes one purchase per year, this means that approximately 17,550,000 contact lens purchases (45 million × 39% = 17,550,000) are made from sellers other than the prescriber.
Based on prior discussions with industry, approximately 73% of sales by non-prescriber sellers require verification, and prescribers affirmatively respond (by notifying the seller that the prescription is invalid or incorrect) to approximately 15% of those verification requests. Using a response rate of 15%, the FTC therefore estimates that prescribers' offices respond to approximately 1,921,725 verification requests annually [(17,550,000 purchases × 73%) × 15% = 1,921,725 responses]. Additionally, some prescribers may voluntarily respond to verification requests and confirm prescriptions (as opposed to simply letting the prescription passively verify). Because correcting or declining incorrect prescriptions is mandated by the Rule and occurs in response to approximately 15% of requests, staff assumes that prescribers voluntarily confirm prescriptions less often and confirm at most an additional 15% of prescriptions (and, in all likelihood, significantly less). Using a combined response rate of 30%, the FTC estimates that prescribers' offices respond to approximately 3,843,450 requests annually.
According to prior industry comments,
[
10
]
responding to verification requests requires approximately five minutes per request. Using that data, we estimate that these responses require an additional 320,288 hours annually [(3,843,450 × 5 minutes) / 60 minutes = 320,288 hours]. Based on investigations and anecdotal comments, FTC staff is aware that many verification requests are handled by office staff rather than by the prescribers themselves. FTC staff, however, does not possess reliable information as to what percentage of verification requests are performed by prescribers or their staff, and thus will allocate all such hours to prescribers, even though this may result in an estimated labor cost that is higher than in actuality.
Lastly, the Rule and FCLCA also impose recordkeeping requirements on prescribers' offices. First, they must maintain signed confirmations, or signed consent to electronic prescription delivery, and proof that such prescriptions were delivered via email, text, or patient portal for a period of three years. For purposes of PRA analysis, the Commission has used the assumption that all prescriber offices require a full minute to store and maintain each confirmation record and a full minute to store and maintain each consent to electronic prescription delivery and proof of electronic
(
printed page 65212)
prescription delivery.
[
11
]
The Commission thus allots an additional 750,000 annual hours for prescribers' offices to store and maintain records of patient confirmations and consents. The Commission believes these labor hours are most likely performed by prescribers' office staff.
The Rule also requires prescribers to document the specific medical reasons for setting a contact lens prescription expiration date shorter than the one-year minimum established by the FCLCA. This burden is likely to be nil because the requirement applies only in cases when the prescriber invokes the medical judgment exception, which is expected to occur infrequently, and prescribers are likely to record this information in the ordinary course of business as part of their patients' medical records. As mentioned previously, the OMB regulation that implements the PRA defines “burden” to exclude any effort that would be expended regardless of a regulatory requirement.
Combining all hours spent annually disclosing prescriptions to consumers, obtaining confirmations of prescription release from consumers, obtaining affirmative consent to electronic prescription delivery from consumers, responding to verification requests, and maintaining records as required by the Rule, we estimate a total of 2,070,288 hours for all contact lens prescribers to comply with the Rule [750,000 prescription-release hours + 187,500 confirmation-collection hours + 62,500 electronic-delivery-consent hours + 320,288 verification-response hours + 750,000 recordkeeping hours = 2,070,288 hours]. Of this total, we estimate 1,070,288 are labor hours performed by prescribers and 1,000,000 are labor hours performed by prescribers' clerical office staff.
2. Sellers
As noted above, a seller may sell contact lenses only in accordance with a valid prescription that the seller has (a) received from the patient or prescriber or (b) verified through direct communication with the prescriber. The FCLCA also requires sellers to retain prescriptions and records of communications with prescribers relating to prescription verification for three years.
As stated previously, there are approximately 17,550,000 sales by non-prescriber sellers annually and approximately 73% of such sales require verification. Therefore, sellers verify approximately 12,811,500 orders annually and retain two records for such sales: the verification request and any response from the prescriber. Staff estimates that sellers' verification and recordkeeping for those orders will entail a maximum of five minutes per sale. At an estimated five minutes per sale to each of the approximately 12,811,500 orders, contact lens sellers will spend a total of 1,067,625 burden hours complying with this portion of the requirement [(12,811,500 × 5 minutes) / 60 minutes = 1,067,625 hours].
Approximately 27% of sales to non-prescriber sellers do not require verification and thus require only that the seller retain the prescription provided. Staff estimates that this recordkeeping burden requires at most one minute per order (in truth, in many cases this retention is electronic and automatic and will not require any time) for 4,738,500 orders [17,550,000 sales × 27%], resulting in 78,975 recordkeeping burden hours [(4,738,500 orders × 1 minute) / 60 minutes = 78,975 hours].
Combining burden hours for all orders [1,067,625 hours + 78,975 hours], staff estimates a total of 1,146,600 hours for contact lens sellers. It is likely that this estimate overstates the actual burden because it includes the time spent by sellers who already keep records pertaining to contact lens sales in the ordinary course of business, and those whose records are generated and preserved automatically when a customer orders online, which staff believes is the case for many online sellers.
Estimated total labor cost burden:
Approximately $133,334,992.
This figure is derived from applying hourly wage figures for optometrists, ophthalmologists, and office clerical staff to the burden hours described above. This estimate is higher than the $117,606,598 labor cost estimate submitted to OMB in 2023 due to wage increases for optometrists, ophthalmologists, and office staff, and an increase in the percentage estimate of contact lens sales made by sellers other than the prescriber.
According to Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), salaried optometrists earn an average wage of $68.05 per hour, ophthalmologists—which are listed by BLS under “surgeons”—earn an average wage of $146.47 per hour, and general office clerks earn an average wage of $22.32 per hour.
[
12
]
Based on our knowledge of the industry and the number of optometrists and ophthalmologists in the United States, we assume that of the 1,070,288 total prescriber labor hours relating to the Rule's prescription release requirement (750,000 hours) and response to verification requests (320,288 hours), optometrists are performing 85% of such hours and ophthalmologists are performing the remaining 15% of prescriber hours. We credit general office clerks for performing the remaining hours, both for prescribers' offices (1,000,000 hours) and for non-prescriber sellers (1,146,600 hours). Based on these assumptions and estimates above, the estimated total labor cost attributable to the Rule is approximately $133,334,992 [($68.05 × 909,745 optometrist hours = $61,908,147) + ($146.47 × 160,543 ophthalmologist hours = $23,514,733) + ($22.32 × 1,000,000 prescribers' office clerk hours = $22,320,000) + ($22.32 × 1,146,600 sellers' office clerk hours = $25,592,112) = $133,334,992].
Estimated annual non-labor cost burden:
$640,575.
Staff believes that the Rule's disclosure and recordkeeping requirements described above impose negligible capital or other non-labor costs, as the affected entities are likely to have the necessary supplies and/or equipment already (
e.g.,
prescription pads, patients' medical charts, facsimile machines and paper, telephones, and recordkeeping facilities such as filing cabinets or other storage) to perform those requirements. The 2020 Rule amendments, however, modified the Rule to require that sellers who use automated verification messages record the calls and preserve the recordings for three years. The Commission does not believe that requiring sellers who use automated messages for verification to record the calls and preserve them will create a substantial burden. The requirement will not require additional labor time, since the calls will be for the same duration as they were previously, but may require capital and other non-labor costs to record the calls and store them electronically. Based on comments supplied during the Rule modification process, the Commission estimates the
(
printed page 65213)
cost to record each verification call at five cents apiece.
[
13
]
Based on survey data, approximately 39% of contact lens purchases are from a source other than the prescriber. Assuming that each of the 45 million contact lens wearers in the U.S. makes on purchase per year, this would mean that approximately 17,550,000 contact lens purchases are made annually from sellers other than the prescribers. And since approximately 73% of sales by non-prescriber sellers require verification, this means that approximately 12,811,500 contact lens purchases would require verification calls, faxes, or emails. The Commission does not possess information as to the percentage of verifications completed by telephone versus fax or email, and thus for purposes of this analysis will assume that all verifications are performed via phone and deliver automated messages that are subject to the call-recording requirement. Based on the aforementioned assumptions, the Commission estimates that the requirement to record automated telephone verification messages will cost sellers, in aggregate, $640,575 (12,811,500 × $.05).
Combining the annual labor cost burden with the non-labor cost burden, the total cost burden of the Rule is estimated at $133,975,567 ($133,334,992 + $640,575 = $133,975,567). This is higher than the $118,197,898 cost submitted to OMB in 2023 due to rising wage rates and an increase in the estimated percentage of sales to non-prescriber sellers.
To put the total cost in perspective, a recent survey estimated that the U.S. contact lens market revenue is approximately $4.4 billion as of 2025, and growing at a healthy pace.
[
14
]
Therefore, the total cost burden estimate of $133,975,567, imposed by the Rule, while not insubstantial, represents just approximately 3% of the overall retail revenue generated.
Request for Comment
Pursuant to Section 3506(c)(2)(A) of the PRA, the FTC invites comments on: (1) whether the disclosure and recordkeeping requirements are necessary, including whether the information will be practically useful; (2) the accuracy of our burden estimates, including whether the methodology and assumptions used are valid; (3) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (4) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information.
For the FTC to consider a comment, we must receive it on or before December 14, 2026. Your comment, including your name and your state, will be placed on the public record of this proceeding, including the
https://www.regulations.gov
website.
You can file a comment online or on paper. Due to heightened security screening, postal mail addressed to the Commission will be subject to delay. We encourage you to submit your comments online through the
https://www.regulations.gov
website.
If you file your comment on paper, write “Contact Lens Rule, PRA Comment, P145403” on your comment and on the envelope, and mail it to the following address: Federal Trade Commission, Office of the Secretary, 600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Mail Stop H-144 (Annex E), Washington, DC 20580.
Because your comment will become publicly available at
https://www.regulations.gov
,
you are solely responsible for making sure that your comment does not include any sensitive or confidential information. In particular, your comment should not include any sensitive personal information, such as your or anyone else's Social Security number; date of birth; driver's license number or other state identification number, or foreign country equivalent; passport number; financial account number; or credit or debit card number. You are also solely responsible for making sure that your comment does not include any sensitive health information, such as medical records or other individually identifiable health information. In addition, your comment should not include any “trade secret or any commercial or financial information which . . . is privileged or confidential”—as provided by Section 6(f) of the FTC Act,
15 U.S.C. 46(f)
, and FTC Rule 4.10(a)(2),
16 CFR 4.10(a)(2)
—including, in particular, competitively sensitive information, such as costs, sales statistics, inventories, formulas, patterns, devices, manufacturing processes, or customer names.
Comments containing material for which confidential treatment is requested must (1) be filed in paper form, (2) be clearly labeled “Confidential,” and (3) comply with FTC Rule 4.9(c). In particular, the written request for confidential treatment that accompanies the comment must include the factual and legal basis for the request and must identify the specific portions of the comment to be withheld from the public record.
See
FTC Rule 4.9(c). Your comment will be kept confidential only if the General Counsel grants your request in accordance with the law and the public interest. Once your comment has been posted publicly at

,
we cannot redact or remove your comment unless you submit a confidentiality request that meets the requirements for such treatment under FTC Rule 4.9(c), and the General Counsel grants that request.
The FTC Act and other laws that the Commission administers permit the collection of public comments to consider and use in this proceeding as appropriate. The Commission will consider all timely and responsive public comments that it receives on or before December 14, 2026. Title:
Qualifying Advanced Energy Project Credit—Notice 2023-18.
OMB Control Number:
1545-2151.
Regulation Project Number:
Notice 2023-18, Notice 2024-36.
Abstract:
IRS Notice 2023-18, as clarified and modified by subsequent guidance, establishes the § 48C(e) Qualifying Advanced Energy Project Credit Allocation Program. The program authorizes the allocation of $10 billion in tax credits for qualified investments in eligible advanced energy projects, including at least $4 billion reserved for projects located in designated energy communities. Eligible projects generally include investments to establish, expand, or re-equip industrial or manufacturing facilities that produce or recycle clean energy technologies, reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 20 percent, or process, refine, or recycle critical materials. To participate in the § 48C(e) program, taxpayers must submit project information to the Department of Energy (DOE) for technical review and recommendation and to the IRS for credit allocation and certification. Required submissions include a concept paper and § 48C(e) application, as applicable, as well as documentation demonstrating that an allocated project satisfies the program's certification requirements and notification when the project is placed in service. Notice 2023-18 has been clarified and modified by subsequent IRS guidance, including Notice 2024-36, which established procedures for the second allocation round and updated the program's technical and administrative requirements.

Environmental Protection Agency
40 CFR Part 751
[EPA-HQ-OPPT-2026-7327; FRL-13574-01-OCSPP]
RIN 2070-AL45
AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or Agency) is proposing to extend certain compliance dates applicable to certain entities subject to the regulation of trichloroethylene (TCE) under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) until December 31, 2027, including for certain chemical processors in meeting the prohibition compliance deadline for the processing of TCE, industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing aid, and associated wastewater disposal; and for refrigerant manufacturers in meeting the compliance deadline for phasing down
(
printed page 65149)
TCE feedstock in the production of HFC-134a. This proposed compliance extension would allow for necessary and reasonable transition periods for regulated entities under TSCA section 6(d).
DATES:
Comments must be received on or before November 13, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Submit your comments, identified by docket identification (ID) number EPA-HQ-OPPT-2026-7327, using the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
As required by the Administrative Procedure Act at
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(4)
, a plain language summary of the rule is available at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the online instructions for submitting comments. Do not submit electronically any information you consider to be Confidential Business Information (CBI) or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute. Additional instructions on commenting or visiting the docket, along with more information about dockets generally, is available at
https://www.epa.gov/​dockets/​
.

.
For general information contact:

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Executive Summary
A. Does this action apply to me?
You may be potentially affected by this rule if you manufacture, process, distribute in commerce, use, or dispose of TCE, or products containing TCE. TSCA section 3(9) defines the term “manufacture” to mean “to import into customs territory of the United States (as defined in general note 2 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States), produce, or manufacture.” Therefore, unless expressly stated otherwise, importers of TCE are subject to provisions regulating manufacture of TCE once the chemical enters the customs territory of the United States. Potentially affected entities may be included in the following lists of North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) codes:
Wood Window and Door Manufacturing (NAICS code 321911);
Other Basic Inorganic Chemical Manufacturing (NAICS code 325180);
Medicinal and Botanical Manufacturing (NAICS code 325411);
All Other Miscellaneous Chemical Product and Preparation Manufacturing (NAICS code 325998);
Rubber and Plastics Hoses and Belting Manufacturing (NAICS code 326220);
Rubber Product Manufacturing for Mechanical Use (NAICS code 326291); and
Storage Battery Manufacturing (NAICS code 335911).
B. What is the agency's authority for taking this action?
Under TSCA section 6(a) (
15 U.S.C. 2605(a)
), if EPA determines through a TSCA section 6(b) risk evaluation that a chemical substance presents an unreasonable risk of injury to health or the environment under the conditions of use, EPA must by rule apply one or more requirements listed in TSCA section 6(a) to the extent necessary so that the chemical substance or mixture no longer presents such risk under the conditions of use. EPA must specify compliance dates under TSCA section 6(d) (
15 U.S.C. 2605(d)
) for any TSCA section 6(a) rule. For TCE, EPA promulgated a final risk management rule under TSCA section 6(a) in 2024 (“2024 TCE Final Rule”) (Ref. 1) and an interim final rule extending compliance dates for two specific TCE conditions of use in 2025 (“2025 TCE Interim Final Rule”) (Ref. 2). Each of these TSCA section 6(a) actions include compliance dates pursuant to TSCA section 6(d). This action proposes to alter some of the compliance dates finalized in 2024 or finalized in subsequent amended rulemakings. Unless provided otherwise by law, agencies may change existing positions (
e.g.,
reconsider, revise, or rescind prior rules) provided that they acknowledge the change in position, offer a reasoned explanation for the change, and take any serious reliance interests into account.
See, e.g., FDA
v.
Wages & White Lion Invs., L.L.C.,
145 S. Ct. 898, 917 (2025);
Encino Motorcars
v.
Navarro,
579 U.S. 211, 221 (2016);
FCC
v.
Fox Television Stations, Inc.,
556 U.S. 502, 515 (2009);
Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n
v.
State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.,
463 U.S. 29 (1983). For the reasons set out in Units II and III of this preamble, EPA is proposing to revise select compliance dates. EPA is not aware of any serious reliance interests regarding this proposal.
C. What action is the agency taking?
EPA is proposing to amend
40 CFR 751.305
and
40 CFR 751.313
to extend the prohibition compliance dates for processing TCE as a reactant/intermediate, processing for and industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing aid in: process solvent used in battery manufacture, process solvent used in polymer fiber spinning, fluoroelastomer manufacture and Alcantara manufacture, extraction solvent used in caprolactam manufacture, precipitant used in beta-cyclodextrin manufacture (hereinafter referred to as “industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing aid”), and the disposal of TCE from such processing or uses to industrial pre-treatment, industrial treatment, or publicly owned treatment works from December 18, 2026, to December 31, 2027.
EPA is also proposing to amend
40 CFR 751.307
to extend the compliance timeframe for a step in the phase-out of processing TCE as an intermediate to manufacture HFC-134a. Specifically, EPA is proposing to extend the compliance deadline from June 7, 2027, to December 31, 2027, for each manufacturer of HFC-134a via processing TCE as an intermediate to process TCE at an annual volume no greater than 75 percent of the baseline.
EPA is also proposing to amend
40 CFR 751.321
to amend the compliance deadline for downstream notification, and the text required to be present in the SDS, to accurately reflect the new prohibition compliance deadline for processing TCE as a reactant/intermediate, processing for and industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing aid, and the disposal of TCE from such processing or uses to industrial pre-treatment, industrial treatment, or publicly owned treatment works. The new text would be required to be updated 30 days after the publication of the final rule.
D. Why is the Agency taking this action?
EPA is proposing to address ongoing difficulties associated with compliance dates for the 2024 TCE Final Rule and 2025 Interim Final Rule for certain chemical processors and refrigerant manufacturers due to challenges with the implementation of the respective prohibition and phaseout, in order to provide a reasonable transition period to no longer process TCE. As detailed further in Unit III.A.1, soon after publication of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, chemical processors and chemical manufacturers explained to EPA that the prohibition on processing TCE as a
(
printed page 65150)
reactant/intermediate, and associated wastewater disposal, would cause significant hardships to the chemical manufacturing sector because byproduct TCE at levels above the regulatory threshold is regularly transferred between sites during the manufacture of other chemicals (Refs. 3, 4 and 5).
EPA is also concerned about the prohibition on the processing for and industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing aid with the same compliance date, as EPA believes it may also warrant a more reasonable compliance timeframe for chemical processing. Due to the regular transfer of byproduct TCE between sites during the manufacture of other chlorinated solvents, a prohibition on processing TCE on December 18, 2026, could have significant negative impacts on the production of other chlorinated solvents in the United States (Ref. 3).
Separately, after publication of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, EPA received information from processors of TCE who manufacture HFC-134a about the continued need for high production of the refrigerant past the 2024 Final Rule's phaseout compliance dates (Ref. 6). As discussed further in Unit III.A.2, HFC-134a manufacturers now need a longer transition period so they can continue using a higher volume of TCE feedstock in order to meet demand for national security and critical infrastructure (Ref. 6). EPA's proposed amendment to the compliance deadline for downstream notification, and the text required to be present in SDSs, is being modified to accurately reflect the new prohibition compliance deadlines for processing being proposed in this action.
E. What are the incremental economic impacts?
EPA evaluated the potential incremental economic impacts and determined that these changes would have minimal impacts on the estimated costs and benefits of the existing actions and would primarily result in a delay when those costs and benefits begin accruing. Quantified costs are expected to be the same as estimated in the 2024 TCE Final Rule but will not be incurred until the proposed compliance date extensions expire. Relying on the cost estimates in section 7 of the economic analysis of the TCE Final Rule (Ref. 7), EPA estimates that the proposed extension of compliance dates would result in present value cost savings of $0.62-0.65 million (2024$ in 2026), forgone health benefits of $3,795 to $7,844 (2025$), and annualized cost savings of $ 0.04-0.06 million (2024$ in 2026, 3%-7% discount rate respectively, 20-year time horizon). EPA notes that, in the event that alternative compliance timeframes are finalized in response to comments received on this proposal, these impacts would be modified accordingly (
e.g.,
cost savings likely increase as the duration of the compliance timeframe extension increases).
II. Background
On December 17, 2024, EPA published the 2024 TCE Final Rule under TSCA section 6(a) to address unreasonable risk to human health (
89 FR 102568
) (FRL-8317-02-OCSPP). The 2024 TCE final rule prohibits the manufacture (including import), processing, and distribution in commerce of TCE for all uses (industrial, commercial, and consumer), while including longer compliance timeframes with reasonable worker protections for some processing and industrial and commercial uses until the prohibitions come into effect, so that TCE no longer presents an unreasonable risk to workers, occupational non-users, consumers, and bystanders.
After publication of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, EPA was made aware of a previously unidentified use of TCE as a processing aid in the manufacture of nuclear fuel and promulgated an interim final rule in September of 2025 to amend the prohibition compliance deadlines until September 15, 2028, to provide a reasonable transition period for that use (Ref. 2). EPA additionally extended the deadlines for disposal of TCE to wastewater for processors of TCE as a reactant/intermediate and certain processors and industrial and commercial users of TCE as a processing aid to December 18, 2026, to match the prohibition compliance date for these processing conditions of use.
EPA received three TSCA section 21 petitions concerning the 2024 TCE Final Rule: from American Chemistry Council (ACC) on May 29, 2025 (withdrawn September 19, 2025) (Refs. 3 and 8); from PPG Industries, Inc. on March 24, 2025 (withdrawn June 11, 2025) (Refs. 4 and 9); and from the Alliance for a Strong U.S. Battery Sector and Microporous on April 30, 2025 (withdrawn July 25, 2025) (Refs. 5 and 10). While these petitions were withdrawn, EPA recognizes the potential merits of certain requests contained in these petitions and is planning to address them in amendments to the rule through a future notice-and-comment rulemaking.
After issuing the TCE Final Rule, EPA received petitions for review that were consolidated in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit. EPA has since announced its intention to reconsider the TCE Final Rule.
III. Provisions of This Proposed Rule
For any TSCA section 6(a) rule, EPA must specify mandatory compliance dates that are “as soon as practicable,” while allowing for “a reasonable transition period.”
15 U.S.C. 2605(d)(1)(B)
and
(E)
. EPA acknowledges that it is proposing a change in position from the 2024 TCE Final Rule and the 2025 TCE Interim Final Rule. EPA intended that the compliance timeframes in these rules would be as soon as practicable while allowing for a reasonable transition period (see Unit I.E of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, and Unit III of the 2025 TCE Interim Final Rule). However, the Agency did not fully anticipate the challenges that certain entities are now experiencing: for chemical processors in meeting the prohibition compliance deadline for the processing of TCE, industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing aid, and associated wastewater disposal (Unit III.A); and for refrigerant manufacturers in meeting the compliance deadline for phasing down TCE feedstock in the production of HFC-134a (Unit III.B). Accordingly, EPA proposes that the compliance dates detailed in this Unit would be more feasible and workable, and compliant with EPA's obligations under TSCA section 6(d) for TCE, than those finalized in 2024 or amended in 2025.
A. Processing TCE as a Reactant/Intermediate, Industrial and Commercial Use of TCE as a Processing Aid, and Their Associated Wastewater Disposal
EPA is proposing to amend the compliance deadline for the prohibition on processing TCE as a reactant/intermediate and the industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing aid in certain chemical manufacturing to December 31, 2027. EPA is also proposing to amend the compliance deadline for the prohibition on the associated disposal of TCE to wastewater by processors of TCE and processors and industrial and commercial users of TCE as a processing aid to December 31, 2027.
In the 2024 TCE Final Rule, EPA finalized a prohibition on processing and distributing in commerce (including making available) of TCE as of June 16, 2025 (
40 CFR 751.305(b)(2)
). EPA also finalized extended phaseouts for processing of TCE as a reactant/intermediate and processing for and the industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing aid to continue until December 2026 (40 CFR
(
printed page 65151)
751.305(b)(9)(i)), and an exclusion from all prohibitions and restrictions for processing (including reuse) of TCE as a byproduct when that TCE byproduct is processed within a site-limited, physically enclosed system that is part of the same overall manufacturing process from which the byproduct TCE was generated (
40 CFR 751.301(c)
).
After the publication of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, EPA received a Section 21 petition from the ACC regarding the exclusion on byproduct reprocessing and the wastewater disposal associated with processing TCE (Ref. 3). In response, in the 2025 TCE Interim Final Rule EPA amended the compliance deadline from September 15, 2025, to December 18, 2026, for the prohibition on disposal of TCE to wastewater for processors of TCE as a reactant/intermediate and processors for and industrial and commercial users of TCE as a processing aid for certain industrial sectors. This action aligned the disposal prohibition with the December 18, 2026, prohibition on such uses in the 2024 Final Rule. This change responded to the concerns raised to EPA that processing conditions of use also involve disposal of TCE to wastewater that inadvertently was not similarly subject to the same compliance deadline (Ref. 2).
Through the Section 21 Petition and subsequent engagement, EPA was made aware after the 2024 final rule that byproduct TCE that is present in feedstock streams is sent by railcar between facilities to be further processed. This usually occurs between facilities of the same company, where one site has chemical manufacturing capabilities that another does not (Refs. 3, 8, 11 and 13). If the prohibition on processing TCE goes into effect on December 18, 2026, then the processing of byproduct TCE that travels between sites will be prohibited, along with disposal of this byproduct TCE to wastewater. Disposal of this byproduct TCE would therefore require incineration; if all byproduct TCE that is currently reused in a different facility must be incinerated, it would cause significant implementation concerns, including exceeded permit limitations and potential facility closures. Petitioners have indicated that the inability to send unpurified chlorinated solvent product streams with byproduct TCE between facilities would significantly disrupt the national supply chain by disproportionately impacting operations in the manufacture of other chlorinated solvents which unintentionally produce TCE as a byproduct (importantly perchloroethylene, carbon tetrachloride, methylene chloride, and 1,2-dichloroethane) in the United States (Refs. 3, 8, 11 and 13). In the 2024 TCE Final Rule and 2025 TCE Interim Final Rule EPA did not anticipate these implications.
As such, EPA is proposing to amend the compliance deadline for the prohibition on processing TCE as a reactant/intermediate and the wastewater disposal associated with such processing TCE until December 31, 2027, so that regulated entities would not be held in non-compliance with the relevant requirements in the 2024 TCE Final Rule and the 2025 TCE Interim Final Rule. EPA is also proposing to amend the compliance deadline for the prohibition on industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing aid because EPA believes, based on ACC's comments, that this condition of use also needs a longer transition period. These ongoing difficulties (see Unit I.D.2) in complying with the prohibitions and restrictions of the TCE final rule, particularly the need to transfer byproduct chemicals off site, warrant a longer reasonable transition period for this group of uses than EPA expected in 2024 or 2025. Given the two years provided for this compliance date in the 2024 TCE rule, EPA considers this extension of no more than one year to be appropriate because it is “as soon as practicable,” while allowing for “a reasonable transition period” (
15 U.S.C. 2605(d)(1)(B)
and
(E)
). Separately, EPA has initiated a rulemaking under RIN 2070-AL41 through which the Agency is reconsidering various elements of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, including various workplace exposure controls and prohibitions on certain industrial and commercial uses.
B. Processing TCE as an Intermediate for the Manufacture of HFC-134a
EPA is proposing to amend the compliance deadline for the first phaseout reduction of the processing of TCE as an intermediate for the manufacture of HFC-134a (1,1,1,2-tetrafluroethane; CASRN 811-97-2). Under the 2024 TCE Final Rule, stakeholders processing TCE to manufacture HFC-134a would have to cut the amount of TCE feedstock they use to 75% of their baseline by June 7, 2027. EPA is proposing to amend the compliance deadline so that this reduction in TCE feedstock would instead occur by December 31, 2027.
At the time of publication of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, the public comments EPA had received from the regulated community supported this phaseout schedule. After the publication of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, EPA received new information from Orbia Fluor & Energy Materials (Orbia) regarding the continued need for HFC-134a for military, industrial, and medical applications at rates higher than the 2024 TCE final rule phaseout accounted for (Refs. 6 and 12). Since the publication of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, the 2024 TCE final rule phaseout is no longer in alignment with the AIM Act phasedown because Orbia has received more allowances and anticipates receiving further allowances under the AIM Act to manufacture HFC-134a than initially anticipated (Ref. 6). The demand for HFC-134a from users in critical infrastructure and national security applications is now expected to remain significant through the early 2030s (Ref. 12).
By proposing to amend the compliance deadline for the first phasedown reduction in TCE feedstock volume to be in December instead of June 2027, EPA intends to allow time for a reasonable transition period given the changes in AIM Act allowances received for HFC-134a manufacture. This new compliance deadline will allow manufacturers of HFC-134a to meet needs from critical infrastructure and national security users while allowing for a transition that has a reasonable timeframe and will not produce unintended negative consequences. It is important to amend this compliance date because if the June 2027 date is not changed, HFC-134a manufacturers must otherwise begin curtailing their production of the refrigerant before the demand abates, negatively impacting critical infrastructure and national security application needs. Given the two and a half years provided for this compliance date in the 2024 TCE rule, EPA considers this extension of no more than 6 and a half months to be appropriate because it is “as soon as practicable,” while allowing for “a reasonable transition period” (
15 U.S.C. 2605(d)(1)(B)
and
(E)
).
Separately, EPA has initiated a rulemaking under RIN 2070-AL41 through which the Agency is reconsidering various elements of the 2024 TCE final rule, including stakeholders' larger issues with the use of TCE for HFC-134a manufacturing.
C. Downstream Notification
In keeping with the proposed new prohibition compliance deadline for processing TCE as a reactant/intermediate in chemical manufacturing, processing for and industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing aid in certain chemical manufacturing, and the disposal of TCE
(
printed page 65152)
from such processing or uses to industrial pre-treatment, industrial treatment, or publicly owned treatment works, EPA also proposes to amend the downstream notification requirements of the 2024 TCE Final Rule to accurately reflect the restrictions on TCE. Accurate downstream notification is necessary to spread awareness throughout the supply chain of the restrictions on use of TCE under TSCA, as well as provide information to commercial end users about allowable uses of TCE until the prohibition compliance dates. EPA recognizes that the 2024 TCE Final Rule and 2025 Interim Final Rule compliance deadlines for updating the SDS of June 16, 2025, and December 16, 2025, respectively, have already passed and as such, manufacturers, processors, and distributors in commerce of TCE would need to update or amend their SDS shortly after doing so already. EPA proposes that 30 days from the publication of the final rule is a practicable time to update the SDS for manufacturers, processors, and distributors in commerce of TCE.
IV. Requests for Comment
EPA is requesting public comment on all aspects of this proposal. EPA notes that the proposed compliance dates may be subject to change depending on the timing of the final rulemaking and public comment.
1. EPA requests comment on the changes proposed in this action, including whether stakeholders have any serious reliance interests that may be impacted and, if so, how such interests should be accounted for in any final action.
2. EPA requests comment on a stakeholder requested alternative compliance deadline of December 18, 2028, for the TCE uses that this rule proposes to extend, and whether there is a basis that this longer deadline, compared to the proposed date of December 31, 2027, would be “as soon as practicable,” while allowing for “a reasonable transition period.” (
15 U.S.C. 2605(d)(1)(B)
and
(E)
) (Ref. 13).
3. EPA requests comment on an expedited (
e.g.,
14 day) or immediate effective date of this extension rule because the December 18, 2026, compliance deadline is fast approaching.

VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews
Additional information about these statutes and Executive Orders can be found at
https://www.epa.gov/​laws-regulations/​laws-and-executive-orders
.
A.
Executive Order 12866
: Regulatory Planning and Review and
Executive Order 13563
: Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review
This action is a significant regulatory action that was submitted to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review under Executive Orders 12866 (
58 FR 51735
, October 4, 1993) and 13563 (
76 FR 3821
, January 21, 2011). Any changes made in response to
Executive Order 12866
review have been documented in the docket.
B.
Executive Order 14192
: Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation
This action is expected to be an
Executive Order 14192
deregulatory action because the action is expected to result in cost savings, as discussed in Unit I.E.
C. Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA)
This action does not impose any new information collection activities or burden subject to OMB review and approval under the PRA,
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
However, this action defers the costs associated with paperwork and
(
printed page 65153)
recordkeeping burden for an existing information collection because the delayed compliance dates alter the time horizon of the collection's analysis. Burden is defined in
5 CFR 1320.3(b)
. OMB has previously approved the information collection activities contained in the existing regulations and associated burden under OMB Control No. 2070-0232 (EPA ICR No. 2775.02). An agency may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to a collection of information that requires OMB approval under PRA, unless it has been approved by OMB and displays a currently valid OMB control number. The OMB control numbers for EPA's regulations in
title 40 of the CFR
, after appearing in the
Federal Register
, are listed in
40 CFR part 9
, and included on the related collection instrument or form, if applicable.
D. Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)
I certify that this action will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the RFA,
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.
In making this determination, EPA concludes that the impact of concern for this action is any significant adverse economic impact on small entities, and the Agency is certifying that this rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities because the rule relieves regulatory burden on the small entities subject to the rule. This action would extend the compliance date for the prohibition on processing TCE as a reactant/intermediate and the industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing aid and their associated disposal until 2028, the compliance date for the first phase of the phaseout of TCE processing in the manufacture of HFC-134a until 2028, and the compliance deadline for downstream notification and the text required to be present in SDSs for TCE starting 30 days after publication of the final rule. We have therefore concluded that this action will relieve regulatory burden for all directly regulated small entities.
E. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA)
This action does not contain an unfunded mandate as described in UMRA,
2 U.S.C. 1531-1538
, and does not significantly or uniquely affect small governments. The costs involved in this action are estimated not to exceed $187 million in 2024$ ($100 million in 1995$, adjusted for inflation using the GDP implicit price deflator) or more in any one year. EPA estimates the annualized cost savings of extending compliance dates in this action to be $0.04-0.06 million.
F.
Executive Order 13132
: Federalism
This action does not have federalism implications as specified in
Executive Order 13132
(
64 FR 43255
, August 10, 1999) because it will not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
G.
Executive Order 13175
: Consultation and Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments
This action does not have Tribal implications as specified in
Executive Order 13175
(
65 FR 67249
, November 9, 2000) because it does not have substantial direct effects on one or more Indian Tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes. Thus,
Executive Order 13175
does not apply to this action.
H.
Executive Order 13045
: Protection of Children From Environmental Health Risks and Safety Risks
Executive Order 13045
(
62 FR 19885
, April 23, 1997) directs federal agencies to include an evaluation of the health and safety effects of the planned regulation on children in federal health and safety standards and explain why the regulation is preferable to potentially effective and reasonably feasible alternatives. This action is not subject to
Executive Order 13045
because it is not a significant regulatory action under section 3(f)(1) of
Executive Order 12866
, and because the EPA does not believe the environmental health or safety risks addressed by this action present a disproportionate risk to children.
Nevertheless, as in the 2024 TCE final rule, EPA's Policy on Children's Health applies to this action. The environmental health or safety risks addressed by the 2024 TCE final rule present a disproportionate risk to children due to TCE's developmental toxicity, as described in Unit VIII.G of that rule. However, this action would not alter the requirements of the final rule promulgated in 2024 that addresses the unreasonable risks presented by TCE under its conditions of use. Rather, this action would delay when entities must comply with certain provisions in order to provide a reasonable transition period for compliance as required under TSCA section 6(d)(1)(E). Information on how the Policy was applied in the 2024 TCE final rule and on that action's health and risk assessments is available under Units II.C., II.D. and IV.A of the final rule as well as in the 2020 Risk Evaluation, and the Economic Analysis for the final rule.
I.
Executive Order 13211
: Actions Concerning Regulations That Significantly Affect Energy Supply, Distribution, or Use
This action is not a “significant energy action” as defined in
Executive Order 13211
(
66 FR 28355
, May 22, 2001) because it is not likely to have a significant adverse effect on the supply, distribution or use of energy.
J. National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act (NTTAA)
This action does not involve technical standards under NTTAA section 12(d),
15 U.S.C. 272
. EPA determined that the 2024 TCE final rule involves environmental monitoring or measurement for occupational inhalation exposures and, consistent with the Agency's Performance Based Measurement System, decided not to require the use of specific, prescribed analytic methods. However, this action would simply extend compliance dates as described in Unit III.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice of intent to prepare a PEIS, open a public scoping period, and hold public scoping meetings.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969, as amended (NEPA) and FAA Order 1050.1G,
FAA National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures,
FAA is announcing its intent to prepare a PEIS analyzing Space Exploration Technologies Corp.'s (SpaceX) proposal to increase Starship-Super Heavy operations at the Boca Chica Launch Site at Starbase, TX and expand Starship landing and expenditure locations. Subsequent license modifications or renewals under
14 CFR part 400
are within the scope of the PEIS, and the issuance of temporary airspace closures associated with the Proposed Action are included in FAA's Federal Action. FAA is requesting comments concerning the scope and content of the PEIS. A Draft PEIS will be released for public review and comment at a later date.
DATES:
FAA invites interested agencies, organizations, Native American Tribes, and members of the public to submit comments on alternatives and impacts and on relevant information, studies, or analyses with respect to the proposed agency action. The public scoping period starts with the publication of this Notice in the
Federal Register
. To ensure sufficient time to consider issues identified during the public scoping period, comments should be submitted by one of the methods listed under
ADDRESSES
no later than November 30, 2026. All comments will receive the same attention and consideration in the preparation of the PEIS.
ADDRESSES:
Comments, statements, or questions concerning scoping issues may be provided to FAA as follows:
Federal E-Rulemaking Portal:
http://www.regulations.gov
.
Search for Docket No. FAA-2026-12808 to retrieve the docket and follow the instructions to submit a comment. Please note that all comments submitted to the docket will be posted on the internet without changes, including any personal identifying information provided.
By U.S. mail to:
Ms. Amy Hanson, FAA Environmental Protection Specialist, SpaceX Boca Chica, c/o Kimley-Horn, 767 Eustis Street, Suite 100, St. Paul, MN 55114.
We encourage the submission of comments electronically through the Federal E-Rulemaking Portal. If comments are submitted electronically, it is not necessary to also submit a hard copy. All comments received will be posted without change to
http://www.regulations.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
Starship-Super Heavy is composed of two stages:
Super Heavy is the first stage
(
printed page 65290)
(or booster), and Starship is the second stage. SpaceX proposes to increase Starship-Super Heavy launch, as well as Super Heavy and Starship landing operations at the Boca Chica Launch Site at Starbase, TX. In addition, SpaceX proposes to expand Starship landing and expenditure locations to support the evolving needs of the Starship program and broader space exploration objectives. Currently, SpaceX is authorized by FAA to conduct up to 25 annual launches and 50 total annual landings (25 of the Starship and 25 of the Super Heavy) per year at the Boca Chica Launch Site at Starbase, TX. The Boca Chica Launch Site at Starbase, TX is an exclusive-use launch site that serves as SpaceX's primary research, development, and flight test launch facility for Starship-Super Heavy. Additional information can be found on the project website at:
https://www.faa.gov/​space/​stakeholder_​engagement/​spacex_​starship/​activity_​archive
.
Proposed Action
This PEIS will evaluate a maximum annual capacity of up to 456 annual launches originating from and up to 912 annual landings at the Boca Chica Launch Site at Starbase, TX.
Phase 1 would include up to 100 annual launches and up to 200 annual landings (100 of the Starship and 100 of the Super Heavy). Launches and landings could occur at any day or time of the week. As the vehicle continues to mature and reliability improves, launch and landing rates are expected to increase. Starship and Super Heavy are designed to require minimal post-flight refurbishment.
Phase 2 would include up to 456 launches originating from, and 912 annual landings at, the Boca Chica Launch Site at Starbase, TX. Launches could occur at any time of day, but would only occur Monday through Friday. This phase represents a mature program launching more than 100 times annually and would be implemented within several years. These launch and landing thresholds represent the maximum annual number of landings that could occur at the Boca Chica Launch Site at Starbase, TX, regardless of the launch origin, and bound the analysis in this PEIS.
SpaceX's Proposed Action within the context of this PEIS is to increase launch and landing operations at the Boca Chica Launch Site at Starbase, TX and expand Starship landing and expenditure locations to support the evolving needs of the Starship-Super Heavy program and broader space exploration objectives. The landing thresholds outlined herein represent the maximum annual number of landings that could occur at the Boca Chica Launch Site at Starbase, TX, regardless of the launch origin. Any currently unforeseen, future proposed increase in launch or landing cadence would require additional NEPA review. Super Heavy would either land at the launch site, soft water land in the Gulf of America, or be intentionally expended during flight. Starship would either land at the launch site; soft water land in the Gulf of America or in the broad open ocean; or be expended in the broad open ocean. Launches may occur during the day or night. For the purposes of the PEIS analysis, it is assumed that half of the launches and landings would occur during the day (7 a.m. to 10 p.m.) and half would occur at night (10 p.m. to 7 a.m.).
Starship-Super Heavy launch trajectories would be specific to each particular mission. Approved trajectories would be based on launch vehicle performance and characteristics and would satisfy
14 CFR Chapter III
regulations. Launch azimuths for the Starship-Super Heavy (the initial direction of travel for the vehicle for launch) would range from 40 degrees to 115 degrees, from a reference of due north at 0 degrees and due east at 90 degrees. Super Heavy landing trajectories would also be within the Starship-Super Heavy launch azimuth range. Starship landing trajectories would range from 155 degrees to 185 degrees and 240 degrees to 340 degrees.
The potential environmental impacts of all proposed operational activities, including those from launches and landings, will be analyzed in the PEIS. The PEIS will evaluate the potential environmental impacts associated with aviation emissions and air quality; biological resources (including fish, wildlife, and plants); coastal resources; Department of Transportation Act, Section 4(f); Land and Water Conservation Fund Act, Section 6(f); farmlands; hazardous materials, solid waste, and pollution prevention; historical, architectural, archaeological, and cultural resources; land use; natural resources and energy supply; noise and noise-compatible land use; socioeconomics and children's health and safety risks; visual effects; and water resources (including wetlands, floodplains, surface waters, groundwater, and wild and scenic rivers). This analysis will consist of an evaluation of potential reasonably foreseeable impacts resulting from the Proposed Action, as compared to a No Action Alternative.
Concurrently with the NEPA process, FAA is initiating National Historic Preservation Act Section 106 consultation to determine the potential effects of the Proposed Action on historic properties. In addition, FAA is consulting with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regarding potential impacts on federally listed threatened and endangered species. FAA is also consulting with the National Marine Fisheries Service under Section 7 of the ESA and the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act for potential impacts on protected marine species. Pursuant to the U.S. Department of Transportation Act of 1966, the PEIS will comply with the requirements of Section 4(f) of the Act (codified at
49 U.S.C. 303
), as applicable.
Alternatives
FAA Order 1050.1G defines reasonable alternatives as those that are technically and economically feasible, meet the purpose and need for the Proposed Action, and, where applicable, meet the goals of the applicant. Prior NEPA documents have established the Boca Chica Launch Site at Starbase, TX as an approved location for Starship-Super Heavy operations. The Boca Chica Launch Site at Starbase, TX already has the necessary infrastructure to support launch operations, therefore other sites are not reasonable alternatives and do not meet the purpose and need of this project. Given these facts, the only alternative to the Proposed Action as described in this PEIS is the No Action Alternative.
Under the No Action Alternative, FAA would not modify SpaceX's launch license for Starship- Super Heavy launch and reentry operations from the Boca Chica Launch Site at Starbase, TX and would not issue any additional associated temporary airspace closures. In this scenario, SpaceX would be permitted to operate at the cadence approved in the 2025
Final Tiered Environmental Assessment and Mitigated Finding of No Significant Impact and Record of Decision for SpaceX Starship/Super Heavy Vehicle Increased Cadence at the SpaceX Boca Chica Launch Site in Cameron County, Texas.
Potential impacts associated with the No Action Alternative will be analyzed in the PEIS.
Scoping Meetings
FAA will hold four IN-PERSON public scoping meetings and one VIRTUAL public scoping meeting. The meetings will allow the public to receive information on the Proposed
(
printed page 65291)
Action and provide comments to the record.
The IN-PERSON meetings will be held on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, and Thursday, November 19, 2026. The November 17, 2026, meetings will be held from 1:00 p.m.-3:00 p.m. and 5:30 p.m.-7:30 p.m. (Central) at the Texas Southmost College, Jacob Brown Auditorium, 600 International Blvd., Brownsville, TX 78520. The November 19, 2026, meetings will be held from 1:00 p.m.-3:00 p.m. and 5:30 p.m.-7:30 p.m. (Central) at the Port Isabel Event & Cultural Center, 309 Railroad St, Port Isabel, TX 78578. The IN-PERSON meetings will consist of an open house information-station format wherein FAA will provide information describing the purpose of the scoping meetings, project schedule, opportunities for public involvement, the Proposed Action and alternatives summary, and environmental resource area summary. The public will have the opportunity to provide verbal comments to a court reporter or written comments via a written comment form at one of several commenting stations at any time during the meetings.
A VIRTUAL meeting will be held on November 18, 2026; 5:30 p.m.-7:30 p.m. (Central); the URL and call-in number for the meeting will be provided in advance on FAA's project website:
https://www.faa.gov/​space/​stakeholder_​engagement/​spacex_​starship
.
The virtual meeting will consist of a closed-captioned auto-run presentation describing the purpose of the scoping meetings, project schedule, opportunities for public involvement, Proposed Action and alternatives summary, and environmental resource area summary. The pre-recorded presentation will be run at the beginning of the meeting, followed by an opportunity for formal comments. Members of the public may provide comments verbally during the virtual meeting; comments received via the chat function will not be part of the public record. A moderator will facilitate verbal comments. English-Spanish translation services for verbal comments will be provided. Both English and Spanish versions of the presentation will be made available to the public on FAA's project website no later than November 10, 2026. If additional accommodations for the public meetings are needed beyond the planned Spanish translation services, please submit a request by November 2, 2026, to the project email address:
spacexbocachica@icf.com
.
More information regarding the scoping meetings, is available on FAA's project website:
https://www.faa.gov/​space/​stakeholder_​engagement/​spacex_​starship
.
Marcus Ward,
Division Manager, Safety Assurance Division, Commercial Space Transportation, Federal Aviation Administration.

7 CFR part 340
, “Introduction of Organisms and Products Altered or Produced Through Genetic Engineering Which Are Plant Pests or Which There Is Reason to Believe Are Plant Pests,” Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) regulates, among other things, the introduction (importation, interstate movement, or release into the environment) of organisms and products altered or produced through genetic engineering that are plant pests or that there is reason to believe are plant pests. Such organisms and products are considered “regulated articles.” Section 340.6(a) of the regulations (
7 CFR 340.6(a)
) provides that any person may submit a petition to APHIS seeking a determination that an article should not be regulated under
7 CFR part 340
.
APHIS received a petition (APHIS Petition Number 25-205-01p) from Ball Horticultural Company (BHC) seeking a determination of nonregulated status for African marigold (
Tagetes erecta
) event pBALL123-022-BE113, designated as pBALL123, which has been developed using genetic engineering to produce red flower petals. The petition provides information in support of petitioners' position that pBALL123 is unlikely to pose a plant pest risk and therefore should not be regulated under APHIS' regulations in
7 CFR part 340
.
As part of our decision-making process regarding the organism's regulatory status, APHIS prepared a draft plant pest risk assessment (PPRA) to assess the plant pest risk of the organism.
APHIS published the petition and draft PPRA in the
Federal Register
(
91 FR 6179
, APHIS-2026-0001) and accepted public comments from February 11, 2026, through April 13, 2026. APHIS received 3 comments by the close of the comment period that were posted to the docket. APHIS received comments from a horticultural industry organization, a non-governmental organization, and an unaffiliated individual. Of the 3 comments posted to the docket, two were in support of deregulation of pBALL123, and one was in opposition.
Determination
Based on APHIS' evaluation in the PPRA of information and data submitted by BHC in its petition, available scientific data, and public comments received in response to the petition and draft PPRA, APHIS has determined that pBALL123 is unlikely to pose a greater plant pest risk than the nonmodified comparator and therefore is no longer subject to the regulations in
7 CFR part 340
governing the introduction of certain organisms developed using genetic engineering.
Copies of the signed determination, PPRA, and response to comments, as well as the previously published petition and supporting documents, are available as indicated in the
ADDRESSES
and
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
sections of this notice.

and
7781-7786
;
31 U.S.C. 9701
;
7 CFR 2.22
,
2.80
, and
371.3
.)

AGENCY:
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
ACTION:
Interim final rule.
SUMMARY:
This interim final rule (IFR) amends Department of Homeland Security (DHS) regulations to expedite termination of refugee status when DHS determines an alien was not a refugee within the meaning of section 101(a)(42) of the Immigration and Nationality Act at the time of admission to the United States. The response period to a Notice of Intent to Terminate (NOIT) is reduced from thirty to ten days. These changes aim to restore integrity to the immigration system, mitigate risks to national security and public safety, and prevent fraud and exploitation.
DATES:
This IFR is effective on October 14, 2026. Written comments and related materials must be submitted on or before November 13, 2026. The electronic Federal Docket Management System will accept comments prior to midnight Eastern Time at the end of that day.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments on the entirety of this rulemaking package, identified by DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0397, through the Federal eRulemaking Portal:
https://www.regulations.gov
. Follow the website instructions for submitting comments.
Comments must be submitted in English, or an English translation must be provided. Comments that will provide the most assistance to USCIS in implementing these changes will reference a specific portion of the Interim Final Rule, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include data, information, or authority that support such recommended change. Comments submitted in a manner other than the one listed above, including emails or letters sent to DHS or USCIS officials, will not be considered comments on the Interim Final Rule and may not receive a response from DHS. Please note that DHS and USCIS cannot accept any comments that are hand-delivered or couriered. In addition, USCIS cannot accept comments contained on any form of digital media storage devices, such as CDs/DVDs and USB drives. USCIS is also not accepting mailed comments at this time. If you cannot submit your comment by using
https://www.regulations.gov
,
please contact the Regulatory Coordination Division, Office of Policy and Strategy, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Department of Homeland Security, by telephone at (240) 721-3000 for alternate instructions.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Security, Public Safety, and Global Vetting Division (SPSG), Office of Policy & Strategy, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), DHS, 5900 Capital Gateway Drive, Camp Springs, MD 20746; telephone (240) 721-3000. Individuals with hearing or speech impairments may access the telephone number above via TTY by calling the toll-free Federal Information Relay Service at 711.

I. Public Participation
DHS invites all interested parties to participate in this rulemaking by submitting written data, views, comments and arguments on all aspects
(
printed page 65078)
of this IFR. DHS also invites comments that relate to the economic, environmental, or federalism effects that might result from this IFR. Comments must be submitted in English, or an English translation must be provided. Comments that will provide the most assistance to USCIS in implementing these changes will reference a specific portion of the IFR, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include data, information, or authority that support such recommended change. Comments submitted in a manner other than the one listed above, including emails or letters sent to DHS or USCIS officials, will not be considered comments on the IFR and may not receive a response from DHS.
Instructions:
If you submit a comment, you must include the agency name (U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services) and the DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0397 for this rulemaking. Regardless of the method used for submitting comments or material, all submissions will be posted, without change, to the Federal eRulemaking Portal at

,

You may wish to consider limiting the amount of personal information that you provide in any voluntary public comment submission you make to DHS. For additional information, please read the Privacy and Security Notice available at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
