I. Executive Summary
A. Basis and Purpose
DHS's mission is to safeguard the American people, our homeland, and our values with honor and integrity. In service of that mission, DHS protects the United States from threats by terrorists, criminals, smugglers, transnational criminal organizations, failed-state actors, and unpredictable lone offenders that constitute present and future threats to public safety and national security.
USCIS issues EADs to certain classes of aliens. These documents are valid for a specified period. Aliens who intend to continue their employment beyond the date specified on their EAD must generally file an application to renew their employment authorization and/or EAD.
The automatic extension of the validity of an EAD grants the alien the benefit of extending his or her expired employment authorization and/or EAD merely by filing a timely renewal EAD application and without first completing adjudicative review and related vetting, including resolution of any derogatory information identified during the vetting process. That is, the automatic extension allows for the granting of the benefit without USCIS first performing the following actions: an eligibility determination, completing vetting and screening checks, resolving potential hits of derogatory information in connection with the alien, and a determination that the employment authorization should be granted in the exercise of discretion, if applicable.
On October 30, 2025, DHS issued an IFR titled, “Removal of the Automatic Extension of Employment Authorization Documents,” with a request for comment.
See
90 FR 48799
(Oct. 30, 2025). The IFR amended DHS regulations to end the practice of automatically extending the validity of EADs for aliens in certain employment authorization categories who timely filed an application to renew their EAD. After careful consideration of the public comments submitted in connection with the IFR, DHS is reaffirming and finalizing the IFR without changes. The rationale and reasoning provided in the preamble for the IFR remains unchanged with respect to the regulatory amendments, and DHS, therefore, adopts such reasoning also to support this final rule.
In reaffirming and finalizing the changes made in the IFR, the purpose of this rule remains the same as articulated in the IFR: to prioritize the proper vetting and screening of aliens and ensure continued eligibility before granting a new period of employment authorization and/or a new EAD by ending the practice of automatically extending the validity of employment authorization and/or EADs for certain employment authorization categories.
Ending the practice of providing automatic extensions of EADs is consistent with Section 16 of President Trump's directive in Executive Order (E.O.) 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion, which directs the Secretary of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Secretary of State and the Attorney General, to take all appropriate action to align any departmental activities with the policies set out by the President and to ensure, among others, “that employment authorization is provided in a manner consistent with section 274A of the Immigration and Nationality Act (
8 U.S.C. 1324a
), and that employment authorization is not provided to any unauthorized alien in the United States.”
[
1
]
It is also consistent with Section 2 of
E.O. 14161
, Protecting the United States From Foreign Terrorists and Other National Security and Public Safety Threats, which directs the Secretary of State, in coordination with the Secretary of Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National Intelligence to “identify all resources that may be used to ensure that all aliens seeking admission to the United States, or who are already in the United States, are vetted and screened to the maximum degree possible.”
[
2
]
B. Legal Authority
The legal basis of this rulemaking is found in section 103(a) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA),
8 U.S.C. 1103(a)
, which authorizes the Secretary to administer and enforce the immigration and nationality laws and establish such regulations as the Secretary deems necessary for carrying out such authority, and section 101(b)(1)(F) of the Homeland Security Act (HSA),
6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F)
, which establishes as a primary mission of DHS the duty to “ensure that the overall economic security of the United States is not diminished by efforts, activities, and programs aimed at securing the homeland.”
C. Summary of the Major Provisions of the Regulatory Action
This final rule adopts the IFR as final, without any changes, after careful consideration of the comments received. Accordingly, DHS is adopting as final the following changes that the IFR has made:
Revised the heading of
8 CFR 274a.13(d)
to clearly indicate that the up-to-540-day automatic extension period only applies to renewal EAD applications filed before October 30, 2025.
Added new
8 CFR 274a.13(e)
. The new provision explains that, unless otherwise provided in
8 CFR 274a.13(d)
, by law, or through a
Federal Register
notice for Temporary Protected Status (TPS)-related employment documentation, the validity period of an expired or expiring Employment Authorization Document and/or employment authorization will not be automatically extended by a renewal EAD application filed on or after October 30, 2025.
DHS explained in the IFR that the IFR did not impact the validity of EADs that were automatically extended prior to October 30, 2025. It also explained that the IFR did not impact automatic extensions of EADs and/or employment authorization provided by law or
Federal Register
notices, such as those for TPS applicants pursuant to section 244 of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1254a
, and
8 CFR part 244
.
[
3
]
This final rule similarly does not impact these provisions.
D. Costs and Benefits
This final rule has been designated a “significant regulatory action” and economically significant as defined under section 3(f)(1) of
E.O. 12866
, because its annual effects on the economy may exceed $100 million in any year of the analysis. Accordingly, this rule has been reviewed by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB).
(
printed page 65308)
This final rule reaffirms and finalizes changes made by the IFR to DHS regulations to end the practice of automatically extending the validity of employment authorization documents (Forms I-766 or EADs) for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew their EAD in certain employment authorization categories. The purpose of this change is to prioritize the proper vetting and screening of aliens and ensure continued eligibility before granting a new period of employment authorization and/or a new EAD. This final rule does not affect the validity of EADs that were automatically extended prior to the IFR. In previous rules providing for the automatic extension of EADs based on the timely filing of a renewal EAD application, DHS attempted to stabilize aliens' earnings and avoid labor turnover costs of employers. However, as explained in the IFR, the Department has shifted focus to prioritizing public safety and national security, and ensuring that aliens continue to be eligible and merit a favorable exercise of discretion, as applicable, before being granted continued employment authorization.
See
90 FR 48799
,
48816
(Oct. 30, 2025).
DHS has prepared two types of quantified estimates of the impacts generated by this final rule. For a single 18-month window (starting in May 2027) from about 20,000 to 33,000 EADs are estimated to lapse, based on several assumptions. This rule may result in some EAD holders incurring a loss of earnings (“reduced earnings”) because of USCIS process delays for renewal EAD applications, as under this rule there could be disruption to their earnings due to a lapsed EAD. Such earnings loss to aliens could comprise beneficial transfers to other U.S. workers if the substitution of the latter for the former is relatively frictionless. Additionally, to the extent this rule affects EAD holders' jobs going unfilled, there will be impacts to tax transfers from businesses and employees to the Federal Government.
[
4
]
This rule will also generate labor turnover costs to businesses that employ the affected-lapsed EAD holders, as under this rule there would be a disruption to the EAD holders' employment authorization and/or document validity. In conducting these estimates DHS emphasizes that variation in factors involved in the impact, including impact processing times, filing volumes, the timing of renewal filings, and underlying benefit requests, will cause variation in the impacts.
Due to variation in future populations and process times, there is likely to be substantial variation in the impact estimates. For this reason, DHS develops wide ranges capturing a high and low bound for the estimates, in terms of the means (expected value). This rule is estimated to result in $138.1 million in lost productivity costs to employers that are not able to easily replace aliens with lapsed EADs, costs of $312.1 million to U.S. employers from potential labor turnover, transfers due to earnings changes worth $138.1 million from employment-authorized aliens to replacement workers and is expected to generate tax reduction impacts of $14.5 million over an 18-month period. Approximately 1,700 and 2,800 employers are estimated to be impacted.
Section V.B. provides an A-4 accounting statement supporting the analysis and the accompanying economic analysis details the data and methodology supporting the impact estimates.
II. Background
A. Legal Authority
The Secretary of Homeland Security's (Secretary) authority for the regulatory amendments made in this final rule are found in various sections of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1101
et seq.,
and the HSA,
Public Law 107-296
, 116 Stat. 2135 (codified in part at
6 U.S.C. 101
et seq.
).
General authority for issuing this rule is found in section 103(a) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1103(a)
, which authorizes the Secretary to administer and enforce the immigration and nationality laws and establish such regulations as the Secretary deems necessary for carrying out such authority, as well as section 102 of the HSA,
6 U.S.C. 112
, which vests all of the functions of DHS in the Secretary and authorizes the Secretary to issue regulations.
[
5
]
Further authority for this rule is found in:
Section 208(d)(2) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(2)
, which provides the Secretary with authority to grant employment authorization, in his or her discretion, to applicants for asylum if 180 days have passed since filing an application for asylum;
Section 214 of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1184
, including section 214(a)(1) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1184(a)(1)
, which authorizes the Secretary to prescribe, by regulation, the time and conditions of the admission of nonimmigrants;
Section 244(a)(1)(B) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1254a(a)(1)(B)
, which states that the Secretary shall authorize employment and provide evidence of employment authorization for aliens who have been granted Temporary Protected Status;
Section 274A(b) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1324a(b)
, which provides for the employment verification system and outlines employment eligibility verification requirements;
Section 274A(h)(3)(B) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1324a(h)(3)(B)
, which recognizes the Secretary's authority to extend employment authorization to aliens in the United States;
[
6
]
and
Sections 100003(c) and 100012(a) of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act,
Public Law 119-21
(July 4, 2025), which limit the validity period of any employment authorization for aliens granted TPS under section 244 of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1254a
, to either a period of one year or for the duration of the designation of TPS, whichever is shorter.
B. Automatic Extension of Employment Authorization and Documentation
Before November 2016,
8 CFR 274a.13(d)
stated that USCIS would adjudicate an EAD application within 90 days of receipt. If USCIS did not adjudicate the EAD application within that timeframe, the alien was eligible to request an interim EAD with a validity period not to exceed 240 days.
[
7
]
On November 18, 2016, as part of DHS's efforts to implement the American Competitiveness in the
(
printed page 65309)
Twenty-first Century Act of 2000 (AC21), DHS published a final rule that eliminated Interim EADs and replaced them with a maximum 180-day automatic extension period for certain renewal applicants.
[
8
]
C. Increasing the Automatic Extension Period From a Maximum of 180 Days to a Maximum of 540 Days
Since the promulgation of the final rule authorizing up to 180-day automatic extension period for certain renewal EAD applicants, USCIS' ability to process both initial and renewal EAD applications within USCIS' targeted processing times was adversely impacted by a variety of temporary circumstances.
[
9
]
In May 2022
[
10
]
and April 2024,
[
11
]
DHS temporarily increased the automatic extension from up to 180 days to up to 540 days. The May 2022 and April 2024 temporary final rules were intended to reduce the number of renewal EAD applicants eligible for an automatic extension of their EAD validity under
8 CFR 274a.13(d)
experiencing lapses in their employment authorization and/or EAD validity because of USCIS processing delays.
DHS also issued a final rule in December 2024
[
12
]
that indefinitely increased the up to 540-day automatic extension for certain applications pending on May 4, 2022, or properly filed on or after May 4, 2022. That rule was intended to reduce the effects of unknown future circumstances that could significantly impact EAD renewal processing times.
[
13
]
D. The 2025 Interim Final Rule Removed Automatic Extensions for Certain Employment Authorization Documents
The IFR amended DHS regulations to end the practice of automatically extending the validity of certain EADs.
See
8 CFR 274a.13(e)
. The IFR did not impact the automatic extensions already granted to renewal EAD applicants under
8 CFR 274a.13(d)(1)
, if the renewal EAD application was filed before October 30, 2025.
See
8 CFR 274a.13(d)
. The IFR also did not impact automatic extensions otherwise provided by law or in an applicable
Federal Register
notice regarding procedures for renewing TPS-related employment documentation pursuant to section 244 of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1254a
, and
8 CFR part 244
.
14
See
8 CFR 274a.13(e)
.
The IFR made two changes to the regulations governing EAD, as discussed below.
1. Added New
8 CFR 274a.13(e)
The IFR added a new paragraph (e) that went into effect immediately with the publication of the IFR on October 30, 2025. With
8 CFR 274a.13(e)
, DHS eliminated the practice of providing automatic extension periods for employment authorization and/or EAD validity for up to 540 days for renewal applications filed on or after October 30, 2025. Therefore, renewal EAD applicants no longer receive an up to 540-day automatic extension of their employment authorization and/or EAD validity if they file their application on or after October 30, 2025.
See
8 CFR 274a.13(e)
.
Except as otherwise provided by law, in
8 CFR 274a.13(d)
, or in accordance with an applicable
Federal Register
notice regarding procedures for renewing TPS-related employment documentation, an alien's employment authorization and/or EAD validity will expire as explained in the following paragraphs:
For those aliens who are employment authorized incident to status under
8 CFR 274a.12(a)
, unless otherwise provided by law, their EAD will expire on the day after the end validity date stated on the face of the EAD.
See
8 CFR 274a.13(e)(1)
. Because the alien's employment authorization is tied to the alien's status in the United States, the alien's employment authorization will not expire on the date indicated on the EAD. Instead, the alien's employment authorization will expire or terminate on the same date the alien's status in the United States expires or terminates.
For example, an alien in L-2 nonimmigrant status as the spouse of an L-1 nonimmigrant is employment authorized incident to status.
See
INA sec. 214(c)(2)(E),
8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(2)(E)
. If the L-2 nonimmigrant chooses to apply for an EAD to evidence his or her employment authorization, the EAD will expire as of the date indicated on the face of the EAD. In some cases that may be the same date as the expiration of the L-2's nonimmigrant status. But in other cases, the L-2 status expiration date may be after the EAD expiration date, particularly if the L-2 nonimmigrant travelled outside of the United States after obtaining an EAD and, upon return to the United States, was provided a new status expiration date that will expire after the EAD expires.
[
15
]
In that scenario, the L-2 nonimmigrant would remain employment authorized while in L-2 nonimmigrant status, even after the EAD expires, but the expired EAD would no longer be a valid document to evidence the L-2 nonimmigrant's employment authorization.
[
16
]
Once the alien is no longer in L-2 status (for example, the L-2 nonimmigrant status expires), the alien would no longer be employment authorized as an L-2 nonimmigrant because such employment authorization is dependent on being in L-2 nonimmigrant status.

E. Severability
In issuing this final rule, like the IFR, DHS continues to intend that the rule's various provisions be considered severable from one another to the greatest extent possible. For instance, if a court of competent jurisdiction were to hold that ending the practice of automatically extending the validity of employment authorization and/or EADs for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew their employment authorization and/or EAD in certain employment categories may only be applied to a particular category of renewal EAD applicants or in a particular circumstance, DHS would intend for the court to leave the remainder of the rule in place with respect to all other covered persons and circumstances. DHS's overarching goal is to militate against threats to national security and public safety and to ensure that employment authorization and/or EADs are provided only after USCIS conducts adequate vetting and determines that the alien continues to be eligible and merits a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable.

IV. Response to Public Comments on the Interim Final Rule
A. Summary of Comments
When issuing the IFR, DHS invited the public to participate in the rulemaking by submitting post-promulgation comments on every aspect of the rule. DHS provided a 33-day comment period following the publication of the IFR. DHS received 653 public comment submissions in the Federal eRulemaking Portal site under Docket ID Number USCIS-2025-0271
[
23
]
in response to the rulemaking.
Comments were submitted by a range of entities and individuals, including attorneys and legal service providers, applicants, individual commenters, professional organizations, unions, advocacy groups, religious organizations, research and community organizations, and State and local government agencies or elected officials. Some commenters expressed support for the rule or offered suggestions for improvement. Some expressed general opposition to the rule, and some offered alternatives. For some of the public
(
printed page 65311)
comments, DHS could not ascertain whether the commenter supported or opposed the IFR. Finally, some commenters addressed topics outside the scope of this rulemaking.
DHS carefully reviewed all the public comments received in response to the IFR and addresses relevant comments in this final rule, grouped by subject area.
B. Comments in Support of the Rule
Comment:
Several commenters supported the rule based on national security concerns, citing the need for proper vetting of nonimmigrant workers. Specifically, they stated that the rule would allow for thorough vetting of nonimmigrants before DHS extends their authorization to work in the United States. Commenters called the rule a “critical” measure to support the safety and security of the public. One commenter emphasized that working in the United States is a privilege, not a right, while another said that safety and national security should be government's highest priority.
Several commenters supported the rule based on concerns about fraud and abuse in the visa system, stating, for example, that it would help deter potential fraud and abuse by preventing aliens from remaining in the workforce for extended periods without final adjudication of their eligibility.
Multiple commenters supported the rule based on concerns about protecting job opportunities for American citizens. A commenter stated that automatic extensions keep nonimmigrant workers employed without timely reevaluation, allowing them to compete with American workers for positions while requiring renewed authorization before continuing employment ensures that only eligible aliens remain in the workforce.
Response:
DHS agrees that this rule safeguards the process to fully evaluate the applicants in order to determine continued eligibility, identify national security and public safety concerns, and enhance fraud prevention through robust vetting and screening processes. This administration prioritizes the safety of the American people. Ensuring that employment authorization and/or EADs are provided only after USCIS conducts adequate vetting and determines that the alien continues to be eligible and merits a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable, better protects national security, public safety, and the integrity of the immigration system. This rule is part of a larger DHS effort to reduce frivolous, fraudulent, and otherwise non-meritorious EAD filings and focus adjudicatory and other resources on ensuring national security and program integrity.
C. Comments in Opposition to the Rule and Mixed Comments
1. DHS Legal Authority
i. DHS Statutory Authority and Congressional Intent
Comment:
Multiple commenters requested that the rule be withdrawn stating that the rule contradicts DHS's statutory mandate, including the mandate to ensure that “the overall economic security of the United States is not diminished by efforts . . . aimed at securing the homeland” under
6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F)
. Many of these commenters stated that, consistent with this statutory mandate, DHS recently concluded that a 540-day automatic EAD extension was necessary to protect employers and workers from lapses in work authorization due to USCIS delays, and DHS previously found that even the 180-day extension established under the 2016 Final Rule was not enough time to avoid harmful gaps in work authorization.
Response:
DHS disagrees that this rule is inconsistent with DHS's statutory mandate, including the mandate under
6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F)
. According to
6 U.S.C. 111(b)
, DHS's primary mission includes preventing terrorist attacks within the United States, reducing the vulnerability of the United States to terrorism, minimizing the damage, and assisting in the recovery, from terrorist attacks that occur within the United States, and ensuring that the overall economic security of the United States is not diminished by efforts, activities, and programs aimed at securing the homeland.
See
6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(A)
, (B), (C), and (F). While the provision does not specifically define “economic security,” another provision within
6 U.S.C. Chapter 1
(Homeland Security Organization), defines “economic security” as the “condition of having secure and resilient domestic production capacity, combined with reliable access to the global resources necessary to maintain an acceptable standard of living and to protect core national values.”
See
6 U.S.C. 474(c)(2)
.
[
24
]
In addition, DHS is charged with the implementation of section 274A of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1324a
, preventing unlawful employment of aliens. This rule, which is part of an effort to secure the homeland, supports DHS's mission as provided by Congress in
6 U.S.C. 111(b)
and section 274A of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1324a
, ensures lawful employment, and supports the overall national and economic security of the United States.
Ending the practice of providing automatic extension of employment authorization and/or EADs enhances the benefit integrity in adjudications of employment authorization requests and better protects public safety and national security by ensuring that aliens are properly vetted and determined to be eligible (and merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable), for employment authorization before such authorization is provided to the alien. The automatic extension of an EAD grants the benefit of extending an alien's expired employment authorization and/or EAD merely by filing a timely renewal EAD application and without first completing adjudicative review and related vetting, including resolution of any derogatory information identified during the vetting process. That is, the benefit is granted without USCIS first performing the following actions: an eligibility determination, completing vetting and screening checks, resolving potential hits of derogatory information in connection with the alien, and a determination that the employment authorization should be renewed in the exercise of discretion, if applicable. Without the IFR and this final rule, aliens could still obtain an automatic extension despite derogatory information that could flag them as national security or public safety risks. Automatic extensions, therefore, pose a security risk.
DHS is charged with combating unauthorized employment in accordance with section 274A of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1324a
, which Congress implemented, among other reasons, because of the detrimental negative effect that unauthorized employment and illegal immigration has on the United States and the national economy.
[
25
]
Sections 103 and 274A of
(
printed page 65312)
the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1103(a)
and
8 U.S.C. 1324a
, among other provisions, provide DHS and USCIS with considerable flexibility to administer and enforce the INA, including granting employment authorization and the issuance of an EAD. There is no generally applicable statutory mandate that requires DHS to provide an automatic extension. As explained in the IFR, the automatic extension carries the risk that employers unwittingly continue to employ a worker whose employment authorization is in fact no longer valid.
See
90 FR at 48810. This includes that aliens may no longer be entitled to employment authorization because they no longer have an underlying status which entitles them to work. Additionally, vetting every alien before granting an immigration benefit, including employment authorization, has been one of the key considerations of Congress.
[
26
]
The rule does not eliminate employment authorizations or prevent eligible aliens from obtaining EADs for employment purposes or proof of identity; or from seeking and maintaining authorized employment. The rule does not reduce economic security. To the contrary, the rule supports the condition of having secure and resilient domestic production capacity, and protects core national values, as directed by Congress, with U.S. workers who are legally authorized to work. Therefore, the IFR is consistent with DHS's statutory mandate, including the mandate at
6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F)
, because it appropriately balances the need for security and vetting while maintaining overall EAD eligibility practices.
DHS is cognizant that prior rulemakings stated that DHS believed, at the time, that taking immediate action and providing automatic extensions of employment authorization supported USCIS' (as a component of DHS) statutory mission to administer employment authorization effectively, and as a measure to ensure that the overall economic security was not diminished by potentially harmful gaps in employment authorizations.
See, e.g.,
89 FR 101208
,
101209
(Dec. 13, 2024);
89 FR 24628
,
24629
and
24651
(Apr. 8, 2024). As explained in this response, and throughout this rule, DHS believes that the factual situation underlying prior rules, in particular the Dec. 13, 2024 rule, have significantly changed, including that DHS has taken significant steps to reduce the flood of filings of EADs that overwhelmed USCIS' adjudicative resources.
[
27
]
Furthermore, the 2024 final rule made the automatic extension period permanent based on the presumption that harmful gaps would occur given the operational realities at the time.
[
28
]
Even if the 2024 final rule had taken into account the security posture of the United States, it was unclear how the rule furthered the economic security given that the rule was based on potential harm to individual applicants and their employers, rather than the broader national economy. It is thus unclear how removing the automatic extension period, which improves the security posture of the United States and is consistent with immigration laws, would undermine the overall economic security of the United States.
Comment:
A commenter asserted that removing the automatic extension of employment authorization without ensuring timely adjudication would strip lawfully authorized noncitizens
[
29
]
of their ability to work due to USCIS processing delays, which, according to the commenter, contradicts the intent of the INA and the “right” to work in the United States. Another commenter stated that the IFR incorrectly states that the rule is consistent with section 274A of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1324a
. Another commenter stated that it seems illegal to deny someone a renewal when they have followed the law and have filed the renewal application in a timely manner.
Response:
DHS disagrees with these commenters' assertions. This final rule and the IFR are consistent with section 274A of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1324a
, which, among other things, recognizes the Secretary's authority to grant employment authorization in his or her discretion. DHS disagrees with the commenter's assertion that aliens have a broadly applicable “right” to work in the United States. Rather, the INA makes clear that aliens, to lawfully work in the United States, must be so authorized by law or a grant of employment authorization by the Secretary.
See
INA 274A(h)(3),
8 U.S.C. 1324a(h)(3)
. Contrary to the commenters' assertions, this rule does not impact whether DHS will renew an alien's employment authorization; it only removes an intermediate automatic extension of the EAD period. If DHS determines that the alien is eligible for continued employment authorization and merits a favorable exercise of discretion, as applicable, DHS may grant the renewal of employment authorization. This final rule merely ends the practice of automatically granting the benefit of continued employment authorization without USCIS first performing the following actions: eligibility determination, completing vetting and screening checks, resolving potential hits of derogatory information in connection with the alien, and a determination that the employment authorization should be granted in the exercise of discretion, if applicable.
Comment:
A commenter stated that, when providing the ability for asylum
(
printed page 65313)
