A commenter stated, without pointing to specific provisions, that the IFR should be discontinued because its policy changes do not reflect the law or the intent of the law or even the will of the people who voted for candidates who would make immigration changes.
Response:
DHS disagrees with the commenters' assertion. Section 208(d)(2) of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(2)
, expressly states that “[a]n applicant for asylum is not entitled to employment authorization,” though it also provides the Secretary with authority to grant employment authorization, in his or her discretion, to applicants for asylum if 180 days have passed since filing an application for asylum. The IFR, and this final rule, clearly outline the legal authority for this change, and are consistent with the Secretary's discretionary authority regarding the grant of employment authorization for asylum applicants and the duration of such authorization.
ii. Constitutional Concerns
Comment:
Multiple commenters expressed that the IFR raises First Amendment concerns, because the IFR suggests that USCIS must evaluate whether renewal applicants “bear hostile attitudes” toward U.S. citizens, culture, government, institutions, or founding principles. The commenters reasoned that employment authorization may not be conditioned on ideological conformity and that agency action on unconstitutional factors may not be sustained as it is constitutionally questionable and impermissible. Another commenter stated that an ideological screening regime for work authorization renewals would further entrench USCIS in DHS's “troubling pattern” of suppressing First Amendment rights in the name of national security and opens the door for USCIS to profile individuals.
Response:
DHS disagrees with the commenters. Citizens and aliens may object to various statutes, regulations, and policies and express those objections publicly. This rule neither penalizes individuals for protected political beliefs or associations nor subjects them to activities such as ideological screenings or profiling. This rule does not abridge the freedom of speech, of the press, or of association or peaceful assembly. Rather, it ends the practice of automatically granting the benefit of continued employment authorization without USCIS concurrently performing the following actions: eligibility determination, completing vetting and screening checks, resolving potential hits of derogatory information in connection with the alien, or a determination that the employment authorization should be renewed in the exercise of discretion, if applicable.
DHS notes that freedom of speech for aliens is not absolute.
See, e.g.,
INA sec. 212(a)(3)(B)(i)(VII),
8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(3)(B)(i)(VII)
(stating that any alien who endorses or espouses terrorist activity, or persuades others to endorse or espouse terrorist activity or support a terrorist organization, is inadmissible), and INA sec. 212(a)(6)(C)(ii),
8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(6)(C)(ii)
(stating that any alien who falsely represents, or has falsely represented, himself or herself to be a citizen of the United States for any purpose or benefit under Federal or State law is inadmissible). DHS has a compelling interest in vetting and screening aliens before granting a benefit request, particularly when such request is granted in USCIS' discretion, as applicable.
DHS also notes that a challenge to the First Amendment cannot lie unless an individual establishes that he or she faces a “credible threat of prosecution” specifically for his or her speech, “under a statute [or rule] that appears to render the [individual]'s arguably protected speech illegal.”
See, e.g., Am. Library Ass'n
v.
Barr,
956 F.2d 1178, 1194 (D.C. Cir. 1992). As indicated above, that is not the case in this scenario as neither section 274A of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1324a
, nor the associated regulations, renders any form of speech illegal or attempts to directly or indirectly regulate or penalize speech. Rather, the IFR and this final rule subject all EAD renewal applicants to the same vetting and screening procedures used for initial applications or those applicants who were not previously eligible for an automatic extension of their renewal employment authorization and/or EAD.
Comment:
Several commenters raised concerns related to due process. Referencing the Fifth Amendment, a commenter stated that the IFR undermines the right to due process and the right to seek asylum by eliminating automatic extensions, which will cause large numbers of asylum seekers and other immigrants to lose employment authorization through no fault of their own. Another commenter said the rule replaces due process with guilt by association and abandons any pretense of a fair and rational immigration system. Other commenters expressed concerns about due process related to the immediate effective date of the IFR, stating that implementation of the IFR appears to be designed to reflect and further the current administration's policies and efforts toward “creating and enhancing chaos and dysfunction.”
Response:
DHS disagrees with the commenters' assertions that the IFR, and this final rule by virtue of reaffirming and finalizing the IFR, undermine due process or the ability of aliens to request asylum, or that it will cause large numbers of asylum seekers or other aliens to lose employment authorization.
In general, the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution protects due process rights to a government benefit if the alien has an entitlement to it, but a benefit is not a protected entitlement if government officials may grant or deny it in their discretion.
See Town of Castle Rock, Colorado
v.
Gonzales,
545 U.S. 748, 756 (2005). There is no generally applicable statutory mandate to grant automatic extensions of employment authorizations. DHS and USCIS have been provided with considerable flexibility and discretion under section 103 and 274A of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1103(a)
and
8 U.S.C. 1324a
, among other provisions, to administer and enforce the INA, including granting employment authorization. Therefore, there is generally no cognizable due process interest in matters related to automatic extensions of employment authorizations and/or EADs. Additionally, contrary to the commenter's assertion, the rule does not suggest guilt by association or that the immigration system is unfair or irrational. A fair and rational immigration system ensures that aliens are sufficiently vetted, and any background hits are resolved before a determination is made that the alien is eligible for an extension of his or her employment authorization and/or an EAD and merits a favorable exercise of discretion, as applicable. The examples provided in the IFR do not suggest guilt by association. Rather, those examples highlight the importance and urgency of ensuring that aliens are not granted employment authorization until appropriate adjudicative review has been completed, and the risks to the national security and public safety if such benefits are granted automatically.
DHS also disagrees with the assertion that immediate implementation of the IFR was designed or intended to create chaos or dysfunction. DHS explained in the IFR why it was implementing the
(
printed page 65314)
rule with immediate effect. DHS concluded that the good cause exceptions in
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
and
(d)(3)
apply to the IFR and that delaying the implementation of the IFR until the conclusion of notice and comment procedures and the delayed effective date would be impracticable and contrary to public interest.
See
90 FR 48814
(Oct. 30, 2025). DHS also explained that the IFR was issued with an immediate effective date because the rule clearly implicates the foreign affairs policy of the United States, and that notice and comment procedure as well as a 30-day delayed effective date would result in undesirable international consequences.
See
90 FR 48816
(Oct. 30, 2025).
iii. International Law and Refugee Protections
Comment:
Several commenters stated that the IFR violates refugee protections, including the 1967 Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees and the Refugee Act of 1980.
[
30
]
One of these commenters said the Refugee Act of 1980 specifically enshrines the right of refugees to work, obtain documentation, and access education, and UNHCR Guidance makes clear that asylum seekers awaiting adjudication of their cases are to be afforded the right to work. The commenter said asylum seekers must obtain EADs to work while their cases are pending, and gaps in EADs restrict the enjoyment of these rights either by directly impacting the right to safe work, or because many services require documentation for which an EAD may be the only form of proof available.
Another commenter stated that eliminating the automatic extension was contrary to Article 34 of the 1951 Refugee Convention, because the resulting loss of employment and the bar of legal employment impede assimilation and naturalization of refugees. The commenter also said the IFR was contrary to Article 33's nonrefoulement, and the Refugee Convention's and Protocol's mandate to facilitate access to fair and efficient refugee status determination procedures that function as a safeguard against refoulement. The commenter reasoned that by undermining asylum seekers' ability to meet their basic needs through legal employment while their claims are pending, the rule obstructs access to a fair asylum procedure and risks forcing aliens to abandon their claims, potentially resulting in their return to the country of persecution.
A commenter stated that cutting off work authorization from people fleeing persecution contradicts our legal obligations and longstanding values.
Response:
DHS disagrees that ending the practice of granting automatic extensions for EAD renewals is inconsistent with the United States' international obligations related to refugee protections, including the Refugee Convention and its Protocol and the Refugee Act of 1980. Although the United States is party to the 1967 Protocol, which incorporates, among others, Articles 17, 33, and 34 of the 1951 Refugee Convention, the treaty is not self-executing and is not directly enforceable in U.S. law. It is the domestic implementing law that governs. The Supreme Court and other case law makes clear that the Protocol serves only as a useful guide in determining congressional intent in enacting the Refugee Act of 1980, because the Act sought to bring U.S. law into conformity with the Protocol.
See, e.g., INS
v.
Stevic,
467 U.S. 407, 428 n.22 (1984);
Khan
v.
Holder,
584 F.3d 773, 783 (9th Cir. 2009). The United States Congress implemented U.S. obligations with respect to certain provisions of the Refugee Convention in the Refugee Act of 1980, including in sections 208, 235, and 241 of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1158
,
1225
and
1231
, and DHS regulations, including
8 CFR part 208
and
1208
. Section 208(d)(2) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(2)
, provides the Secretary with authority to grant employment authorization, in his or her discretion, to applicants for asylum if 180 days have passed since filing an application for asylum.
The IFR is limited in scope, merely ending the practice of automatically extending the validity of employment authorization and/or EADs for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew their EAD in certain employment categories. There is no mandate under international or United States law that DHS provide an automatic extension of employment authorization and/or EAD validity for aliens filing renewal EAD applications, and certainly not without adequately being vetted for continued eligibility. Aliens with a pending asylum application are permitted to still apply for employment authorization as nothing in this rule restricts the ability to apply for an EAD.
[
31
]
Rather, the IFR, and this final rule, are consistent with the Secretary's discretionary authority regarding the grant of employment authorization for asylum applicants and the duration of such authorization, and with international obligations, including the favorable treatment of those seeking refuge from persecution in their countries. DHS finally notes that asylees (but not those with pending asylum applications), refugees, and certain other aliens are “qualified aliens” for purpose of receiving public benefits to cover basic needs under Title IV of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996.
[
32
]
Therefore, even if there are gaps in employment on account of adjudication delays, these aliens may be able to obtain public benefits.
Comment:
A commenter referenced Article 17 of the Refugee Convention, which provides that refugees lawfully in the territory of the host state (which would include not only asylees and resettled refugees, but all aliens pursuing asylum claims who apply for renewal EADs), shall be the accorded the “most favorable treatment accorded to nationals of a foreign country in the same circumstances.” The commenter stated that, because the rule does not end all automatic extensions of the validity period of EADs for those applying for renewal (for example, TPS-based EAD validity extensions through FRN), it provides refugees applying to renew their EADs less favorable treatment than other foreign nationals. The commenter concluded that the rule is therefore issued in violation of Article 17 of the Refugee Convention and should be withdrawn.
(
printed page 65315)
Response:
DHS disagrees with the commenters. The United States implemented the “Wage-earning and Employment” provision of Article 17 of the 1951 Refugee Convention (as incorporated through the 1967 Protocol) through sections 207 and 208 of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1157
,
1158
, and implementing regulations at
8 CFR 207
,
208
and
274a
. Refugees (and asylees)
[
33
]
have the right to employment authorization upon arrival, with minimal restrictions and are provided a pathway to lawful permanent residency because their status in the United States is permanent. This approach aligns with Article 17's requirements and complies with the U.S. obligation including that these individuals are not subject to more restrictive conditions than other foreign nationals in similar circumstances. Even if Article 17 were imposing a binding obligation, nothing in Article 17 requires DHS to provide employment authorization to noncitizens seeking refugee status or asylum before DHS or an immigration judge has made a final determination that they meet requirements for asylum or refugee status and grant the alien's application.
TPS applicants do not have the same protections and legal definition as refugees and asylees. Aliens granted TPS and TPS applicants are only temporarily in the United States on account of the Secretary's designation under section 244 of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1254a
, and
8 CFR part 244
. As part of the TPS statute, Congress provided employment authorization for purposes of the entire designation period.
See
INA sec. 244(a)(1)(B) and (2),
8 U.S.C. 1254a(a)(1)(B)
and
(2)
. To comply with the law enacted by Congress, DHS is typically extending employment authorization via a
Federal Register
notice. However, TPS applicants still must apply for the renewal employment authorization document as part of the redesignation to obtain evidence of employment. Additionally, TPS may be terminated, and TPS never leads to permanent residency.
See
INA sec. 244(b)(3)(B), (h),
8 U.S.C. 1254a(b)(3)(B)
, (h). Thus, upon termination of TPS, TPS beneficiaries and applicants may lose employment authorization in the United States.
See
8 CFR 244.12
and
13
. Refugees (and asylees) once granted, do not typically lose their refugee status and thus, their right to employment and path to lawful permanent residency and eventually citizenship. Therefore, the implementation scheme and the termination of automatic extension is not contrary to the United States international obligations.
2. DHS Justification and Need for the Rule
i. Security Rationale for the Rule
a. General Security Rationale Comments
Comment:
Multiple commenters said the IFR rests on a single asserted justification: the desire to complete vetting and security checks before approving an individual's
[
34
]
work permit renewal, and DHS offers no other policy rationale for eliminating automatic extensions. Commenters stated the IFR is a reversal in policy without new evidence or a reasoned explanation and violates the APA. The commenters stated that DHS's sole rationale suffers from numerous problems and reveals a significant mismatch between the concern asserted and the real-world purpose and impact of automatic extensions.
Additional commenters stated that DHS's security rationale for the IFR contradicts findings in its own 2024 Final Rule, which did not identify any adverse impact of automatic extensions on USCIS' ability to conduct security checks. Commenters stated that DHS offers no credible rationale for this new finding. Some commenters also stated that this rule ignores that DHS narrowly tailored the prior automatic extensions to certain applicants who applied for EAD renewals, which “reasonably assured” the agency that the individual remained eligible for employment authorization and protected the program from abuse.
Response:
DHS does not agree that the IFR is a “reversal of policy without new evidence or a reasoned explanation,” that the justification for the rule is a “mismatch between the concern asserted and the real-world purpose and impact of automatic extensions,” or that DHS failed to consider important aspects of the program. DHS, in the IFR, explained that it is ending the practice of providing automatic extensions of employment authorization documents to enhance integrity in adjudications of employment authorization requests and better protect public safety and national security by ensuring that aliens are properly vetted and determined to continue to be eligible (and merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable), for employment authorization before such authorization is provided to the alien. The Department also explained the permissibility of the change and specifically acknowledged and considered reliance interests that applicants could have engendered by the prior policy and explained why the policy considerations outweighed these interests. The IFR and this final rule reflect a continuation and refinement of DHS's longstanding focus on security, fraud prevention, and benefit integrity in the employment authorization context.
In 2016, DHS eliminated the interim EAD and replaced it with the 180-day automatic extension of employment authorization and explained that it would support the Department's vital mission of securing the nation from the many threats it faces. Therefore, DHS determined that the elimination of both the 90-day EAD processing timeframe and the issuance of interim EADs was necessary.
[
35
]
This change in 2016 reflected DHS's “continued attention to security and commitment to improving adjudication processes, including technological advances in document production, to reduce fraud and address threats to national security.”
See
81 FR 82398
(Nov. 18, 2016) (AC21 Final Rule). DHS implemented the automatic extension of employment authorization to avoid gaps in employment without compromising national security and public safety given the context at the time. However, the automatic extension of employment authorization and/or EADs, whether 180 days or 540 days, extends employment authorization based solely on the filing of a renewal EAD application, before USCIS has completed full vetting, resolved any derogatory information, and determined continuing eligibility for the benefit. Today, concerns regarding national
(
printed page 65316)
security, public safety, and integrity of immigration benefits are at a high point, and the President has directed DHS, through Executive Orders 14159 and 14161, to vet and screen aliens to the maximum extent possible and to ensure that employment authorization is not provided to unauthorized aliens.
[
36
]
DHS notes there is no statutory requirement for USCIS to automatically extend EADs.
DHS has provided a reasonable explanation for changing its policy, namely by giving greater weight to different policy considerations than in the past. DHS has concluded that, owing to current conditions and presidential directives, the security and program-integrity risks inherent in automatic extensions must be given greater weight than the benefits and different temporary circumstances that motivated prior rules. Given the inherent national security and public safety concerns that flow from granting immigration benefits (including EADs) to aliens before determining continued eligibility, DHS believes that rescinding the automatic extension of employment authorization and/or EADs is a necessary remedy. Ending the practice of providing automatic extensions of employment authorization and/or EADs enables DHS to better protect the public's safety and enhance benefit integrity.
b. Lack of Evidence Supporting Security Rationale
Comment:
Numerous commenters stated that DHS did not present evidence or data supporting the claim that automatic extensions pose security risks or that eliminating extensions would meaningfully enhance screening. Multiple commenters stated that the absence of any such evidence demonstrates that the purported problem does not exist. Several commenters wrote that for nearly 10 years, millions of workers have worked under automatic extensions, but the IFR provided no evidence showing that this system allowed security risks to persist or resulted in later security-based denials.
Response:
DHS disagrees with the commenters' assertions. DHS explained in its AC21 Final Rule nearly 10 years ago that it was prioritizing national security and fraud concerns by eliminating the interim EAD and the mandated EAD 90-day processing timeframe. Specifically, DHS noted that “any reduction in the level of eligibility and security vetting before issuing evidence of employment authorization, whether on an interim basis or otherwise, would both be contrary to its core mission and undermine the security, quality, and integrity of the documents issued.”
[
37
]
Consistent with that rationale, and as explained in the IFR, DHS now believes that eliminating the automatic extension of employment authorization and/or EADs will ensure that all identity verification, public safety and security related checks are completed, and that a determination has been made that the applicant continues to be eligible and merits a favorable exercise of discretion, as applicable, before renewing employment authorization and/or an EAD. The IFR also clearly explained the relevance of the Boulder incident and its connection to the automatic extension,
[
38
]
and why the measure was justified. Maintaining automatic extensions based upon the filing of an EAD renewal application would be inconsistent with DHS's stated benefit integrity, security and fraud-prevention objectives.
Comment:
Many commenters stated that DHS's reliance on a single anecdotal incident involving an individual in Boulder, Colorado, was insufficient evidence to justify a policy reversal negatively affecting hundreds of thousands of law-abiding workers and their employers. Commenters wrote that DHS did not demonstrate that the incident involved an automatic extension or how eliminating automatic extensions would have prevented this incident.
Response:
DHS disagrees that the IFR relied on insufficient evidence to justify the IFR's policy change as alleged by commenters. The concern addressed by the IFR and this final rule is that, under the automatic extension framework, an alien's employment authorization and/or EAD validity could be extended for up to 540 days based only on the filing of a renewal application and without having fully vetted the alien for eligibility, including background and security checks. When employment authorization is automatically extended before those checks are complete, aliens who may no longer qualify for the benefit, or who present public safety or national security concerns, are able to remain employment-authorized. This allows aliens who could be public safety or national security threats to use associated documentation to potentially obtain other credentials, such as driver's licenses, and use such document, in turn, to engage in nefarious activities. For example, an alien could rent a car by using the driver's license obtained with an automatically extended EAD as an identity document and subsequently use the car to perpetrate a terrorist attack or other criminal activity. As explained in the IFR and throughout this final rule, DHS has found that these public safety and national security concerns outweigh the interim impacts that may result from a temporary lapse in an individual aliens' employment authorization and/or documentation while USCIS completes refreshed vetting, evaluates any new derogatory information, and determines that the alien remains eligible and continues to merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable.
The IFR references the attack by an alien against peaceful demonstrators in Boulder, Colorado, as a concrete example of an alien in possession of an automatic extension that highlighted the urgent need to mitigate additional public safety emergencies, as well as the importance of ensuring aliens are not granted employment authorization until adjudicative review has been completed. The alien responsible for the Boulder, Colorado, incident was the beneficiary of an automatic extension of his employment authorization, and is thus one example of an alien who remained employment authorized without having undergone full vetting for eligibility or security concerns. Attacks, such as the one in Boulder, Colorado, are tough to predict, but they may not be impossible to stop with proper and thorough vetting and intelligence sharing among government agencies each time an alien is seeking immigration benefits.
[
39
]
DHS is prioritizing the completion of vetting
(
printed page 65317)
prior to granting an immigration benefit to ensure public safety and national security and to mitigate the immediate risks posed to Americans. Ending automatic extensions based on the filing of an EAD renewal application alone addresses that systemic vulnerability. It ensures that continued employment authorization and its documentation is conferred only after USCIS has completed refreshed vetting, evaluated any new derogatory information, and determined that the alien remains eligible and continues to merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable. As discussed in the Executive Summary, President Trump has directed DHS to “vet and screen to the maximum degree possible” all aliens within the United States and ensure that “employment authorization is not provided to any unauthorized alien.”
[
40
]
In line with presidential priorities, DHS is prioritizing program integrity, public safety, and national security and believes the benefits of eliminating automatic extensions of EADs outweigh the risks of potential temporary lapses in employment authorization.
c. Prior Vetting of Renewal Applicants and Existing Security Measures
Comment:
One commenter stated that DHS “offered no credible evidence of security risks associated with” the automatic extension of employment authorization and/or EADs, and that the IFR therefore “lacks any substantive rationale.” Other commenters claimed the security rationale for the rule is inadequate given that aliens applying for EAD renewals have already been vetted. Some commenters said many EAD holders are also likely to have other pending applications before USCIS with evidentiary submissions, background, and identity documents that allow for additional agency vetting.
Response:
DHS disagrees that the IFR lacks a rationale. DHS is prioritizing the completion of proper vetting before issuing immigration benefits and cannot continue to extend employment authorization or EADs without determining that the applicant continues to be eligible and, when applicable, merits a favorable exercise of discretion, regardless of any prior vetting that may have been conducted in connection with past or pending benefit requests. DHS is not required by statute to provide an automatic extension of employment authorization and/or EADs. Rather, DHS is exercising its authority to structure employment authorization processes in a manner that ensures the integrity of the immigration benefit provided, and better advances national security, public safety, and program integrity.
Comment:
Commenters wrote that the IFR misstates how security vetting works, stating that all relevant background check processes occur independently of whether a worker has an unexpired EAD. The commenter said many security flags require follow up investigation, interagency coordination, and a full review of classified or sensitive information that can take considerable time to evaluate, and these assessments occur within the structured adjudicative framework, not during the mechanical, threshold review of an EAD-renewal request.
Response:
DHS disagrees with the premise of these comments. While some background checks and security review processes may be ongoing, others are initiated when USCIS receives a request and are completed in connection with that adjudication. There are no statutory or other regulatory limitations on USCIS' authority to conduct background and security checks to determine eligibility for employment authorization. Additionally, background checks and vetting can be a lengthy process that may require additional time to resolve or to make an eligibility determination. For USCIS to renew an immigration benefit, the applicant must meet the relevant eligibility standards and merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable. All individuals who apply for immigration benefits, including applications for employment authorization, are required to submit and sign the application authorizing the release of any information from their records that USCIS may need to determine eligibility for the benefit sought. By signing and submitting the form to USCIS, the applicant consents to verification by USCIS, as well as use of information to determine initial or continued benefit eligibility. Given the, at times, lengthy vetting process, the previous practice allowed automatic extension of EADs to aliens that would otherwise be found ineligible after USCIS initiates or resolves background check information.
The previous practice of automatically extending employment authorization for a period of up to 540 days prioritized EAD backlog management over program integrity, public safety and national security. Requiring completion of adjudicative review before extending employment authorization and/or EADs better aligns with DHS's vetting responsibilities and the policy priorities of enhancing program integrity, public safety, and national security.
Comment:
Multiple commenters stated that USCIS remains free to conduct continuous vetting during the renewal process and deny the renewal application and terminate employment authorization immediately should it identify new information indicating a security concern.
Some commenters stated that DHS already has the capability to perform continuous screening and vetting, such as through ATLAS and the Continuous Immigration Vetting (CIV) program, which allow for ongoing information sharing and monitoring of individuals in the immigration system, stating these systems can identify security concerns at any time, not just during the renewal application process.
Response:
DHS continues to implement various strategies to address public safety and national security concerns. These efforts include, but are not limited to, the use of continuous screening and vetting capabilities, interagency information-sharing, and enhancements to identity and security verification processes. However, these tools do not obviate the need to complete appropriate vetting and screening before extending employment authorization. Conducting background checks, whether continuously or at certain intervals (for example, when an alien again applies for an immigration benefit), is only one part of the overall vetting and screening process.
Furthermore, derogatory information identified during the background check process must still be reviewed and resolved.
[
41
]
DHS believes that before any immigration benefit is granted, such as an extension of employment authorization and/or an EAD, USCIS should complete the vetting and screening process and determine that the alien continues to be eligible for the benefit and merits a favorable exercise of discretion, as applicable.
Comment:
A commenter stated that the rule discounts the multiple layers of
(
printed page 65318)
vetting and monitoring tools that are already being conducted by employers to identify potential security threats, including Form I-9 verification, E-Verify participation, and criminal background checks.
Response:
DHS will not delegate to employers its responsibility to enhance program integrity and better protect public safety and national security. The varying levels of vetting by different employers are not a substitute for the vetting that USCIS conducts. USCIS has information-sharing agreements with various agencies within the U.S. government and foreign partners. Therefore, vetting from an employer is typically not comparable to USCIS access and vetting. In addition, Form I-9 and E-Verify are not used for national security and public safety vetting. Form I-9 is required for all U.S. employers to document identity and employment authorization for every worker hired. E-Verify is a voluntary program that electronically compares the information on Form I-9 with SSA and DHS records to confirm employment eligibility.
[
42
]
Criteria for security checks and vetting depend upon the immigration benefit sought as well as various other factors, and each benefit request has its own requirements and vulnerabilities. DHS does not believe that renewing employment authorization should be an exception to the stated policy objectives of better protecting public safety and national security and ensuring continued eligibility and that the applicant warrants a favorable exercise of discretion (as applicable) prior to issuing immigration benefits. USCIS is exercising its full authority to investigate immigration benefit requests filed by aliens who may pose risks to the national security and public safety of the United States while adhering to the provisions of the INA and applicable laws, as outlined in DHS Delegation of Authority 0150.1 and 15006.
[
43
]
The elimination of automatic extensions of employment authorization and/or an EAD based on the filing of a renewal application is one component of this broader effort to enhance program integrity and safeguard the United States.
d. Rule Would Not Strengthen Security
Comment:
One commenter said justifying the rule under “the guise of national security is ironic” because the rule's likely consequence in derailing the livelihoods of aliens may push them to violate the law for survival. Another commenter stated that most of the public safety and national security risk created by malicious aliens stems from their presence in the United States rather than their ability to work and encouraged DHS to study how significant the risk associated with income generated through lawful employment is compared to the risk associated with presence on U.S. soil. A commenter stated that DHS implicitly assumes that unemployment is the antidote to potential crime when common sense and empirical evidence provides the opposite is true.
Response:
DHS disagrees with the comment that this rule will result in derailing the livelihoods of aliens and the insinuation that it may push individuals to become criminals to survive.
As explained in the IFR, DHS has taken significant steps to reduce the overall EAD filings that followed the unprecedented flood of illegal immigration into the United States during previous years.
[
44
]
For example, DHS has narrowed the use of parole and better aligned TPS and related programs with statutory criteria. As a result, initial EAD applications have significantly declined since 2025. USCIS has also seen a decline in the number of filings in the largest EAD categories that were formerly eligible for automatic extensions based on the filing of a renewal EAD application, as shown in Table 1.
(
printed page 65319)
The two largest categories of Form I-765 applicants are those with pending asylum applications (C08) and those with pending adjustment of status applications (C09). Together these categories made up approximately 80% of all I-765 applicants from January 2025 through the end of June 2026.
[
45
]
Table 1 shows how C08 and C09 filings have decreased since the start of the current administration in January 2025. USCIS received a total of 240,060 C08 filings in January 2025, which decreased to 32,472 in June 2026.
[
46
]
Similarly, USCIS received a total of 64,106 C09 filings in January 2025, which decreased to 36,455 in June 2026. USCIS notes the decreased EAD filing rates support the point made in the IFR that the potential lapse, and in particular the duration of any lapse, is speculative and could be outweighed by the harm posed by automatic extensions.
Finally, DHS regularly publishes detailed statistics on its activities,
[
47
]
but declines to perform a study of the additional risk to national security caused by income aliens generated through lawful employment for multiple reasons. For example, isolating and quantifying the incremental risk attributable solely to income derived from lawful employment—as distinct from the risk associated with presence, travel, associations, unauthorized employment, or other activities—would present significant methodological and data limitations. The relevant population would be small, sensitive national security information would constrain the availability and use of underlying case data, and it would be difficult to draw statistically meaningful conclusions.
DHS acknowledges the commenter's view that the primary public safety and national security risk posed by malicious actors arises from their presence in the United States and not solely from their continuing ability to work. Even so, DHS considers it important and appropriate to use its authorities to reduce risks associated with both presence and employment. Access to lawful employment can provide malicious actors with financial resources, routine cover for their activities, and access to certain workplaces and facilities. Limiting the ability of aliens with potentially malicious intent to retain EADs and/or employment authorization, and to lawfully work and generate income, without full vetting is therefore a meaningful component of DHS's broader efforts to safeguard benefit integrity, national security and public safety.
For these reasons, DHS continues to view measures that reduce the likelihood that malicious actors can obtain or rely on employment authorization and related secure documentation as worthwhile.
Comment:
Some commenters stated that, if the goal is to strengthen vetting integrity, the logical solution is to expedite case processing so that all
(
printed page 65320)
background checks and reviews are completed more quickly. One commenter also stated that workers should be able to maintain their employment authorization and support their families while vetting occurs.
Response:
DHS undertakes every effort to complete case processing as expeditiously as possible while being conscious of the importance of vetting every benefit requestor thoroughly for eligibility, including vetting for criminal activity and other security risks. DHS believes screening, vetting, and determining continued eligibility before granting a renewal of employment authorization and/or documentation is essential to enhance program integrity and better protect public safety and national security. Such processes, however, especially given the volume of initial and renewal EAD applicants that USCIS encounters, necessarily take time. Note that expediting a case generally means that USCIS would move the benefit request to the front of the processing queue to the detriment of those who may have filed earlier but does not otherwise change the time needed to properly conduct screening and vetting and determine continued eligibility. To the extent that these commenters suggest that USCIS should expedite all EAD renewal applications and thus put renewal EAD applications in front of other applications in the processing queue, DHS maintains that this would not be a viable solution and would not enhance program integrity or better protect public safety and national security.
Comment:
Multiple commenters stated that the security benefit of the rule is incremental because renewal applicants have already been robustly vetted and will not be re-vetted until the EAD renewal is adjudicated, stating that this second vetting by USCIS occurs even if EAD extensions are automatic.
Response:
USCIS must ensure that all aliens who request immigration benefits from USCIS are eligible for the benefit sought, merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable, and do not pose a threat to national security or public safety. It is necessary and within USCIS' authority to continue investigating immigration benefit requests and to assess whether an applicant has established ongoing eligibility and warrants favorable discretion, if applicable, and whether they pose a risk to the national security and public safety of the United States, before issuing immigration benefits. This includes renewal applications for employment authorization and/or EADs, which may reveal new derogatory information or changed circumstances that were not present at the time of the initial grant.
Comment:
One commenter stated that the IFR would cause DHS resources to be spent on EAD processing while people remain in the United States without decisions on their ability to stay, stating that the rule “punishes applicants, families, communities, and employers for USCIS' failure to timely process applications.” Another commenter similarly stated that the rule “does not meaningfully improve homeland security” and would divert resources rather than supporting security or operational efficiency.
Response:
DHS is dedicated to ensuring that all aliens who enter and remain in the United States do not present threats to national security or public safety. USCIS plays an instrumental role in preventing terrorists and other bad actors from harboring in the United States, and screening and vetting should be prioritized over purely expedient adjudications to that end. DHS will continue to work to reduce frivolous, fraudulent, and meritless EAD filings to free up adjudicatory and other resources to better ensure national security and program integrity. Therefore, DHS does not agree that focusing resources on careful EAD renewal adjudications “diverts” resources from security; rather, such adjudications are themselves a core security function of USCIS.
e. Other Comments on Security Rationale
Comment:
Some commenters expressed concern with DHS's rationale that bad actors could benefit from EADs being automatically extended and the income generated from working to support “nefarious activities,” stating that it is speculative, discriminatory, and perpetuates anti-immigrant rhetoric. A commenter said this is particularly dangerous language for Asian American communities who face a persistent narrative as the “perpetual foreigner” and will only contribute to that “pernicious stereotype” and support unfounded suspicions that Asians are agents of foreign governments.
Response:
DHS disagrees with the commenters' assertions. DHS ended the practice of providing automatic extension of employment authorization and/or EADs based on the filing of a renewal EAD application to ensure continued eligibility and prioritizing the proper vetting and screening of aliens in furtherance of its mission. This rule does not target Asian American communities or any other specific group of aliens. Instead, this rule, as written, applies to all aliens who were eligible for the automatic extension of their employment authorization and/or EADs under former
8 CFR 274a.13(d)
. As explained in the IFR and this final rule, DHS is prioritizing the completion of vetting prior to granting an immigration benefit to enhance program integrity and better protect public safety and national security. The examples provided in the IFR illustrated the broader concern that extending employment authorization before completing vetting can allow aliens who may present public safety or national security risks to retain employment authorization. Ending automatic extensions based on the filing of an EAD renewal application ensures that continued employment authorization is conferred only after USCIS has completed renewed vetting, evaluated any new derogatory information, and determined that the alien remains eligible and continues to merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable. DHS believes that the program integrity, public safety, and national security benefits of eliminating automatic extensions of EADs outweigh the risks of potential temporary lapses in employment authorization.
Comment:
Commenters stated that, while DHS repeatedly cites purported national security concerns as justification for the IFR, the “underemphasized yet explicit” motivation for the IFR is a reduction in EAD filings overall. They stated that the rule is intended to generally deter immigration, specifically for asylum seekers, and that DHS ignores that asylees and refugees are authorized employment even if the expiration date on their EAD has passed. One commenter stated that, while DHS claims it is ending the practice of automatically renewing EADs for refugees and asylees to take a “uniform approach” and avoid “the potential for confusion” of employers, it does not quantify the potential confusion or justify why it cannot at least provide automatic renewals for refugees and asylees, who are authorized to work incident to their status.
The commenters concluded that the IFR is meant to undermine and frustrate those with legal work authorization and will cause unnecessary lapses in work authorization creating unreasonable obstacles, citing DHS's referenced goal of providing a “comprehensive policy solution” and stating the rule is actually intended to unnecessarily confuse employers, frustrate immigrants' ability to work, and push more into “dire straits.” Another commenter questioned enhanced security as the true intent of
(
printed page 65321)
the rule, suggesting other motives such as intentionally causing aliens to fall out of status and lose their jobs.
Response:
DHS disagrees with the commenters that the goal of this rule is to reduce EAD filings overall, generally deter immigration or to “unnecessarily confuse employers” and “frustrate immigrants' ability to work.” As previously stated, the purpose of this rule is to prioritize the proper vetting and screening of aliens, to ensure continued eligibility, and to confirm that applicants continue to merit favorable exercises of discretion, if applicable, before granting new periods of employment authorization and/or new EADs by ending the practice of automatically extending the validity of employment authorization and/or EADs.
DHS recognizes that aliens who are granted asylum or refugee status are authorized employment incident to their asylum or refugee status. As explained in the IFR, aliens who are authorized employment incident to their status
[
48
]
and are maintaining their respective immigration status, such as asylees and refugees, will continue to be employment authorized while maintaining their immigration status, regardless of the expiration date on their EAD. Aliens who are authorized employment incident to status will continue to have the choice to file Form I-765 to obtain EADs for proof of identity. As stated in the IFR, DHS is taking a uniform approach for all aliens by ending the practice of providing automatic extensions of employment authorization and/or EADs.
Comment:
One commenter said that eliminating automatic extensions does not serve
E.O. 14159
, Protecting the American People Against Invasion, which orders DHS and other agencies to ensure that employment authorization is not provided to any unauthorized alien in the United States. The commenter said eliminating automatic extensions has no impact on this mandate, as the purpose of such automatic extensions is to afford USCIS the time and resources to make a robust determination in compliance with its statutory and regulatory obligations in cases where aliens were already approved for employment authorization.
Response:
DHS maintains that this rule accomplishes the mandate of
E.O. 14159
. This executive order directs the Secretary of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Secretary of State and the Attorney General, in Section 16 to take all appropriate action to align any departmental activities with the policies set out by the President, to ensure that “employment authorization is not provided to any unauthorized alien in the United States.” As stated in the IFR and this rule, ending the practice of providing automatic extensions of EADs is consistent with this instruction in
E.O. 14159
because a previous grant of employment authorization does not mean that an applicant remains indefinitely eligible for employment authorization, and it is necessary to review eligibility to ensure that an alien's circumstances have not changed such that the alien is no longer eligible. Granting automatic extensions of employment without proper vetting and full adjudication to ensure continued eligibility is not consistent with
E.O. 14159
or with current priorities.
ii. Consistency in USCIS Rationale and Reversal of Longstanding Policy
Comment:
Multiple commenters wrote that USCIS says it does not expect delays in processing EAD renewals in the future, but also says it must end automatic extensions on EADs now because it needs more time to finish security checks. Commenters said both cannot be true. Commenters also stated that, if DHS expects continued delays, then ending automatic extensions will push employees out of work authorization simply because the government cannot finish adjudicating these cases fast enough. These commenters said courts invalidate rules when an agency's reasoning is contradictory and the agency offers no adequate justification for the inconsistency, with some commenters citing
F.C.C.
v.
Fox Television Stations, Inc.
Also referencing this purported inconsistency, multiple commenters stated that DHS's conclusion that EAD applications will decline and that more adjudicative resources will reduce EAD renewal processing times ignores that those same resources will be available at the initial stage to address any red flags. Thus, the commenter said DHS's purported need for fuller investigations at the renewal stage will be even less necessary moving forward. The commenter said the claim also cannot be reconciled with the Department's historic position that it can complete sufficient investigations promptly, given sufficient resources.
Multiple commenters said the IFR rejects and contradicts the policies of both the 2016 and the recent 2024 rules, the purpose of which was to mitigate the harm to workers and employers caused by interruptions in work authorization, without adequate explanation, justification, or alternative remedies. One commenter specified that the IFR cites no data showing sustained reductions in renewal processing times, no new performance metrics, and no analysis demonstrating that the long-recognized adjudication challenges identified in 2016 and again in 2024 have materially changed.
Response:
DHS disagrees with the commenters' assertion that the reasoning in the IFR, and this final rule, is contradictory or unjustified. DHS notes the IFR does not state that “USCIS does not expect delays in processing EADs.” Instead, DHS explained it has taken measures to address floods of filings from TPS beneficiaries and other applicants, and that DHS expects that overall filing rates for initial and renewal EADs are likely to substantially decline, freeing up adjudicative resources to reduce renewal EAD processing times.
[
49
]
USCIS routinely evaluates filing volumes relative to adjudicative resources and reallocates workloads to address priorities as appropriate and feasible, including between initial and renewal EAD filings. The IFR explains that, while USCIS continues to work to improve processing times and reduce backlogs, DHS has determined that automatic extensions are inconsistent with ensuring continued eligibility or with current security and vetting priorities. DHS believes that the reasoning provided in the IFR is appropriate and that the purpose of the IFR has been adequately justified. Ending automatic extensions based on the filing of an EAD renewal application ensures that continued employment authorization is conferred only after USCIS has completed renewed vetting, evaluated any new derogatory information, and determined that the alien remains eligible and continues to merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable. DHS believes that the program integrity, public safety, and national security benefits of eliminating automatic extensions of EADs outweigh the risks of potential temporary lapses in employment authorization.
As discussed in greater detail in response to a previous comment in Section IV.C.2.i.a. of this preamble, the decision to end automatic extensions reflects a change in how DHS balances operational efficiency and continuity of employment against these security and benefit integrity concerns rather than an inconsistency in DHS's underlying commitment to timely adjudications.
DHS expects that overall, EAD filing rates will substantially decline and free up adjudicative resources to reduce
(
printed page 65322)
renewal EAD processing times. Decreasing processing times would result in a reduced need for aliens filing renewal EAD applications to rely on an automatic extension of their EAD to avoid potential lapses. Since the IFR became effective on October 30, 2025, USCIS has seen a steady decrease in overall EAD filings.
See
Table 1 in Section IV.C.2.i.d. of this preamble. USCIS notes that decreased EAD filing rates support the point made in the IFR: that the potential for an alien to have a lapse, and in particular the duration of any lapse, is speculative and could be outweighed by the harm posed by automatic extensions.
iii. Lack of Acknowledgement of the Backlog and Other Operational Realities
Comment:
Multiple commenters stated that the IFR ignores that backlogs persist today and provides no projections or plans to reduce the backlogs that necessitate automatic extension. Some of these commenters said the IFR incorrectly portrays backlogs as a future “scenario,” but processing delays are significant. A commenter stated that external analyses reinforce the conclusion that long delays in EAD adjudication are a documented, ongoing reality and, despite this record, DHS offers no empirical data showing in the IFR that processing times have improved enough to make automatic extensions unnecessary. A commenter stated that external analyses reinforce the conclusion that long delays in EAD adjudication are a documented, ongoing reality and, despite this record, DHS offers no empirical data showing in the IFR that processing times have improved enough to make automatic extensions unnecessary. Some commenters referenced DHS backlog data in asserting the value of the automatic extension mechanism and the rule's lack of acknowledgement of the backlog. Another commenter stated that, while striving for timely adjudication is a worthy goal, it does not eliminate the need for automatic extensions, and USCIS should not eliminate the regulatory provision of automatic extensions in its entirety.
Response:
DHS is ending the automatic extension of employment authorization and EADs not because USCIS has completed its backlog of pending cases, but rather because DHS is prioritizing ensuring continued eligibility and proper vetting. However, USCIS will continue to work through its backlog of cases without unnecessarily granting immigration benefits to those who may be ineligible or threaten the public safety and national security of the United States.
DHS acknowledged the EAD backlog in the IFR, stating that most of the backlog resulted from prior policy decisions that resulted in an overwhelming number of initial and subsequent renewal EAD filings.
[
50
]
DHS discussed potential future backlog scenarios while also acknowledging the current backlogs in each of those rules. Specifically, DHS provided data in the 2024 TFR to project the impact of the asylum filing surges and backlogs to consider possible renewal EAD application filing behaviors and the impact throughout the effective period of the 2024 TFR.
See
89 FR 24628
(Apr. 8, 2024). DHS discussed the same data in the 2024 Final Rule.
See
89 FR 101208
(Dec. 13, 2024). These rules attempted to mitigate the impact of potential future renewal EAD processing backlogs that could have been caused by a variety of circumstances, and DHS used those data projections to estimate the impact of codifying the automatic extension period increase from up to 180 days to up to 540 days. DHS has reassessed that conjectural approach and determined that, notwithstanding ongoing backlogs, automatic extensions are not an appropriate mechanism given the associated security and integrity risks.
As discussed elsewhere in this preamble, DHS has taken significant steps to reduce the overall EAD filings that followed the unprecedented flood of illegal immigration into the United States during previous years.
[
51

(

iii. Procedural Fairness
Comment:
Many commenters expressed concerns about the procedural fairness of applicants losing work authorization due to USCIS processing times. Specifically, some commenters said that the IFR would punish people who are following the law, complying with immigration procedures, or, more generally, “have done everything right,” losing status through “no fault of their own.” Likewise, several commenters remarked that the current automatic extension policy helps prevent nonimmigrants from being punished for delays beyond their control. A few commenters said that removing automatic extensions without addressing processing delays would be unjust.
A few other commenters remarked that the IFR would contradict administrative equity or fairness. Other commenters said that the rule would contradict DHS's own acknowledgement that interruptions in work authorization cause “substantial and unnecessary harm.” A couple of commenters said that the rule would penalize law abiding applicants due to an extreme individual case.
Response:
DHS recognizes that many renewal applicants diligently comply with filing requirements and that delays in adjudication may not be within their control. DHS also acknowledges that prior rulemakings, including the 2016 and 2024 rules, sought to mitigate the impact of processing delays on workers and employers by providing automatic extensions of employment authorization and/or EADs.
However, as explained in the IFR, DHS has reassessed the balance between continuity of employment authorization and the need to ensure that immigration benefits are granted only after appropriate vetting and eligibility determinations. There is no statutory entitlement to an automatic extension of employment authorization. Employment authorization in the relevant categories is generally discretionary and time-limited, and renewal requires a new adjudication. The IFR and this final rule do not deny renewal to eligible applicants; they simply require that continued employment authorization be based on an approved renewal application rather than on the mere filing of that application.
DHS has determined that granting automatic extensions without updated vetting and adjudication is inconsistent with its mission and with E.O.s directing DHS to ensure that employment authorization is not provided to unauthorized aliens and that all aliens in the United States are vetted and screened to the maximum degree possible. While DHS is mindful of the hardships that may arise from temporary lapses in employment authorization, the need to protect national security and public safety, and to enhance the integrity of immigration benefits, justifies discontinuing automatic extensions.

(

[
84
]
and again in finalizing this rule. However, DHS has concluded that the need to ensure proper vetting and screening, and continued eligibility, before granting renewed employment authorization and issuing secure evidence of that authorization outweighs the risk that some applicants might experience a temporary lapse in employment authorization and/or EAD validity. DHS also determined that extending this benefit without updated adjudication and screening is inconsistent with its mission and with E.O.s
[
85
]
directing DHS to ensure that employment authorization is not provided to unauthorized aliens and that aliens in the United States are vetted and screened to the maximum degree possible.
Nevertheless, DHS emphasizes that this rule does not eliminate eligibility for employment authorization or prevent eligible aliens from obtaining initial or renewal EADs. Rather, it ends the practice of automatically extending employment authorization and/or EAD validity for up to 540 days based solely on the filing of a renewal application, without completion of adjudicative review and related vetting, including resolution of any derogatory information. Continued employment authorization will now depend on USCIS' approval of a renewal application, after USCIS has determined that the alien continues to be eligible and continues to merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable.
This rule also does not change underlying eligibility standards for immigration benefits, public benefits, or educational programs, and it does not restrict aliens from seeking assistance for which they are otherwise eligible under Federal or State law. Certain categories of aliens, such as refugees and asylees, remain “qualified aliens” for specified public benefits under existing statutes, and those authorities are unchanged by this rule. Likewise, this rule does not alter the ability of States, localities, or private organizations to provide charitable or humanitarian assistance.
DHS also notes that, independent of this rule, it has taken steps to reduce the extraordinary EAD filing volumes driven by prior policies, including narrowing the use of parole and aligning TPS designations with statutory criteria. DHS expects that overall EAD filing rates (initial and renewal) will substantially decline because of those actions, freeing adjudicative resources to reduce renewal EAD application processing times. For example, initial and renewal EAD applications for the largest EAD categories that were formerly eligible for automatic extensions have significantly reduced since the start of 2025.
See
Table 1 in Section IV.C.2.i.d. of this preamble.
Accordingly, the decreased EAD filing rates support the point made in the IFR that any claims about an increase in the number and duration of employment authorization and/or EAD lapses are speculative and outweighed by the harm posed by automatic extensions.
USCIS also publishes current case processing time information on its website.
[
86
]
Proper planning by applicants, such as monitoring EAD expiration dates, consulting posted processing times, and filing renewal applications as soon as permitted by regulation and form instructions, can further mitigate the risk and duration of any lapses in employment authorization.
Overall, DHS recognizes the seriousness of the hardships described by commenters but concludes that, on balance, the national security, public safety, and benefit integrity interests served by ending automatic EAD extensions outweigh the potential adverse impacts associated with temporary lapses in employment authorization and/or EAD validity.

One commenter asserted that some of the immigrant population is already experiencing significant levels of trauma and stress from immigration enforcement activity, and that the IFR would only exacerbate such feelings.
Many commenters shared concerns about nonimmigrants' increased level of vulnerability to exploitation by employers and landlords, as well as human trafficking, sexual harm, and abuse owing to the IFR's elimination of automatic extensions. For example, multiple commenters said that loss of employment authorization makes nonimmigrants vulnerable to exploitative working conditions. Some commenters remarked that if aliens lose their ability to work legally, they may seek under the table work or unlawful employment. Commenters warned that this leaves such individuals vulnerable to exploitation, explaining that these jobs often have lower wages, minimal labor protections, and abusive conditions which they may be afraid to report due to unlawful status. They also indicated that 84.9 percent of unauthorized immigrants reported not being paid time and a half for overtime labor, and 37.1 percent reported being victims of minimum wage violations. The commenter added that many employers of unauthorized workers do not carry workers compensation insurance, meaning that employees may be responsible for covering their own medical costs in the case of work-related injury. The commenter added that since USCIS recently ended a program that protected whistleblowers, unauthorized employees are now less likely to report various types of abuse. A different commenter added that forcing applicants into unlawful employment may also impact their eligibility for future immigration benefits, putting them in a long-term position of vulnerability.
Response:
DHS recognizes that uncertainty about employment authorization and potential lapses in income can contribute to stress, anxiety, and other mental health challenges, particularly for individuals who may already have experienced trauma or instability. DHS also recognizes that economic insecurity and lack of lawful employment opportunities can increase vulnerability to exploitation by unscrupulous employers, landlords, or others, and may heighten risks of trafficking, abuse, or other harm.
The IFR and this final rule do not deny eligible aliens access to employment authorization or to the underlying immigration benefits for which they qualify. Rather the IFR, affirmed by this final rule, removes only the automatic extension mechanism that previously allowed aliens to remain employment authorized for up to 540
(
printed page 65329)
days based solely on a pending renewal application, without completion of updated vetting and adjudication. As described throughout this preamble, DHS has determined that such automatic extensions present an unacceptable security and program integrity risk because they confer significant benefits before USCIS has completed vetting and screening, resolved any derogatory information, determined continued eligibility and that the applicant merits a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable.
DHS cannot structure its regulatory framework on the assumption that aliens and/or employers will respond to temporary lapses in employment authorization by engaging in unauthorized employment or other unlawful conduct. The INA prohibits the knowing employment of unauthorized aliens and establishes consequences for both employers and aliens who violate those provisions. While DHS recognizes that some aliens may face difficult choices if a lapse occurs, DHS does not condone unauthorized employment or believe that it is an appropriate response to a temporary lapse in employment authorization.
DHS shares commenters' concerns about exploitation and abuse. DHS, including through components such as ICE and USCIS' fraud detection and victim protection programs, will continue to enforce laws related to human trafficking, forced labor, and other forms of exploitation, and to coordinate with the Department of Labor and other agencies on enforcement. Existing protections for victims of trafficking, crime, and abuse (including T and U nonimmigrant classifications and VAWA) are unaffected by this rule. Nothing in this rule diminishes DHS's commitment to identify and assist victims or to support the investigation and prosecution of traffickers and other offenders.
DHS recognizes that some aliens may experience heightened stress or vulnerability if their employment authorization temporarily lapses. However, DHS has concluded that the need to ensure that employment authorization is extended only after appropriate vetting and adjudication, consistent with current national security and public safety priorities, justifies ending automatic extensions. DHS also expects that reductions in overall EAD filing volumes may help limit the frequency and length of lapses and that timely filing and planning by applicants can further reduce uncertainty. For reduced filing volumes,
see
Table 1 in Section IV.C.2.i.d. of this preamble.
c. Identification, Driver's Licenses, and Access to Services
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concerns that lapses in employment authorization and the associated use of employment authorization documents would hinder nonimmigrants' abilities to obtain or renew their driver's licenses, open and access bank accounts, obtain or renew health insurance, enroll in educational programs and training, and interact with law enforcement. Commenters remarked that lack of a driver's license could interfere with critical daily activities for nonimmigrants, such as taking children to school, commuting to work, or attending doctors' appointments or immigration hearings. A few commenters shared that in many cases, nonimmigrants require driver's licenses to perform their job duties and that, without a valid driver's license, nonimmigrants may be pushed to drive without a license, compromising road safety.
Response:
DHS acknowledges that EADs are commonly used by aliens as identity and, in some contexts, status documents for State-issued driver's licenses and identification cards, financial services, and other purposes. Under the prior automatic extension framework, an EAD that was facially expired could be treated as unexpired for certain purposes if accompanied by a Form I-797C receipt notice, including obtaining a driver's license. As explained in the IFR, DHS determined that continuing that practice and the use of automatically extended EADs is no longer appropriate.
This rule does not change State authority to determine which documents are acceptable for issuance of driver's licenses or other State identification, nor does it amend the Department's REAL ID regulations for issuance of driver's licenses or identification cards acceptable for federal official purposes defined in the REAL ID Act. It does, however, make clear that, for renewal applications filed on or after October 30, 2025, a pending Form I-765 and associated receipt notice will no longer operate to automatically extend EAD validity under DHS regulations. An EAD that is facially expired will not be treated as unexpired for employment or immigration purposes unless it qualifies for an automatic extension under
8 CFR 274a.13(d)
based on a renewal application filed before October 30, 2025, or is otherwise extended by law or an applicable
Federal Register
notice (for example, certain TPS-related documents).
The rule does not prevent eligible aliens from seeking or renewing EADs, nor does it prohibit States or other entities from accepting alternative forms of identification or documentation where permitted by law.
DHS also expects that, as overall EAD filing volumes decline and renewal processing times improve, the risk and duration of lapses will be reduced. USCIS has already seen a decline in filing rates for the main EAD categories that were eligible for automatic extensions.
See
Table 1 in Section IV.C.2.i.d. of this preamble.
DHS concludes that the security and benefit integrity gains from ensuring that EADs used as evidence of identity and work authorization reflect a recent adjudication and completed vetting outweigh the potential risks associated with discontinuing automatic extensions.
