a. Employer Burdens, Business Continuity, and Sector Specific Concerns
Comment:
Multiple commenters argued that loss of automatic extensions will increase Form I-9 compliance complexity, cause turnover and productivity losses, exacerbate existing shortages in health care, education, agriculture, manufacturing, etc., and impose particular burdens on small employers.
Commenters expressed opposition to removing automatic extensions, stating that such a change would cause significant disruption to employers, including operational inefficiencies (loss of productivity and delays), administrative burdens, staffing gaps, human capital costs and retention, civil penalties, and compliance burdens as employees await renewal decisions without work authorization. A few commenters stated that employers could violate Form I-9 compliance rules due to unclear authorization statuses.
Multiple commenters asserted that the IFR would exacerbate existing labor shortages and projected a continued decrease in labor force participation rates through at least 2030, cautioning that the IFR could worsen such shortages by preventing asylum seekers from working during EAD processing and removing vetted workers. One commenter stated that labor shortages would negatively impact the U.S. economy, hinder growth and contribute to inflationary pressures. Another commenter stated that a decline of 2 million immigrant workers between 2019 and 2021 contributed to labor
(
printed page 65330)
shortages across sectors, including a labor shortage in the construction industry valued at $10.8 billion, reasoning that the IFR would replicate such labor shortages across every industry. A commenter stated that until public and private sector efforts could fully meet industry demand, the United States would need additional workers to fill jobs left vacant by the domestic workforce, expressing concern that ending the EAD extension could further disrupt workforce stability and business continuity for manufacturers. Many commenters stated that the removal of automatic extensions would negatively impact critical industries and sectors of the U.S. economy that rely on foreign workers, including agriculture, technology, energy, manufacturing, logistics, transportation, hospitality, education, and construction. Several commenters expressed concern about the impact on healthcare and healthcare workers, noting that even a brief lapse in employment authorization disrupts patient care, clinic operations, and community health access. One commenter remarked about how the IFR will adversely affect teaching hospitals and academic health systems that employ EAD workers.
Other commenters expressed concerns that the IFR would undermine labor unions, collective bargaining, and workforce stability by disrupting bargaining units that include immigrant workers with EADs, stating that increased risk of sudden job loss among workers would strain unions' ability to enforce workplace standards, forcing them to devote more resources to protecting vulnerable workers and addressing instability caused by the IFR.
Multiple commenters expressed the importance of automatic extensions for business continuity amid persistent government processing delays and stated that the IFR would impose unnecessary burdens and costs, especially on smaller companies without in-house legal departments. Some commenters stated that the rule would force employers to conduct extensive contingency planning and workforce audits to prepare for potential lapses in work authorization. Specifically, a commenter stated that groups such as asylees, who are authorized to work incident to status, may still be asked to show an EAD to their employer, and further reasoned that the IFR could still cause employer confusion and job loss among these groups. Other commenters stated that eliminating automatic EAD extensions would cause businesses to lose workers and cited to a USCIS analysis establishing that EAD extensions previously saved U.S. employers an estimated $3.5 billion by avoiding labor turnover.
Numerous commenters expressed concern that employers would be forced to terminate employees due to administrative delays in processing EAD renewals. Commenters stated that previous sudden reversals of work permit rules have created confusion for employers and caused them to make rash decisions based on misinformation about changing Federal regulations, leading to erroneous layoffs where workers with valid EADs were dismissed because employers did not understand how to comply with current rules. A commenter said that such impacts would exacerbate the ongoing teacher shortage crisis.
Response:
DHS recognizes that some sectors, including healthcare, education, manufacturing, agriculture, hospitality, and technology, and unionized workplaces may be particularly sensitive to interruptions in workforce continuity.
This rule does not change employers' underlying obligations under section 274A of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1324a
, and
8 CFR part 274a
to hire only individuals who are authorized to work in the United States, to verify employment eligibility, and to reverify employment authorization when existing documentation expires.
By ending automatic extensions for renewal applications filed on or after October 30, 2025, this rule ensures that employment authorization will be evidenced by a secure, unexpired document issued following adjudication. This reduces the risk that employers will rely on outdated or invalid documentation, and it aligns with DHS's responsibility to ensure that employment authorization and/or an EAD is provided only after USCIS has completed appropriate vetting and determined continued eligibility.
To ensure that workplaces and businesses have a clear understanding of the requirements of the IFR, DHS has updated the Handbook for Employers (M-274) and related guidance to assist employers in understanding these changes and properly completing Form I-9. Employers are responsible for ensuring I-9 compliance for all of their employees, including updates to the I-9 verification process.
[
87
]
DHS acknowledges that, where renewal adjudications are not completed before current EADs expire, some employers may face temporary staffing gaps and associated costs. These can include lost productivity, overtime for remaining staff, recruitment and training for temporary or replacement workers, and internal administrative costs associated with planning, auditing, and compliance. DHS discussed these categories of impacts in the IFR and in the economic analysis accompanying this rule and recognizes there may be negative impacts for some employers.
[
88
]
DHS outlined the difficulties in estimating the number of EADs that would lapse in the Section V.B.1. of this preamble. However, in this final rule DHS has made estimates of economic impacts and emphasizes that there is likely to be variation in the impacts, due to factors such as dynamic process times, filing volumes, and filing behavior. For this reason, DHS provides a wide range for the estimates.
DHS has determined that these operational burdens are outweighed by the national security, public safety, and benefit integrity concerns associated with automatic EAD extensions. Automatic EAD extensions allow employment authorization and/or EAD validity to continue for up to 540 days based solely on a pending renewal application, before USCIS has completed updated background checks and adjudication. Considering current security priorities and E.O.s directing enhanced vetting of aliens already present in the United States, DHS has concluded that continued reliance on automatic extensions is not an acceptable means of managing adjudication backlogs.
Independent of this rule, DHS has taken steps expected to reduce initial and renewal EAD filing volumes by narrowing the use of parole and aligning TPS and related policies with statutory text. As discussed previously in response to comments, DHS anticipates that overall EAD filings will decline and that adjudicative capacity can increasingly be focused on timely renewal adjudications.
DHS notes that an applicant may request that USCIS expedite the adjudication of an application that is under USCIS jurisdiction.
[
89
]
USCIS considers all expedite requests on a case-by-case basis and generally requires documentation to support such
(
printed page 65331)
requests.
[
90
]
The decision to expedite is within the sole discretion of USCIS.
[
91
]
Expediting a case generally means that USCIS would adjudicate a benefit ahead of others, including those who may have filed earlier, so USCIS carefully weighs the urgency and merit of each expedite request.
[
92
]
DHS recognizes the concerns raised by employers, unions, and industry groups and will continue to monitor implementation and processing times. Nonetheless, DHS concludes that ensuring that renewed employment authorization is granted only after complete vetting and adjudication is necessary to better protect national security and public safety and to enhance the integrity of the employment verification system. Adhering to a system that prioritizes national security, public safety, and benefit integrity outweighs the potential risks and additional burdens that applicants and their employers may face by a potential temporary lapse in employment authorization.
b. Immigrant Contributions to the Economy and Macroeconomic and Local Economic Impacts of the Rule
Comment:
Numerous commenters stated that the IFR ignores the vital economic contributions of immigrants, and operational realities that the work authorization is a critical tool to successfully integrate aliens into the United States and contribute to the economy. Commenters also stated that the IFR is disrupting businesses that employ these aliens and thereby losing the economic contribution of immigrants. For example, commenters discussed the positive impacts that asylees and refugees make to the U.S. economy and stated that this population contributed more revenue than they cost in expenditures to the U.S. government. Another commenter said that in 2023, New York State's immigrant population represented about 23 percent of the total population and paid $74.8 billion in taxes, thus demonstrating that immigrants are productive members of the workforce. The commenter also stated that a lapse in employment authorization could mean that they would lose their homes, face hunger, contribute less taxes to state and the federal government or would otherwise become vulnerable (such as incurring negative health effects). Another commenter said that immigrant workers are a key driver of New York City's economy, making up 36 percent of the population; accounting for 37 percent of total wage, salary, and business income; and in 2021, contributed tens to hundreds of billions of dollars in taxes and spending to the city and state. An additional commenter identified in-migration of workers, including asylum seekers and other immigrants, as one of the few positive trends offsetting the rapid exit of older workers and emphasized that many economic development strategies depend on immigrants' continuous access to work authorization. Other commenters highlighted potential impacts on the economy, pointing out that asylum seekers and refugees work in sectors that face shortages and pay billions in taxes, and that immigrants will add $7 trillion to the economy over the next decade.
Commenters raised concerns about the macroeconomic impacts of eliminating automatic extensions of EADs, such as undermining U.S. economic competitiveness, innovation capacity, and national interests by forcing workers into temporary unemployment. Other commenters predicted that the IFR would lead to negative economic impacts, including reduced tax revenue, costs to taxpayers, supply chain disruptions, reduced consumer spending, the risk of a recession, and job losses. Some commenters expressed general concern that the IFR will reduce economic productivity and destabilize the workforce and the economy, considering that one in five U.S. workers is an immigrant who relies on EADs.
Commenters said that the IFR would significantly increase States' healthcare costs by driving up the uninsured rate among immigrants, who already face limited access to Medicaid and Affordable Care Act coverage. The commenters remarked that with lapses in work authorization eliminating employer-sponsored insurance, States could bear nearly $280 billion in uncompensated care costs. The commenters also stated that the IFR would adversely impact the States' ability to enforce their laws, reasoning that legal workers with lapses in work authorization would increasingly enter the underground economy and become less likely to report labor and civil rights violations and discussed how this would interfere with the States' ability to enforce their labor and civil rights laws, because effective enforcement relies on employees' ability and willingness to report violations.
A commenter said the IFR would have significant negative consequences on the federal budget and federal agencies such as the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and Department of Labor (DOL) because the IFR would reduce the amount of taxable income reported to the IRS when applicants face prolonged lapses in employment authorization, diminishing federal revenue and complicating federal fiscal projections. The commenter further asserted that cutting off work authorization for aliens awaiting renewal would push thousands of workers into unauthorized employment or out of the workforce entirely and consequently increase DOL's investigatory burdens.
Furthermore, commenters highlighted a range of potential negative impacts on the local and state economy, such as disrupting the workforce and hindering an alien's ability to maintain consistent employment, which, in turn, could directly affect essential community services, including infrastructure projects, healthcare, and public safety. A commenter highlighted that immigrants play a major role in entrepreneurship. Another commenter remarked that Maine stands to lose an economic boom they are currently experiencing if immigrant workers lose work authorization.
While expressing concerns about the impacts the IFR's regulatory changes would have on the economy, multiple commenters requested a return to previous practices allowing automatic extension of EAD validity periods.
Response:
DHS agrees that immigrants, including aliens who were eligible for the automatic extension of their employment authorization and/or EAD for up to 540 days, make important contributions to the national and local economies through their labor, entrepreneurship, tax payments, and consumer spending; and that continuity of lawful employment can benefit workers, employers, and communities. DHS also acknowledges the many cited studies, data points, and experiences to support their claims about these contributions.
As the commenters noted, prior DHS rulemakings, including the 2022 and 2024 temporary final rules and the 2024 final rule, emphasized the economic and operational benefits of automatic extensions as a tool to mitigate the effects of EAD processing delays. Those rules estimated that automatic extensions could reduce wage losses for affected workers, avoid turnover costs for employers, and maintain tax contributions that might otherwise be impacted by lapses in employment authorization. In adopting those measures, DHS gave significant weight to the economic and labor market
(
printed page 65332)
advantages of continuity of employment.
The IFR and this final rule in contrast reflect a reassessment of that policy and how to balance those economic considerations against DHS's core responsibilities for national security, public safety, and benefit integrity. DHS has determined that continued use of automatic extensions, which allow employment authorization and the related use of secure documentation to continue for up to 540 days based solely on the filing of a renewal application, before USCIS has completed updated vetting, resolved any derogatory information, and determined that the alien remains eligible and continues to merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable, is not consistent with DHS's current policy priorities reflected in, among others,
E.O. 14159
[
93
]
and 14161.
[
94
]
Those E.O.s direct DHS to vet and screen aliens already present in the United States to the maximum degree possible, to ensure that employment authorization is not provided to unauthorized aliens, and to identify all resources that may be used to ensure that all aliens who are already in the United States, are vetted and screened to the maximum degree possible.
Accordingly, ending the practice of providing automatic extension of employment authorization documents enhances the benefit integrity in adjudications of employment authorization requests and better protects public safety and national security by ensuring that aliens are properly vetted and determined to continue to be eligible (and merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable) for employment authorization before such authorization is provided to the alien. DHS emphasizes that it is charged with combating unauthorized employment in accordance with section 274A of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1324a
, which Congress implemented, among other reasons, because of the detrimental negative effect that unauthorized employment and illegal immigration has on the United States and the economy.
[
95
]
In light of these directives, DHS is now placing greater weight on security and benefit integrity considerations.
DHS recognizes that ending automatic extensions may result in temporary lapses in employment authorization and/or EAD validity for some renewal applicants if the adjudication of their renewal EAD application is not completed before their current EAD expires. Those lapses can lead to lost wages for affected workers, lost output and turnover costs for employers, and associated reductions in payroll and income tax contributions for the duration of the lapse. DHS also acknowledges that such impacts may be more pronounced in certain localities, sectors, or communities where EAD holders represent a substantial share of the workforce, and that employers and governments may face transitional challenges as they adjust to this change.
While DHS faces uncertainty in projecting the size of any future affected population and the magnitude of resulting macroeconomic impacts, under several assumptions DHS has estimated the impacted population and cost-impacts for a specific window of time. As explained in the IFR and earlier in this preamble, EAD processing times have fluctuated over recent years due to changes in application volumes, programmatic policies, resource levels, and court orders. DHS has also undertaken significant policy changes, such as narrowing the use of parole and better aligning TPS and related programs with statutory criteria, that are expected to materially reduce initial and renewal EAD filings over time. Given this evolving environment, DHS estimates of the number of renewal applicants who might experience lapses in the absence of automatic extensions population, and the resultant impact estimates, likely face significant variation. For this reason, we clearly articulate the assumptions and inputs relied upon to make the estimates and provide ranges for them.
With respect to commenters' concerns about reduced tax revenues and increased uncompensated care, DHS acknowledges that lower earned income during periods when some workers are not employed could reduce certain tax payments and contributions toward employer-sponsored health coverage for those individuals. At the same time, total tax receipts and healthcare costs depend on numerous factors across the broader economy, and DHS cannot attribute or forecast such aggregate effects with sufficient precision to support a quantitative estimate specific to this rule.
DHS also does not agree that ending automatic extensions will necessitate or require a shift of large numbers of workers into unauthorized employment.
[
96
]
While DHS acknowledges that unauthorized work can create an underground labor market where exploitation is more likely and enforcement more difficult, this rule does not require or condone unauthorized employment. The INA prohibits the knowing employment of unauthorized aliens and establishes consequences for both employers and aliens who engage in such conduct.
See
INA sec. 274A,
8 U.S.C. 1324a
;
8 CFR part 274a
. DHS will continue to enforce those provisions, as well as coordinate with the Department of Labor and other agencies on labor-rights enforcement and protection of workers, regardless of immigration status. Nothing in this rule alters existing worker-protection authorities or the ability of Federal, State, or local entities to investigate and remedy labor law violations.
DHS further notes that this rule does not change underlying eligibility criteria for employment authorization or prevent renewal applicants from obtaining employment authorization and/or an EAD. Eligible aliens remain able to apply for and receive renewed EADs, and, once those renewals are approved, continue contributing economically through lawful employment. DHS expects that other policy changes that DHS has made will reduce EAD filing volumes, and when combined with ongoing process improvements and careful resource allocation within USCIS, will lessen the frequency and duration of any future lapses in employment authorization and/or EADs.
[
97
]
DHS has seen falling
(
printed page 65333)
numbers of I-765 applications since October 2025.
See
Table 1 in Section IV.C.2.i.d. of this preamble.
Renewal applicants can further reduce their risk of a temporary lapse in employment authorization by filing as early as permitted under applicable regulations and form instructions, ensuring that their application includes all evidence needed to establish continued eligibility so that processing is not delayed by a Request for Evidence, and by keeping informed of current processing-time information posted by USCIS.
[
98
]
Proper planning by applicants, together with anticipated reductions in overall EAD demand, may help mitigate the extent of any temporary disruptions.
As discussed above, DHS believes the public safety, national security and benefit-integrity benefits of eliminating automatic extensions outweigh the potential macroeconomic and local economic costs identified by commenters. Ending the practice of providing automatic extension of employment authorization documents enhances the benefit integrity in adjudications of employment authorization requests and better protects public safety and national security by ensuring that aliens are properly vetted and determined to continue to be eligible (and merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable) for employment authorization before such authorization is provided to the alien.
iii. Relief for Specific Immigration Categories
a. Impact on Refugees, Asylees, Asylum Seekers, Unaccompanied Alien Children (UACs), and Other Humanitarian Categories
Comment:
Multiple commenters stated that refugees, asylees, TPS beneficiaries, VAWA self-petitioners, and unaccompanied children will be disproportionately harmed by gaps in work authorization because of their vulnerability, limited access to public benefits, which makes work authorization crucial to their wellbeing, and reliance on work to support themselves, safety, and integration. A commenter indicated that the IFR would not only destabilize the workforce, but would inflict unconscionable distress and cause lasting harm to refugees, asylees (including those with pending claims) and other humanitarian entrants and their families, solely on account of the government's processing delay and the impact of lapses in employment on this population.
Some commenters expressed concern that asylum seekers of specific nationalities including Haitians, Ukrainians, Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders, and Afghans were disproportionally affected by the IFR. Additionally, some of these commenters indicated that these aliens did not enter through an unknown or informal process but known, vetted and humanitarian programs, and are law-abiding and productive individuals that benefited the government and the economy. For that reason—while at the same time acknowledging the Department's interest in benefit integrity, security vetting, and aligning policies with recent executive directives emphasizing enforcement and careful screening, a commenter advocated for a narrow, risk-sensitive approach that preserves the core logic of the interim final rule while avoiding an “all or nothing” outcome for the vetted humanitarian population.
Another commenter remarked that the removal of the automatic extension of EADs would have severe consequences for those obtaining status through the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA), in particular Asian American and Pacific Islander women, who are particularly vulnerable to these harms, as work interruptions can force them into unsafe situations or dependence on abusive partners. Others indicated that access to employment authorization offers safety, stability, and a better quality of life for survivors of gender-based violence. One commenter explained that abusers commonly misuse the immigration system, for example, by threatening to withhold, withdraw, or sabotage immigration filings, as a means of control and intimidation, and predicted the rule would exacerbate this problem. This submission called attention to backlogs in adjudicating EAD renewal applications and predicted hardships for survivors and families due to lapses in employment.
A commenter expressed concern that unaccompanied children and youth would be negatively impacted. The commenter said that young protection seekers, even those not yet eligible to work, often rely on EADs as a form of government identification to access essential social services and care such as psychological, education, and housing services. The commenter also said that EADs “facilitate critical access to jobs and training opportunities for older youth.”
Response:
DHS understands that refugees, asylees, asylum applicants, TPS beneficiaries, VAWA self-petitioners, unaccompanied children, and other humanitarian populations may be particularly vulnerable to hardship if they experience lapses in employment authorization and/or EAD validity. As recognized in the IFR for purposes of all applicants, including those in humanitarian programs, DHS is cognizant that a lapse in employment authorization and/or EAD validity may impact individual aliens, and their families. Many applicants in the United States may have fled persecution, violence, or disaster, may have limited access to public benefits, and often rely heavily on employment authorization to support themselves and their families and to integrate into their communities.
This rule does not eliminate access to employment authorization for any of these categories. Refugees and asylees (not including asylum applicants) remain employment authorized incident to their status under
8 CFR 274a.12(a)
; they may continue to work so long as they maintain that status, regardless of the expiration date on any EAD issued as evidence of that authorization. Similarly, aliens with a pending asylum application may apply for employment authorization in accordance with the regulations provided at
8 CFR part 208
and
8 CFR part 274a
. TPS beneficiaries likewise receive employment authorization consistent with section 244 of the Act,
8 U.S.C. 1254a
, and its implementing regulations at
8 CFR 244
, and TPS-related extensions of documentation may continue to be provided by law or
Federal Register
notice. This rule does not change those underlying eligibility frameworks.
The IFR and this final rule simply end the practice of automatically extending the validity of EADs and, for categories not authorized incident to status, attendant employment authorization based solely on the filing of a renewal application on or after October 30, 2025, except where extensions are provided by law or
Federal Register
notice (such as certain TPS-related documents). DHS has determined that automatic extensions of employment authorization and/or EADs, even for vulnerable populations, present the same underlying concern: they allow continued employment authorization and use of secure documentation for up to 540 days based solely on a pending renewal application, before USCIS has determined continued eligibility and that the applicant merits a favorable exercise of discretion (if applicable) in
(
printed page 65334)
light of any new information, including potential criminal or other derogatory information.
Consistent with Executive Orders
[
99
]
and the Department's mission, DHS does not believe that it is reasonable to maintain a separate automatic extension regime for particular categories of applicants, while at the same time addressing this core security and benefit integrity issue. Even a risk-based approach for humanitarian programs, as a commenter suggested, would fail to address the core concern that some aliens could continue employment authorization, and potentially use associated documents to obtain other benefits, without updated vetting and adjudication. The Department has instead chosen a uniform approach that applies the same principle across affected categories.
DHS acknowledges that some asylum applicants and other humanitarian applicants may experience temporary lapses in employment authorization if renewal adjudications are not completed before their current EADs expire. Asylum applicants, in particular, may have limited access to public benefits under existing statutes, and gaps in income may be difficult to absorb. DHS considered these factors but concluded that they did not outweigh the need to ensure that each renewal of employment authorization and/or an EAD is granted only after USCIS has completed appropriate vetting and determined that the applicant continues to be eligible and continues to merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable.
DHS notes that, separate from this rule, asylum and refugee status confers or may lead to eligibility for certain public benefits under existing law, and certain other vulnerable groups may be eligible for specialized support programs.
[
100
]
Those frameworks are not altered by this rule.
In addition, DHS has taken steps to reduce incentives for frivolous or non-meritorious filings that might delay adjudications for bona fide humanitarian applicants, thereby seeking to improve processing for those with meritorious claims. For example, in the past four years, USCIS has seen alarming new filing trends, including a 360% overall increase in VAWA self-petition filings.
[
101
]
When unqualified aliens misuse the VAWA program, it causes significant processing delays, harming survivors with legitimate claims.
[
102
]
On December 22, 2025, USCIS took steps to address these issues by updating guidance in the USCIS Policy Manual to streamline and clarify the expectations of submitted evidence and reduce the need for Requests for Evidence and Notices of Intent to Deny, among other clarifying changes.
[
103
]
With respect to unaccompanied children and youth, this rule does not change any statutory protections or procedural safeguards applicable to that population.
[
104
]
To the extent that employment-eligible unaccompanied children and youth seek EADs to participate in job training opportunities for valid employment purposes, they remain eligible to apply and, if approved, to work consistent with existing regulations. The IFR and this final rule do not impact or prevent the use of valid EADs as identity documents; they simply end the practice of automatically extending the validity of employment authorization documents for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew their EAD in certain employment authorization categories filed on or after October 30, 2025.
DHS recognizes the heightened vulnerability of humanitarian populations and will continue to administer those programs consistent with statutory protections and humanitarian objectives. However, DHS concludes that the core principle underlying this rule, namely that renewed employment authorization should not be automatically extended without fully completing the adjudicative review and the related vetting, including resolution of any derogatory information identified during the vetting process—must be applied consistently across affected categories to fulfill DHS's national security, public safety, and benefit integrity responsibilities. As explained in detail in the IFR, granting benefits without fully completing the adjudicative review, which includes proper vetting, is contrary to the statutory mission of DHS and poses a threat to the safety and security of the American people.
[
105
]
b. Impact on Employment-Based Nonimmigrants, Their Dependents, and Employment-Based Green Card Applicants
Comment:
Multiple commenters expressed concern about the removal of automatic extensions of EADs for H-4 dependent spouses. Some commenters said that eliminating automatic EAD renewal disproportionately harms women, who make up most H-4 EAD holders. Multiple commenters raised concerns that H-4 nonimmigrants are dependent on their spouses' H-1B status, creating vulnerabilities.
A number of commenters remarked that current processing times for H-4 EAD applications frequently exceed the recommended filing time of 180 days prior to the current EAD's expiration and argued the removal of automatic extensions would result in many aliens losing employment authorization and facing unavoidable work gaps. Commenters said that delays in H-1B processing, from either the Department of Labor or DHS, could adversely affect an H-4 nonimmigrant's status and application for an EAD, complicating timely filing.
Other commenters suggested that removing the automatic extension would significantly reduce the employability of H-4 nonimmigrants and will cause adverse effects including family income and savings disruption, termination of health insurance for spouses and children, possible eviction or inability to meet mortgage obligations, psychological stress and medical hardship, administrative burden on employers managing I-9 reverifications, and work interruptions.
Other commenters said that H-4 EAD holders contribute significantly to the economy through their specialized work and through taxes; have been thoroughly vetted by USCIS; and are actively contributing to their
(
printed page 65335)
communities. The commenters indicated that the lack of a reasonable extension period for a fully vetted and documented population of legal residents is counterproductive to the goals of a stable immigration system. Therefore, one commenter urged DHS to reconsider this IFR, or revert to the previous duration of the automatic extension or extend it to at least 240 days, to align with the current USCIS processing timelines or exempt certain categories like C26 and other legal resident categories who are already vetted multiple times.
Other commenters highlighted the effects of the IFR on business as they are relying on a stable and authorized workforce to meet client commitments, drive innovation, and support U.S. economic growth. This commenter concluded that the IFR would primarily affect H-4 and L-2 dependents whose EAD renewals already face significant processing delays, which in turn disrupts projects, increases administrative burdens and cause significant financial and emotional distress to the employees and their families. Many also believed that they could lose their authorization to work, impacting them and the U.S. citizens they employ. Many urged USCIS to retain the automatic extensions to reduce backlogs and improve adjudication, reduce disruptions to businesses, including small-businesses, and increase America's global competitiveness.
Response:
This rule does not change the underlying eligibility of H-4, L-2, or other employment-based dependents to apply for employment authorization and/or EAD. This final rule also does not alter the eligibility of employment-based adjustment applicants to seek EADs while their Form I-485 applications are pending. For nonimmigrants whose employment authorization is incident to status and not necessarily evidenced by an EAD (for example, certain L-2 spouses with appropriate notation on their Form I-94), that authorization continues for so long as the underlying nonimmigrant status remains valid, irrespective of any separate EAD. For those whose employment authorization is granted under
8 CFR 274a.12(c)
, renewal of that authorization remains discretionary and time limited.
As is the case for all nonimmigrant classifications who were eligible to receive an automatic extension of the validity of employment authorization documents prior to the IFR, this rule eliminates only the practice of providing an automatic extension of the EAD validity and, where applicable, attendant employment authorization based solely on a timely filed renewal EAD application on or after October 30, 2025. DHS acknowledges that, given current and historical processing times for some dependent and employment-based EAD categories, as well as the steps needed to fully adjudicate and vet an application, there may be a risk that USCIS may not complete adjudication of every renewal application before the prior card expires. In such cases, affected dependents and adjustment applicants may experience temporary lapses in employment authorization and associated impacts on income, benefits, and career continuity. Employers may also face disruptions if they are unable to retain those employees pending renewal.
DHS has carefully weighed these impacts against its responsibility to ensure that renewed employment authorization is granted only after USCIS has completed appropriate vetting and determined that the applicant continues to be eligible and merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable. Automatic extensions for H-4, L-2, and employment-based adjustment applicants present the same underlying security and program integrity concerns as automatic extensions for other categories: they allow continued employment authorization and use of facially expired secure documentation for up to 540 days based solely on a pending application, before USCIS has determined continued eligibility in light of any new information, including potential ineligibility for employment authorization or potential criminal or other derogatory information.
For these reasons, DHS declines to preserve automatic extensions of any length for any subset of renewal EAD applicants, including employment-based- dependents or adjustment applicants.
[
106
]
Providing carve outs would perpetuate the core concern that some aliens could continue employment authorization, and potentially use associated documents to obtain other benefits, without updated vetting and adjudication. The Department has instead chosen a uniform approach that applies the same principle across affected categories.
DHS notes that many employment-based EADs are linked to other benefit requests (for example, principal nonimmigrant extensions or adjustment applications) and that USCIS is engaged in efforts to streamline and coordinate processing where operationally feasible. USCIS will continue to explore process improvements to further reduce the potential for future backlogs, including the potential for expanded use of premium processing or other tools where authorized by statute, while ensuring that security and integrity are not compromised.
DHS recognizes the important economic and personal contributions of employment-based nonimmigrants, their families, and adjustment applicants, and the disruption that lapses in employment authorization may cause for these aliens, their employers, or to the businesses that these aliens may have opened and operated based on their EAD. Nevertheless, DHS concludes that the need to ensure that renewed employment authorization is extended only after full adjudicative review for continued eligibility (including whether the applicant merits a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable) and vetting, consistent with current national security and public safety priorities, justifies ending automatic extensions for these categories as well and outweighs the potential impacts of temporary lapses in employment authorization.

7. Recommendations for the Automatic Extension and EAD Validity Period
Several commenters encouraged DHS to explore alternative solutions that better balance national security, economic stability, and human dignity.
i. Maintain the Automatic Extension, Including Various Lengths of the Extension Period
Comment:
Many commenters urged DHS to withdraw the IFR and instead maintain the automatic extension policy. Some commenters stated that keeping the automatic extension policy is necessary to protect workers and their families from losing continuity of employment caused by processing delays and protecting the economic and strategic interests of the United States. Multiple commenters reasoned that the automatic extension should be retained until reliable EAD renewal processing benchmarks (for example, less than 90 days) are consistently met.
Numerous commenters said DHS should at a minimum restore the up-to-180-day automatic extension period. Other commenters recommended various extension periods, including up to 120 days, up to 180 days, or up to 240 days, rather than removing extension periods entirely to better align with the current USCIS processing timelines and ensure minimal workforce disruption.
Response:
DHS declines to adopt the commenters' suggestions. Keeping a reduced automatic extension period would conflict with DHS's overriding concern that granting employment authorization benefits to aliens without those aliens being properly vetted and determined to continue to be eligible (and merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable) based on a complete adjudicative review is contrary to the DHS mission to enhance benefit integrity and protect public safety and national security.
[
111
]
As explained in the IFR,
[
112
]
if DHS pursued these options, aliens with derogatory information flagged during the background check process would nevertheless still obtain an automatic extension of some lengths (such as 180 or 240 days). These extensions pose a security vulnerability and undermine benefit integrity. As with the up to 540-day automatic extension, any automatic extension duration would not eliminate the risk that an alien who wished to fund nefarious activities could continue to work lawfully and generate money. These same aliens could use their automatically extended employment authorization and/or EADs to obtain valid identity documents, which would make it easier to commit conduct detrimental to the United States.
ii. Consecutive EAD Validity Periods
Comment:
Numerous commenters recommended implementing consecutive EAD validity periods so that applicants could file early without losing work authorization, time, and money. Commenters reasoned that under the current system, when aliens file well in advance of expiration, USCIS routinely issues overlapping validity periods rather than starting the new approval period at the end of the existing authorization period resulting in early filers losing usable work authorization time. Some commenters concluded that consecutive EAD validity periods would allow aliens to apply far in advance, provide USCIS with a longer adjudication window, and preserve the full period of authorized employment.
Similarly, another commenter reasoned that EADs should be issued for longer validity periods to reduce the frequency of renewals, stating that a 1-year EAD is, in practice, effective for only 6 months as renewal adjudication typically requires approximately 6 months. The commenter wrote that the IFR ignores the operational realities, that, although USCIS may accept EAD renewals filed more than 180 days before expiration, the agency issues overlapping—not consecutive—validity periods, effectively cutting into the card's usable time and forcing applicants into an ever earlier renewal cycle.
Response:
DHS considered the alternatives suggested by the commenters but will not adopt them. DHS's top priority is the robust vetting of all aliens in our country to better protect the safety of American workers and the public at large. The IFR, and this final rule, will enhance public safety by ensuring proper vetting before issuing renewal EADs, which are important benefits, and improve program integrity. DHS is enhancing its vetting and screening efforts, increasing its ability to detect aliens with potentially harmful intent, deter fraud, and place removable aliens into proceedings. USCIS uses all provisions under the law, to the extent permissible under the law, to deny benefits to those who are a risk to public safety and national security. This includes more frequent vetting of aliens, including more frequent determinations that an alien granted an EAD continues to remain eligible for employment
(
printed page 65337)
authorization and, as applicable, continues to merit a favorable exercise of discretion. DHS believes that it would be inconsistent with these policy goals for USCIS to issue, concurrently or in close proximity, multiple EADs to the same alien with consecutive validity periods or to issue EADs with longer validity periods, as the commenters suggest. Consecutive EADs based on the filing of multiple renewal applications, concurrently or in close proximity, would be tantamount to one EAD with a longer validity period. The result of these alternatives would be less frequent vetting and eligibility determinations, which would be directly contrary to DHS's stated policy goal of the IFR and this final rule.
iii. Allowing Application Filing Earlier Than 180 days
Comment:
Some commenters recommended extending the filing window for EAD renewals beyond the current 180 days prior to expiration to mitigate processing risks. A few commenters said USCIS should allow EAD renewals to be filed 12 months prior to expiration.
Response:
Although USCIS generally recommends that applicants not file requests to renew EADs more than 180 days before the expiration of their EADs, there is no prohibition on filing the form before a certain date ahead of expiration. However, USCIS does not postdate the renewal EAD in relation to an applicant's current EAD's validity period. Therefore, applicants who file and have their EAD applications adjudicated further ahead of the expiration of their current EADs may have less of a risk of incurring gaps in their employment authorization but may also have a shorter combined employment authorization validity period.
USCIS is committed to continuing to explore processing efficiencies, including possible expansion of premium processing for some or all affected populations.
iv. Enhanced Vetting
Comment:
Some commenters said DHS should implement enhanced vetting, such as ongoing security checks for applicants, without eliminating automatic extension of EADs. Other commenters recommended DHS maintain the automatic extension of EADs for up to 540 days while renewal applications are adjudicated, but conduct vetting on a “particularized basis,” noting that USCIS can use its discretionary authority to cancel an extension in individual cases when and if derogatory information or other concerns arise.
Response:
In service of the DHS mission, and to ensure that DHS grants benefits only after having thoroughly vetted in the context of the renewal application and full adjudicative review for continued eligibility (including, as applicable, whether the applicant merits a favorable exercise of discretion), DHS declines to adopt these recommendations. DHS has determined that automatic extensions are not compatible with its current security and benefit integrity priorities, even in an environment where enhanced vetting tools are used. DHS will grant renewed employment authorization only after USCIS has reviewed a completed application, conducted the appropriate checks, resolved any derogatory information, and determined that the applicant continues to be eligible and continues to merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable. Even if DHS were to cancel the extension in individual cases, as the commenter suggests, the alien would still have had the benefit of a renewed EAD, even if for a short time, without proper vetting and a full eligibility adjudication, which is contrary to the DHS mission to enhance benefit integrity and better protect public safety and national security. Any automatic extension of employment authorization and/or EAD validity based solely on the filing of a renewal application, even if subsequently cancelled or terminated, would not eliminate the risk that an alien who wished to fund nefarious activities could continue to work lawfully and generate money, even though the alien may not be eligible for the renewal EAD in the first place. Thus, DHS believes granting a benefit without completely and fully finishing the adjudicatory process (including vetting) would make it easier for aliens engaged in nefarious activity to commit conduct detrimental to the United States and will not adopt the commenter's suggestion.
8. Processing Capacity and Timelines
i. Timely Processing of Renewals
Comment:
A few commenters stated support for the IFR but urged USCIS to ensure timely processing of renewals, so workers and employers do not experience unintended lapses in employment authorization. A commenter added that if the process cannot be completed within 180 days of application, then the IFR is “very unfair.” Many commenters said USCIS should be required to adjudicate and process all EAD applications more quickly. Multiple commenters recommended a specific timeframe (for example, under 90 days or under 6 months/180 days) be set for renewals to ensure timely processing. A commenter stated that efficient, timely processing is the only measure that genuinely improves both security and economic stability.
Response:
DHS remains committed to timely processing applications without lowering security and vetting standards or benefit integrity. DHS understands the importance of timely processing and strives to adjudicate applications as efficiently as possible. However, a variety of factors can affect processing times, such as security vetting requirements and the total number of applications pending review. USCIS continually monitors its resource allocations and makes adjustments, as appropriate and feasible to ensure customer service. However, DHS cannot commit to a maximum processing time in all cases given the need for thorough review of each application to ensure that USCIS only grants employment authorization after full vetting and screening of the applicant, including resolution of any derogatory information, and determining that the alien continues to be eligible for employment authorization and/or an EAD and to merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable.
DHS notes that we expect overall EAD filing rates (initials and renewals) are likely to substantially decline given actions DHS has taken to align policy with statutory text. DHS anticipates that this decline will free up adjudicative resources to reduce renewal EAD processing times and the need for renewal EAD applicants in the longer term to rely on an automatic extension of their EAD to avoid lapses in employment authorization and/or EAD validity due to processing delays.

Even if additional resources were to further improve processing times, they would not eliminate the core security and program-integrity risk inherent in granting automatic extensions without a full adjudication of the application.

10. Other Alternatives and Recommendations
Comment:
A commenter discussed Continuous Immigration Vetting (CIV) as a more effective timely identification of national security and public safety risks than point-in-time screening and vetting that occurs only upon application submissions. Multiple commenters asked why DHS cannot utilize “concurrent vetting,” an apparent reference to CIV, as an alternative to the procedures implemented by the IFR. Commenters noted that DHS currently employs CIV in some contexts. Specifically, commenters noted that, “DHS already has a system that protects security while letting people keep working, and it has not explained why it cannot keep using it.”
Response:
DHS appreciates the commenters' focus on the role of CIV and other automated screening tools in enhancing national security and public safety. CIV is an event-based vetting tool that automates and streamlines the process of notifying USCIS of potential derogatory information in Government databases that may relate to individuals in USCIS systems, as new information is discovered.
[
135
]
DHS agrees that continuous screening and vetting capabilities (including systems such as CIV and ATLAS, along with interagency information sharing) are important components of DHS's security efforts.
However, these tools are not a substitute for the full adjudicative process that occurs when USCIS considers a new application for an immigration benefit, including a renewal of employment authorization. Continuous vetting may identify new information or trigger further review, but it does not, by itself, resolve questions of eligibility (including whether the alien warrants a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable), assess all relevant evidence, or provide the structured context in which USCIS officers make determinations about continued eligibility and the exercise of discretion, if applicable. Eligibility determinations are complex and require an officer to examine all the facts and evidence of a case prior to a finding. Vetting, like CIV, is one part of the overall process.
A core concern addressed by the IFR and this final rule is that automatic extensions of EADs allow employment authorization to continue for up to 540 days based solely on the filing of a renewal application, without USCIS first completing adjudicative review and the related vetting, including the resolution of any derogatory information. That is, the benefit is granted without USCIS first performing the following actions: an eligibility determination, completing vetting and screening checks, resolving potential hits of derogatory information in connection with the alien, and a determination that the employment authorization should be granted in the exercise of discretion, if applicable. Even with continuous vetting in place, an alien could remain work authorized under an automatic extension and use that authorization to obtain or maintain other documents, such as driver's licenses, including REAL ID compliant driver's licenses in some jurisdictions, during a period when USCIS has not yet reevaluated eligibility in light of any new information or changed circumstances.
Accordingly, DHS has determined that automatic extensions are not compatible with its current security and benefit integrity priorities, even in an environment where CIV and other continuous vetting tools are used. Those tools complement but do not replace the requirement that renewed employment authorization be granted only after USCIS has completed the actions discussed above. Therefore, DHS declines to rely on CIV as a basis for retaining automatic extensions of EADs.
Comment:
Multiple commenters requested that USCIS withdraw or delay the implementation of the IFR until DHS could guarantee timely EAD processing for all categories.
Several commenters requested a grace period or transitional period to mitigate the abrupt impacts of the IFR. Some commenters reasoned that the IFR provided no grace period for applicants who relied on the prior policy at the time of filing, imposing undue hardship on individuals and families who would face employment gaps threatening their livelihoods and financial security.
Some commenters requested specific transitional measures, including:
Granting the automatic extension to all applicants whose renewal applications were postmarked before the effective date of the rule, even if received later;
Delaying the effective date of the IFR by at least 90 days;
Providing a transition period of at least 12 months for employers and employees to adjust workforce planning and compliance systems;
A phased transition to prevent work authorization gaps during EAD adjudication; and
Coordinating with the Department of Health and Human Services, the Health Resources and Services Administration, the Department of Veterans Affairs, and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to assess workforce impacts prior to full implementation.
A few commenters urged DHS to delay implementation and open a full notice and comment period.

DHS understands that the IFR and this final rule, and any resulting gaps in continued employment authorization, may have adverse impacts on employers and applicants to the extent that individuals experience disruptions in employment. However, as stated earlier in the preamble DHS expects that overall EAD filing rates will substantially decline and free up adjudicative resources to reduce renewal EAD processing times. Decreasing processing times would result in a reduced need for aliens filing renewal EAD applications to rely on an automatic extension of their EAD to avoid potential lapses. DHS notes that USCIS has, as expected, seen a steady decrease in overall EAD filings since
(
printed page 65341)
January 2025.

Table 1 in Section IV.C.2.i.d. of this preamble.

Ultimately, granting benefits without proper vetting and full adjudication is contrary to the DHS mission to enhance benefit integrity and better protect public safety and national security.
[
136
]
DHS believes that these policy goals outweigh concerns about potential backlogs and operational challenges that may result in a temporary lapse of employment authorization and/or EAD validity. Therefore, DHS declines to adopt the commenters' suggested transitional measures or otherwise delay implementation of this rule.

Further, additional outreach would not address the fact that employers do not receive direct notice if their alien employees' pending EAD renewal applications have been denied, which creates a risk that employers could unwittingly engage in unauthorized employment and provide income to aliens with potentially nefarious motives.
After considering these concerns, DHS determined that continued reliance on the 540-day automatic extension, even with expanded outreach and educational materials, would not sufficiently address these compliance and program integrity risks. DHS will continue to provide clear, accessible information about employment authorization validity through its public-facing resources.
DHS notes that the justification for the IFR and this final rule is to enhance benefit integrity and better protect public safety and national security. 11. Administrative Procedure Act
i. “Good Cause” for Bypassing the Notice and Comment Period
Comment:
Numerous commenters stated that DHS failed to demonstrate valid “good cause” to bypass the standard notice and comment process. Commenters said that immediate implementation without notice and comment rulemaking represents a “significant procedural failure.” Two commenters requested that USCIS reconsider the decision to immediately implement the IFR and that fair advance notice should be given in the future.
Other commenters stated that the described “security vulnerability that could allow bad actors to continue to work and generate income to potentially finance nefarious activities that pose an imminent threat to the American public” had no causal connection to the automatic extension, was speculative, unsupported by any reliable evidence, and at any rate that a single example of potential adverse consequence is insufficient to establish the meticulous and demanding good cause standard. Commenters indicated that the analysis was devoid of specific factual allegations of harm or threat to public safety.
Commenters also indicated that the IFR failed to explain how the incident in Boulder was related to the automatic work authorization extension provision or why this one incident, even if related, would justify the impact the termination of this rule would have on hundreds of thousands of workers and their U.S. employers.
(
printed page 65342)
Many commenters stated that DHS's claim that providing a notice and comment period would cause noncitizens to “rush” to file EAD renewal applications was unfounded. One commenter said that this “rush” is unlikely given that USCIS instructs applicants not to file more than 180 days before their current EAD expires, and because the high renewal fees make rapid, unplanned filings less feasible.
Multiple commenters said that to properly invoke the “good cause” exemption, the claimed harm must be “demonstrable and immediate—like war, health crisis, or economic collapse.” The commenters noted that DHS recognizes that “good cause” has been limited to quantifiable threats, such as in the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks or hurricanes, and that one anecdote is insufficient evidence of “demonstrable and immediate” harm at the scale of economic collapse. They also asserted that DHS failed to establish that the attack would not have occurred in the absence of automatic renewals, or that it would have been detected or prevented with additional vetting. Finally, these commenters also indicated that there was no good cause because DHS failed to overcome indisputable evidence that immigrants are less likely to commit crimes than native-born citizens.
Response:
DHS disagrees with the commenters that DHS failed to meet the good cause standard under
5 U.S.C. 553(b)
or that DHS did not provide sufficient factual evidence of a public security risks to justify bypassing notice and comment procedures. DHS maintains that, under the totality of the circumstances, bypassing notice and comment procedures under
5 U.S.C. 553(b)
was justified to act swiftly and expeditiously, as notice and comment procedures would have been impracticable or contrary to public interest.
DHS also disagrees that the IFR was devoid of specific factual allegations of harm or threat to public safety, that the harm was speculative, and that the solution of the IFR was not rationally connected to the need for immediate action. The IFR clearly explained the relevance of the Boulder incident and its connection to the automatic extension,
[
140
]
and why the measure was justified, notwithstanding the impact of the automatic extension's termination on aliens and employers. DHS notes that it has now considered all comments received on the IFR and responded to them in this preamble, thereby providing the notice and comment process sought by commenters.
[
141
]
DHS believes that commenters may have misunderstood the risks associated with granting automatic extensions of an alien's expired employment authorization and/or EAD that is merely based on the timely filing of a renewal EAD application but not on fully vetting an applicant's eligibility or background. As explained in the IFR, aliens could obtain an automatic extension even if they no longer qualified for employment authorization and/or an EAD. Examples include if the alien no longer possessed the underlying status, had derogatory information that would render them ineligible for employment authorization, or would not merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable. These aliens could properly file a timely renewal application to obtain the benefit of continued employment authorization and/or an EAD for up to 540 days. This would allow aliens who could be public safety or national security threats to use associated documentation to potentially obtain other credentials, such as driver's licenses, and use it to engage in nefarious activities.
Unfortunately, aliens committing harmful acts and those engaging in nefarious activities do not operate on a schedule that aligns neatly with them seeking benefits applications. They may or may not engage in harmful activity post-approval of an application granting immigration status. Attacks, such as the one in Boulder, Colorado, are tough to predict, but they may not be impossible to stop with proper and thorough vetting and intelligence sharing among government agencies each time an alien is seeking immigration benefits.
[
142
]
Congress has long emphasized the importance of vetting each and every applicant before an immigration benefit is granted.
[
143
]
Fully vetting each applicant during every USCIS encounter helps identify patterns, flags activities, alerts officials to potential threats, and protects U.S. residents from harm. The attack in Boulder, Colorado—committed by an alien in possession of an EAD that was automatically extended—provided clear evidence of the ongoing public emergency, exposed the security vulnerability of the automatic extension, and demonstrated that every time USCIS is granting a benefit without fully vetting an applicant, an opportunity is lost to detect bad actors and protect the public. The public's response to the Boulder event underscored the urgency to act to safeguard public safety,
[
144
]
and DHS acted accordingly.
If DHS had announced the change, and followed the standard rulemaking procedures, the automatic extension process would have continued during the time spent developing this final rule. During that period, aliens with unresolved derogatory information could have obtained an automatically extended EAD. Even if USCIS had ultimately denied the actual application, the documents related to the automatically extended EAD would remain in possession of the affected alien, even if they were engaging in nefarious activity. Indeed, the automatically extended EAD may have given the attacker the very thing that enabled him to follow through with the attack in the first place. This demonstrates that the threat of attacks, as shown by the events in Boulder,
(
printed page 65343)
Colorado, is real, immediate, and ongoing.
If DHS had announced the rulemaking, DHS believes that aliens would have rushed to file renewal EAD applications to obtain automatic extensions before the rule's effective date. DHS does not believe that USCIS' instructions to renewal applicants to file 180 days before the expiration of their authorization would have helped in this regard as it would have been unclear how quickly a final rule would be issued by DHS.
Similarly, DHS does not agree that renewal fees necessarily make rapid, unplanned filings less feasible. Historically, increased filing fees have not depressed the number of individuals seeking immigration benefits, and fee waivers are still available for some applicants.
[
145
]
For these reasons, allowing automatic extension to continue for the duration of the notice and comment period would have been irresponsible given the high threat level.
[
146
]
It would also have been contrary to the public interest, impeding DHS's ability to fully execute its functions—to vet every EAD applicant with each application to prevent terrorist attacks and grant immigration benefits only to eligible aliens.
Finally, DHS is not aware of any case law—and the commenters did not cite to any—requiring that good cause can only be demonstrated if there has been more than one incident that causes an emergency or that the demonstrable and immediate harm must be of the scale of an “economic collapse” or a 9/11-type of event. Similarly, the government is not required to prove that the Boulder, Colorado attack would not have occurred in the absence of automatic extension renewals. The applicable APA standard is whether “notice and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.”
[
147
]
This standard is met when,
inter alia,
there is an emergency; when delay caused by the APA's notice and comment procedures would result in serious harm to life, property or an immediate threat to the public safety; or when announcing the rule would have hurt the public interest.
[
148
]
DHS has met the standard.
Immediately ending the practice and acting expeditiously given the security posture was a reasonable measure. As is noted throughout this rulemaking, this rule does not remove the alien's ability to seek and obtain employment authorization in accordance with current laws and regulations. To address the prior flood of EAD applications, as discussed earlier, this administration has taken significant actions that are expected to result in fewer EAD applications and shorter renewal EAD processing times.
[
149
]
Additionally, the issuance of employment authorization and/or an EAD depends largely on the applicant timely filing a renewal EAD application with sufficient evidence to establish eligibility. Thus, early and timely filing of a renewal application may allow the alien to mitigate or reduce the risk for the alien, the alien's family, and the alien's employer. DHS does not anticipate, nor have commenters provided evidence, that the IFR will adversely impact hundreds of thousands of workers and their U.S. employers. This assessment considers efforts to reduce the number of filings through policy and operational measures, as well as expected improvements in processing resulting from the overall reduction in filings. While DHS cannot rule out the potential for temporary lapses in employment authorization, DHS believes that the program integrity, public safety, and national security benefits of eliminating automatic extensions of EADs outweigh the risks of potential temporary lapses in employment authorization.
Immediately ending the practice of providing automatic extensions resulted in continued improvement in program integrity by ensuring that employment authorization is provided in a manner consistent with the laws of the United States, allowed the agency to properly perform its adjudicative function, and immediately closed the gap in the security vulnerability that the automatic extension created.

Comment:
Many commenters stated that the IFR disregarded significant reliance interests that DHS itself reaffirmed when it issued a permanent 540-day automatic extension less than one year before the IFR. Commenters said the 2025 IFR eliminates extensions entirely, imposing consequences DHS recently deemed economically harmful and operationally unworkable. v.

Response:
DHS disagrees with the assertion that the IFR did not sufficiently consider the reliance interests of the regulated public on the prior rules that provided for automatic extension of EADs and/or employment authorization based on a timely filed renewal application. The IFR specifically discussed and acknowledged reliance interests and explained why DHS has determined that any reliance interests are outweighed by the removal of automatic extensions for aliens in certain employment authorization categories.
See
90 FR 48809-10
. In preparing this final rule, DHS further considered all comments that articulated specific reliance interests.
DHS believes that the benefits of this rule to the United States outweigh any reliance interests held by the alien, his or her family, the employer or the public at-large in the automatic extensions of EADs to avoid temporary lapses in employment authorization and/or EAD validity. The Federal Government has a duty to protect U.S. national security, public safety, and the integrity of immigration benefits, and in the context of the IFR and this final rule, to better ensure that employment authorization is provided in a manner consistent with prohibiting the unlawful employment of aliens. Any reliance interest in the prior regulatory framework and policy does not outweigh the need to protect public safety and the integrity of immigration benefits and employment authorization.
vi. Failure To Consider Alternatives
Comment:
A commenter argued that DHS's rejection of two alternatives ((1) returning to a 180-day automatic work permit extension period and (2) issuing interim EAD cards) without substantive analysis and based upon unsubstantiated risks to national security does not satisfy the APA's requirement of “meaningful consideration of alternatives.”
Response:
DHS disagrees with the commenter's assertion that it did not meaningfully consider reasonable alternatives. These were reasonable alternatives for DHS to consider since they are prior DHS policies. As DHS explained in the IFR, and reiterates in this final rule, these and the other sub regulatory alternatives mentioned above suffer the same flaws as the up-to-540-day automatic extension. The automatic extension of an EAD, whether for 180 days, 540 days, or through the issuance of an interim EAD, grants the benefit of extending an alien's expired employment authorization and/or EAD merely by filing a timely renewal EAD application. That is, the benefit is granted without USCIS first performing the following actions: an eligibility determination, completing vetting and screening checks, resolving potential hits of derogatory information in connection with the aliens, and a determination that the employment authorization should be granted in the exercise of discretion, if applicable. If DHS pursued these options, aliens with derogatory information flagged during the background check process would nevertheless still obtain an automatic extension of 180 days, or an interim EAD, even if derogatory information cannot be reviewed and resolved, and their application denied, before the alien's EAD expires. These automatic extensions therefore pose a security vulnerability that could allow bad actors to continue to work and generate income to potentially finance nefarious activities that pose an imminent threat to the American public.
Comment:
Multiple commenters stated that the IFR failed to consider reasonable alternatives to eliminating automatic extensions entirely, which violates the standards of “rational decision-making” required under the APA. A commenter said DHS did not articulate any consideration of alternative, sub-regulatory means to achieve increased security for the American public, such as providing direction to staff to prioritize the vetting of EAD renewal applications, which
(
printed page 65347)
would be appropriate and a better option to meet the agency's security goals than the rule's termination of the post-2024 practice of providing automatic extensions of employment authorization and/or EADs for 540 days for eligible aliens who timely filed. A commenter stated that DHS ignores the straightforward solution of printing extension confirmations on secure paper or commonsense alternatives such as issuing multiple EADs with consecutive validity periods or improving USCIS data systems to identify and expedite renewal applications for applicants whose EAD will imminently expired, and that rejecting a simple administrative fix in favor of a rule that foreseeably creates widespread employment interruptions reflects precisely the sort of arbitrary and capricious decision-making the APA prohibits.
Another commenter said that DHS's failure to address consecutive EAD validity periods underscores the inadequacy of its “proper planning” rationale and confirms that the agency did not meaningfully consider reasonable, less disruptive alternatives, which is in violation of the APA.
Response:
DHS considered the alternatives suggested by the commenters but declined to adopt them. This administration's priority is the robust vetting of all aliens in our country to better protect the safety of American workers and the public at large. The IFR, and this final rule, will enhance public safety by ensuring proper vetting before issuing renewal EADs, which are important benefits, and improve program integrity. DHS is enhancing its vetting and screening efforts, increasing its ability to detect aliens with potentially harmful intent, deter fraud, and place removable aliens into proceedings. DHS uses all applicable provisions under the law, to protect the United States from those who are a risk to public safety and national security. This includes more frequent vetting of aliens, including more frequent determinations that an alien granted an EAD continues to remain eligible for employment authorization, and continues to merit a favorable exercise of discretion, as applicable. DHS believes that it would be inconsistent with these policy goals for USCIS to issue, concurrently or in close proximity, multiple EADs to the same alien with consecutive validity periods. Essentially, this would allow an alien to submit multiple EAD applications at or around the same time, and consecutive EADs would be tantamount to one EAD with a longer validity period. The result of this alternative would be less frequent vetting and eligibility determinations, which would be directly contrary to DHS's stated policy goal of the IFR and this final rule.
DHS does not agree that identifying and expediting renewal applications for applicants whose EAD will imminently expire is a reasonable alternative. Such an approach, even if operationally feasible, would simply encourage and incentivize applicants to wait until the last minute before filing the EAD renewal application. Expediting the applications of those who wait to file would have the unintended consequence of delaying the adjudication of those who filed six months in advance of their EAD expiration. DHS does not believe it is reasonable to reward applicants who wait until the last minute to file their renewal EAD application by moving those applications to the front of the processing queue to the disadvantage of other applicants who filed months in advance.
Furthermore, DHS does not agree that a reasonable alternative is to issue evidence of an automatic extension of employment authorization on secure paper, as that would not further the policy goal of more frequently vetting, screening, and adjudicating continued eligibility and that the alien continues to merit a favorable exercise of discretion, as applicable. Secure paper would also not resolve the issue DHS noted in the IFR
[
162
]
pertaining to the risks associated with automatic extension of employment authorization and the potential for employer confusion as to when the automatic extension of employment authorization ends. The potential confusion stems from the fact that the alien, not their employer, is the party to the renewal application and is the one notified if the renewal application is denied. Their employer is not separately notified and is dependent on notification from the alien that their renewal application has been denied and they are no longer employment authorized. If the alien does not immediately notify their employer, the employer could unknowingly employ an alien who is no longer authorized to work in the United States. The use of secure paper to print evidence of the automatic extension would have no effect on this issue, or the need to ensure more frequent vetting and screening and that the alien continues to be eligible for employment authorization and merits a favorable exercise of discretion, as applicable.
