, Protecting the American People Against Invasion (Jan. 20, 2025),
90 FR 8443
,
8446
(Jan. 29, 2025), which put the public on notice that it was the President's priority to take all appropriate action to alien any departmental activities with the policies set out by the President and to ensure, among others, “that employment authorization is provided in a manner consistent with section 274A of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1324a
, and that employment authorization is not provided to any unauthorized alien in the United States.”
Additionally, on Jan. 20, 2025, the President also issued
E.O. 14161
, Protecting the United States from Foreign Terrorists and other National Security and Public Safety Threats, which directs the coordination among the departments to identify all resources that may be used to ensure that all aliens seeking admission to the United States, or who are already in the United States, are vetted and screened to the maximum degree possible. Commenters stated that the post-promulgation comment period offered by DHS was insufficient to bypass the APA's notice and comment procedures. Courts have repeatedly held that such after-the-fact opportunities
(
printed page 65348)
cannot substitute for prior notice and comment. Once a rule takes effect, the ability to influence the agency's decision-making is, as a practical matter, diminished. The commenters added that pre-promulgation notice and comment are not optional—they are statutory prerequisites for a legislative rule to be valid, especially in this instance where the IFR will have far reaching effects. Response:
DHS disagrees with the commenters that allowing for post-promulgation comments when issuing the IFR may be insufficient for purposes of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and that the rule may be invalid or otherwise procedurally deficient. Unless a statutory exception to notice and comment rulemaking applies, the APA requires agencies to publish a notice of proposed rulemaking in the
Federal Register
before the rule has legal effect.
See
5 U.S.C. 553(b)
. The APA requires that the notice of proposed rulemaking contain reference to the legal authority under which the rule is proposed and either the terms or substance of the proposed rule or a description of the subjects and issues involved.
See
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(2)-(3)
. DHS has complied with the requirements under the APA. The IFR explained the relevant issues and the Department's rationale why it was ending the automatic extensions of employment authorizations and/or EADs under
8 CFR 274a.13
. DHS also demonstrated that it had good cause to bypass standard notice and comment procedures under the APA. With the issuance of the IFR, DHS invited the public to participate in the rulemaking, thus giving stakeholders an opportunity to provide comments on every aspect of this rule, including potential modifications. DHS is now considering all comments received on the IFR and responded to them in this preamble, thereby providing the notice and comment process sought by commenters. DHS thus has met every statutory requisite for the IFR and this final rule to be a properly issued legislative rule under the APA.
[
163
]
Comment:
Several commenters expressed that the issuance of the rule as an IFR with immediate effect that same day deprived stakeholders of any meaningful opportunity to review, comment, or prepare for compliance.
Response:
As stated in the IFR, DHS issued the IFR without prior notice or public procedures because DHS was invoking the “good cause” exception under the APA,
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)

See
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
. Both provisions allow an agency to publish a measure immediately if acting expeditiously is warranted. DHS further explained in the IFR why it was necessary for the agency to move so expeditiously in promulgating and implementing this rule. With the issuance of the IFR, however, DHS invited the public to participate in the rulemaking, thus giving stakeholders an opportunity to provide comments on every aspect of this rule, including potential modifications. DHS has now considered all comments received on the IFR and responded to them in this preamble, thereby providing the notice and comment process sought by commenters. Furthermore, DHS also explained in the IFR that the regulatory amendment involves a foreign affairs function under
5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1)
and that therefore, the agency may forego notice and comment rulemaking and a delayed effective date. Therefore, the IFR and this final rule complied with the process required under the APA for rules that are excepted from notice and comment.

i. Methodology
Comment:
Many commenters stated that the IFR fails to provide any substantive economic impact analysis of eliminating automatic EAD extensions and did not reconcile its position with DHS's recent finding that automatic extensions yield substantial economic benefits.

.

Response:
DHS believes it conducted an analysis in full compliance with
E.O. 12866
, and DHS described that this rule would affect those aliens who would no longer receive an automatic EAD extension. DHS did designate the IFR as a “significant regulatory action” and economically significant as defined under section 3(f)(1) of
E.O. 12866
, because its annual effects on the economy may exceed $100 million in any year of the analysis. Although there is likely to be variation and uncertainty in populations and filing behavior, DHS estimated in this final rule the number of EADs that are expected to lapse, and the estimated duration of the lapse, for a specific 18-month window based on some specific assumptions.
See
Section V.B.1 of this preamble for more information.
In previous rules, DHS attempted to stabilize aliens' earnings and avoid labor turnover costs of employers. DHS also continues to work to improve processing times and reduce backlogs. However, the Department has shifted focus to prioritizing public safety, national security and benefit integrity. Due to this shift, DHS acknowledges that there will be impacts to EAD renewal applicants for the classes covered in the previous extension actions and their employers. DHS disagrees with the comment that this rule would destabilize up to one-fifth of the national labor force and the employers, tax revenues, and economic activity that depend on that workforce or that the discussion about remittances in the IFR is inconsistent with DHS statistics. The reference in the IFR to the total percentage of foreign-born workers in the United States was in the context of the foreign affairs exception and a broader discussion about the significance of remittances, including by aliens affected by this rule, on foreign affairs. This rule applies directly to certain categories of renewal applications that were previously provided automatic extensions and not, as the commenter suggests, to every foreign-born worker in the U.S. economy.
ii. Impact on Individuals
Comment:

Another commenter stated that recent and proposed immigration policies will raise the cost of goods and services for U.S. families.
Response:

Due to this shift, DHS acknowledges that there will be impacts on a portion of the U.S. labor force. The commenter further stated even short lapses could cause thousands of dollars in lost wages per worker and major operational disruptions. Response:
DHS agrees that this rule reverses some of the impacts described in the prior automatic extension rules. As DHS acknowledged in the IFR, temporary lapses in employment authorization and/or EAD validity could result in cost and transfer impacts such as lost compensation to workers, transfers between workers losing their employment authorizations to replacement workers, employers' lost productivity when they are not able to quickly replace employees with lapses, and turnover costs for employers to find replacement employees.
DHS's 2024 final rule analysis projected that automatic extensions would prevent a significant number of future lapses, but anticipated that lapses would generally cease beginning in April 2026, even without the 540-day extension.
[
165
]
DHS acknowledges that the December 2025 reduction in EAD validity periods may lead to more frequent renewal applications, potentially affecting this projection.
[
166
]
However, recent declines in the affected population and changes in filing behavior make it nearly impossible to reliably estimate the number and duration of lapses.
DHS has concluded that the need to ensure proper vetting and screening, and continued eligibility, before granting renewed employment authorization and issuing secure evidence of that authorization outweighs the risk that some applicants might experience a temporary lapse in employment authorization and/or EAD validity. The prior automatic extension framework allowed aliens to continue working for up to 540 days based solely on a pending renewal application, during which time USCIS might identify, but not yet resolve, derogatory information bearing on eligibility or security concerns. DHS has determined that extending this benefit without updated adjudication and screening is inconsistent with its mission and with E.O.s directing DHS to ensure that employment authorization is not provided to unauthorized aliens and that aliens in the United States are vetted and screened to the maximum degree possible.
[
167
]
DHS disagrees with the comment that this rule would destabilize up to one-fifth of the national labor force and the employers, tax revenues, and economic activity that depend on that workforce. This rule applies directly to certain categories of renewal applications that were previously eligible for automatic extensions.
iv. Other Comments on the RIA
Comment:
A commenter asked that USCIS suspend further action with the rule until it prepares and publishes a full RIA, an Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis, and reopen the comment period for 60 days following the publishing of those materials.
Response:
DHS published an RIA in the IFR providing a qualitative assessment of benefits, transfers, and costs. In that analysis, DHS acknowledged the possibility that some renewal applicants could experience EAD lapses. However, due to factors such as population changes, reduced filings, shorter validity periods for certain EADs, DHS determined that the conditions are too uncertain to accurately estimate the number or duration of lapses. Additionally, lower filing volumes may allow DHS to address the backlog more rapidly.
While many renewal applicants covered by the two TFRs who received automatic extensions may have eventually obtained five-year EADs, projecting how many new and renewal EADs will be subject to the 18-month validity period is highly speculative. As a result, DHS cannot reliably estimate processing times, which are essential for calculating lapses and their duration.
Within the IFR, DHS referenced prior analyses from the TFRs and 2024 final rule to demonstrate that it is aware of the past situations of large lapses, but could not use prior historical data to
(
printed page 65351)
forecast the IFR's impact. Assuming prior spikes in EAD filings would continue is inconsistent with recent data.
See
Table 1 in Section IV.C.2.i.d. of this preamble. Therefore, at the time of the IFR and the issuance of this final rule, DHS could not reliably estimate the number or duration of lapsed EADs.
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.
) requires agencies to prepare an initial regulatory flexibility analysis when issuing a notice and comment rulemaking. DHS disagrees with the claims that a proper regulatory flexibility analysis was not conducted. The RFA's regulatory flexibility analysis requirements apply only to those rules for which an agency is required to publish a general notice of proposed rulemaking pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553
or any other law. DHS did not issue a notice of proposed rulemaking for this action. Accordingly, DHS is not required to either certify that this IFR would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities nor conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis. DHS acknowledged that this interim final rule directly regulates individuals, and individuals are not defined as “small entities” by the Regulatory Flexibility Act. The rule indirectly impacts certain employers if, in the future, processing times exceed the expiration dates of EADs.
DHS used the IFR, in part, to address prior policy decisions that resulted in the filing of an overwhelming and unmanageable number of EAD applications making it more important than ever to conduct complete and thorough vetting of applicants, including those filing for renewal EADs, to mitigate potential risks to public safety and national security. DHS understands that the IFR and this final rule, and any resulting gaps in continued employment authorization, may have adverse impacts on employers and applicants. However, as DHS noted in the IFR, DHS expects that overall EAD filing rates (initials and renewals) are likely to substantially decline given actions DHS has taken in support of presidential directives, freeing up adjudicative resources to reduce renewal EAD processing times and the need for renewal EAD applicants in the longer term to rely on an automatic extension of their EAD to avoid lapses in employment authorization and/or EAD validity due to processing delays.
In addition, proper planning by an applicant, and monitoring of EAD processing times, may allow the alien to mitigate the risk for the alien, the alien's family, as well as the alien's employer that the alien will experience prolonged lapses in their employment authorization and/or EAD validity. Proper planning may ameliorate the risk of losing valid employment authorization, as well as the disruption and associated instability with business continuity or other financial harm for employers and the community. Ultimately, granting benefits without proper vetting and full adjudication is contrary to the DHS mission to enhance benefit integrity and better protect public safety and national security.
[
168
]
DHS believes that this concern justifies potential backlogs and operational challenges that may result in a temporary lapse in employment authorization and/or EAD validity.
As explained, DHS has complied with the requirements of the APA and RFA. Therefore, DHS will not adopt the commenters' suggestions to withdraw the IFR, delay the implementation of the IFR or this final rule, and provide an additional comment period.

14. Paperwork Reduction Act
Comment:
A commenter said that eliminating the automatic extension directly affects two OMB-approved information collections: Form I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification (OMB Control No. 1615-0047) and Form I-765 Application for Employment Authorization (OMB Control No. 1615-0040/0016). The commenter said the rule does not appear to include Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) notices proposing revisions to these collections or revised burden estimates and DHS must either (a) publish PRA notices with revised burden and cost estimates aligned to the rule's effects, or (b) explain why no change occurs and provide data supporting that assertion. Proceeding without PRA compliance is a defect.
Response:
DHS has considered the comment asserting that this rule triggers new information collection requirements under the PRA for Form I-9, Employment Eligibility Verification (OMB Control No. 1615-0047), and Form I-765, Application for Employment Authorization (OMB Control No. 1615-0040).
Under the PRA, an agency must obtain OMB approval when it seeks to “collect information” from 10 or more persons, or when it revises an existing collection in a way that changes the information requested, who must respond, how often they must respond, or the estimated burden of responding. This rule does none of those things.
The rule does not change the Form I-765 itself, the data elements on the form, the categories of individuals who file it, or the circumstances under which it must be filed. Aliens who seek initial or renewal employment authorization and/or EAD in the affected categories will continue to use the same form, with the same instructions, to request the same benefit. The rule changes only the regulatory consequence that previously flowed automatically from the filing of certain renewal applications, not the information collected on Form I-765 or the obligation to file the form in the first place.
This rule also does not amend the requirements that govern employers' use of Form I-9. Employers are required under section 274A of the INA and
8 CFR 274a.2
to complete Form I-9 for each new hire and to reverify employment authorization when previously presented documentation expires. Those obligations exist independent of this rule. While the elimination of automatic extensions may result in some employers conducting reverification at different times than they would have under the prior automatic-extension framework, the scope and content of the information collected on Form I-9 are unchanged. The rule does not add any new fields to Form I-9, does not create a new reverification requirement, and does not expand the universe of employers subject to the Form I-9 provisions. Accordingly, it does not revise the underlying information collection approved under OMB Control No. 1615-0047.
This rule does not require DHS or employers to collect new categories of information, does not increase the frequency with which individuals must submit information to DHS beyond what is already required to seek or renew an EAD, and does not impose new recordkeeping or reporting requirements on employers beyond existing Form I-9 obligations.
Consistent with the IFR's PRA discussion and the PRA section of this final rule, DHS concludes that this rule does not introduce a new collection of information or revise an existing collection within the meaning of the PRA and that no new or amended OMB approval is required.

This final rule reaffirms and finalizes changes made by the IFR to DHS regulations to end the practice of automatically extending the validity of employment authorization documents (Forms I-766 or EADs) for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew their EAD in certain employment authorization categories. The purpose of this change is to prioritize the proper vetting and screening of aliens and ensure continued eligibility before granting a new period of employment authorization and/or a new EAD. This final rule does not affect the validity of EADs that were automatically extended prior to the IFR. In previous rules providing for the automatic extension of EADs based on the timely filing of a renewal EAD application, DHS attempted to stabilize aliens' earnings and avoid labor turnover costs of employers. However, as explained in the IFR, the Department has shifted focus to prioritizing public safety and national security, and ensuring that aliens continue to be eligible and merit a favorable exercise of discretion, as applicable, before being granted continued employment authorization.

DHS has prepared two types of quantified estimates of the impacts that could be generated by this final rule. For a single 18-month window (starting in May 2027) from about 20,000 and 33,000 EADs are estimated to lapse, based on several assumptions. This rule may result in some EAD holders incurring a loss of earnings (“reduced earnings”) because of USCIS process delays for renewal EAD applications, as under this rule there could be disruption to their earnings due to a lapsed EAD. Such earnings loss to aliens could comprise beneficial transfers to other U.S. workers if the substitution of the latter for the former is relatively frictionless. Additionally, to the extent this rule affects EAD holders' jobs going unfilled, there will be impacts to tax transfers from businesses and employees to the Federal Government.

Module B
The purpose of this rulemaking is to prioritize benefits integrity and the proper vetting and screening of aliens before granting a new period of employment authorization and/or a new EAD by ending the practice of automatically extending the validity of employment authorization and/or EADs for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew their EAD in certain employment authorization categories. While prior automatic extensions reduced the risk of employers employing aliens with lapsed employment authorization and/or EAD validity, this final rule will also reduce the risk that affected employers will continue to employ an alien who is no longer authorized to work. For example, within their automatic extension period, an alien's application could have been adjudicated and denied. The obligation is on the alien employee to notify his or her employer that he or she is no longer work authorized, which puts employers at risk of unknowingly employing an unauthorized alien. Absent the IFR and this final rule, employers assess the applicability of the automatic extension based in part on a non-secure document (such as Form I-797C, Notice of Action, which is printed on plain paper). With this final rule ending the practice of providing automatic extensions based on the timely filing of a renewal EAD application, DHS is reducing the potential for fraud and instances where employers unknowingly employ aliens beyond their employment authorization and/or EAD validity.
This rule reverses some of the impacts described in the prior automatic extension rules. Employment lapses could result in cost and transfer impacts such as lost compensation to workers, transfers between workers losing their employment authorizations to replacement workers, employers' lost productivity when they are not able to quickly replace employees with lapses, and turnover costs for employers to find replacement employees. In the following section, DHS discusses impacts but cannot reliably quantify these impacts due to uncertainty.
As was described earlier in the Affected Population section, DHS determined that an expected impact of this final rule is that some EADs will lapse while the alien's renewal EAD application is pending with USCIS. In this section, the estimated lapse is developed into a quantified impact, which will constitute an earnings change to aliens. The employment lapse impacts, a loss of income to aliens, could result in either transfers of compensation to other workers or costs to employers, depending on employers' ability to replace workers with lapsed employment authorization and/or EAD validity. In cases where, in the absence of an automatic extension period, businesses would have been able to easily find reasonable labor substitutes for aliens with a lapsed employment authorization and/or EAD validity, this rule results in transfers of the earnings of affected aliens to others, who might fill in for or replace the renewal EAD applicants during their earnings lapse. This could result in losses to native-owned businesses and their native employees. Labor Turnover Cost Impacts
This final rule is expected to generate labor turnover costs to some employers of affected EAD holders. DHS bases the assessment of these impacts on the assumption that the estimated population of aliens with lapsed EADs because of this final rule would involuntarily separate from an employer, or otherwise cease employment, and that the separation or cessation would not be due to other factors.
Employment separations or cessation can generate labor turnover costs to employers. First are the direct or “hard” costs that involve separation and replacement costs. These include exit interviews, severance pay, and costs of temporarily covering the employee's duties and functions with other employees, which may require overtime or temporary staffing. The replacement costs typically include expenses of advertising positions, search and agency fees, screening applicants, interviews, background verification, employment testing, hiring bonuses, and travel and relocation costs. Once hired, employers face additional training, orientation, and assessment costs.
Second, direct costs involve loss of productivity and possibly profitability due to operational disruptions, which can include errors from employees that may temporally fill the position. A third cost segment is a type of indirect cost that encompasses loss of institutional knowledge, networking, and impacts to work-culture, morale, and interpersonal relationships. This last type of cost is almost impossible to measure quantitatively.
[
207
]
There are studies and reports concerning labor turnover costs available from Human Resource entities that are cited across correspondent literature, and turnover cost can be measured in slightly different ways. The turnover cost is generally reported as a share of annual earnings or an actual cost per employee. Usually, these reports measure the more direct, or hard costs associated with turnover and not intangible effects such as worker morale or lost productivity. Many reports cite a 2012 Center for American Progress (CAP) report that surveyed more than 30 studies that considered both direct (
e.g.,
separation and replacement) and indirect (
e.g.,
loss of institutional knowledge) costs.
The CAP and other reports confirm three central aspects of turnover cost: (1) that they vary substantially across industries and jobs; (2) that they tend to grow (in absolute and percentage terms) according to skill level and earnings; and (3) that they are higher for salaried workers compared to hourly wage earners.
[
208
]
The report notes that specialized technical jobs and highly paid jobs in line with senior or executive levels, which involve high levels of education, credentials, and stringent hiring criteria, can generate disproportionately high replacement costs that can reach more than 100 percent of the salary—compared to jobs with low educational and technical requirements.
[
209
]

DHS has no reason to believe that there has been a substantive change to this figure.
Some of the impacts of this rule will depend on whether businesses will be able to find replacement labor for the positions the affected renewal EAD applicants are expected to lose if they experience a lapse in employment authorization and/or employment authorization documentation due to this rule. If businesses can find replacement labor from the pool of the unemployed, the only monetized costs of this rule to society is for costs resulting from labor
(
printed page 65365)
turnover. If businesses cannot find replacement labor, the monetized costs of the rule would also include lost productivity due to a lack of available labor.
DHS estimates that reduced earnings to renewal EAD applicants ranges from $17.1 million to $900.8 million with a primary estimate of $276.2 million depending on the wages and other compensation the renewal EAD applicants earn, the number of renewal EAD applicants affected, and the duration of the lapse in employment authorization and/or employment authorization documentation that may occur because of this rule.
[
212
]
DHS uses estimates of the earnings as a measure of either: (1) transfers of this compensation from the affected population to others in the labor market, but are not already employed; or (2) a proxy for businesses' costs from lost productivity, depending on whether businesses would be able to find replacement labor for affected renewal EAD applicants due to this rule.
DHS does not know what the next best labor alternative would be for businesses when lapses occur due to this rule. Accordingly, DHS does not know the portion of the overall effects of this rule that are transfers or costs. To begin, DHS describes the two extreme scenarios, which provide the bounds for the range of effects.
Scenario 1:
If, under the effect of this rule with potential lapsed EADs, all businesses would have been able to immediately find reasonable labor substitutes for the positions the renewal EAD applicants lost, businesses lose little or no productivity. Accordingly, this rule could result in $276.2 million (primary estimate, undiscounted) being transferred from affected renewal EAD applicants to workers currently in the labor force (whom are not presently employed full time) or induced back into the labor force and this rule would result in $0 costs to businesses for prevented productivity losses.
Scenario 2:
Conversely, if all businesses would be unable to, within the period of analysis, find reasonable labor substitutes for the position the EAD holder filled, then businesses would lose productivity. Accordingly, $276.2 million is the estimated monetized costs from this rule for productivity losses and this rule will result in $0 being transferred from affected renewal EAD applicants to replacement labor. Because under this scenario businesses would not have been able to find replacement labor, the rule may also result in additional costs to employers for profit losses; and may result in a reduction in tax transfer payments from businesses and employees to the government. DHS has not estimated all potential tax effects but notes that earnings of $276.2 million would result in employment tax losses to the Federal Government (
i.e.,
Medicare and Social Security) of $29.0 million.
In both scenarios, whether without this rule employers would have been able to find replacement labor or not, DHS assumes that businesses would have incurred labor turnover costs for having to search for a replacement for affected renewal EAD applicants. Accordingly, DHS estimates the rule will also result in additional labor turnover costs to businesses of $312.1 million.
Table 7 below summarizes these two scenarios and the primary estimate of this rule. Because DHS does not know the overall proportion of businesses that would have been able to easily find replacement labor in the absence of this rule, for DHS's primary estimate we assume that replacement labor would have been immediately found for half of all renewal EAD applicants and not found for the other half (
i.e.,
an average of the two extreme scenarios described above). The June 2026 unemployment and job openings data indicate there are as many jobs available as there are people looking for jobs.
[
213
]
Accordingly, we believe the impacts of this rule will likely skew towards Scenario 1, with the rule resulting in mostly transfers of compensation from renewal EAD applicants to other workers and turnover costs for employers.
(
printed page 65366)
C. Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.
), as amended by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996, requires Federal agencies to consider the potential impact of regulations on small businesses, small governmental jurisdictions, and small organizations during the development of their rules. The term “small entities” comprises small businesses, nonprofit organizations that are independently owned and operated and are not dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with populations of less than 50,000. The RFA's regulatory flexibility analysis requirements apply only to those rules for which an agency is required to publish a general notice of proposed rulemaking pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553
or any other law.
[
214
]
DHS did not issue a notice of proposed rulemaking for this action. Accordingly, DHS is not required to certify either that this final rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities nor conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis.
Further, this final rule directly regulates individuals, and individuals are not defined as “small entities” by the Regulatory Flexibility Act. The rule indirectly impacts certain employers if, in the future, processing times exceed the expiration dates of EADs.
DHS is unsure what backlogs may continue in the future; however, DHS anticipates that, due to other DHS actions described in Section IV.C. of this final rule, it is possible that the backlog may end. If the backlogs are eliminated outside of this rule, employers will no longer be indirectly impacted by this final rule.
In the alternate scenario of a backlog in renewal EAD processing, some employers could experience indirect costs or transfer effects. The transfers would be in the form of lost compensation (wages and benefits). A portion of this lost compensation might be transferred from renewal EAD applicants to others who are currently in the U.S. labor force. A portion of the effects of this rule would also be borne by companies that would have continued to employ renewal EAD applicants had they been in the labor market longer; however, they were unable to find available replacement labor. These companies may incur an indirect cost, as they will be losing the productivity and potential profits the EAD applicant would have provided. Companies may also incur opportunity costs by having to choose the next best alternative to the immediate labor the applicant would have provided and by having to pay workers to work overtime hours. DHS does not know what this next best alternative may be for those companies. If companies can find reasonable labor substitutes for the positions the alien occupied, they will bear little or no costs. Conversely, if companies are unable to find reasonable labor substitutes for the position the applicant would have maintained then there would be no transfers and companies may experience turnover costs or other disruptions.

H. Family Assessment
DHS has reviewed this rule in line with the requirements of section 654 of the Treasury and General Appropriations Act, 1999,
[
217
]
enacted as part of the Omnibus Consolidated and Emergency Supplemental Appropriations Act, 1999.
[
218
]
DHS has systematically reviewed the criteria specified in section 654(c) of the Treasury and General Appropriations Act by evaluating whether this regulatory action: (1) impacts the stability or safety of the family, particularly in terms of marital commitment; (2) impacts the authority of parents in the education, nurture, and supervision of their children; (3) helps the family perform its functions or substitutes governmental activity for the function; (4) affects disposable income or poverty of families and children; (5) only financially impacts families, if at all, to the extent such impacts are justified; (6) may be carried out by State or local government or by the family; or (7) establishes a policy concerning the relationship between the behavior and personal responsibility of youth and the norms of society. If the agency determines a regulation may negatively affect family wellbeing, then the agency must provide an adequate rationale for its implementation.
As articulated in the IFR and this final rule, DHS is discontinuing the practice of providing an automatic extension of the EAD or employment authorization upon the filing of a renewal EAD application because it grants a benefit without an eligibility determination, without completing vetting and screening checks and without resolving the potential hits and derogatory information. DHS has determined that the implementation of this regulation may potentially negatively affect family wellbeing as outlined in section 654 of the Treasury General Appropriations Act, 1999. Specifically, the IFR and this final rule has the potential to affect disposable income of families and children, and therefore, also impacts the family financially. However, DHS believes that it has an adequate rationale for its implementation. DHS believes that the consequences of the IFR and this final rule, the possibility that an alien is not authorized to work during the pendency of the alien's renewal EAD application and thus, that families have less disposable income, are justified in light of the national security and public safety risk that automatically issuing immigration benefits, such as an automatic extension of an EAD, poses to the public. Additionally, DHS is not removing the alien's ability to obtain a renewal of their employment authorization and/or EAD. DHS is also not preventing eligible aliens from obtaining an EAD for purposes such as proof of identity. The issuance of a renewal EAD depends in large part on the applicant's timely application for a renewal EAD. The proper planning by the alien, and monitoring of EAD processing times, allows the alien to timely file a renewal EAD application far enough in advance of their EAD expiration date, which may mitigate the risk that the alien could experience a lapse in their employment authorization and/or EAD validity and have to temporarily stop working. For these reasons, DHS believes that the benefit this rule provides by improving the security posture as it relates to the issuance of automatic extensions outweighs the impact, if any, on families and their children. Better
(
printed page 65368)
protecting public safety and national security before providing immigration benefits, such as automatic extensions of employment authorizations based on the filing of a renewal EAD application, is paramount.

DHS and its components analyze proposed regulatory actions to determine whether the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA),
42 U.S.C. 4321
,
et seq.,
applies and, if so, what degree of analysis is required. DHS Directive 023-01 Rev. 01 “Implementing the National Environmental Policy Act” (Dir. 023-01 Rev. 01) and Instruction Manual 023-01-001-01 Rev. 01 (Instruction Manual)
[

]
establish the policies and procedures that DHS and its components use to comply with NEPA.
NEPA allows Federal agencies to establish, in their NEPA implementing procedures, categories of actions (“categorical exclusions”) that experience has shown do not, individually or cumulatively, have a significant effect on the human environment and, therefore, do not require an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement.
[
220
]
The Instruction Manual, Appendix A lists the DHS Categorical Exclusions.
[
221
]
Under DHS NEPA implementing procedures, for an action to be categorically excluded, it must satisfy each of the following three conditions: (1) The entire action clearly fits within one or more of the categorical exclusions; (2) the action is not a piece of a larger action; and (3) no extraordinary circumstances exist that create the potential for a significant environmental effect.
[
222
]
This final rule responds to public comments provided in response to the IFR and adopts the IFR as final without change. This final rule therefore retains the changes made to the DHS regulations by the IFR, discontinuing the practice of providing an automatic extension of employment authorization and/or EAD validity upon the filing of a renewal EAD application. Through the IFR, and now this final rule, DHS is ending the practice of providing automatic extensions of EADs to prioritize the completion of vetting and eligibility screening of aliens before granting a new period of employment authorization and/or a new EAD.
This final rule is strictly administrative and procedural. DHS has reviewed this final rule and finds that no significant impact on the environment, or any change in environmental effect will result from the amendments being promulgated in this final rule.
Accordingly, DHS finds that the promulgation of this final rule's amendments to current regulations clearly fits within categorical exclusion A3 established in DHS's NEPA implementing procedures as an administrative change with no change in environmental effect, is not part of a larger Federal action, and does not present extraordinary circumstances that create the potential for a significant environmental effect. Therefore, regulatory amendments are categorically excluded from further NEPA review.

                             DHS utilized the SAS JMP PRO 17 software. The “State Space Smoothing” suite utilizes machine learning algorithms to offer the best model information criterion to assess fit and forecasting technique for queued time series data, given dozens of potential model specifications. Based on the
Akaike Information Criterion
(AIC) DHS forecasted the data via a
multiplicative error-multiplicative (undamped) trend, non-seasonal
component (MMN) setup. The MMN model fits five parameters, but these are not reported here since the goal is limited to forecasting and not hypothesis testing. The fit results are very good according to the diagnostics:
R-squared
= .932, AIC = 405.6, and the residuals display no discernable pattern and are purged of serial correlation (at any lag, as all
p
-values of the
Ljung-Box
statistic are far greater than .05). In principal DHS could rely on each prediction interval around a monthly forecast to develop an aggregate range. In practice, the intervals applicable to the data are not plausible, for the following reasons. The standard error is large to begin with due to some sharp movements in the underlying data; and with a downward trending time series, the standard error takes on increasing relative weigh as the forecast values decline. The result is a “division by zero” issue in which the lower bound is pulled towards zero. But the increased relative weight of standard error does not discriminate between the upper and lower bounds, and it therefore enacts a proportional effect to the upper level, causing it to diverge on an unstable path. For this reason, the forecast prediction interval at a 95% confidence level is not reliable.

This period was chosen as it is the more recent period in which automatic extension was generally not in place. The percentages shown are averages for both forms taken together (a weighted average) and display very little variation. The renewal (filing) rate was conceptually and practically more difficult. The average renewal filing rate over the same period was high for the C8 (77.6%) but low for the C9 (13.1%). The existence of a large difference in filing rates is not problematic per se, but the composition of the two filings has changed substantially over time, meaning that relying on the past averages in inadequate. For example, in the period of analysis the C8 comprised 15.2% of the two forms in terms of approvals. But, due to a surge in C8 filings, one can glean from the data in Table 1 that that form has taken on a much larger share. Therefore, DHS proceeded by developing a weighted average based on what is possible in the near future. Specifically, workflow projections estimated by OPQ place the shares of the two forms at 41.9 percent and 58.1 percent, in order, for FY 2026 through FY 2028. Multiplying these shares by the afore reported renewal rates yields weight factors of .325 and .076, in order, which sum to the relied upon 40.1 percent. Nuclear Regulatory Commission
[NRC-2026-4720]
AGENCY:
Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
ACTION:
Biweekly notice.
SUMMARY:
Pursuant to section 189a.(2) of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended (the Act), the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is publishing this regular biweekly notice. The Act requires the Commission to publish notice of any amendments issued, or proposed to be issued, and grants the Commission the authority to issue and make immediately effective any amendment to an operating license or combined license, as applicable, upon a determination by the Commission that such amendment involves no significant hazards consideration (NSHC), notwithstanding the pendency before the Commission of a request for a hearing from any person.
DATES:
Comments must be filed by November 13, 2026. A request for a hearing or petitions for leave to intervene must be filed by December 14, 2026. This biweekly notice includes all amendments issued, or proposed to be issued, from September 15, 2026, to September 28, 2026. The last biweekly notice was published on September 29, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments by any of the following methods; however, the NRC encourages electronic comment submission through the Federal rulemaking website.
Federal rulemaking website:
Go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and search for Docket ID NRC-2026-4720. Address questions about Docket IDs in
Regulations.gov
to Bridget Curran; telephone: 301-415-1003; email:
Bridget.Curran@nrc.gov
.
For technical questions, contact the individual(s) listed in the
For Further Information Contact
section of this document.
Mail comments to:
Office of Nuclear Material Safety and Safeguards, Mail Stop: TWFN-5-A85, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Washington, DC 20555-0001, ATTN: Guidance and Publications Branch.
For additional direction on obtaining information and submitting comments, see “Obtaining Information and Submitting Comments” in the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section of this document.
(
printed page 65268)

.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Obtaining Information and Submitting Comments
A. Obtaining Information
Please refer to Docket ID NRC-2026-4720, facility name, unit number(s), docket number(s), application date, and subject when contacting the NRC about the availability of information for this action. You may obtain publicly available information related to this action by any of the following methods:
Federal Rulemaking Website:
Go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and search for Docket ID NRC-2026-4720.
NRC's Agencywide Documents Access and Management System (ADAMS):
You may obtain publicly available documents online in the ADAMS Public Documents collection at
https://www.nrc.gov/​reading-rm/​adams.html
.
To begin the search, select “Begin ADAMS Public Search.” For problems with ADAMS, please contact the NRC's Public Document Room (PDR) reference staff at 1-800-397-4209, at 301-415-4737, or by email to
PDR.Resource@nrc.gov
.
The ADAMS accession number for each document referenced (if it is available in ADAMS) is provided the first time that it is mentioned in this document.
NRC's PDR:
The PDR, where you may examine and order copies of publicly available documents, is open by appointment. To make an appointment to visit the PDR, please send an email to
PDR.Resource@nrc.gov
or call 1-800-397-4209 or 301-415-4737, between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. eastern time (ET), Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
B. Submitting Comments
The NRC encourages electronic comment submission through the Federal rulemaking website (
https://www.regulations.gov
). Please include Docket ID NRC-2026-4720, facility name, unit number(s), docket number(s), application date, and subject, in your comment submission.
The NRC cautions you not to include identifying or contact information that you do not want to be publicly disclosed in your comment submission. The NRC will post all comment submissions at
https://www.regulations.gov
as well as enter the comment submissions into ADAMS. The NRC does not routinely edit comment submissions to remove identifying or contact information.
If you are requesting or aggregating comments from other persons for submission to the NRC, then you should inform those persons not to include identifying or contact information that they do not want to be publicly disclosed in their comment submission. Your request should state that the NRC does not routinely edit comment submissions to remove such information before making the comment submissions available to the public or entering the comment into ADAMS.
II. Notice of Consideration of Issuance of Amendments to Facility Operating Licenses and Combined Licenses and Proposed No Significant Hazards Consideration Determination
For the facility-specific amendment requests shown in this notice, the Commission finds that the licensees' analyses provided, consistent with section 50.91 of title 10 of the
Code of Federal Regulations
(10 CFR) “Notice for public comment; State consultation,” are sufficient to support the proposed determinations that these amendment requests involve NSHC. Under the Commission's regulations in
10 CFR 50.92
, operation of the facilities in accordance with the proposed amendments would not (1) involve a significant increase in the probability or consequences of an accident previously evaluated; or (2) create the possibility of a new or different kind of accident from any accident previously evaluated; or (3) involve a significant reduction in a margin of safety.
The Commission is seeking public comments on these proposed determinations. Any comments received within 30 days after the date of publication of this notice will be considered in making any final determinations.
Normally, the Commission will not issue the amendments until the expiration of 60 days after the date of publication of this notice. The Commission may issue any of these license amendments before expiration of the 60-day period provided that its final determination is that the amendment involves NSHC. In addition, the Commission may issue any of these amendments prior to the expiration of the 30-day comment period if circumstances change during the 30-day comment period such that failure to act in a timely way would result, for example in derating or shutdown of the facility. If the Commission takes action on any of these amendments prior to the expiration of either the comment period or the notice period, it will publish in the
Federal Register
a notice of issuance. If the Commission makes a final NSHC determination for any of these amendments, any hearing will take place after issuance. The Commission expects that the need to take action on any amendment before 60 days have elapsed will occur very infrequently.
A. Opportunity To Request a Hearing and Petition for Leave To Intervene
Within 60 days after the date of publication of this notice, any person (petitioner) whose interest may be affected by any of these actions may file a request for a hearing and petition for leave to intervene (petition) with respect to that action. Petitions shall be filed in accordance with the Commission's “Agency Rules of Practice and Procedure” in
10 CFR part 2
. Interested persons should consult
10 CFR 2.309
. If a petition is filed, the Commission or a presiding officer will rule on the petition and, if appropriate, a notice of a hearing will be issued.
Petitions must be filed no later than 60 days from the date of publication of this notice in accordance with the filing instructions in the “Electronic Submissions (E-Filing)” section of this document. Petitions and motions for leave to file new or amended contentions that are filed after the deadline will not be entertained absent a determination by the presiding officer that the filing demonstrates good cause by satisfying the three factors in
10 CFR 2.309(c)(1)(i)
through
(iii)
.
If a hearing is requested, and the Commission has not made a final determination on the issue of no significant hazards consideration, the Commission will make a final determination on the issue of no significant hazards consideration, which will serve to establish when the hearing is held. If the final determination is that the license amendment request involves no significant hazards consideration, the Commission may issue the amendment and make it immediately effective, notwithstanding the request for a hearing. Any hearing would take place after issuance of the amendment. If the final determination is that the license amendment request involves a significant hazards consideration, then any hearing held would take place before the issuance of the amendment unless the Commission finds an imminent danger to the health or safety of the public, in which case it will issue an appropriate order or rule under
10 CFR part 2
.
A State, local governmental body, Federally recognized Indian Tribe, or designated agency thereof, may submit
(
printed page 65269)
a petition to the Commission to participate as a party under
10 CFR 2.309(h)
no later than 60 days from the date of publication of this notice. Alternatively, a State, local governmental body, Federally recognized Indian Tribe, or designated agency thereof, may participate as a non-party under
10 CFR 2.315(c)
.
For information about filing a petition and about participation by a person not a party under
10 CFR 2.315
, see ADAMS Accession No. ML20340A053 (
https://adamswebsearch2.nrc.gov/​webSearch2/​main.jsp?​AccessionNumber=​ML20340A053
) and the NRC's public website (
https://www.nrc.gov/​about-nrc/​regulatory/​adjudicatory/​hearing.html#participate
).
B. Electronic Submissions (E-Filing)
All documents filed in NRC adjudicatory proceedings, including documents filed by an interested State, local governmental body, Federally recognized Indian Tribe, or designated agency thereof that requests to participate under
10 CFR 2.315(c)
, must be filed in accordance with
10 CFR 2.302
. The E-Filing process requires participants to submit and serve all adjudicatory documents over the internet, or in some cases, to mail copies on electronic storage media, unless an exemption permitting an alternative filing method, as further discussed, is granted. Detailed guidance on electronic submissions is located in the “Guidance for Electronic Submissions to the NRC” (ADAMS Accession No. ML13031A056), and on the NRC's public website (
https://www.nrc.gov/​site-help/​e-submittals.html
).
To comply with the procedural requirements of E-Filing, at least 10 days prior to the filing deadline, the participant should contact the Office of the Secretary by email at
Hearing.Docket@nrc.gov
,
or by telephone at 301-415-1677, to: (1) request a digital identification (ID) certificate, which allows the participant (or their counsel or representative) to digitally sign submissions and access the E-Filing system for any proceeding in which it is participating; and (2) advise the Secretary that the participant will be submitting a petition or other adjudicatory document (even in instances in which the participant, or their counsel or representative, already holds an NRC-issued digital ID certificate). Based upon this information, the Secretary will establish an electronic docket for the proceeding if the Secretary has not already established an electronic docket.
Information about applying for a digital ID certificate is available on the NRC's public website (
https://www.nrc.gov/​site-help/​e-submittals/​getting-started.html
). After a digital ID certificate is obtained and a docket is created, the participant must submit adjudicatory documents in the Portable Document Format. Guidance on submissions is available on the NRC's public website (
https://www.nrc.gov/​site-help/​electronic-sub-ref-mat.html
). A filing is considered complete at the time the document is submitted through the NRC's E-Filing system. To be timely, an electronic filing must be submitted to the E-Filing system no later than 11:59 p.m. ET on the due date. Upon receipt of a transmission, the E-Filing system time-stamps the document and sends the submitter an email confirming receipt of the document. The E-Filing system also distributes an email that provides access to the document to the NRC's Office of the General Counsel and any others who have advised the Office of the Secretary that they wish to participate in the proceeding, so that the filer need not serve the document on those participants separately. Therefore, applicants and other participants (or their counsel or representative) must apply for and receive a digital ID certificate before adjudicatory documents are filed in order to obtain access to the documents via the E-Filing system.
A person filing electronically using the NRC's adjudicatory E-Filing system may seek assistance by contacting the NRC's Electronic Filing Help Desk through the “Contact Us” link located on the NRC's public website (
https://www.nrc.gov/​site-help/​e-submittals.html
), by email to
MSHD.Resource@nrc.gov
,
or by a toll-free call at 1-866-672-7640. The NRC Electronic Filing Help Desk is available between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m., ET, Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
Participants who believe that they have good cause for not submitting documents electronically must file an exemption request, in accordance with
10 CFR 2.302(g)
, with their initial paper filing stating why there is good cause for not filing electronically and requesting authorization to continue to submit documents in paper format. Such filings must be submitted in accordance with
10 CFR 2.302(b)-(d)
. Participants filing adjudicatory documents in this manner are responsible for serving their documents on all other participants. Participants granted an exemption under
10 CFR 2.302(g)(2)
must still meet the electronic formatting requirement in
10 CFR 2.302(g)(1)
, unless the participant also seeks and is granted an exemption from
10 CFR 2.302(g)(1)
.
Documents submitted in adjudicatory proceedings will appear in the NRC's electronic hearing docket, which is publicly available on the NRC's public website (
https://ehd.nrc.gov
), unless otherwise excluded pursuant to an order of the presiding officer. If you do not have an NRC-issued digital ID certificate as previously described, click “cancel” when the link requests certificates and you will be automatically directed to the NRC's electronic hearing docket where you will be able to access any publicly available documents in a particular hearing docket. Participants are requested not to include personal privacy information such as social security numbers, home addresses, or personal phone numbers in their filings, unless an NRC regulation or other law requires submission of such information. With respect to copyrighted works, except for limited excerpts that serve the purpose of the adjudicatory filings and would constitute a Fair Use application, participants should not include copyrighted materials in their submission.

Notice.
SUMMARY:
This notice sets forth the schedule and proposed agenda for a virtual meeting of the Manufactured Housing Consensus Committee (MHCC) to be held on October 27, 2026, and October 28, 2026, from 11:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Eastern Daylight Time (EDT). The meeting is open to the public. The agenda provides an opportunity for interested parties to comment on the business before the MHCC.
DATES:
The MHCC meeting will be held on October 27, 2026 and October 28, 2026, from 11:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Eastern Daylight Time (EDT).
ADDRESSES:
The meeting will be held via teleconference. The teleconference number for the meeting is:
Phone:
(669) 444-9171.
Meeting ID
: 865 0804 1852.
To access the webinar, use the following link:
https://us06web.zoom.us/​j/​86508041852
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Mary Jo Houton, Administrator, Office of Manufactured Housing Programs, Department of Housing and Urban Development, 451 7th Street SW, Room 9252, Washington, DC 20410, telephone (202) 708-6423 (this is not a toll-free number). HUD welcomes and is prepared to receive calls from individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing, as well as from individuals with speech or communication disabilities. To learn more about how to make an accessible telephone call, please visit
https://www.fcc.gov/​consumers/​guides/​telecommunications-relay-service-trs
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
Notice of these meetings is provided in accordance with the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA) and implementing regulations.
5 U.S.C. 1009(a)(2)
,
41 CFR 102-3.150
. The Manufactured Housing Consensus Committee (MHCC) was established by the National Manufactured Housing Construction and Safety Standards Act of 1974. Public Law 93-383, 88 Stat. 633, codified at
42 U.S.C. 5401
et seq.
This Act was later amended by the Manufactured Housing Improvement Act of 2000 (
Pub. L. 106-569
, 114 Stat. 2944). Under
42 U.S.C. 5403
, the purposes of the MHCC are to:
(1) Provide periodic recommendations to the Secretary to adopt, revise, and interpret the Federal manufactured housing construction and safety standards in accordance with subsection 5403(a);
(2) Provide periodic recommendations to the Secretary to adopt, revise, and interpret the procedural and enforcement regulations, including regulations specifying the permissible scope and conduct of monitoring, in accordance with subsection 5403(b); and
(3) Be organized and carry out its business in a manner that guarantees a fair opportunity for the expression and consideration of various positions and for public participation.
The MHCC is deemed an advisory committee not composed of Federal employees.
Public Comment
Interested parties wishing to make comments on the business of the MHCC are encouraged to register by or before Wednesday, October 21, 2026, by contacting HUD's Administering Organization (AO) for the MHCC, Home Innovation Research Labs; Attention: John Peavy and Tynica Stefun, 400 Prince Georges Blvd., Upper Marlboro, MD 20774, or email to
mhcc@homeinnovation.com
or call 1-888-602-4663. Written comments should be submitted on or before Monday, October 19, 2026, to give MHCC members an opportunity to review the comments and come prepared to the meeting. Timely submission of comments will allow adequate opportunity to consider stakeholder input and help facilitate meaningful discussions. The MHCC strives to accommodate citizen comments to the extent possible within the time constraints of the meeting agenda. Advance registration is strongly encouraged. The MHCC will provide an opportunity for public comments on specific matters before the MHCC.
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's (HUD), Office of Manufactured Housing Programs, is providing an opportunity for the MHCC to discuss standards for new rules it is responsible to promulgate under the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, enacted on July 11, 2026, which amends the Manufactured Housing Construction and Safety Standards Act of 1974 (Section 603 (
42 U.S.C. 5402
) and Section 604 (
42 U.S.C. 5403
). Specifically, HUD seeks the input of the MHCC to identify the necessary changes to the standards for manufactured housing as it relates to the removal of the permanent chassis on the lowest floor, including anticipated costs and benefits. HUD also seeks MHCC input on state certifications and recertification that verify that certain state laws treat manufactured homes without a chassis in parity with manufactured homes with a chassis.
HUD is scheduling this meeting with the MHCC to allow robust discussion, analysis, and consideration as the committee is responsible for providing recommendations to the Secretary for the purposes of proceeding with changes to the standards. This meeting is scheduled for two days to provide sufficient time for thorough consideration and collection of MHCC recommendations. HUD, therefore, strongly encourages active participation by committee members, stakeholders, and other interested parties.

Office of the Secretary
[Docket ID: DOD-2026-OS-2217]
AGENCY:
Office of the Secretary, Department of Defense, (DoD).
ACTION:
Notice of a new matching program.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Privacy Act of 1974, as amended, and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) guidance on computer matching, the DoD is providing notice of the establishment of a new matching program. Pursuant to the Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (PIIA), DoD, including its component Defense Finance and Accounting Service (DFAS), is establishing a new matching program consisting of the computerized comparison of its system of records for the Military Retirement—Combat Related Special Compensation program with the Do Not Pay (DNP) Working System, which is administered by Treasury's Bureau of the Fiscal Service. This matching program will enable the DoD program to compare records maintained in its system of records with records maintained in the DNP Working System for the purposes of identifying and preventing improper payments.
DATES:
Comments will be accepted on or before November 13, 2026. This proposed action will be effective the day following the end of the comment period unless comments have been received from interested members of the public that require modification and republication of the notice. This new matching program will be effective through September 10, 2029.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments, identified by docket number and title, by any of the following methods:
* Federal Rulemaking Portal:
http://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the instructions for submitting comments.
* Mail:
Department of Defense, Office of the Director of Administration and Management, Oversight and Compliance Directorate, Regulatory Division, 4800 Mark Center Drive, Attn: Mailbox 24, Suite 05F16, Alexandria, VA 22350-1700.
Instructions:
All submissions received must include the agency name and
(
printed page 65186)
docket number for this
Federal Register
document. The general policy for comments and other submissions from members of the public is to make these submissions available for public viewing on the internet at
http://www.regulations.gov
as they are received without change, including any personal identifiers or contact information.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
James Cochran, System Manager, 8899 E 56th St., Indianapolis, IN 46249-0150, Phone (800) 321-1080.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Computer Matching and Privacy Protection Act of 1988 amended the Privacy Act of 1974 (5 United States Code (U.S.C.) 552a) by establishing procedural safeguards for agencies' use of records in computerized matching. The Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (
31 U.S.C. 3351
et seq.
) provides the authority to waive the requirements for matching agreements in certain cases. Pursuant to this authority, the Secretary of the Treasury, after consulting with the OMB Director, authorized the issuance of a four-year waiver of the requirement for entering into a matching agreement for programs that meet the criteria in OMB Memorandum M-25-32. DoD has determined that the DNP matching program for the Military Retirement—Combat Related Special Compensation (PIIA Program ID: DOD-0045) is eligible for this waiver.
Participating Agencies:
The DoD, through DFAS, will match records against the DNP Working System, maintained by the Bureau of the Fiscal Service at the U.S. Department of the Treasury.
Authority for Conducting the Matching Program:
The Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (
31 U.S.C. 3351
et seq.
) and OMB Memorandum M-25-32. The Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (
31 U.S.C. 3351
et seq.
) establishes the DNP Initiative and requires, for the purposes of identifying and preventing improper payments, each executive agency to have access to, and use of, the relevant databases in DNP to verify payment or award eligibility. Additional applicable authorities for this matching program include
Executive Order 13520
, Reducing Improper Payments (
74 FR 62201
);
Executive Order 14249
, Protecting America's Bank Account Against Fraud, Waste, and Abuse (
90 FR 14011
); and OMB Memorandum M-25-32, Preventing Improper Payments and Protecting Privacy Through Do Not Pay. Additional information regarding the authorities for the collection and maintenance of information for each of the DoD programs that will conduct matches with the DNP Working System are contained within the systems of records notices listed below.
Purpose(s):
The purpose of the matching program is to identify and prevent improper payments by verifying through DNP prepayment or pre-award eligibility.
Categories of Individuals:
Applicants for, or recipients of, Federal funds from the Military Retirement—Combat Related Special Compensation program.
Categories of Records:
Data elements to be matched include applicant's name, Social Security Number (SSN) or Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN), address, date of birth, and payment/banking information. These data elements include all the records involved in the matching program.
System(s) of Records:
The records contained within the DNP Working System are maintained in the Treasury system of records, Bureau of the Fiscal Service .017—Do Not Pay Payment Verification Records (
85 FR 11776
). The DoD records involved in this matching program are maintained in the following system of records: T7347b, Defense Military Retiree and Annuity Pay System Records (
74 FR 696
), (
90 FR 54312
).
Dated: October 8, 2026.
Stephanie J. Bost,
Alternate OSD Federal Register Liaison Officer, Department of Defense.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice of a new matching program.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Privacy Act of 1974, as amended, and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) guidance on computer matching, the DoD is providing notice of the establishment of a new matching program. Pursuant to the Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (PIIA), DoD, including its component Defense Finance and Accounting Service (DFAS), is establishing a new matching program consisting of the computerized comparison of its system of records for the Military Retirement—Retired Pay program with the Do Not Pay (DNP) Working System, which is administered by Treasury's Bureau of the Fiscal Service. DATES:
Comments will be accepted on or before November 13, 2026. Department of Defense
Office of the Secretary
[Docket ID: DOD-2026-OS-2220]
AGENCY:
Office of the Secretary, Department of Defense (DoD).
ACTION:
Notice of a new matching program.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Privacy Act of 1974, as amended, and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) guidance on computer matching, the DoD is providing notice of the establishment of a new matching program. Pursuant to the Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (PIIA), DoD, including its component Defense Health Agency, is establishing a new matching program consisting of the computerized comparison of its system of records for the Military Health Benefits—TRICARE Medicare Eligible Program (TMEP) with the Do Not Pay (DNP) Working System, which is administered by Treasury's Bureau of the Fiscal Service. This matching program will enable the DoD program to compare records maintained in its system of records with records maintained in the DNP Working System for the purposes of identifying and preventing improper payments.
DATES:
Comments will be accepted on or before November 13, 2026. This proposed action will be effective the day following the end of the comment period unless comments have been received from interested members of the public that require modification and republication of the notice. This new matching program will be effective through September 10, 2029.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments, identified by docket number and title, by any of the following methods:
*
Federal Rulemaking Portal:
http://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the instructions for submitting comments.
*
Mail:
Department of Defense, Office of the Director of Administration and Management, Oversight and Compliance Directorate, Regulatory Division, 4800 Mark Center Drive, Attn: Mailbox 24, Suite 05F16, Alexandria, VA 22350-1700.
Instructions:
All submissions received must include the agency name and docket number for this
Federal Register
document. The general policy for comments and other submissions from members of the public is to make these submissions available for public viewing on the internet at
http://www.regulations.gov
as they are received without change, including any personal identifiers or contact information.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Ms. Laura White, Accounting Officer, Oracle Federal Financials, DHA/SP&FO/J8, 16401 E Centretech Pkwy., Aurora, CO 80011, Phone # (303) 676-3877.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Computer Matching and Privacy Protection Act of 1988 amended the Privacy Act of 1974 (
5 U.S.C. 552a
) by establishing procedural safeguards for agencies' use of records in computerized matching. The Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (
31 U.S.C. 3351
et seq.
) provides the authority to waive the requirements for matching agreements in certain cases. Pursuant to this authority, the Secretary of the Treasury, after consulting with the OMB Director, authorized the issuance of a four-year waiver of the requirement for entering into a matching agreement for programs that meet the criteria in OMB Memorandum M-25-32. DoD has determined that the DNP matching program for the Military Health Benefits—TRICARE Medicare Eligible Program (TMEP) (PIIA Program ID: DOD-0030) is eligible for this waiver.
Participating Agencies:
The DoD, through Defense Health Agency, will match records against the DNP Working System, maintained by the Bureau of the Fiscal Service at the U.S. Department of the Treasury.
Authority for Conducting the Matching Program:
The Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (31 United States Code (U.S.C.) 3351
et seq.
) and OMB Memorandum M-25-32. The Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (
31 U.S.C. 3351
et seq.
) establishes the DNP Initiative and requires, for the purposes of identifying and preventing improper payments, each executive agency to have access to, and use of, the relevant databases in DNP to verify payment or award eligibility. Additional applicable authorities for this matching program include
Executive Order 13520
, Reducing Improper Payments (
74 FR 62201
);
Executive Order 14249
, Protecting America's Bank Account Against Fraud, Waste, and Abuse (
90 FR 14011
); and OMB Memorandum M-25-32, Preventing Improper Payments and Protecting Privacy Through Do Not Pay. Additional information regarding the authorities for the collection and maintenance of information for each of the DoD programs that will conduct matches with the DNP Working System are contained within the systems of records notices listed below.
Purpose(s):
The purpose of the matching program is to identify and prevent improper payments by verifying through DNP prepayment or pre-award eligibility.
Categories of Individuals:
Applicants for, or recipients of, Federal funds from the Military Health Benefits—TRICARE Medicare Eligible Program (TMEP) program.
Categories of Records:
Data elements to be matched include applicant's name, Social Security Number (SSN) or Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN), address, date of birth, and payment/banking information. These data elements include all the records involved in the matching program.
System(s) of Records:
The records contained within the DNP Working System are maintained in the Treasury system of records, Bureau of the Fiscal Service .017—Do Not Pay Payment Verification Records (
85 FR 11776
). The DoD records involved in this matching program are maintained in the following system of records: EDTMA 04, Medical/Dental Claim History Files (
80 FR 65720
), (
90 FR 54312
).
(
printed page 65189)
Dated: October 8, 2026.
Stephanie J. Bost,
Alternate OSD Federal Register Liaison Officer, Department of Defense.

title: Schedules of Controlled Substances: Temporary Placement of 7- Hydroxymitragynine and Mitragynine Pseudoindoxyl Above a Specified Threshold in Schedule I
abstract: The Administrator of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) is issuing this notice of intent to publish a temporary order to schedule 7-hydroxymitragynine and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (including their isomers, esters, ethers, salts, and salts of isomers, esters, and ethers, whenever the existence of such isomers, esters, ethers, and salts is possible) when either substance alone, or their combined amount if both are present, is above a specified threshold, in schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA). Based on a different threshold provided by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) in July of 2025, DEA published a notice of intent to temporarily schedule 7-hydroxymitragynine above that lower threshold on July 7, 2026. Additionally, DEA published a temporary order placing mitragynine pseudoindoxyl without a threshold in schedule I of the CSA on August 26, 2026. On October 8, 2026, HHS sent a letter recommending that DEA place of the CSA 7-hydroxymitragynine and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl in schedule I when either substance alone, or their combined amount if both are present, is above a new specified threshold. Based on the October 8, 2026 letter, DEA is issuing this notice of intent. While the new threshold recommended by HHS would permit certain products to remain in the marketplace without being subject to schedule I controls, neither HHS nor DEA has made a finding that these substances are safe to use at below-threshold levels. When a temporary order is issued, it will impose the regulatory controls and administrative, civil, and criminal sanctions applicable to schedule I controlled substances on persons who handle (manufacture, distribute, reverse distribute, import, export, engage in research, conduct instructional activities or chemical analysis with, or possess) or propose to handle 7- hydroxymitragynine and/or mitragynine pseudoindoxyl above the specified threshold. In a separate document contained in this issue of the Federal Register, DEA is withdrawing the July 7, 2026 notice of intent related to 7-hydroxymitragynine. The August 26, 2026 temporary order placing mitragynine pseudoindoxyl in schedule I of the CSA without a threshold remains in effect until either it expires or the new temporary order is published and the previous order is withdrawn, whichever occurs first.
