,
referencing DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0529. You may also sign up for email alerts on the online docket to be notified when comments are posted or a final rule is published.
II. Background
A. Purpose and Summary of the Proposed Regulatory Action
The purpose of this proposed rule is to remove
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
. That regulation instructs USCIS officers to give deference to a prior determination of a petitioner's, applicant's, or beneficiary's eligibility when adjudicating a request filed on Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, involving the same parties and the same underlying facts.
[
1
]
This requirement most often applies when a petitioning employer seeks to extend a petition for an alien's employment or authorized stay in the United States under the same previously approved nonimmigrant worker classification. Under the current regulation, USCIS must generally defer to the prior determination of eligibility for the nonimmigrant worker classification unless there was a material error, a material change, or new material information.
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
.
When DHS promulgated
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
, the agency stated that petitioners would “continue to have the burden to present all required and relevant evidence” to establish eligibility for the requested nonimmigrant worker classification notwithstanding the prior approval.
See Modernizing H-1B Requirements, Providing Flexibility in the F-1 Program, and Program Improvements Affecting Other Nonimmigrant Workers,
89 FR 103054
,
103093
(Dec. 18, 2024). The agency also stated that “deference does not equate to a lack of USCIS review of the petition.”
Id.
DHS now believes, however, that the practical effect of the deference regulation is inconsistent with those statements. In particular, the deference regulation and policy effectively shift the burden from the petitioner to the USCIS officer to justify departing from a prior approval. DHS is also concerned that the deference policy has had the practical effect of encouraging USCIS officers to prioritize consistency with prior approvals and efficiency in adjudication of extension requests rather than fully exploring all facts and evidence to ensure continued eligibility for the nonimmigrant worker benefit. As a result, DHS believes that some petitioners have interpreted the deference policy as reducing their obligation to demonstrate continued eligibility for the requested nonimmigrant worker classification when seeking an extension of a prior approval. Overall, the deference regulation and policy risk undermining program integrity by potentially reducing scrutiny of extension requests of nonimmigrant worker classifications, thereby potentially perpetuating erroneous prior approvals and creating an environment in which fraudulent and meritless petitions are less likely to be detected before approval.
See
Section III of this preamble.
Therefore, DHS proposes to remove
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
. DHS believes that this change would better align DHS regulations and USCIS adjudicatory practice with the agency's longstanding interpretation of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA or Act), which places the burden of proof in establishing eligibility for all immigration benefits on the petitioner.
See
INA sec. 291,
8 U.S.C. 1361
;
Matter of Chawathe,
25 I. & N. Dec. 369, 375 n.7 (USCIS AAO, 2010) (“The burden of proving eligibility for the benefit sought remains entirely with the applicant”). Removing the deference requirement would also help to ensure that USCIS officers fully review the facts and evidence in every case to ensure continued eligibility. Overall, DHS believes that this change would promote more complete adjudications, strengthen program integrity in the adjudication of nonimmigrant worker benefits, reduce the risk of perpetuating erroneous approvals, and support the Administration's broader efforts to better protect U.S. workers and more faithfully enforce the immigration laws enacted by Congress.
[
2
]
B. Legal Authority
The Secretary of Homeland Security (Secretary)'s authority for these proposed regulatory amendments is found in various sections of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1101
et seq.,
and the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (HSA),
Public Law 107-296
, 116 Stat. 2135,
6 U.S.C. 101
et seq.
General authority for issuing this proposed rule is found in section 103(a) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1103(a)
, which authorizes the Secretary to administer and enforce the immigration and nationality laws and establish such regulations as the Secretary deems necessary for carrying out such authority, as well as section 102 of the HSA,
6 U.S.C. 112
, which vests all of the functions of DHS in the Secretary and authorizes the Secretary to issue regulations.
[
3
]
Further authority for these proposed regulatory amendments is found in:
Section 214(a)(1) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1184(a)(1)
, which authorizes the Secretary to prescribe, by regulation, the time and conditions of the admission of nonimmigrants;
Section 214(c)(1) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(1)
, which,
inter alia,
authorizes the Secretary to prescribe how an importing employer may petition for nonimmigrant workers, as well as the form of the petition and the information that an importing employer must provide in the petition;
Section 235(d)(3) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1225(d)(3)
, which authorizes “any immigration officer . . . to administer oaths and to take and consider evidence of or from any person
(
printed page 65121)
touching the privilege of any alien or person he believes or suspects to be an alien to enter, reenter, transit through, or reside in the United States or concerning any matter which is material and relevant to the enforcement of [the INA] and the administration of [DHS]”;
Section 287(b) of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1357(b)
, which authorizes the taking and consideration of evidence “concerning any matter which is material or relevant to the enforcement of [the INA] and the administration of [DHS]”;
Section 402 of the HSA,
6 U.S.C. 202
, which charges the Secretary with “[e]stablishing and administering rules
[
4
]
. . . governing the granting of visas or other forms of permission . . . to enter the United States” and “[e]stablishing national immigration enforcement policies and priorities”;
see also
HSA sec. 428,
6 U.S.C. 236
; and
Section 451(a)(3) and (b) of the HSA,
6 U.S.C. 271(a)(3)
and
(b)
, transferring to USCIS the authority to adjudicate petitions for nonimmigrant status, establish policies for performing that function, and set national immigration services policies and priorities.
C. Extensions of Stay and Petition Validity
Many aliens come to the United States under a nonimmigrant visa classification. Some of these classifications permit aliens to be employed or otherwise provide services in the United States for temporary periods.
See
INA secs. 101(a)(15) and 214,
8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)
and
1184
. Each classification for purposes of employment or otherwise performing services in the United States has its own eligibility requirements and requirements related to the period of admission or status, maintenance of status, the ability to change jobs or employers, and the ability to extend nonimmigrant status.
Id.
For certain nonimmigrant visa classifications, a petitioner seeking the services of an alien beyond the previously granted period of admission may file an extension of stay request on Form I-129, Petition for Nonimmigrant Worker.
[
5
]
8 CFR 214.1(c)(1)
. An extension of stay is ordinarily only granted if the alien is still in, and has maintained, his or her nonimmigrant status at the time the request is filed.
8 CFR 214.1(c)(6)
. When requesting an extension of stay on Form I-129, the petitioner must submit evidence that the alien maintained his or her status along with all other initial evidence specified in the regulations and in accordance with form instructions.
See
8 CFR 214.1(c)(1)
,
(6)
; Form I-129 Instructions, Instructions for Petition for Nonimmigrant Worker,
https://www.uscis.gov/​sites/​default/​files/​document/​forms/​i-129instr.pdf
(Sept. 9, 2026).
An extension of stay request is often submitted together with a request for an extension of petition validity, which is a request to allow the alien to continue to work for his or her current employer in the same nonimmigrant classification.
[
6
]
The petition extension and extension of stay request are filed on Form I-129 along with evidence of continued eligibility for the nonimmigrant classification, and all other initial evidence specified in the regulations and in accordance with form instructions.
[
7
]
A request for an extension of petition validity follows a previous finding of eligibility for the nonimmigrant classification. Although there is a previous finding of eligibility, the burden of proof in any immigration request—including a request for an extension of petition validity—remains on the petitioner.
See
INA sec. 291,
8 U.S.C. 1361
.
[
8
]
Officers are not bound to approve subsequent petitions seeking immigration benefits where eligibility has not been demonstrated, merely because of a prior approval.
[
9
]
The prior approval may have been erroneous, in which case giving deference to that prior determination of eligibility because the adjudicating officer was not aware of the error may perpetuate unmeritorious approvals. Even if the prior approval was not erroneous, the burden of proof remains on the petitioner to establish eligibility in each benefit request. USCIS decides each matter according to the evidence of record on a case-by-case basis.
[
10
]
Despite these well-established principles, the regulation at
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
instructs USCIS officers to give deference to a prior determination of eligibility when adjudicating a request filed on Form I-129 involving the same parties and the same underlying facts unless the officer determines that there was a material error involved with a prior approval, a material change in circumstances or eligibility requirements, or new, material information that adversely impacts eligibility. As discussed in Section III. of this preamble, DHS believes that the deference regulation is in tension with the statutory requirement that the petitioner must bear the burden to demonstrate eligibility for an immigration benefit, and it may unduly limit adjudicating officers' inherent fact-finding authority in certain cases.
D. History of Deference in USCIS Adjudications
While the codification of deference was relatively recent, USCIS has had a history of implementing and rescinding deference through a series of policy actions beginning in 2004. First, in April 2004, USCIS issued a memorandum discussing the significance of prior USCIS adjudications.
See
USCIS, “The Significance of a Prior CIS Approval of a Nonimmigrant Petition in the Context
(
printed page 65122)
of a Subsequent Determination Regarding Eligibility for Extension of Petition Validity,” HQPRD 72/11.3 (Apr. 23, 2004). This memorandum, while recognizing USCIS' authority to question prior determinations and that each matter must be decided according to the evidence of record on a case-by-case basis, first set out the policy instructing adjudications officers to give deference to a prior determination of eligibility in matters relating to an extension of nonimmigrant petition validity involving the same parties (petitioner and beneficiary) and the same underlying facts, unless there was material error, a substantial change in circumstances, or new material information.
In October 2017, USCIS issued a memorandum which rescinded the 2004 guidance, expressing concerns that the 2004 memorandum improperly shifted the burden from the petitioner to USCIS.
See
USCIS, “Rescission of Guidance Regarding Deference to Prior Determinations of Eligibility in the Adjudication of Petitions for Extension of Nonimmigrant Status,” PM-602-0151 (Oct. 23, 2017). In the 2017 memorandum, USCIS also expressed concerns that the deference policy unduly limited adjudicating officers' inherent fact-finding authority in certain cases.
In April 2021, USCIS reinstituted its deference policy and incorporated it into the USCIS Policy Manual.
See
USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 2, Part A, Chapter 4 “Extension of Stay, Change of Status, and Extension of Petition Validity.” The policy manual acknowledges that officers are not required to approve subsequent petitions where eligibility has not been demonstrated strictly because of a prior approval but stressed that they should defer to prior determinations involving the same parties and underlying facts. According to the policy manual, if an officer determines that deference to a prior approval is not appropriate, the officer must acknowledge the previous approval(s) in the denial, Request for Evidence (RFE), or Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) and articulate the reason for not deferring to the previous determination (for example, due to a material error, change in circumstances, or new adverse material information).
See id.
Officers must provide the petitioner with an opportunity to respond to the new information consistent with
8 CFR 103.2(b)(16)(i)
.
See id.
In December 2024, DHS codified its deference policy at
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
through the final rule
Modernizing H-1B Requirements, Providing Flexibility in the F-1 Program, and Program Improvements Affecting Other Nonimmigrant Workers,
89 FR 103054
(Dec. 18, 2024) (Modernization Final Rule). Current
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
states that when adjudicating a Form I-129, Petition for Nonimmigrant Worker, involving the same parties and the same underlying facts, USCIS gives deference to its prior determination of eligibility unless there is a material error, a material change, or new material information that adversely impacts eligibility.
III. Discussion of Proposed Rule
DHS proposes to remove its regulation at
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
, and the deference policy, which instructs USCIS officers to give deference to a prior determination of the petitioner's or beneficiary's eligibility when adjudicating a request filed on Form I-129 involving the same parties and the same underlying facts, unless there was a material error, a material change, or new material information that adversely impacts eligibility.
[
11
]
This proposed change would apply to all benefit requests filed using Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker. This proposal would not prohibit USCIS officers from considering a prior approval where relevant. Rather, it would remove the requirement that officers begin from a position of deference to the prior approval. DHS believes that this change would better ensure that officers fully consider all relevant facts and evidence to ensure continued eligibility, and adjudicate each petition or request on a case-by-case basis to determine whether the petitioner has met its burden of proof to demonstrate continued eligibility for the benefit. Overall, DHS believes that removing deference would enhance program integrity and thereby better protect the interests of U.S. workers, consistent with this Administration's priorities.
A. Restoring the Proper Allocation of the Burden of Proof
Removing deference would better align DHS regulations with the agency's longstanding interpretation of section 291 of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1361
, which places the burden of proof on the petitioner or applicant to establish eligibility for each immigration benefit sought.
See also Matter of Chawathe,
25 I. & N. Dec. 369, 375 n.7 (USCIS AAO, 2010) (“The burden of proving eligibility for the benefit sought remains entirely with the applicant.”). Although an agency may establish reasonable evidentiary presumptions,
see e.g., Reno
v.
Flores,
507 U.S. 292, 313 (1993), any such presumption must be consistent with the statutory text and scheme,
see Lin
v.
U.S. Dep't of Justice,
494 F.3d 296, 308 (2d Cir. 2007) (en banc). Whether or not the deference regulation is consonant with the statute, DHS now believes that it has the practical effect of shifting the burden of proof from the petitioner to the agency, in tension with section 291 of the INA,
8 U.S.C. 1361
, with respect to the eligibility criteria that Congress intended the agency to determine for each immigration benefit sought.
When DHS promulgated
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
, the agency stated that petitioners would continue to have the burden to demonstrate continued eligibility for the requested nonimmigrant worker classification.
See
89 FR 103094
. In practice, however, the deference policy effectively shifts the burden from the petitioner to the adjudicating officer who must identify a material error or change in circumstances to justify deviating from the prior approval.
[
12
]
In effect, this creates a default position that the prior approval was correct, and the petitioner and beneficiary remain eligible for the benefit unless the officer finds that an enumerated exception to the deference policy applies (
i.e.,
that there was a material error, material change in circumstances or eligibility requirements, or new, material information that adversely impacts eligibility). This structure effectively shifts the burden from the petitioner to
(
printed page 65123)
the adjudicating officer. Instead of requiring the petitioner to establish that the alien is eligible to continue to work in the United States under a nonimmigration classification, the deference regulation and policy effectively require the officer to justify why the prior approval should not control.
B. Enhancing USCIS Officer Fact-Finding Authority
Removing deference would also better ensure that USCIS officers review the facts and evidence in every case to ensure continued eligibility before approving a petition extension and granting an extension of stay request. The deference policy suggests that a less than thorough review of each case may be acceptable and gives the impression of unduly limiting adjudicating officers' inherent fact-finding authority. Some officers may view deference as a restriction on their ability to consider all the facts of the case. Rather than taking appropriate action if eligibility was not demonstrated in the petition (such as issuing an RFE), some officers may simply grant the benefit absent glaring errors or changes as a result of the deference policy.
Indeed, as shown in Table 3
infra,
the RFE rate increased by 2.9 percent more than the RFE rate for the comparison group after the deference policy was rescinded in 2017. DHS acknowledges that other changes unrelated to deference may have, in part, contributed to this increased RFE rate. However, DHS believes that it is reasonable to conclude that the rescission of the deference policy was one of the contributing factors for this increased RFE rate. This increase is consistent with DHS's concern that the deference policy has had the effect of discouraging some officers from requesting additional evidence even in cases where the petitioner has not established eligibility for the nonimmigrant worker classification in connection with the current request.
An adjudicating officer's fact-finding authority should not be constrained by any prior petition approval. Instead, officers should thoroughly review a petition for eligibility and request additional documentation as appropriate based on the merits of each case, consistent with USCIS policy regarding requests for evidence, notices of intent to deny, and the adjudication of petitions for nonimmigrant benefits. Because deference may be viewed as a default position upon beginning review of certain filings, the deference policy may, in some cases, have had the unintended effect of limiting the ability of officers to conduct a thorough review of the facts and limiting assessment of eligibility in each case. While officers may, of course, reach the same conclusion as in a prior decision, they should not be compelled to do so as a default starting point.
[
13
]
In addition, deference increases the risk of officers not discovering material errors in prior adjudications. Although the deference policy allows officers to deviate from the prior decision if there was a material error, if officers limited their review of the cases before them because of an assumption that the prior decision was correct, it would necessarily limit the discovery of material error. Deferring to a determination of eligibility for nonimmigrant worker classification that was made potentially up to several years before the adjudication of the petition extension, and that may be based on inaccurate or outdated facts or adjudicated under regulations which have changed since the original approval was issued, is inconsistent with this Administration's efforts to strengthen the integrity of the nonimmigrant worker system.
USCIS does not believe additional officer training or clarification on how to apply deference would sufficiently address these concerns. As discussed earlier in this preamble, USCIS has a history of applying deference over several years. Prior to its codification in the regulations in 2024, the deference policy was in place at USCIS from 2004 until its rescission in 2017 and was reinstituted in 2021. Therefore, USCIS officers generally have had training and operational guidance on how to adjudicate petitions with the deference policy in place. Training, however, is not the issue or solution. Rather, any deference requirement itself conveys a fundamental tension with an officer's obligation to conduct a fulsome review to ensure that the petitioner met its burden before granting a nonimmigrant worker benefit. Indeed, the deference policy was based in part on a desire to increase efficiency by reducing the officer's need to revisit prior determinations of eligibility. That efficiency, however, has had the unintended effect of discouraging officers from thoroughly reviewing a case when adjudicating extension requests for nonimmigrant worker classifications. DHS now believes that the deference policy is inconsistent with ensuring that officers fully evaluate eligibility in every case, which is necessary to protect the integrity of the immigration benefits system and the interests of U.S. workers by ensuring that petitioners and beneficiaries are eligible for the requested nonimmigrant worker benefit.
C. Strengthening Program Integrity
DHS also believes that deference may undermine program integrity, including by creating opportunities for unscrupulous petitioners to submit fraudulent or misleading petitions for nonimmigrant worker benefits. For example, an unscrupulous filer might submit a petition of questionable merit, hoping that if it is approved, the approval can be used as an anchor for later filings involving similar facts, related beneficiaries, or the same employer. They may even file multiple of these types of petitions and use the fact pattern that is the most advantageous or that is the most quickly approved. Similarly, a petitioner might overstate the beneficiary's role, compensation, or qualifications in the first filing, expecting that once approved, future filings will receive less scrutiny. Further, petitioners may be less forthcoming about changes affecting their business operations or the proffered position (such as reduced operations, loss of contracts, altered job duties, or other compliance issues) if they believe a prior approval is binding. If deference is expected, the petitioner may be incentivized to file extensions without fully disclosing those changes.
Indeed, USCIS data provides some support for the concern that deference may undermine program integrity by reducing scrutiny in some cases and contributing to an environment in which misleading, non-compliant, or fraudulent extensions of nonimmigrant worker petitions are more likely to be approved. For example, the data demonstrate higher percentages of fraud and non-compliance identified in the
(
printed page 65124)
H-1B and L-1A programs since the time when USCIS reinstituted its deference policy and incorporated it into the USCIS Policy Manual.
[
14
]
Specifically, for H-1B extension cases from FY 2022 through FY 2025, the overall combined percentage of non-compliance and/or fraud among H-1B sites visited during USCIS administrative and targeted site visits was 22.39 percent. In comparison, when USCIS had a policy of no deference, the overall combined percentage of H-1B non-compliance and/or fraud among H-1B sites visited during FY 2018 through FY 2020 was 16.77 percent.
[
15
]
For L-1A extension cases, the overall combined percentage of non-compliance and/or fraud among L-1A sites visited during USCIS administrative and targeted site visits from FY 2022 through FY 2025 was 24.46 percent. In comparison, the overall combined percentage of L-1A non-compliance and/or fraud among L-1A sites visited from FY 2018 through FY 2020 was 18.37 percent.
[
16
]
In other words, during the years that USCIS had a policy of deference, the combined percentage of non-compliance and/or fraud among sites visited in the H-1B and L-1A programs was higher than in the years that USCIS did not have a policy of deference. This trend reflected in a subset of H-1B and L-1A extension filings supports the concern that deference undermines program integrity in potentially limiting USCIS' ability to thoroughly review an extension petition on a case-by-case basis, which in turn may incentivize frivolous or fraudulent filings that falsely assert no material change. While DHS acknowledges that other factors besides or in addition to deference may have led to this higher percentage of identifying fraud or non-compliance, it is reasonable to conclude that deference was one of the contributing factors.
Removing deference would potentially disincentivize fraudulent filings and help restore the integrity of the lawful immigration system. This, in turn, would also better protect U.S. workers by ensuring that petitions for nonimmigrant workers are only approved if eligibility is established by the petitioner based on evidence submitted in support of each petition.
D. Reconsideration of the Deference Policy
DHS acknowledges the history of the deference policy and its recent codification at
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
in the Modernization Final Rule. DHS also acknowledges that some of the statements in this proposed rule represent a shift from statements made in the Modernization Final Rule. In the Modernization Final Rule, some commenters voiced concern that codifying deference would constrain USCIS officers' fact-finding authority.
See
89 FR 103093
. Commenters stated that USCIS officers should not be constrained in requesting additional evidence in the adjudication process. They also stated that requiring USCIS officers to confirm all material facts before granting a benefit request would serve as a fraud detection mechanism and deterrent.
At the time, DHS disagreed with the commenters' concerns.
Id.
However, DHS has reconsidered the issue since publication of the Modernization Final Rule and now believes that codification of the deference policy may have had the unintended effect of appearing to constrain USCIS officers' fact-finding authority, leading some USCIS officers to conduct a less than fulsome review, and thus undermining the agency's efforts to detect and deter fraud.
[
17
]
In the NPRM proposing to codify deference, DHS stated that the benefits of deference included promoting consistency and efficiency for both USCIS and its stakeholders, and creating predictability for petitioners and beneficiaries. DHS now believes that these benefits were overstated and were not adequately weighed against the negative impacts of deference. It is not clear that the codification of deference actually promoted consistency and efficiency in adjudication, and to any extent that it did, it did so at the expense of program integrity. As discussed in this preamble, deference may incentivize non-meritorious filings, give the appearance of unduly limiting adjudicators' inherent fact-finding authority, and increase the risk that erroneous prior approvals continue to serve as the basis for granting extension petitions for nonimmigrant workers. Quite simply, the deference policy is inconsistent with this Administration's focus on restoring the integrity of the legal immigration system to better protect U.S. workers by ensuring that only petitioners and beneficiaries who meet eligibility criteria and demonstrate eligibility are granted nonimmigrant worker benefits.
E. Reliance Interests and Alternatives Considered
DHS recognizes that some U.S. employers and nonimmigrant workers may assert reliance interests in the continuation of the deference policy. For example, U.S. employers that expect the continued approval of their Form I-129 petitions may have made business arrangements based on an assumption that these nonimmigrant workers would be able to continue working for them. Similarly, nonimmigrant workers may have made career and/or personal plans in the United States based on the assumption that they would be able to continue their employment and legal presence in the United States.
DHS has considered these reliance interests but believes that any such interests are limited. The deference regulation does not itself guarantee approval of an extension. Conversely, removing deference does not substantively change eligibility for the requested immigration benefit. This proposed change would not deprive U.S. employers of their ability to continue employing nonimmigrant workers, nor would it deprive nonimmigrant workers of their ability to continue working and living in the United States, so long as they are able to establish continued eligibility and obtain necessary approvals to continue such employment. Petitioners and beneficiaries do not have a legitimate expectation that an erroneous or unsupported prior approval would continue to result in future approvals.
To the extent there are legitimate reliance interests in the continuation of deference, DHS believes the negative impacts of the deference policy, as discussed in this preamble, outweigh the potential benefits to employers and aliens who may seek to rely on deference as codified at
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
. DHS believes that its interest in restoring integrity to the immigration system, including by ensuring that USCIS adjudicators conduct fulsome reviews of all benefits requests before granting a benefit, far outweighs any interest a petitioner or beneficiary may have in expecting continued approvals. This is especially true when deference increases the risk of USCIS failing to identify petitioners and beneficiaries who were not eligible for approval in the first place. DHS
(
printed page 65125)
therefore believes that removing
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
and ending the deference policy is necessary to ensure the integrity of the legal immigration system, which in turn better protects U.S. workers.
DHS considered an alternative to removing the deference regulation whereby DHS would revise the regulation to more clearly state that USCIS has discretion whether to apply deference. This could be accomplished by revising the regulatory text to state that USCIS “may give deference in its discretion” instead of “USCIS gives deference” as currently stated at
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
. However, DHS is not proposing this alternative because it would likely create unnecessary confusion and uncertainty for both petitioners and USCIS officers as to whether deference should be applied. Further, this alternative would not adequately address the concerns with deference discussed above in Section III.A through III.C of this preamble. Overall, DHS believes that removing deference entirely is the most practical alternative to enhance program integrity, including by ensuring that the burden remains on the petitioner to establish eligibility for the requested immigration benefit, and that USCIS adjudicators thoroughly review each nonimmigrant worker extension request on its own merits before extending the benefit.
IV. Statutory and Regulatory Requirements
A. Executive Orders 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review), 13563 (Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review), and 14192 (Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation)
Executive Orders 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review) and 13563 (Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review) direct agencies to assess the costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits.
Executive Order 13563
emphasizes the importance of quantifying both costs and benefits, of reducing costs, of harmonizing rules, and of promoting flexibility.
Executive Order 14192
(Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation) directs agencies to significantly reduce the private expenditures required to comply with Federal regulations and provides that “any new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.”
The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) has not designated this rule as a “significant regulatory action,” under section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
. Accordingly, OMB has not reviewed it.
This proposed rule is not an
Executive Order 14192
regulatory action because it is being issued with respect to an immigration-related function of the United States. The proposed rule's primary direct purpose is to implement or interpret the immigration laws of the United States (as described in INA sec. 101(a)(17),
8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(17)
) or any other function performed by the U.S. Federal Government with respect to aliens.
See
OMB Memorandum M-25-20, “Guidance Implementing Section 3 of
Executive Order 14192
, titled `Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation' ” (Mar. 26, 2025).
Summary of Changes
The proposed rule would remove the deference provision at
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
, which currently instructs USCIS officers to give deference to a prior determination for Form I-129 requests when the parties and underlying facts remain the same, unless there was a material error, a material change, or new material information that adversely impacts eligibility. As a result of a more thorough review of each petition, the number of requests for evidence (RFE) is expected to increase, resulting in additional time burden for petitioners to submit additional supporting documentation and evidence. The rule would also impose costs on petitioners by lengthening adjudication times and increasing uncertainty regarding continued employment. DHS estimates that the rule would produce new annual costs to petitioners of approximately $133,987 due to an increase in RFEs. In addition, the rule would impose costs on USCIS by increasing the adjudicative workload and operational costs, as officers would spend more time reassessing eligibility issues previously reviewed and may issue an increased number of RFEs, thereby increasing overall resource demands.
There are primary benefits associated with removing the deference policy. Removal would clarify and reinforce that the statutory burden of proof remains on the petitioner, not the agency. Removal would also encourage a more thorough review of each petition and its supporting evidence. Implementing a more thorough review process is expected to improve the ability to detect prior errors, inconsistencies, or indicators of fraud, and to eliminate the need to determine when deference applies. For the broader public and the immigration system, the change is expected to enhance confidence in the integrity and reliability of the adjudication process and align with agency priorities related to system integrity and protection of U.S. workers' interests. Background and Population
The purpose of this proposed rule is to remove
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
, which instructs USCIS officers to give deference to a prior determination of the petitioner's, applicant's, or beneficiary's eligibility when adjudicating a request filed using Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, involving the same parties and the same underlying facts, unless there was a material error, a material change, or new material information that adversely impacts eligibility.
The USCIS deference policy was first implemented and applied from April 2004 to October 2017. In April 2004, USCIS issued a memorandum directing officers to generally give deference to prior approvals when adjudicating petitions for extensions involving the same petitioner, the same beneficiary, and the same underlying facts.
See
USCIS, “The Significance of a Prior CIS Approval of a Nonimmigrant Petition in the Context of a Subsequent Determination Regarding Eligibility for Extension of Petition Validity,” HQPRD 72/11.3 (Apr. 23, 2004). While recognizing that each case must be decided on its own merits and that prior decisions could be revisited, the policy established that officers should defer to that prior determination of eligibility absent material error, substantial changed circumstances, or new material information.
Id.
In October 2017, USCIS issued a memorandum rescinding the April 2004 guidance.
See
USCIS, “Rescission of Guidance Regarding Deference to Prior Determinations of Eligibility in the Adjudication of Petitions for Extension of Nonimmigrant Status,” PM-602-0151 (Oct. 23, 2017). The agency expressed concern that the deference policy improperly shifted the burden of proof away from the petitioner and unduly restricted officers' fact-finding authority.
Id.
From October 2017 to April 2021, officers were not instructed to defer to prior approvals and instead were instructed to make new determinations of eligibility without relying on earlier decisions.
USCIS reinstated the deference policy in April 2021 and incorporated it into the USCIS Policy Manual.
See
USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 2, Part A, Chapter 4 “Extension of Stay, Change of Status, and Extension of Petition Validity.” The manual instructs officers to generally defer to prior approvals involving the same parties and the same underlying facts, unless there was a material error in the prior decision, a material change in circumstances, or new material information that adversely impacts the petitioner's or beneficiary's eligibility.
Id.
Then, in December 2024, DHS codified the reinstated policy at
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
in the H-1B Modernization Final Rule, requiring deference to prior determinations in such cases unless one of the exceptions applies.
See
89 FR 103054
(Dec. 18, 2024).

Costs and Benefits of the Proposed Rule
DHS expects that the proposed rule would generate both quantified and unquantified costs and benefits, assessed relative to a baseline in which the existing deference policy remains in effect.
Quantified Costs
Quantified costs are captured as the additional time burden on petitioners resulting from more frequent RFEs. Removing the deference policy requires officers to more thoroughly assess eligibility, which may result in officers requesting additional documentation more often to independently verify eligibility for each extension request. Each RFE increases the time burden on petitioners, who must review the notice, collect and organize documents, and prepare and submit a response. To estimate the increase in RFEs attributable to removal of the deference policy, DHS uses historical data from October 1, 2013, to April 27, 2021, covering periods when the deference policy was in effect (October 1, 2013, to October 11, 2017) and when it was not in effect (October 12, 2017, to April 27, 2021).

Unquantified Costs
Petitioners may experience longer adjudication times and increased uncertainty regarding continued employment when seeking extensions of stay and petition validity. Based on the average of the last four fiscal years (FY 2022-FY 2025), the difference in processing time between petitions with and without an RFE is 64 days; therefore, we use the additional processing time associated with petitions that receive an RFE, which is 64 calendar days.
[
27
]
These longer timelines can delay the final decision, making it difficult for workers and employers to plan project timelines, staffing levels, and work assignments. During this extended period, petitioners may face added uncertainty as to the beneficiary's longer-term employment authorization and status, which could create operational challenges for employers, such as workforce planning and project scheduling and increase stress for workers who may have to wait significantly longer for clarity on their ability to continue employment beyond that already authorized. In cases where a petition to extend the beneficiary's stay has been timely filed, if the petition remained pending when the beneficiary's status expired, the beneficiary may remain in the United States in an authorized period of stay while awaiting the adjudication of the petition filed on their behalf and may be eligible to continue to work.
See, e.g.,
8 CFR 274a.12(b)(20)
. The costs to beneficiaries then would be more related to unpredictability regarding when their petition is adjudicated.
DHS recognizes that removing deference may lead petitioners to devote additional time and resources to preparing extension petitions. USCIS did not find evidence that the Form G-28 filing rate increased as a result of removing deference.
[
28
]
However, petitioners may take additional steps to ensure that submissions are complete and well-organized at the outset, instead of merely relying on a prior approval. These efforts may help petitioners satisfy their burden of proof and may reduce the likelihood of deficiencies, but they may also impose unquantified costs in the form of additional staff time, attorney time, or other preparation costs. DHS is unable to quantify this cost with the available data.
Unquantified Benefits
Removing
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
and the deference policy would clarify and reinforce that the statutory burden of proof remains on the petitioner rather than on the agency, consistent with the statute.
See
INA sec. 291,
8 U.S.C. 1361
;
Matter of Chawathe,
25 I. & N. Dec. 369, 375 n.7 (USCIS AAO, 2010) (“The burden of proving eligibility for the benefit sought remains entirely with the applicant”). This benefits the agency by underscoring that officers are not obligated to approve subsequent petitions seeking immigration benefits where eligibility has not been demonstrated, merely because of prior approval. Removing the deference policy would also compel adjudication officers not to rely on incomplete or outdated facts, and supports more accurate, record-based decisions. Clear allocation of the burden of proof can also promote more complete, better-organized filings, and may reduce the risk of erroneous approvals of extension petitions.
Moreover, removing deference would reinforce DHS's authority to conduct a full, current review of the evidence in each petition, improving the ability to identify ineligibility or indicators of fraud. When officers need not defer to prior approvals, they can better evaluate documentation and eligibility criteria based on updated information, policies, or patterns that may not have been apparent at the time of the earlier decision. This full-scope review could help reveal discrepancies between past and current filings, highlight evolving risk indicators, and identify potential mistakes in prior decisions. This approach would strengthen program integrity by helping the agency to correct mistakes, detect emerging fraud schemes, and refine guidance and training based on issues identified through ongoing examination of repeat filers.
Removing deference would also benefit the public and the broader immigration system by reinforcing that each petition is evaluated on the current record, which could increase confidence in the integrity of adjudications. Members of the public would have more assurance that approvals are not simply carried forward from prior decisions but are based on current facts and applicable standards. At the same time, removing deference would maintain the integrity of the immigration system and advance policies that better protect the interests of U.S. workers by supporting more accurate, evidence-driven decisions and reducing the risk that outdated or erroneous prior approvals continue to serve as the basis for granting immigration benefits.
(
printed page 65130)
Alternatives Considered
This proposed rule seeks to clarify and reinforce that the statutory burden of proof remains on the petitioner, encourage a more thorough review of each petition and its supporting evidence, and better protect the integrity of the legal immigration system. DHS believes that removing deference would impose relatively small additional compliance costs and that the resulting benefits it provides justify these costs. Therefore, DHS believes that removing the deference provision for extension of stay petitions would be the most effective way to achieve the goals of this rulemaking.
DHS considered an alternative to revise the deference regulation to more clearly state that USCIS has discretion whether to apply deference. DHS is not proposing this alternative because it would likely create unnecessary confusion and uncertainty for both petitioners and USCIS. Instead, DHS believes that removing deference entirely is the most practical alternative to enhance program integrity, including by ensuring that the burden remains on the petitioner to establish the nonimmigrant alien worker's eligibility to continue working in the United States, and that USCIS adjudicators thoroughly review each nonimmigrant worker extension request on its own merits before granting the benefit. DHS did not consider other alternatives. DHS welcomes public comments on this issue.

1. A Description of the Reason Why the Action by the Agency Is Being Considered
The purpose of this proposed rule is to remove
8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)
and the deference policy which instructs USCIS officers to give deference to a prior determination of the petitioner's, applicant's or beneficiary's eligibility when adjudicating a request filed on Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, involving the same parties and the same underlying facts, unless there was a material error, a material change, or new material information that adversely impacts eligibility. This proposed change would better align the regulation with the statute, which places the burden of proof in establishing eligibility on the petitioner.

3. A Description and, Where Feasible, an Estimate of the Number of Small Entities to Which the Proposed Changes Would Apply

For purposes of this analysis, DHS relied on H-1B petitioner data as the best available source of employer-level information. Form I-129 is used for several nonimmigrant worker classifications; however, DHS does not have sufficiently reliable employer-level data for all non-H-1B classifications to conduct a comparable small entity analysis across all Form I-129 petitioners. H-1B petitions account for more than 75 percent of all Form I-129 filings and include employer-level data that allow DHS to evaluate petitioner size. Because H-1B filings constitute the majority of Form I-129 petitions and provide the most reliable available data for assessing small entity impacts, DHS used H-1B petitioner data as a reasonable proxy for the broader Form I-129 petitioner population. The unquantifiable cost of this rule is the increased uncertainty and potential operational disruption associated with longer adjudication times for extension petitions that receive an RFE. Based on FY 2022 through FY 2025 data, petitions with an RFE took an average of 64 additional calendar days to process, which may affect employer planning for staffing, project timelines, and work assignments, as well as workers' uncertainty regarding their longer-term employment authorization and status.
The quantifiable cost is the opportunity cost of employer time spent preparing and submitting additional RFEs resulting from the expected increase in RFEs. As discussed in the “Quantified Costs” section of the RIA, DHS estimates that the annual increase in costs to petitioners would be $133,987 across all affected employers for preparing additional supporting documentation and evidence to re-establish eligibility for an estimated 6,044 additional RFEs. DHS identified 22,748 unique employers affected by this rule. DHS estimates the cost per RFE by dividing the total estimated annual cost of $133,987 by the estimated increase in RFEs attributable to this rule, 6044, resulting in an estimated cost of approximately $22 per RFE. Because the median number of petitions filed by small entities is one,
[
34
]
a small entity that receives an RFE due to the removal of deference would need to spend time submitting additional supporting documentation and evidence and would incur an estimated cost of approximately $22. As shown in Table 3, the RFE rate during the period when the deference policy was not in effect was 23.4 percent. DHS therefore estimates that approximately 23.4 percent, or 3,637, of the small entities potentially affected by the rule would incur costs as a result of this rule. The estimated cost would be approximately $22 per affected small entity. Therefore, although the rule may affect a substantial number of small entities, DHS does not expect the economic impact on affected small entities to be significant. DHS welcomes public comments on this analysis, particularly those comments that would provide further insight into the quantified costs of this proposed rule.
4. A Description of the Projected Reporting, Recordkeeping, and Other Compliance Requirements of the Proposed Rule, Including an Estimate of the Classes of Small Entities That Will Be Subject to the Requirement and the Types of Professional Skills Necessary for Preparation of the Report or Record
The proposed rule would increase compliance requirements primarily by increasing the number of RFEs associated with extension of stay petitions, because officers would no longer apply deference to prior approvals and would instead more thoroughly examine eligibility for each request. As a result, certain petitioners would need to review RFE notices more frequently, collect and organize additional supporting documentation, and maintain more robust records of prior approvals and ongoing eligibility. DHS anticipates that these activities would generally be carried out by an HR specialist, an in-house attorney, or an outsourced attorney, who would be responsible for analyzing the RFEs, assembling the required documentation, and preparing timely, complete responses on behalf of the petitioner.
5. An Identification of All Relevant Federal Rules, to the Extent Practical, That May Duplicate, Overlap, or Conflict With the Proposed Rule
DHS is unaware of any duplicative, overlapping, or conflicting Federal rules, but invites the public to provide comments and information regarding any such rules.
6. A Description of Any Significant Alternatives to the Proposed Rule That Accomplish the Stated Objectives of Applicable Statutes and That Minimize Any Significant Economic Impact of the Proposed Rule on Small Entities
DHS did not consider any alternatives to the proposed rule other than revising the regulatory text to more clearly state that USCIS has discretion whether to apply deference. However, this alternative would not accomplish the stated objectives of this proposed rule. DHS believes that removing deference would impose relatively small additional compliance costs and that the resulting benefits justify these costs.

Difference-in-difference (DID) is a quasi-experimental research design that makes use of longitudinal data from treatment and control groups to obtain an appropriate counterfactual to estimate a causal effect. AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines that countervailable subsidies are being provided to SRF Limited (SRF), a producer and exporter of polyethylene terephthalate film, sheet, and strip (PET film) from India. The period of review (POR) is January 1, 2024, through December 31, 2024. In addition, Commerce is rescinding the review with respect to nine companies. Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results.
DATES:
Applicable October 14, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jack Vachon or Suresh Maniam, AD/CVD Operations, Office I, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-3572 or (202) 482-0176, respectively.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On July 1, 2002, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the countervailing duty order on PET film from India.
[
1
]
On August 22, 2025, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the notice of initiation of an administrative review of the
Order.
[
2
]
On September 30, 2025, Commerce selected Polyplex Corporation, Ltd. (Polyplex) and SRF as the mandatory respondents in this administrative review.
[
3
]
On November 20, 2025, interested parties timely withdrew their review request for with respect to all companies under review except SRF; the petitioners did not withdraw their request for review regarding SRF.
[
4
]
Therefore, on November
(
printed page 65170)
25, 2025, because SRF was the only company remaining for which a review was requested and not withdrawn, we sent the initial questionnaire to SRF as it is the sole mandatory respondent in this review.
[
5
]
Due to the lapse in appropriations and Federal Government shutdown, on November 14, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by 47 days.
[
6
]
Additionally, due to a backlog of documents that were electronically filed via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS) during the Federal Government shutdown, on November 24, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by an additional 21 days.
[
7
]
On May 15, 2026, Commerce extended the deadline for issuing the preliminary results of this review to no later than September 30, 2026.
[
8
]
On September 30, 2026, Commerce further extended the deadline for the preliminary results by seven days, until October 7, 2026.
[
9
]
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this investigation,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
[
10

A list of topics discussed in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is included in Appendix I to this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via ACCESS, which is available to registered users at
http://access.trade.gov

In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/​frnotices
.
Scope of the Order
The merchandise covered by the
Order
is PET film from India. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Partial Rescission of Administrative Review
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.213(d)(1)
, Commerce will rescind an administrative review, in whole or in part, if the parties that requested a review withdraw the request within 90 days of the date of publication of the notice of initiation. Commerce received timely filed withdrawal requests with respect to nine companies. Because the withdrawal requests were timely filed, and no other parties requested a review of these companies, in accordance with
19 CFR 351.213(d)(1)
, Commerce is rescinding this review of the
Order
with respect to the nine companies. For a complete list of companies for which we are rescinding this administrative review,
see
Appendix II.
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this administrative review in accordance with section 751(a)(1)(A) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). For each subsidy program found countervailable, we preliminarily find that there is a subsidy (
i.e.,
a financial contribution by an “authority” that gives rise to a benefit to the recipient, and that the subsidy is specific).
[
11
]
For a full description of the methodology underlying our conclusions, including our reliance, in part, on adverse facts available (AFA) pursuant to sections 776(a) and (b) of the Act,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.

Disclosure
Commerce intends to disclose its calculations and analysis performed to interested parties for these preliminary results within five days of any public announcement or, if there is no public announcement, within five days of the date of publication of this notice in accordance with
19 CFR 351.224(b)
.
Public Comment
Case briefs or other written comments may be submitted to the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance. Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.309(c)(1)(ii)
, we have modified the deadline for interested parties to submit case briefs to Commerce to no later than 21 days after the date of the publication of this notice.
[
12

Rebuttal briefs, limited to issues raised in the case briefs, may be filed not later than five days after the date for filing case briefs.
[
13

Interested parties who submit case briefs or rebuttal briefs in this review must submit: (1) a table of contents listing each issue; and (2) a table of authorities.
[

All briefs must be filed electronically using ACCESS. An electronically filed document must be received successfully in its entirety in ACCESS by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on the established deadline.
As provided under
19 CFR 351.309(c)(2)(iii)
and
(d)(2)(iii)
, we request that interested parties provide at the beginning of their briefs a public executive summary for each issue raised in their briefs.
[
15

Further, we request that interested parties limit their public executive summary of each issue to no more than 450 words, not including citations. We intend to use the public executive summaries as the basis of the comment summaries included in the issues and decision memorandum that will accompany the final results in this administrative review. We request that interested parties include footnotes for relevant citations in the public executive summary of each issue. Note that Commerce has amended certain of its requirements pertaining to the service of documents in
19 CFR 351.303(f)
.
[
16
]
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.310(c)
, interested parties who wish to request a hearing must submit a written request to the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance, filed electronically via ACCESS by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time within 30 days after the date of publication of this notice. Requests should contain: (1) the party's name, address, and telephone number; (2) the number of participants, and whether any participant is a foreign national; and
(
printed page 65171)
(3) a list of issues to be discussed. Oral presentations at the hearing will be limited to issues raised in the briefs. If a request for a hearing is made, Commerce will inform parties of the scheduled date for the hearing.
[
17
]
Assessment Rates
In accordance with section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.221(b)(4)(i)
, we preliminarily determined subsidy rates in the amounts shown above for SRF. Upon completion of the administrative review, consistent with section 751(a)(1) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.212(b)(2)
, Commerce shall determine, and CBP shall assess, countervailing duties on all appropriate entries covered by this review. We intend to issue assessment instructions to CBP no earlier than 35 days after the date of publication of the final results of this review in the
Federal Register
. If a timely summons is filed at the U.S. Court of International Trade, the assessment instructions will direct CBP not to liquidate relevant entries until the time for parties to file a request for a statutory injunction has expired (
i.e.,
within 90 days of publication).
For the companies for which the review is rescinded with these preliminary results, we will instruct CBP to assess countervailing duties on all appropriate entries at a rate equal to the cash deposit of estimated countervailing duties required at the time of entry, or withdrawal from warehouse, for consumption, during the period January 1, 2024, through December 31, 2024, in accordance with
19 CFR 351.212(c)(1)(i)
. Commerce intends to issue appropriate assessment instructions directly to CBP no earlier than 35 days after the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
.
Cash Deposit Requirements
In accordance with section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act, Commerce also intends upon publication of the final results, to instruct CBP to collect cash deposits of the estimated countervailing duties in the amount shown for SRF on shipments of subject merchandise entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the date of publication of the final results of this review. If the rate calculated in the final results is zero or
de minimis,
no cash deposit will be required on shipments of the subject merchandise entered or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the date of publication of the final results of this review.
For all non-reviewed firms, CBP will continue to collect cash deposits of estimated countervailing duties at the all-others rate or the most recent company-specific or all-others rate applicable to the company, as appropriate. These cash deposit requirements, when imposed, shall remain in effect until further notice.
Final Results
Unless extended, we intend to issue the final results of this administrative review, which will include the results of our analysis of the issues raised in the case briefs, within 120 days of publication of these preliminary results in the
Federal Register
, pursuant to section 751(a)(3)(A) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.213(h)(1)
.
Notification to Importers
This notice also serves as a preliminary reminder to importers of their responsibility under
19 CFR 351.402(f)
to file a certificate regarding the reimbursement of antidumping duties prior to liquidation of the relevant entries during this review period. Failure to comply with this requirement could result in Commerce's presumption that reimbursement of antidumping duties occurred and the subsequent assessment of double antidumping duties.
Notification to Interested Parties
These preliminary results of review are issued and published in accordance with sections 751(a)(1) and 777(i)(1) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.213
and
351.221(b)(4)
.

SUMMARY:
This notice provides guidance to U.S. Customs and Border Protection regarding the assessment of “U.S. content” for products of Canada and Mexico that qualify for preferential tariff treatment under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, for purposes of implementing tariffs pursuant to Proclamation 11032 of June 1, 2026.
DATES:
The guidance set out in in this notice is effective with respect to products that are entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern Time on October 14, 2026.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On June 1, 2026, the President issued Presidential Proclamation 11032 entitled “Further Adjusting the Tariff Regimes for Imports of Aluminum, Steel, and Copper into the United States” (
91 FR 34085
) (Proclamation). The Proclamation modifies the tariff regimes for metal products imposed in Presidential Proclamation 9704, as amended, Proclamation 9705, as amended, and Proclamation 10962, as amended, and directs the Secretary of Commerce (Secretary) to issue guidance to U.S. Customs and Border Protection regarding the assessment of “U.S. content” for purposes of implementing tariffs pursuant to clause (2)(d) of the Proclamation. The Secretary has delegated this duty to the Deputy Assistant Secretary for Technology Security.
Guidance to U.S. Customs and Border Protection Regarding the Assessment of “U.S. Content” for Purposes of Implementing Tariffs Pursuant to Clause (2)(d) of Proclamation 11032 of June 1, 2026
The Department of Commerce advises that, for purposes of implementing clause (2)(d) of the Proclamation, the term “U.S. content” means the following:
1. The value of the product attributable to parts wholly obtained, entirely produced, or substantially transformed in the United States, and
2. To the extent not otherwise accounted for in (1), the value of the product attributable to steel that was melted and poured in the United States, aluminum that was smelted and cast in the United States, and/or copper that was smelted and cast in the United States.
Questions regarding the application of this Notice to a specific product may be directed to U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

I. Default Determination
Under
21 CFR 1301.43

21 CFR 1301.43(a)
& (c)(1). In the absence of a demonstration of good cause, a registrant who fails to timely file an answer also is “deemed to have waived their right to a hearing and to be in default.”
21 CFR 1301.43(c)(2)
. Unless excused, a default is deemed to constitute “an admission of the factual allegations of the [OSC].”
21 CFR 1301.43(e)
.
Here, the OSC notified Registrant of her right to file a written request for hearing, and that if she failed to file such a request, she would be deemed to have waived her right to a hearing and be in default. RFAAX 1, at 8 (citing
21 CFR 1301.43
). According to the Government's RFAA, Registrant failed to request a hearing. RFAA, at 1-2. Thus, the Agency finds that Registrant is in default and therefore has admitted to the factual allegations in the OSC.
21 CFR 1301.43(e)

B. Discussion
Pursuant to
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)
, the Attorney General is authorized to suspend or revoke a registration issued under
21 U.S.C. 823
“upon a finding that the registrant . . . has had his [or her] State license or registration suspended . . . [or] revoked . . . by competent State authority and is no longer authorized by State law to engage in the . . . dispensing of controlled substances.” With respect to a practitioner, DEA has also long held that the possession of authority to dispense controlled substances under the laws of the state in which a practitioner engages in professional practice is a fundamental condition for obtaining and maintaining a practitioner's registration.
Gonzales
v.
Oregon,
546 U.S. 243, 270 (2006) (“The Attorney General can register a physician to dispense controlled substances `if the applicant is authorized to dispense . . . controlled substances under the laws of the State in which he practices.' . . . The very definition of a `practitioner' eligible to prescribe includes physicians `licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted, by the United States or the jurisdiction in which he practices' to dispense controlled substances. [21 U.S.C.] 802(21).”). The Agency has applied these principles consistently.
See, e.g., Ashley Vermillion, N.P.,
91 FR 35270
(2026);
Benson Sergiles, P.A.,
90 FR 32016
(2025);
Mark D. Beale, M.D.,
85 FR 48564
(2020).
[
5
]
According to Indiana statute, and subject to exceptions irrelevant here, “[e]very person who dispenses or proposes to dispense any controlled substance within Indiana must have a registration issued by the [Indiana Board of Pharmacy] in accordance with the board's rules.” Ind. Code § 35-48-3-3(b) (2025). Further, “dispense” means “to deliver a controlled substance to an ultimate user or research subject by or pursuant to the lawful order of a practitioner and includes the prescribing, administering, packaging, labeling, or compounding necessary to prepare the substance for that delivery.”
Id.
§ 35-48-1.1-11 (2025).
Here, the undisputed evidence in the record is that Registrant lacks authority to handle controlled substances in Indiana because her Indiana CSR license is expired. As discussed above, a person must hold an Indiana controlled substance registration to dispense a controlled substance in Indiana. Thus, because Registrant lacks authority to handle controlled substances in Indiana, Registrant is not eligible to maintain a DEA registration. Accordingly, the Agency finds that Registrant's lack of state authority to handle controlled substances provides an independent basis for revocation of Registrant's DEA registration.
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)
.
III. Public Interest Determination
A. Overview of Law
The Attorney General “may deny, suspend, or revoke [a] registration if . . . the [registrant's] registration would be `inconsistent with the public interest.' ”
Gonzales
v.
Oregon,
546 U.S. at 251 (quoting
21 U.S.C. 824(a)(4)
). The Attorney General's “discretion in exercising [the authority to register and deregister practitioners] is spelled out in very broad terms.”
Id.
at 292 (Scalia, J., dissenting);
see also Neumann's Pharmacy, L.L.C.
v.
Drug Enf't Admin.,
167 F.4th 320, 323 (5th Cir. 2026) (“DEA unquestionably has broad authority to deregister pharmacies and substantial discretion to shape policy within statutory bounds.”). In executing this broad mandate, DEA must continuously balance the CSA's public interest goals of curbing the “illegal . . . distribution[ ] and possession[,] and improper use of controlled substances[, which has] a substantial and detrimental effect on the health and general welfare of the American people,” while ensuring that the public has access to medications that “have a useful and legitimate medical purpose and are necessary to maintain the health and general welfare of the American people.”
21 U.S.C. 801(1)
, (2);
see
Joanna R. Lampe, Cong. Rsch. Serv., R45948, The Controlled Substances Act (CSA): A Legal Overview for the 119th Congress (2025),
https://www.congress.gov/​crs-product/​R45948
.
In the case of a practitioner, Congress directed the Attorney General to consider five factors in making the public interest determination.
21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1)(A)-(E)
.
[
6
]
Just as the phrase “inconsistent with the public interest” is broad, the five factors that Congress directed DEA to consider in determining the public interest are similarly broad, suggesting that Congress intended for DEA to have discretion and flexibility to interpret this language as necessary to implement its critical mission to protect the public from drug abuse and diversion.
See Loper Bright Enters.
v.
Raimondo,
603 U.S 369, 394-95 (2024) (noting that “[i]n a case involving an agency . . . the statute's meaning may well be that the agency is authorized to exercise a degree of discretion,” such as where the statute uses terms or phrases like “ `appropriate or reasonable' ” (internal citations omitted)). Indeed, courts have recognized the Agency's broad discretion to deny applications and deregister practitioners for a wide variety of conduct that the Agency has determined is inconsistent with the public interest.
See, e.g., Orusa
v.
Drug Enf't Admin.,
No. 22-3132, 2023 WL 3886403 (6th Cir. June 8, 2023) (physician issuing prescriptions outside the usual course of professional practice and beneath the standard of care);
St. Croix
v.
Drug Enf't Admin.,
No. 21-1116, 2022 WL 2092177 (D.C. Cir. June 10, 2022) (physician failing to maintain adequate records, prescribing controlled substances without a legitimate medical purpose, storing controlled substances at an unregistered location, failing to
(
printed page 65261)
provide effective controls to guard against theft or diversion of these substances);
Suntree Pharmacy
v.
Drug Enf't Admin.,
No. 20-14626, 2022 WL 444357 (11th Cir. Feb. 14, 2022), cert. denied, 143 S. Ct. 305 (2022) (pharmacy filling prescriptions outside the usual course of practice).
The CSA's five public interest factors are considered in the disjunctive.
Gonzales
v.
Oregon,
546 U.S. at 292-93 (Scalia, J., dissenting) (“It is well established that these factors are to be considered in the disjunctive,” quoting
In re Arora,
60 FR 4447
,
4448
(1995));
Robert A. Leslie, M.D.,
68 FR 15227
,
15230
(2003). Each factor is weighed on a case-by-case basis.
David H. Gillis, M.D.,
58 FR 37507
,
37508
(1993);
see Morall
v.
Drug Enf't Admin.,
412 F.3d 165, 181 (D.C. Cir. 2005) (describing the Agency's adjudicative process as “applying a multi-factor test through case-by-case adjudication,” quoting
LeMoyne-Owen Coll.
v.
N.L.R.B.,
357 F.3d 55, 61 (D.C. Cir. 2004)). Any one factor, or combination of factors, may be decisive,
David H. Gillis, M.D.,
58 FR at 37508, and the Agency “may give each factor the weight . . . deem[ed] appropriate in determining whether a registration should be revoked or an application for registration denied.”
Morall,
412 F.3d. at 185 n.2 (Henderson, J., concurring) (quoting
Robert A. Smith, M.D.,
70 FR 33207
,
33208
(2007));
see also Penick Corp.
v.
Drug Enf't Admin.,
491 F.3d 483, 490 (D.C. Cir. 2007).
Moreover, while the Agency is required to consider each of the factors, it “need not make explicit findings as to each one.”
MacKay

Drug Enf't Admin.,

B. Applicable State Law
According to the CSA's implementing regulations, a lawful controlled substance prescription is one that is “issued for a legitimate medical purpose by an individual practitioner acting in the usual course of his professional practice.”
21 CFR 1306.04(a)
;
see Gonzales
v.
Oregon,
546 U.S. at 274;
United States
v.
Hayes,
595 F.2d 258, 260 (5th Cir. 1979),
rehearing den.,
598 F.2d 620 (5th Cir. 1979),
cert. denied,
444 U.S. 866 (1979); RFAAX 1, at 2. “A practitioner must establish and maintain a
bona fide
doctor-patient relationship in order to act `in the usual course of . . . professional practice' and to issue a prescription for a `legitimate medical purpose.'  ”
Dewey C. MacKay, M.D.,
75 FR 49956
,
49973
(2010).
As for state law, Indiana statute requires a practitioner who uses telehealth to establish a provider-patient relationship, and at a minimum, requires obtaining the patient's medical history and other information required to establish a diagnosis. Ind. Code § 25-1-9.5-7; RFAAX 1, at 2. Further, Indiana statute prohibits a prescriber from issuing a prescription for an opioid through telehealth when the prescriber has not previously examined the patient in person. Ind. Code § 25-1-9.5-8; RFAAX 1, at 2.
Additionally, Indiana regulations set the standards for each nurse practitioner, which include, but are not limited to, diagnosing health problems, developing and implementing nursing treatment plans, and using appropriate critical thinking skills to make independent decisions. 848 Ind. Admin. Code § 4-2-1; RFAAX 1, at 2. Indiana regulations also require nurse practitioners to perform a focused history and physical exam on the patient, review records, complete an objective pain assessment tool, and assess the mental health of the patient and risk for abuse. 848 Ind. Admin. Code § 5-4-4; RFAAX 1, at 2.
Lastly, Indiana regulations require that an APRN with prescriptive authority consult Indiana's Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (INSPECT) prior to prescribing an opioid medication to a patient, at least annually thereafter run another report through INSPECT for the patient, and document in the patient's chart whether the INSPECT reports are consistent with the APRN's knowledge of the patient's controlled substance use history. Ind. Admin. Code § 5-4-7; RFAAX 1, at 7.
